SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
A. Executive Summary
In
Executive Order 14273
,
Lowering Drug Prices by Once Again Putting Americans First
, President Trump instructed the Department to propose regulations under ERISA section 408(b)(2) to improve employer health plan transparency into the direct and indirect compensation received by pharmacy benefit managers.
[
1
]
Businesses that provide pharmacy benefit management services (“PBMs,” unless otherwise specified) to ERISA-covered self-insured group health plans have acquired significant influence over prescription drug costs in recent years. By addressing the influence of PBMs and promoting transparent pricing, President Trump's Executive Order aims to create a fairer and more competitive prescription drug market that lowers costs and ensures accountability across the entire healthcare system.
[
2
]
This final rule responds to
Executive Order 14273
and is a part of the Trump Administration's larger initiative to address rising healthcare costs for Americans.
[
3
]
ERISA section 408(b)(2) is a statutory exemption from ERISA's prohibited transaction rules applicable to contracts or arrangements for services. ERISA section 406(a)(1)(C) provides that the furnishing of goods, services, or facilities between employee benefit plans (including group health plans) and parties in interest to the plans is a prohibited transaction.
[
4
]
A person providing services to the plan is a “party in interest” to the plan.
[
5
]
To satisfy the conditions of the exemption, ERISA section 408(b)(2)(A) provides that the service contract or arrangement must be reasonable, the services must be necessary for the establishment or operation of the plan, and no more than reasonable compensation may be paid for the services. In addition, under recent amendments to ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (CAA, 2026), a broad group of service providers to group health plans including PBMs must provide specified disclosures to the group health plan for the services contract or arrangement to meet the reasonableness condition of the exemption.
[
6
]
This final rule implements ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) for PBMs and affiliated brokers and consultants, with respect to the covered plans described in the final rule.
PBMs are the “middlemen” in the pharmaceutical supply chain.
[
7
]
For ERISA-covered self-insured group health plans, PBMs perform a wide range of services including, but not limited to, organizing pharmacy networks, negotiating pharmacy reimbursement amounts and drug rebates,
[
8
]
establishing drug formularies,
[
9
]
processing claims, and managing utilization. In connection with these services, PBMs receive compensation from self-insured group health plans as
(
printed page 69093)
well as from other sources in the pharmaceutical supply chain. Responsible plan fiduciaries of self-insured group health plans (including plan sponsors and other fiduciaries who are responsible for prudently selecting and monitoring service providers)
[
10
]
also commonly rely on brokers or consultants to help them with advice, recommendations, and referrals regarding pharmacy benefit management services. The brokers or consultants may, in some cases, be affiliated with a PBM. They also may receive compensation from sources other than group health plans.
Concerns have existed for many years that PBMs, including in their capacities as brokers and consultants with respect to pharmacy benefit management services, are not fully disclosing their compensation to the responsible plan fiduciaries. These concerns prompted the ERISA Advisory Council to recommend that the Department consider extending its service provider disclosure regulation to require specific disclosures by PBMs.
[
11
]
Congress took that step by amending ERISA section 408(b)(2) to specify disclosure requirements for PBMs and other covered service providers to group health plans.
[
12
]
Additionally, Congress has provided that effective for plan years beginning on or after August 3, 2028, PBMs must pass through rebates, fees, alternative discounts, and other remuneration received from drug manufacturers and other entities to the group health plans that the PBMs are providing services to (or to health insurance issuers on behalf of the plans).
[
13
]
A new ERISA section 726, added to part 7 of ERISA, will require additional, retrospective disclosures by providers of pharmacy benefit management services regarding drug spending and drug utilization under the group health plan, effective for plan years beginning on or after August 3, 2028.
[
14
]
The Department's final rule implementing ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) is intended to provide much needed transparency into contracts and arrangements with PBMs and affiliated brokers and consultants, so that the responsible plan fiduciaries of large ERISA-covered self-insured group health plans can fulfill their statutorily mandated role to determine whether these service contracts or arrangements are reasonable. Under the Department's final rule, these service providers must furnish detailed disclosures to responsible plan fiduciaries of large self-insured group health plans describing their compensation for such services, and advance disclosure of compensation they reasonably expect to receive. The final rule also includes audit provisions designed to ensure that the responsible plan fiduciaries of large self-insured group health plans can verify the accuracy of the disclosures. The responsible plan fiduciaries will be able to use the disclosures in their process of selecting a provider of pharmacy benefit management services, engaging an affiliated broker or consultant, and monitoring these service providers' operations and compliance with contractual obligations.
B. Background
1. Group Health Plan Prescription Drug Coverage
Approximately 136 million Americans receive health coverage through their employers (or their family members' employers) in group health plans covered by ERISA.
[
15
]
Group health plans provide healthcare benefits such as hospitalization, sickness, prescription drugs, vision, and dental. Group health plans provide these benefits by purchasing insurance
[
16
]
or by self-funding
[
17
]
(also known as self-insured) benefits from the employer's general assets or from a funded trust.
Employer pharmacy spending is increasing faster than medical and surgical expenses, representing a growing concern for employers and workers about affordability and adherence. Retail prescription drug spending in the U.S. amounted to nearly $495 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow 7 percent in 2025, but to grow more slowly from 2026 to 2033.
[
18
]
Against this backdrop, employers anticipate an 11 to 12 percent increase in pharmacy costs in 2025 into 2026.
[
19
]
For employer-sponsored group health plans, the cost of prescription drugs is usually shared between the group health plan and the individual participant, where the participant pays a fixed amount (copayment), a percentage of the drug's cost (coinsurance), or the full cost of the drug up to the amount of the annual deductible, if the group health plan applies a deductible. The group health plan's drug formulary identifies the drugs that are covered and organizes the drugs into tiers, with different cost-sharing requirements imposed on
(
printed page 69094)
participants. The tiers often distinguish between generic drugs and brand-name drugs, and plans may have one or more separate tiers for “specialty drugs.”
[
20
]
Managing a group health plan's prescription drug coverage is exceedingly complex due to the vast number of drugs available on the market and the large number of drug manufacturers and pharmacies, among other reasons. Further, the pharmaceutical supply chain involves multiple entities—including drug manufacturers, drug wholesalers, pharmacies, PBMs, payors (
e.g.
, group health plans), and participants—that interact with each other in arrangements that can be quite opaque.
[
21
]
Due to the complexity of the pharmaceutical supply chain and the myriad players involved, responsible plan fiduciaries of group health plans often outsource pharmacy benefit management services. When group health plan benefits are obtained through insurance, pharmacy benefit management services are often integrated with the insurance contract. When group health plans are self-insured, however, the responsible plan fiduciaries may engage a PBM directly, or they may obtain pharmacy benefit management services through a third-party administrator (TPA) or other entity.
2. Pharmacy Benefit Managers' Services Provided to Self-Insured Group Health Plans
PBMs perform numerous services related to self-insured group health plans' prescription drug coverage, including identifying the prescription drugs that will be covered by a plan and negotiating prices with various entities in the pharmaceutical supply chain.
[
22
]
2.1. Formulary Development and Design
PBMs develop a self-insured group health plan's prescription drug formulary,
[
23
]
which is a list of drugs (brand, generic, and specialty) that the self-insured group health plan will cover. A variety of different, tiered cost-sharing requirements may apply to the drugs in the formulary, either through coinsurance (a percentage off list price) or copayments (a fixed price not tied to list price).
[
24
]
Formularies generally balance access to prescription drugs with managing costs, and their development is similar across PBMs in that they often follow a multi-step process involving several distinct committees.
[
25
]
For example, a pharmacy and therapeutics (P&T) committee is often used as an external body of experts who “evaluate clinical and medical literature to select the most appropriate medications for individual disease states and conditions.”
[
26
]
These committees are staffed with healthcare providers including physicians, pharmacists, and patient representatives. Following their analyses, the P&T committee makes recommendations for the PBM's template formulary or for an individual client's custom formulary.
[
27
]
Notably, this is only one of several possible PBM committees that may have influence over formulary design.
[
28
]
There are also formulary review and value assessment committees which review P&T committee recommendations to make formulary placement decisions and trade relations committees which negotiate and approve rebate agreements with drug manufacturers.
[
29
]
In connection with formulary development, PBMs and their affiliates enter into rebate contracts with drug manufacturers and negotiate for rebates and fees on prescription drugs and other remuneration in return for preferred formulary placement.
[
30
]
PBMs use the large number of participants across multiple self-insured group health plans to negotiate with drug manufacturers based on “covered lives,” primarily
(
printed page 69095)
where there are competing therapeutic alternatives.
[
31
]
Rebates are paid to the PBM periodically after the prescriptions are filled and may be passed through to the self-insured group health plan to the extent required by the services contract.
[
32
]
While PBMs historically have negotiated these contracts directly with drug manufacturers, PBM-affiliated group purchasing organizations (GPOs), also known as rebate aggregators, have taken over much of the rebate negotiation function for commercial health plans in return for incremental fees, or for a portion of the rebate that is then shared with the PBM and the self-insured group health plan, pursuant to contractual terms.
[
33
]
Each of the three largest PBMs is part of a vertically integrated entity which owns and controls such GPO subsidiaries. These GPOs are affiliates of their respective PBMs and perform the role of rebate aggregator, and two of these GPOs are currently headquartered outside of the United States.
[
34
]
2.2. Drug Utilization Management
PBMs provide a range of utilization management services—such as prior authorization, step therapy, and quantity limits—to promote medication use, improve clinical outcomes, and control drug costs.
[
35
]
While formularies act as the “menu” of drugs the self-insured group health plan will cover, utilization management techniques dictate the “how” a participant may access drugs prescribed by their healthcare provider. As illustrated above, formularies typically sort drugs into tiers of cost-sharing requirements. Additionally, PBMs may require providers to obtain approval before a drug can be dispensed, a process known as prior authorization. Step therapy, on the other hand, requires participants to try and fail on a less expensive drug first before progressing to another, more expensive option. PBMs may also implement quantity limits that cap the amount of a drug a participant can receive for a particular condition within a given period.
2.3. Pharmacy Contracting and Network Design
PBMs develop pharmacy networks for self-insured group health plans which can be divided into three types of dispensing formats: retail, mail-order, and specialty.
[
36
]
Retail pharmacies, which may be part of a pharmacy chain or independent, purchase prescription drugs from drug manufacturers and drug wholesalers and make them available to self-insured group health plan participants.
[
37
]
Mail-order pharmacies dispense and deliver prescriptions directly to participants and are often utilized for prescription drugs that are taken regularly.
[
38
]
Specialty drugs that meet certain characteristics such as special handling needs or high cost may be provided through a separate pharmacy.
[
39
]
Pharmacy networks can be open (which includes most pharmacies as in-network and apply uniform cost-sharing) or restrictive (which limit in-network status to a narrow group of pharmacies). An open network allows participants to fill prescriptions at nearly any licensed pharmacy nationwide, offering broad convenience and access. This wider access, however, often comes with higher costs for both the plan and its participants, as broader networks may reduce a plan's leverage to negotiate lower reimbursement rates. Recent analysis by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), Congress, and others have highlighted that the largest PBMs utilize restrictive networks to steer participants to their own vertically integrated or PBM-affiliated pharmacies, even when another pharmacy may provide the same or better pricing, raising concerns about diminished competition and potential conflicts of interest.
[
40
]
In developing pharmacy networks, PBMs negotiate reimbursement rates and post-sale adjustment provisions that determine the amount the pharmacy is ultimately reimbursed. The reimbursement rate is typically determined using the lowest price among various indices using the “lesser of” logic, for example, the lesser of: (1) Average Wholesale Price, (2) Wholesale Acquisition Cost, (3) Usual and Customary Price, (4) Submitted Costs, or (5) Maximum Allowable Costs (MAC).
[
41
]
MAC lists represent the amount that a group health plan will pay for generics and, in some cases, brand name drugs with generic equivalents.
[
42
]
MAC lists are often proprietary and are created, maintained, and updated by PBMs exclusively.
(
printed page 69096)
2.4. Claims Administration and Other Services
Finally, PBMs also perform prescription drug claims administration services, which like the other services, are important to a self-insured group health plan's pharmacy benefit program. Claims processing may involve the determination of “(1) whether an individual was an eligible participant: (2) whether the prescribed drug was covered by the plan; (3) whether the participant met his or her deductible; and (4) what the participant's co-payment would be if required by the plan.”
[
43
]
PBMs have developed systems to transmit prescription information between themselves and pharmacies, permitting the rapid processing of claims as prescriptions are being filled.
[
44
]
Other services include adjudicating appeals, plan recordkeeping and regulatory compliance.
[
45
]
3. PBM Contracts and Arrangements With Self-Insured Group Health Plans
When engaging in a request for proposal process, responsible plan fiduciaries of self-insured group health plans receive bids to contract directly with a PBM for services, or they may contract for services with a TPA or other entity (examples discussed herein) that agrees to provide pharmacy benefit management services to the self-insured group health plan.
[
46
]
Some responsible plan fiduciaries also join coalitions or cooperatives that negotiate with PBMs on behalf of a group of employer-sponsored self-insured group health plans.
[
47
]
Negotiating a pharmacy benefit contract is a complex process that requires specialized expertise. Responsible plan fiduciaries, especially those without internal expertise and practices to manage drug benefits, often work with a separate consultant or broker to select and negotiate a direct contractual agreement with the PBM. As a best practice, the Department is of the view that large employers should ensure that strategic financial leaders, including the company's Chief Financial Officer or similarly situated individual(s), both lead and collaborate closely with internal teams in selecting, designing, and engaging in procurement for employee health benefits. This will ensure alignment of health benefits with the company's overall strategic financial plan and assist in addressing rising healthcare costs, improving benefits, and reducing administrative burdens.
Consultant or broker services can include requests for proposals (RFPs), PBM oversight, and PBM audit services.
[
48
]
In some cases, the consultants and brokers receive indirect compensation (
i.e.
, compensation from the PBMs or other sources other than the self-insured group health plan) that create a conflict of interest with respect to their self-insured group health plan customers.
[
49
]
Consulting firms and brokerages reportedly may receive payments on a per prescription or per covered employee basis, or they may share in rebates earned by PBMs.
[
50
]
Consultants may have preferred relationships with certain PBMs which may impact their recommendations.
[
51
]
In addition to the complexity of the negotiations, PBM contracts themselves are complex and responsible plan fiduciaries often lack knowledge of how PBMs operate and how they receive compensation.
[
52
]
For example, PBM contracts may be for one year or multiple years, and may be amended at any point during the contract period if the formulary changes. The contracts may also allow for interim “market checks.”
[
53
]
As described by one source, this involves “a comparison of the aggregate program pricing terms with the market access product types/distribution channels, administrative fees, allowances, other financial guarantees, and rebates to determine if the plan sponsor is receiving competitive market rates.”
[
54
]
The contracts also address the ability of the responsible plan fiduciary to audit the PBM's compliance with the contract.
[
55
]
PBMs often limit a self-insured group health plan's audit rights, however, providing only a sample of records relating to contractual performance,
(
printed page 69097)
requiring that the auditor be approved by the PBM, or that the audit be conducted on-site at a facility chosen by the PBM.
3.1. Administrative Fees and Spread Pricing
PBM compensation arrangements with self-insured group health plans may have multiple components, but the compensation models are sometimes described as falling into two general categories: pass through pricing and spread pricing.
[
56
]
In a pass-through pricing model, self-insured group health plans may pay the PBM the average wholesale price (AWP) for a drug minus a negotiated discount (also referred to as the negotiated rate) plus an administrative fee, which may be structured on a per claim basis, per participant basis, flat rate, or other mechanism.
[
57
]
In a spread pricing model, self-insured group health plans may pay AWP or AWP minus a smaller negotiated discount than in a pass-through model, but will either not pay or pay only a reduced administrative fee.
[
58
]
The PBM will instead retain the spread between the price reimbursed to the pharmacy, which might be based on MAC or a different formula, and the negotiated rate with self-insured group health plans.
[
59
]
The spread pricing model does not utilize an agreed upon AWP for a given drug. Accessing AWP data may be costly, and AWP providers use proprietary, hard-to-verify data sources and methodologies.
[
60
]
Additionally, PBMs typically have not disclosed to the responsible plan fiduciaries either the reimbursement amount paid to pharmacies or the pharmacies' acquisition costs.
[
61
]
Even where a price guarantee is included in a PBM contract, this guarantee may apply on an aggregate basis where PBMs may use periodic true-ups to show compliance with the price guarantee, rather than ensuring each individual prescription is billed at or below the guaranteed price.
[
62
]
One testimony to the ERISA Advisory Council indicated that PBMs may also use complex pricing algorithms in aggregate calculations, which can involve including or excluding certain claims in ways that affect the calculations used to measure the fulfillment of price guarantees.
[
63
]
Some responsible plan fiduciaries may view the spread pricing model as providing potential benefits such as smoothing fluctuations in drug costs, which could reduce unpredictability, compared to models where the full drug costs are passed through to the self-insured group health plan, without applying a price smoothing mechanism.
[
64
]
However, the spread pricing model may be less transparent to responsible plan fiduciaries if there are no disclosures of the differences between the amounts the PBM paid to pharmacies and the amounts charged to the self-insured group health plan, or if pricing guarantees are verified only in the aggregate. Comparatively, in the pass-through model, PBMs charge the plan the same amount they reimburse pharmacies, and compensation is more plainly identified, which some responsible plan fiduciaries characterize as a more “transparent” arrangement.
[
65
]
Some PBMs that offer pass-through pricing also have business models that provide customers with frequent audit
(
printed page 69098)
opportunities and minimal limitations on access to PBM data.
[
66
]
Additionally, as discussed in greater detail later in the Regulatory Impact Analysis, the largest PBMs have become vertically integrated with health insurance companies, pharmacies, drug manufacturers, and other entities.
[
67
]
PBMs sometimes operate affiliated pharmacies and require plan participants to use these affiliated pharmacies for certain prescriptions such as mail-order and/or specialty drugs.
[
68
]
In some ways, the vertically integrated structure can be efficient and cost-effective, but it may affect price competition when participants are required to use a PBM-affiliated pharmacy for certain prescriptions.
[
69
]
With respect to specialty drugs, which are an increasing source of drug spending, the FTC found in a recent study that the three largest PBMs “reimbursed their affiliated pharmacies at a higher rate than unaffiliated pharmacies on nearly every specialty generic drug examined.”
[
70
]
3.2. Payments From Drug Manufacturers
Payments from drug manufacturers are another component of PBM compensation. These types of payments include, but are not limited to, rebates, administrative fees, price protection fees, and so on. These payments are often defined by reference to list price, which incentivizes PBMs to choose high-list price, high-rebate drugs when creating a self-insured group health plan's formulary.
[
71
]
Rebates are discounts on drugs offered by the pharmaceutical manufacturer in return for preferred placement on a self-insured group health plan's formulary; and the extent to which rebates are retained by the PBM or passed through to the self-insured group health plan is negotiated by the parties.
[
72
]
PBMs also earn administrative fees from drug manufacturers when prescriptions are filled based on the utilization of the drugs and plan design decisions made by plan sponsors, including formulary and utilization management strategies.
[
73
]
Price protection fees are an additional rebate that a manufacturer pays the PBM if list prices rise faster than inflation or another agreed upon amount.
[
74
]
To the extent rebates, fees, and other sources of remuneration are passed through to the self-insured group health plan, such amounts can help defray the cost of the healthcare benefits being provided.
[
75
]
However, even if there are contracted obligations requiring that rebates, fees, and other sources of remuneration be passed through to the plans, the responsible plan fiduciaries may benefit from more transparent disclosures to ensure that such amounts are passed through as agreed to under the contract with the PBM, in part due to evolving terminology used in the contracts and or re-routing or recharacterizing of the amounts.
[
76
]
The role of rebate aggregators adds complexity to drug pricing and transparency for disclosure of rebates owed to group health plans.
[
77
]
The rebate payment structure would also benefit from more transparent disclosure for other reasons. One commonly cited concern is that PBMs have an incentive to select certain drugs with high-list prices over others for group health plan formularies due to the size of the rebate payments from drug manufacturers.
[
78
]
In addition to
(
printed page 69099)
providing PBMs with an incentive to select higher priced drugs for the formularies, drug manufacturers offer higher rebates to PBMs to exclude competing products from the formulary.
[
79
]
Disclosure of rebates and other payments from drug manufacturers will enable responsible plan fiduciaries to evaluate the way the PBM has designed the formulary, the extent to which its composition might be influenced by financial incentives, and to determine whether the impacts of these incentives require mitigation to ensure the reasonableness of the contract or arrangement.
Rebates and related PBM formulary practices have also been shown to correspond to increases in the manufacturers' drug list prices.
[
80
]
Drug manufacturers often raise list prices to accommodate rebate demands to secure preferred formulary placement to protect market share, profits, or to recoup the costs for research and development.
[
81
]
While increases in list prices have a marginal impact on self-insured group health plans, as they generally pay a lower price due to rebates and other discounts negotiated by the PBMs, they can be detrimental to participants.
[
82
]
To offset rising drug prices, employers are increasingly shifting towards cost-sharing structures that make participants more sensitive to list prices. Participants in self-insured group health plans often pay the full cost of the drug up to the amount of their annual deductible and a portion of prescription drug costs after the deductible is satisfied, typically in the form of coinsurance. In many self-insured group health plans, coinsurance is often based on list price, resulting in higher out-of-pocket costs for participants.
[
83
]
3.3. Payments From Pharmacies
PBMs receive payments from pharmacies in several different circumstances. If a participant's copay is higher than the total reimbursement owed to the pharmacy, a PBM may “claw-back” the overpayment amount.
[
84
]
For example, if a participant's copayment for a generic drug is $15 dollars, but the PBM has agreed to pay the pharmacy $5, the PBM will “claw-back” the excess $10. In such cases, it is not clear whether such overpayments are generally or ever reimbursed to the self-insured group health plan (or participant).
[
85
]
PBMs also reportedly recoup amounts paid to pharmacies for other reasons, including “network participation fees, fees for non-compliance or lower performance with quality measures, and reimbursement reconciliation.”
[
86
]
A relatively new PBM practice is “effective rate reconciliation,” in which the contractual reimbursement rate paid by a PBM to a pharmacy for dispensing a drug is determined by an aggregate effective rate, typically expressed as a percentage discount from AWP.
[
87
]
The PBM periodically reconciles the payments made to pharmacies at the point of sale with the specified effective rate and will adjust future reimbursement to the pharmacy to account for the difference between the amount paid at the point of sale and the effective rate following the reconciliation.
[
88
]
In addition to generic
(
printed page 69100)
effective rate and brand effective rate, the PBM may also include a “dispensing fee effective rate” for the administrative cost charged by a pharmacy to dispense a drug.
[
89
]
C. Service Provider Arrangements Under ERISA
1. Prohibited Transaction Framework
Responsible plan fiduciaries of group health plans must determine that service provider relationships involving the group health plan meet certain conditions to avoid constituting a prohibited transaction under ERISA. Specifically, unless an exemption applies, the furnishing of goods, services, or facilities between a group health plan and a party in interest to the plan is a prohibited transaction under ERISA section 406(a)(1)(C). A person providing services to the group health plan is defined by ERISA section 3(14)(B) to be a “party in interest” to the group health plan.
ERISA section 408(b)(2) exempts certain arrangements between ERISA-covered plans (including group health plans) and service providers that otherwise would constitute prohibited transactions under ERISA section 406. Section 408(b)(2) provides relief from ERISA's prohibited transaction rules for service contracts or arrangements between a plan and a party in interest if the contract or arrangement is reasonable, the services are necessary for the establishment or operation of the plan, and no more than reasonable compensation is paid for the services.
The Department's regulation under ERISA section 408(b)(2) clarifies the exemption's “necessary service,” “reasonable contract or arrangement,” and “reasonable compensation” conditions.
[
90
]
The regulation also clarifies that the exemption in ERISA section 408(b)(2) does not extend to acts described in ERISA section 406(b) relating to fiduciary conflicts of interest and provides examples illustrating this principle.
[
91
]
In 2012, the Department amended its regulation under ERISA section 408(b)(2) to require parties who are “covered service providers” with respect to pension plans to disclose specified information to a responsible plan fiduciary, in order for certain services contracts or arrangements to be reasonable.
[
92
]
The amended regulation generally requires covered service providers to provide initial disclosure of: the services to be provided; the status of the covered service provider, an affiliate, or a subcontractor as a fiduciary, if applicable; the direct and indirect compensation reasonably expected to be received by the covered service provider, their affiliates and their subcontractors; as well as allocations of compensation reasonably expected to be made among the covered service providers and its affiliates and subcontractors. The amended regulation also establishes ongoing disclosure obligations in the event of a change in the information required to be provided in the initial disclosures and disclosures to be provided upon the written request of the responsible plan fiduciary as needed for the plan to comply with the reporting and disclosure requirements of title I of ERISA. The amended regulation also carries over a provision from the initial regulation regarding termination of the contract or arrangement.
[
93
]
The amended regulation defines a responsible plan fiduciary as a fiduciary with authority to cause the plan to enter into, or extend or renew, a contract or arrangement for the provision of services to the plan.
[
94
]
The Department's amended regulation is accompanied by an administrative class exemption for responsible plan fiduciaries, codified at paragraph (c)(1)(ix), which provides prohibited transaction relief for responsible plan fiduciaries in the event a covered service provider fails to disclose information as required under the regulation. In the absence of an exemption providing otherwise, the service provider's failure to comply with the regulation will result in a prohibited transaction by the responsible plan fiduciary.
[
95
]
In the final rule amending its regulation, the Department reserved paragraph (c)(2) for future guidance on disclosure with respect to welfare plans (including self-insured group health plans). The Department concluded that there were significant differences between service and compensation arrangements for welfare plans and those involving pension plans, and that those differences supported the development of specifically tailored disclosure requirements for welfare plans.
[
96
]
In 2014, the ERISA Advisory Council studied PBM fee disclosures and recommended that the Department should “consider making Section 408(b)(2) Regulations applicable to welfare plan arrangements with PBMs, and thereby deem such arrangements reasonable only where PBMs disclose direct and indirect compensation, including compensation paid among related parties such as subcontractors, in a manner consistent with current Section 408(b)(2) Regulations.”
[
97
]
The report included several findings related to this recommendation, including:
“Plan sponsors of group health plans who testified at the Council hearings were unanimous in their view that they face many challenges managing pharmacy benefits on a cost-effective basis. However, plan sponsors uniformly testified that PBM services are a valuable part of this effort.”
“Testimony submitted to the Council revealed that drug pricing methodologies and PBM compensation are complex and evolving, including rebates, price spreads, discounts, and other payments from retail pharmacy chains and manufacturers. Substantial evidence was submitted to the Council
(
printed page 69101)
from ERISA plan sponsors and others that many PBMs do not fully disclose compensation in a manner which is readily understandable to even the most sophisticated plan sponsors and consultants.”
“Testimony before the Council indicated that some forms of PBM compensation have the potential for creating conflicts of interest. Sponsors of ERISA health plans may or may not be aware of these potential conflicts.”
“ERISA group health plans that contract directly with PBMs frequently use consultants to assist in negotiations with the PBM. Testimony was submitted to the Council that it is common for consultants to receive indirect compensation. The payment of indirect compensation to consultants who are advising plan sponsors in negotiations with the PBM may create the potential for conflicts of interest that may be adverse to the plan sponsor. Sponsors of ERISA health plans may or may not be informed of such indirect compensation.”
“Plan sponsors testified that disclosure of PBM compensation would better enable them to comply with their obligations to determine reasonable compensation under Section 408(b)(2). Nondisclosure creates the potential for impediments to plan sponsors' ability to comply with 408(b)(2).”
The second recommendation of the ERISA Advisory Council related to audits of a PBM's compliance with its contract with the welfare plan.
[
98
]
Specifically, the Council recommended that the Department should “consider issuing guidance to assist plan sponsors in determining whether to and how to conduct a PBM audit of direct and indirect compensation.”
[
99
]
Findings related to this recommendation included identification of the following problem areas, among others:
“The exclusion of auditors who the PBM believes hold hostile views.”
“On-site audits are required at PBM headquarters.”
“PBMs limit the auditor to transcribing notes of documents.”
“Confidentiality agreements can be overly broad and put unnecessary burdens on the parties when they prohibit disclosure of information by an auditor to its client plan.”
“PBMs will not disclose documents requested by some auditors such as PBM contracts with retail pharmacies and drug manufacturers.”
“Access to claims data is restricted.”
“Audit rights restricted to limited periods (such as 2 years).”
“Some necessary data sources such as AWP pricing are not public and access is expensive . . . and disclosure is limited.”
2. Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 408(b)(2) Amendment
In the Consolidated Appropriations Act (CAA), 2021, Congress amended the ERISA section 408(b)(2) statutory exemption to add a new paragraph (B) applicable to certain services arrangements with group health plans, effective December 27, 2021.
[
100

As part of the amendment, Congress designated the pre-existing text as ERISA section 408(b)(2)(A).
[
101

The requirements in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) as originally enacted applied to a group of covered service providers, defined as persons or entities who provide “brokerage services” or “consulting” to group health plans with respect to a list of sub-services including pharmacy benefit management services.
[
102

ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) closely tracks the Department's regulation for pension plan arrangements. It requires disclosure of: the services to be provided; the status of the covered service provider, an affiliate, or a subcontractor as a fiduciary, if applicable; the direct and indirect compensation reasonably expected to be received by the covered service provider, their affiliates and their subcontractors; as well as allocations of compensation reasonably expected to be made among the covered service providers and its affiliates and subcontractors. It also establishes ongoing disclosure obligations in the event of a change in the information required to be provided in the initial disclosures and disclosures to be provided upon the written request of the responsible plan fiduciary as needed for the plan to comply with the reporting and disclosure requirements of title I of ERISA.

D. Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026
1. ERISA Amendments
The Department issued a proposed rule entitled Improving Transparency Into Pharmacy Benefit Manager Fee Disclosure on January 30, 2026.
[
105
]
On February 3, 2026, Congress made further changes to ERISA in the CAA, 2026. Among other things, the CAA, 2026 amended subparagraph (B) of ERISA section 408(b)(2), added a new subparagraph (C) to ERISA section 408(b)(2), and added a new section 726 to ERISA entitled “Oversight of Entities that Provide Pharmacy Benefit Management Services.”
1.1. Amendments to ERISA Section 408(b)(2)
In subparagraph (B) of ERISA section 408(b)(2), the CAA, 2026 revised the definition of covered service provider to remove the words “brokerage services” and “consulting.” This change clarified that providers of pharmacy benefit management services (as well as a broad range of other service providers to group health plans, including third party administrators) are covered service providers and are required to make the disclosures under the statute to rely on the prohibited transaction exemption. Additionally, new language was added to subparagraph (B) stating that a service provider for pharmacy benefit management services that contracts with a health insurance issuer in connection with health insurance coverage for a group health plan is considered an indirect provider of services to the plan and a party in interest under ERISA. This language clarified that providers of pharmacy benefit management services that provide services to fully insured plans through an insurance contract are considered parties in interest that must comply with an exemption to avoid participating in a prohibited transaction. The CAA, 2026 amendments also specified that the Department has authority to issue regulations addressing the time, manner, and content of the disclosures identified in subparagraph (B). The amendments to subparagraph (B) were effective on February 3, 2026, upon enactment of the CAA, 2026.
New subparagraph (C) of ERISA section 408(b)(2) focuses solely on providers of pharmacy benefit management services. Under that subparagraph, which is effective for plan years beginning on or after August 3, 2028, providers of pharmacy benefit management services are required to remit to group health plans (or to the insurance company on behalf of the plan) “100% of rebates, fees, alternative discounts, and other remuneration” received from “any applicable entity” related to the utilization of drugs or drug spending under the plan.
[
106
]
Applicable entities are defined in new ERISA section 726 and generally include: drug manufacturers, rebate aggregators, affiliated group purchasing organizations; affiliates of the plan, health insurance issuer, PBM, or drug manufacturers; and other entities that the Secretary specifies in rulemaking. Subparagraph (C) includes related disclosure and audit provisions.
1.2. New ERISA Section 726
ERISA section 726 provides that certain group health plans must receive a report from providers of pharmacy benefit management services every six months (or, at the plan's request, quarterly) containing detailed information about drug spending under the plan. Relatedly, applicable entities must agree by contract with plans and providers of pharmacy benefit management services (i) not to limit or delay disclosure of information in such a manner as to prevent the provider from making the required reports and (ii) to supply the required information. ERISA section 726 is applicable to plan years beginning on or after August 3, 2028, and the Department, along with the Secretaries of the Treasury and of Health and Human Services, has authority to issue regulations necessary to implement it.
Under ERISA section 726, the report is required for self-insured plans of “specified large employers” (generally with at least 100 employees) and self-insured “specified large plans” (generally with at least 100 participants).
[
107
]
Employers with fully insured plans that meet these size specifications can opt in to receive the report.
[
108
]
Under ERISA section 726, all group health plans regardless of size must also receive certain information from the entity providing pharmacy benefit management services on behalf of the group health plan. All group health plans must receive a summary document of the information required to be provided for self-insured plans of specified large employers and self-insured specified large plans, as specified by the Secretary through guidance, program instruction, or otherwise.
[
109
]
ERISA section 726 also requires that all group health plans regardless of size receive a summary document that plans can provide to participants and beneficiaries upon request by the participant or beneficiary.
[
110
]
Further, ERISA section 726 provides for a limited form of report to be defined by the Secretary for any group health plan established by a plan sponsor that is, or is affiliated with, a drug manufacturer, drug wholesaler, or any other participant in the drug supply chain, “to prevent anti-competitive behavior.”
[
111
]
The required reports for the self-insured group health plans of specified large employers and self-insured specified large plans include a list of drugs for which a claim was filed and related information about costs, compensation, and distribution channel, including information on spread compensation received by the provider of pharmacy benefit management services as well as the total amount received, or expected to be received, by the provider of pharmacy benefit management services from applicable entities in rebates, fees, alternative discounts or other remuneration.
[
112
]
The report must also include a list of each therapeutic class for which a claim was filed and related information about costs, utilization, and formulary placement; for any drug for which gross spending exceeded $10,000 during the reporting period (or the 50 drugs with the highest spending if gross spending exceeded $10,000 during the reporting period with respect to fewer than 50 drugs), information about other drugs in
(
printed page 69103)
the same therapeutic class, rationale for formulary placement and any change in the formulary placement compared to prior year; and for plans, issuers, and providers of pharmacy benefit management services with affiliated pharmacies, information about benefit design that encourages/requires use of mail order, specialty or retail pharmacies, percentage of prescriptions dispensed by such pharmacies, and a list of drugs dispensed along with amount charged to the plan and comparative cost information from other pharmacies.

2. Comments on Interaction With the Department's Rule
Upon enactment of the CAA, 2026, the Department published a notice in the
Federal Register
drawing the public's attention to the new amendments to ERISA and extending the comment period on the proposed rule by an additional 15 days to allow interested persons to address “whether the rule should be adjusted in light of the CAA, 2026 amendments to ERISA, and if so, what adjustments are needed.”
[
114
]
Many commenters responded to the Department on the interaction of the proposed rule and the CAA, 2026, amendments to ERISA. These commenters generally touched on whether the Department should move forward to a final rule or withdraw its proposal, as well as ways that the Department should align provisions of its regulation with the CAA, 2026 amendments.
On the topic of whether the Department should move forward to a final rule or withdraw the proposal, commenters weighed in on both sides. A few commenters advocated for withdrawal of the Department's proposal based on their view that in the CAA, 2026, Congress established a disclosure framework for PBM transparency that rendered the Department's regulatory project unnecessary, or even outside its regulatory authority. Commenters said the CAA, 2026 amendments address the transparency issues that motivated the Department's rulemaking, and the Department should focus its efforts on implementing the CAA, 2026 framework under ERISA section 726 with the Departments of Treasury and Health and Human Services. Some commenters noted the Department could then evaluate whether additional regulation is warranted.
Some commenters also expressed a related concern that if the Department proceeded to a final rule at this time, the rule could end up being duplicative or even conflict with requirements under the CAA, 2026 amendments to ERISA that will become effective several years from now, resulting in compliance inefficiencies and difficulties and confusion for plan fiduciaries. One commenter said that implementing the Department's rule only to later make changes to satisfy the CAA, 2026 amendments would impose operational and financial burdens on the healthcare system. One commenter said these types of compliance burdens would particularly impact mid-market PBMs. Several commenters suggested the Department should at least repropose its rule to ensure its provisions are consistent with the CAA, 2026 amendments.
A few commenters also recognized that providers of pharmacy benefit management services are now clearly covered service providers under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) and expressed concern that such service providers would be required to comply with three sets of disclosure obligations: the statutory provisions of ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), the Department's rule, and ERISA section 726. Another commenter opposed the Department proceeding with a regulation under the prohibited transaction framework because of the potential for penalties such as excise taxes for covered service providers as well as equitable remedies which the commenter said could disrupt the provision of pharmacy benefit management services.
Many more commenters expressed strong support for the proposal and urged the Department to finalize it. Commenters expressed particular support for the proposal's focus on transparency and accountability for providers of pharmacy benefit management services. Commenters also supported supplying plan fiduciaries with disclosures necessary to assess contracts with these providers and to satisfy the fiduciaries' obligations under ERISA. Some commenters expressed the view that the proposal represented an important protection of group health plan participants' interests.
One commenter who supported finalizing the rule noted that the CAA, 2026 provision that amended ERISA to add section 726 did not contain any preemptive language, did not rescind or prohibit rulemaking under ERISA section 408(b)(2), and did not state that the section 726 provisions are exclusive. Commenters also highlighted the distinct purpose of ERISA section 408(b)(2) as a statutory prohibited transaction exemption that requires group health plan fiduciaries to determine the reasonableness of services contracts or arrangements as a reason for the Department to proceed to a final rule. Some commenters identified the initial disclosures in particular as helpful to fiduciaries in discharging this obligation at the time they are entering into a contract and noted there is no counterpart in ERISA section 726. A few commenters also described how certain specific disclosures in the proposed rule would complement, not conflict with, those in ERISA section 726. For example, one commenter said that the pre-contract disclosure of spread pricing at the formulary level in the Department's proposed rule along with the post-transaction drug level reporting on spread under ERISA 726 would work together to allow for prospective fiduciary review as well as retrospective transaction verification. One commenter said the Department's adoption of a final rule at this time would provide impacted parties the opportunity to implement and gain experience with the disclosures in preparation for implementation of the CAA, 2026 amendments.
Regardless of their views on whether the Department should withdraw its proposal or proceed to a final rule, there was consensus among many commenters that if the Department determined to proceed to a final rule, it should align with the CAA, 2026 amendments to the extent possible. Many such commenters focused on alignment with the ERISA section 726 disclosures, including areas of scope, definitions, and timing.
Commenters also discussed the impact of the new subparagraph (C) of ERISA section 408(b)(2) on service provider arrangements. As that provision will require covered service providers to pass through to the group health plans “100% of rebates, fees, alternative discounts, and other remuneration” received from “any applicable entity,” commenters asserted that some of the contractual practices disclosed under the Department's rule would no longer persist after subparagraph (C)'s effective date. One commenter suggested sunsetting some of the disclosures while leaving in place robust audit rights to ensure that compensation is not recharacterized or shifted to avoid the pass-through
(
printed page 69104)
requirements. Other commenters suggested disclosures would still be needed with respect to any compensation not passed through to the group health plan. One commenter said that the definition of “applicable entity” does not specifically include pharmacies and therefore—unless the Department (with the Departments of Treasury and Health and Human Services) uses its regulatory authority to include them within the definition—revenue streams from pharmacies would continue to exist after the rebate-pass through provision takes effect.
3. The Department's Responses
The Department has carefully considered the interaction of its proposal with the CAA, 2026 amendments to ERISA, as well as comments urging withdrawal of the rule, but has determined that it would not be appropriate or prudent to withdraw its proposal in favor of a disclosure regime based solely on ERISA section 726. In making this determination, the Department acknowledges that the disclosures required under new ERISA section 726 have areas of overlap with the disclosures the Department had proposed under ERISA section 408(b)(2). However, the Department believes that, for many of the reasons cited by supportive commenters, it is appropriate to proceed to a final rule on its proposal.
Chiefly, the Department believes that the ERISA section 408(b)(2) disclosures serve a function that is distinct from those in ERISA section 726. First and foremost, the Department's regulation is designed to improve transparency in large self-insured group health plan contracting practices involving providers of pharmacy benefit management services. It will ensure responsible plan fiduciaries can determine the reasonableness of the contract or arrangement by providing them a description of each pharmacy benefit management service to be provided to the covered plan and disclosure of the direct and indirect compensation that service providers contracting for pharmacy benefit management services receive. This is achieved through initial disclosures, at the time of contracting, extension or renewal, as well as semiannual disclosures and audit rights that will support the fiduciaries' ongoing monitoring of the services contract or arrangement. Section 726, on the other hand, is a retrospective disclosure containing detailed information about drug spending and drug utilization under the group health plan that goes beyond the disclosure requirements of the Department's final rule.
Congress' amendments to ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) clarified that providers of pharmacy benefit management services are covered service providers, and the legislation also provided specific authority to the Department to issue regulations addressing time, manner, and content of the disclosures. The fact that Congress added disclosure obligations for providers of pharmacy benefit management to both ERISA section 408(b)(2) and new ERISA section 726 in a single piece of legislation detailing separate, albeit related, disclosure regimes compels the conclusion that Congress meant for both disclosure regimes to coexist. In the Department's view, these two regimes complement each other.
In sum, the Department issues this final rule to implement disclosure obligations under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) with respect to the covered service providers and covered plans described in the rule, thus satisfying the provisions of section 408(b)(2)(B) for those covered service providers and responsible plan fiduciaries. The Department is operating under the authority granted in section 408(b)(2)(B) to regulate the time, manner, and content of those disclosures, applying the statutory framework. The Department has added a provision to the regulation in paragraph (a) to confirm this position.
The Department also acknowledges, as some commenters noted, that the new subparagraph (C) of ERISA section 408(b)(2) requiring pass-through to group health plans of “100% of rebates, fees, alternative discounts, and other remuneration” received from “any applicable entity” is likely to result in changes to pharmacy benefit manager compensation arrangements. The Department considered whether to sunset related disclosure obligations but, as discussed in greater detail below, determined that it would be preferable to retain the disclosure obligations generally as proposed to ensure transparency regarding how the payments are being handled. In this regard, the Department notes that, once in effect, ERISA section 408(b)(2)(C) will require the rebates, fees, alternative discounts, and other remuneration not only to be passed through to the group health plan but also to be fully disclosed to such plan.
[
115
]
Overall, the Department concurs with commenters who stressed the importance of aligning with the CAA, 2026 amendments to avoid inefficiencies and potential confusion on the part of plan fiduciaries. The Department has made a number of changes to the text of the rule to achieve alignment. These changes, which are discussed in greater detail below, include:
Limitation to large self-insured group health plans:
The final rule applies only to self-insured plans of specified large employers and self-insured specified large plans, defined in the same way that such plans are defined in ERISA section 726. This is consistent with the approach in ERISA section 726(b)(2) in which the detailed information about drug spending will be provided to these plans.
Disclosure period:
The final rule provides for disclosures on a semiannual basis or, at the request of the group health plan, quarterly, for consistency with the reporting period in ERISA section 726(b)(1).
Manufacturer payments:
The final rule's disclosures regarding payments from drug manufacturers use the terminology “rebate[s], fee[s], alternative discount[s], or other remuneration” for consistency with the reporting obligation in ERISA section 726(b)(2)(A)(i)(X) and (XI).
Spread compensation:
The final rule's disclosures regarding spread compensation define spread compensation consistently with ERISA section 726(b)(2)(A)(i)(I)-(III).
Drug pricing methodology:
The final rule's disclosures regarding drug pricing methodology use terminology from ERISA section 726(b)(2)(A)(i)(VII).
The Department sought and received thoughtful comments on the extent to which this rule should align with the CAA, 2026. Comments on legal arguments regarding the Department's authority to issue the final rule in light of the CAA, 2026 are discussed along with the Department's responses, in section E.14 of this preamble.
The Department has not aligned the effective date of this final rule with the August 3, 2028 effective date of the CAA, 2026 amendments, as some commenters requested. The Department concurs with commenters who expressed concern about unduly delaying the introduction of much needed transparency in the area of group health plans' contracts with providers of pharmacy benefit management services. Implementing this final rule without delay will benefit responsible plan fiduciaries of self-insured group health plans by providing timely access to the more detailed information required to be disclosed. It will also provide timely guidance to
(
printed page 69105)
covered service providers regarding their compliance with ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), as amended effective February 3, 2026, who may use the guidance in this final rule to determine their own disclosure obligations.
Furthermore, as noted earlier in this preamble, the addition of new subparagraph (C) of ERISA section 408(b)(2) and the addition of section 726 of ERISA under the CAA, 2026 do not take effect until 30 months after the date of enactment. In contrast, Congress' amendments to ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), establishing statutory disclosure requirements for pharmacy benefit management service providers wishing to take advantage of the exemption, became effective upon enactment of the CAA, 2026 on February 3, 2026. In the Department's view, this indicates Congress' intent that responsible plan fiduciaries should have the required disclosures to evaluate the contracts or arrangements with pharmacy benefit management service providers on an earlier timetable. The provisions in this final rule implement the statutory disclosure requirements in section 408(b)(2)(B), dictating against delaying applicability longer than necessary to allow parties to develop compliance structures. Accordingly, the Department has made the final rule effective January 4, 2027, and applicable to plan years beginning after July 1, 2027.
4. ERISA Section 408(b)(2)(B) Compliance
Several commenters urged the Department to acknowledge and highlight that the amendments to ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) are in effect currently. The Department concurs with these commenters that the broader range of service providers to group health plans must make the disclosures outlined in the statute to rely on the exemption, for contracts or arrangements, extensions or renewals, effective as of February 3, 2026. As specified in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), as amended, covered service providers include, in addition to providers of brokerage services and consulting, providers of: pharmacy benefit management services, third-party administration services, insurance services and insurance product selection services (including vision and dental), recordkeeping services, and others.

This final rule implements the requirements of ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), as amended, for the covered service providers and covered plans identified herein. Although the statutory provisions apply to all ERISA-covered group health plans, the Department believes the detailed descriptions of compensation streams and arrangements in this rule that are tailored to the pharmaceutical supply chain will provide particularly valuable information to responsible plan fiduciaries of large, self-insured group health plans. Furthermore, to demonstrate alignment with the statutory disclosures as appropriate following the CAA, 2026 amendments, and in response to commenters requesting additional clarity regarding the application of the disclosure obligations to indirect compensation, the Department has revised the rule to categorize the disclosures in the final rule as either “direct” or “indirect” compensation.

Some commenters asked the Department to offer an enforcement policy for all covered service providers identified in the amended ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), which was effective as of February 3, 2026, as these providers work to come into compliance with the statutory disclosure obligations. Commenters also asked for safe harbors for responsible plan fiduciaries who demonstrate good faith efforts to comply with their obligations with respect to determining the reasonableness of the service contract or arrangement.
The Department concurs that enforcement relief under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) is appropriate as parties develop mechanisms to comply with obligations that became effective when the CAA, 2026 was enacted on February 3, 2026, and believes the appropriate period for a temporary enforcement policy should end on the final rule's applicability date of plan years beginning on or after July 1, 2027. This temporary enforcement policy will apply to all covered service providers and responsible plan fiduciaries of covered plans, each as defined in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), regardless of whether they are covered service providers and plan fiduciaries of covered plans addressed in this final rule. Accordingly, from the period from February 3, 2026 to the applicability date of the final rule, the Department will not treat a covered service provider as defined in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) as having failed to make the required disclosures to a responsible plan fiduciary under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) as long as the covered service provider made disclosures in accordance with a good faith interpretation of ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), as amended. Further, prior to the applicability date of the final rule, the Department will not treat a responsible plan fiduciary of a covered plan as defined in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) as having engaged in a prohibited transaction in entering into a contract or arrangement with a covered service provider as long as the fiduciary acted in accordance with a good faith interpretation of their obligations under ERISA to determine the reasonableness of the contract or arrangement.

As provided in paragraph (b) of the final rule,

While the proposed rule applied to all self-insured group health plans, the final rule further limited the scope to large self-insured group health plans and included a new exception for group health plans established by a plan sponsor that is, or that is affiliated with, a drug manufacturer, distributor, wholesaler, or rebate aggregator (or other purchasing entity designed to aggregate rebates), as discussed in the next sections of the preamble.
1.2.1. Limitation to Large, Self-Insured Group Health Plans
The final rule applies only to self-insured group health plans offered by “specified large employers” and self-insured group health plans that are “specified large plans.” These terms are defined in paragraph (m)
[
122
]
and are generally consistent with those terms in ERISA section 726. A specified large employer means, in connection with a group health plan established or maintained by a single employer, with respect to a calendar year, an employer who employed an average of at least 100 employees on business days during the preceding calendar year and who employs at least 1 employee on the first day of the calendar year. For purposes of counting employees to determine whether an employer is a specified large employer, employees must be counted in accordance with the rules for counting employees and employer aggregation under section 4980H of the Internal Revenue Code and its implementing regulations at
26 CFR 54.4980H
. A specified large plan means a group health plan established or maintained by a plan sponsor described in ERISA section 3(16)(B)(ii) or (iii) that had an average of at least 100 participants on business days during the preceding plan year. Whether a group health plan is a specified large plan is determined by taking the sum of the total number of participants (not including beneficiaries) for each calendar month in the preceding plan year, and dividing by 12. The result, if not a whole number, is then rounded to the next lowest whole number. Self-insured group health plans that are not described in those definitions are not covered plans for purposes of the final rule, but they are covered plans for purposes of the application of the statutory exemption in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) to entities providing pharmacy benefit management services. Accordingly, covered service providers not addressed in this rule must provide the generalized compensation disclosures specified in the statute to rely on the prohibited transaction exemption.
The Department determined to limit the scope of the final rule in response to several different types of comments. First, commenters asked the Department to align the covered plan definition with ERISA section 726. Under ERISA section 726, the larger group health plans (
i.e.,
offered by a specified large employer or a specified large plan) receive a report with detailed information about drug spending while smaller group health plans will receive a summary document that includes information “that the Secretary determines useful to group health plans for purposes of selecting pharmacy benefit management services, such as an estimated net price to group health plan and participant or beneficiary, a cost per claim, the fee structure or reimbursement model, and estimated cost per participant or beneficiary.”

]
In the Department's view, aligning the definition of a covered plan so that only the larger self-insured group health plans receive the detailed disclosures under this final rule is responsive to those comments and is consistent with the Secretary's authority to specify the time, manner and content of the section 408(b)(2)(B) disclosures. Based on that same authority, the Secretary has determined that the smaller self-insured group health plans should receive the generalized compensation disclosures pursuant to ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B).
Limiting the detailed disclosures under the final rule to large, self-insured group plans is also responsive to other comments on the proposal. Commenters expressed the view that smaller employers with limited resources may
(
printed page 69107)
face substantial challenges analyzing the detailed disclosures in the proposal, and having received the detailed disclosures, may face increased litigation risk second guessing their disclosure-related decisions. Other commenters said that providing the detailed disclosures in the proposal would unduly burden smaller providers of pharmacy benefit management services who commonly serve smaller employers.
The Department believes that increased transparency in the area of pharmacy benefit management services is critical but it recognizes that, as a practical matter, the detailed disclosures required under the final rule may be most useful to responsible plan fiduciaries of larger employers, who are more likely to have compliance staff and sufficient resources to analyze the disclosures and take appropriate action. Proceeding with the more limited scope in the final rule is intended to avoid unintended negative consequences for smaller employers as described by some commenters while ensuring they receive disclosures under the statute to determine the reasonableness of the contracts or arrangements, including their covered service providers' compensation.
[

This approach will not result in the smaller self-insured group health plans receiving no disclosures to assist them in selecting a provider of pharmacy benefit management services. These group health plans are covered plans under the statutory exemption in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) and would receive the disclosures required under the statute from covered service providers—including providers of pharmacy benefit management services—wishing to take advantage of the exemption. The disclosures are required at the time of the initial contract or arrangement and any extension or renewal, and include, for example, the services to be provided; the status of the covered service provider, an affiliate, or a subcontractor as a fiduciary, if applicable; and the direct and indirect compensation reasonably expected to be received by the covered service provider, their affiliates and their subcontractors. The statute also provides for disclosure in the event of a change in the information required to be provided in the initial disclosures and for disclosures to be provided upon the written request of the responsible plan fiduciary, as needed for the plan to comply with the reporting and disclosure requirements of Title I of ERISA. Simply put, the covered service providers of these smaller self-insured group health plans, alongside those that serve fully-insured entities through a health insurance issuer, will not be required to provide the disclosures described in the final rule, which are more specific, prescriptive, and detailed with respect to the compensation streams than the disclosure provisions in the statute, but they will still need to follow the statute. As such, after considering comments, the Department believes that these more detailed disclosures are appropriately directed to the responsible plan fiduciaries of larger self-insured group health plans.
1.2.2. Fully Insured Plans
The definition of “covered plan” in the final rule excludes fully insured group health plans because the Department is reserving for future action more detailed regulatory disclosure obligations with respect to these plans. However, these group health plans remain covered plans under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) and therefore covered service providers serving fully insured plans that wish to rely on the statutory prohibited transaction exemption are required to provide the generalized statutory disclosures.
In the proposal, the Department had reserved regulatory disclosure obligations with respect to fully insured group health plans for future action based on the preliminary view that responsible plan fiduciaries may focus on different considerations when contracting with an insurance company for health insurance coverage that integrates prescription drug coverage, as opposed to self-insuring medical care and contracting for pharmacy benefit management services. Specifically, the Department questioned whether responsible plan fiduciaries would find the specific disclosures proposed in the regulation useful when negotiating a fully insured arrangement as to justify the costs associated with the detailed disclosures (both to the covered service provider providing the disclosures and the responsible plan fiduciary reviewing and analyzing the disclosures). The Department also noted its understanding that, in some instances, other relevant reporting and disclosure requirements may apply under State law to the health insurance issuer, either independently under the applicable insurance code, or as part of the issuer's routine form filing review.
In the proposal, the Department sought comments on the relevance of the proposed disclosures to responsible plan fiduciaries of fully insured group health plans. In these arrangements in which services are fully bundled with insurance, the Department assumed that responsible plan fiduciaries discharged their obligation to ensure that the contract or arrangement is reasonable by focusing on premiums, covered benefits, coverage limits, exclusions, and cost-sharing requirements. The proposal further assumed that responsible plan fiduciaries would not, in these circumstances, benefit from the specific disclosures required under the proposal because when the pharmacy benefit management services are fully bundled with insurance, the responsible plan fiduciary has a clearer understanding of the total compensation paid for the services.
Some commenters supported the Department's proposed exclusion of fully insured group health plans as covered plans under the regulation. Commenters said a contract of insurance is different from the services arrangements involving self-insured plans and involves state insurance law oversight (
i.e.
, Medical Loss Ratio requirements). A few commenters also took the position that extending the proposed disclosures to responsible plan fiduciaries of fully insured group health plans would not be legally supportable. One commenter said that, in the case of a fully insured group health plan, the provider of pharmacy benefit management services is a vendor to the insurer and therefore does not have a contractual relationship with the plan. This commenter further argued that, in a fully insured group health plan, the insurer (not the plan) assumes financial risk, administers the benefits, and is responsible for all components of the insurance product. The same commenter also suggested that Congress addressed the mechanisms for fully insured arrangements to receive prescription drug reporting under ERISA section 726.
Many other commenters on the proposal said the Department should extend disclosure obligations under the final rule to covered service providers of fully insured group health plans. Many of these commenters said that excluding fully insured plans would leave fiduciaries without the benefit of the disclosures in the rule despite those fiduciaries having an obligation under ERISA to assess the reasonableness of contractual arrangements. Further, commenters believed that a consistent approach to transparency across self-insured plans and fully insured plans
(
printed page 69108)
was desirable. Some commenters specifically referenced concerns about transparency in connection with the vertical integration of the largest PBMs and health insurance issuers. Other commenters noted that fully insured plans that are offered by specified large employers or that are specified large plans can receive the detailed report required under ERISA section 726 (although such plans must specifically opt in to do so). One commenter said the Department's stated rationale for excluding fully insured plans—which was based on integration with a health insurance contract—was not compelling, on the basis that the rule would apply to other cases where the commenter believed that pharmacy benefits are integrated with medical services, such as in arrangements offered by TPAs.
A few commenters who supported extending disclosure obligations to covered service providers of fully insured group health plans asked the Department to conduct a future rulemaking for these products, acknowledging the differences between fully insured and self-insured contracts and arrangements. One commenter said the Department would have flexibility to tailor disclosures to reflect differences in the fully insured group health plan context. A commenter opposing the expansion of this rule to include fully insured group health plans also expressed the view that fiduciaries making decisions about an insurance contract would not act on the particular disclosures in the Department's proposal.
The Department has carefully considered comments encouraging the Department to extend the final rule's disclosure obligations to covered service providers with respect to fully insured plans. In the Department's view, some of these commenters argued for disclosures to be made to fully insured plans as a matter of policy, without addressing whether the proposed disclosures would be meaningful for responsible plan fiduciaries of fully insured group health plans. The Department believes that arrangements in which pharmacy benefit services are bundled with insurance are distinct from self-insured arrangements offered by TPAs in which pharmacy benefit management services are integrated with medical services, as referenced by one commenter. The bundling with health insurance raises different issues because of the insurance guarantees. When an employer self-insures a group health plan, the employer bears the financial risk of paying claims and managing the plan. To assist with managing the plan, these employers often contract with service providers such as TPAs to process claims and provide other plan administration services. For a fully insured plan, generally the employer purchases a pre-packaged insurance product where the issuer bears the financial risk of covering costs. These differences in financial risk and plan management require a different approach for developing meaningful disclosures for plan fiduciaries of fully insured plans. The Department is persuaded by the commenters who believe further work would need to be done before developing a framework for disclosures to responsible plan fiduciaries of fully insured group health plans.
The Department notes however that, contrary to an assertion by one commenter, providers of pharmacy benefit management services that contract with health insurers providing coverage to fully insured plans are in fact parties in interest and covered service providers, as clarified by the CAA, 2026.
[
