Accordingly, these covered service providers have disclosure obligations under the statute that must be satisfied if they wish to rely on the exemption set forth in ERISA section 408(b)(2).
1.2.3. Other Types of Group Health Plans
Some commenters asked the Department to exclude excepted benefits such as limited scope dental and vision plans from the definition of covered plan. The commenters said that including excepted benefits is inconsistent with the CAA, 2026 amendments to ERISA. A few commenters also asked the Department to clarify whether the rule would apply to Taft-Hartley plans or welfare benefit plans under ERISA section 3(1).
The final rule applies to covered plans which are defined as group health plans under ERISA section 733(a) that are offered by a specified large employer or that are specified large plans, each as defined in paragraph (m), other than a group health plan in which all of the benefits are provided exclusively through a contract or policy of insurance issued by a health insurance issuer. Although excepted benefits are not subject to certain requirements in Part 7 of ERISA, such benefits are “covered plans” subject to the requirements of ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) to the extent that such benefits satisfy the definition of “group health plan” under ERISA § 733(a)(1). The Department notes that in accordance with ERISA section 732(b) and (c), the market requirements of part 7 of ERISA do not apply to a group health plan or a health insurance issuer in the group or individual market in relation to the provision of excepted benefits described in ERISA section 733(c). However, ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) provides that covered plan means a group health plan as defined in ERISA section 733(a). Under ERISA section 733(a) a group health plan is defined as “an employee welfare benefit plan to the extent that the plan provides medical care . . . to employees or their dependents (as defined under the terms of the plan) directly or through insurance, reimbursement, or otherwise.” Section 733(a)(1) of ERISA specifically excludes qualified small employer health reimbursement arrangements.
The definition of a group health plan in ERISA section 733(a) does not exclude excepted benefits, which are defined under ERISA section 733(c)(2). Therefore, excepted benefits are not excluded from the disclosure requirements under this final rule. To the extent that a covered service provider enters a contract or arrangement with an excepted benefit plan, the disclosure obligations required to qualify for a prohibited transaction exemption may apply. Similarly, the definition of group health plan does not exclude Taft-Hartley plans, and such plans are covered plans under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) and this regulation if they meet the size criteria.

(

No commenters articulated why plan fiduciaries of self-insured group health plans sponsored by drug manufacturers or other employers in the drug supply chain should receive detailed disclosures under this final rule. Commenters highlighted that, in recent years, multiple cases have been brought by plan participants claiming that their plan fiduciaries did not fulfill their fiduciary responsibilities regarding PBM services by incurring excessive fees, failing to negotiate better pricing terms for prescription drugs, and not behaving prudently when selecting the plan's PBM.

Although the disclosures under the final rule would assist employers in the drug supply chain in satisfying their fiduciary obligations, the Department is persuaded that Congress' inclusion of this special provision in CAA, 2026 reflects a deliberate judgement that anticompetitive harm could result from those with a direct financial stake in the drug supply chain receiving detailed disclosures. These service providers include TPAs, health insurers, and others involved in the administration of self-insured group health plans' medical claims, such as for hospital stays, surgeries, and chronic treatment, but whose services are unrelated to pharmacy benefit management. Stakeholders had indicated that group health plan fiduciaries may not have access to all claims data, payments to providers, and fee and pricing data that could enable negotiation for cost savings to group health plans and participants.

The Department sought comment on whether it should expand the proposed disclosures to cover additional service providers beyond providers of pharmacy benefit management services; and if so, which service providers should be covered. Additionally, the Department sought comment on whether the disclosures in the proposal would be sufficient to bring transparency into arrangements with those additional service providers or whether additional disclosures would be needed, such as claims data, payments to providers, and other fee and pricing data.
As discussed in section D. of this preamble, shortly after the Department published its proposed rule, Congress amended ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) in the CAA, 2026, which in part clarified which service providers are covered service providers for purposes of the prohibited transaction exemption. The phrase “Brokerage services” was removed and replaced with “Services (including brokerage services),” in subparagraph (AA) of section 408(b)(2)(B)(ii)(I)(bb). The term “Consulting” was removed and replaced with “Other services” in subparagraph (BB) of section 408(b)(2)(B)(ii)(I)(bb). Additionally, in subparagraph (BB) of section 408(b)(2)(B)(ii)(I)(bb), the phrase
(

In response to the CAA, 2026, the Department extended the comment period for the proposed rule to allow stakeholders to address how to harmonize the proposed rule with the new statutory requirements.

Many commenters said the Department should expand the definition of covered service provider to include additional types of service providers. They mentioned TPAs, independent brokers and consultants, insurers, and network vendors, for example. Commenters said the need for transparency was not limited to the context of pharmacy benefit management services, with some commenters also stating that arrangements with other service providers also suffered from undisclosed conflicts of interest, misaligned incentives, and indirect compensation streams that may not be known by the responsible plan fiduciaries. A few commenters said that the compensation flows among various group health plan service providers are inseparable, especially due to vertical integration of service providers and expressed concern that failure to expand the definition of covered service provider would allow parties to evade disclosure obligations and undermine the transparency goals of the rulemaking. Some commenters noted expansion to other types of service providers would be consistent with Congress' action clarifying the broader definition of covered service provider in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B).
Some commenters provided information on the types of disclosures that should be required should the Department expand the final rule to include other covered service providers, especially TPAs with respect to medical claims. Commenters mentioned compensation retained on provider reimbursements; shared savings or gainsharing arrangements; network access or discount fees; repricing or claims-editing fees; and many others. Commenters raised the point that TPAs often receive compensation from network lessors, specialty vendors, and utilization management companies by routing business through those entities, for the plans the TPA serves. These indirect sources of compensation may not be known to plan sponsors as they are not always identified in the contracts between TPAs and plans. Commenters also identified brokers and consultants who advise plans on service provider selection and may receive compensation from selected providers.
Other commenters said the Department should not expand the definition of covered service providers to other types of service providers beyond providers of pharmacy benefit management services. One commenter said that TPA and claims administration services are fundamentally different from pharmacy benefit management services and disclosure issues would not be able to be addressed by expanding the disclosures in the Department's rule which had been developed for providers of pharmacy benefit management services. Another commenter noted that TPAs are included in the proposed rule to the extent they provide pharmacy benefit management services. Commenters also said that Congress had made clear that there is a broader set of covered service providers in the statutory exemption but did not single them out for detailed disclosure obligations.
The Department concurs with commenters who said that broader transparency encompassing additional covered service providers to group health plans would be beneficial and consistent with law. As discussed above, a broad range of covered service providers are now covered service providers for purposes of the statutory exemption in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), including TPAs. Commenters identified multiple types of service providers that contract with group health plans to provide a wide array of services with multiple sources of direct and indirect compensation that group health plan service providers, such as TPAs, may utilize. However, based on the comments identifying the compensation streams that should be disclosed, the Department believes disclosures for the expanded group of covered service providers would best be addressed in a separate regulatory or subregulatory guidance project tailored to those other types of service providers, and will consider adding this project to a future regulatory agenda.
For now, although not covered by this final rule, the Department expects this expanded group of covered service providers to make a good-faith effort to comply with their disclosure obligations under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), in line with the Department's temporary enforcement policy announced herein, in order to rely on the exemption. For example, a TPA providing services to a group health plan for medical management should disclose, pursuant to ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), direct and indirect compensation. This includes direct or indirect compensation such as administrative fees, per-employee-per-month fees, or 340B-related income; provider and network compensation; affiliate, subcontractor, and vertically integrated compensation; data monetization compensation; and payment and recovery compensation.
1.3.2. Compensation of Individuals Who Are Officers, Directors, Employees or Partners
Some commenters noted that the definition of an “affiliate” includes officers, directors, employees, and partners of the covered service provider. These commenters said the final rule should not require disclosure of any individual's compensation in connection with providing pharmacy benefit management services. The Department agrees that compensation of individuals is not the focus of this regulatory project and notes that ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) specifically provides that the requirement to disclose indirect compensation does not extend to compensation received by an employee from an employer on account of work performed by the employee.

The Department has added a similar provision in paragraph (c) of the final rule that specifies that the regulation does not require disclosure of the compensation of individuals who are officers, directors, employees and partners.
1.4. Providers of Pharmacy Benefit Management Services—Paragraph (c)(1)(i)
Paragraph (c)(1)(i) of the final rule defines, as covered service providers, service providers who enter into a contract or arrangement with a covered plan to provide pharmacy benefit management services. Like the proposed rule, the final rule clarifies that this would be the case regardless of whether the services will be performed by the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor.
[
136
]
Thus, the
(
printed page 69111)
final rule recognizes that the pharmacy benefit management services may be performed by the covered service provider, or they may be performed by an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor of the covered service provider. Likewise, the final rule recognizes that compensation in connection with the services may be received by the covered service provider or it may be received by an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor of the covered service provider.
Under this framework, paragraph (c)(1)(i) of the final rule focuses on the entity that has a contract or arrangement with the covered plan to provide any pharmacy benefit management services to that plan—that party is the covered service provider. The Department believes that the service provider directly responsible to the covered plan for the provision of pharmacy benefit management services is the appropriate party to ensure that the required disclosures under the regulation are made. This approach is consistent with ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) as well as the Department's service provider regulation applicable to pension plans (
29 CFR 2550.408b-2(c)(1)
).
[
137
]
In this regard, the Department understands that responsible plan fiduciaries to covered plans may take a number of different approaches in identifying and selecting a provider of pharmacy benefit management services. The covered plan may ultimately contract directly with the entity that will perform the services, or it may enter into a contract with a different entity that agrees to provide the services to the covered plan through an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor. It is common, for example, for responsible plan fiduciaries to work with a consultant or broker to conduct a request for proposal and to assist in negotiations with the providers of pharmacy benefit management services. In that case, the covered plan will enter a contract directly with the PBM.
On the other hand, the Department understands that TPAs may contract directly with covered plans to provide a range of health-care related services, such as creating networks of healthcare providers, negotiating payments rates, and processing and paying health claims. One component of these services may be pharmacy benefit management services. If the TPA contracts with the covered plan to provide pharmacy benefit management services, the TPA would be a covered service provider under this regulation, even if it intends to rely on another provider to perform those services. In that event, the TPA would be responsible for making the disclosures to the responsible plan fiduciary required under the final rule and therefore must be able to obtain information from the provider performing the pharmacy benefit management services necessary for those disclosures.
Covered plans may access pharmacy benefit management services through other similar types of arrangements, where the provider may or may not refer to itself as a TPA. For example, it is common for group health plans to enter level-funded arrangements that have stop-loss policies to emulate characteristics of fully insured arrangements, such as predictable spending, but that are actually self-funded arrangements. These arrangements commonly include pharmacy benefit services and the entity that contracts with the covered plan to provide those services would be the covered service provider. As in the TPA example, even if the entity contracting or arranging with the covered plan is not providing the services itself, it nonetheless would be responsible for making the disclosures to the responsible plan fiduciary required under the final rule, and therefore must be able to obtain information from the provider performing the pharmacy benefit management services necessary for those disclosures.
Questions may arise regarding which party is the covered service provider and which party is the responsible plan fiduciary in the context of a multiple employer welfare arrangement (MEWA).
[
138
]
For MEWAs that are considered single ERISA plans, the responsible plan fiduciary for the covered plan would receive the disclosures from the party that contracts with the covered plan to provide pharmacy benefit management services. In the case of a MEWA that is not considered a single ERISA plan but rather involves a number of covered plans each sponsored by an employer individually, the party operating the MEWA is likely to be the covered service provider that contracts with the individual covered plans to provide pharmacy benefit management services. In that case, the MEWA operator would have the responsibility to make the disclosures required by the final rule to the responsible plan fiduciaries (
i.e.
, the employers or other fiduciary responsible for entering into the contract or arrangement to provide such services),
[
139
]
and therefore must obtain the necessary information from the provider (
e.g.
, as a subcontractor) performing the pharmacy benefit management services.
Covered plans alternatively may access pharmacy benefit management services through employer consortiums or other types of employer groups. The analysis of who the covered service provider is in those arrangements would depend on the details of the arrangement and, specifically, which entity contracts with the covered plan to provide the pharmacy benefit management services. If the consortium or other group assists in negotiating with the provider of pharmacy benefit management services but the covered plan contracts directly with the provider—which the Department believes is the predominant approach—the provider of pharmacy benefit management services would be the covered service provider. However, if the consortium or other employer group were to contract to provide the services to the covered plan, the consortium or other group would be the covered service provider.
Finally, a covered plan may directly contract with more than one entity for pharmacy benefit management services as such services are defined in paragraph (d) of the rule. In such circumstances, the covered plan would thus have more than one PBM, each of which would be a covered service provider and responsible for making its own disclosures with respect to services under its contract or arrangement with the covered plan.
1.4.1. Definition of Pharmacy Benefit Management Services—Paragraph (d)
Paragraph (d) of the final rule
[
140
]
defines pharmacy benefit management services as services necessary for the management or administration of a covered plan's prescription drug benefits (including the covered plan's provision of prescription drugs through the plan's medical benefit), regardless of whether the person, business, or entity
(
printed page 69112)
performing the service identifies itself as a “pharmacy benefit manager.” The definition includes a list of examples of such services, as follows:
acting as a negotiator or aggregator of rebates, fees, discounts and other price concessions for prescription drugs;
establishing or maintaining prescription drug formularies;
establishing or maintaining pharmacy networks, through contract or otherwise, including a mail order pharmacy, a specialty pharmacy, a retail pharmacy, a nursing home pharmacy, a long-term care pharmacy, and an infusion or other outpatient pharmacy, to provide prescription drugs;
performing utilization review and management, including the instituting and processing of prior authorization requests for drugs, step therapy protocols, patient compliance analyses, conducting therapeutic intervention, and administering generic and biosimilar substitution programs.
The definition also includes examples of other services that, in conjunction with any of the services described above, are considered pharmacy benefit management services. These services are:
processing and payment of claims for prescription drugs;
adjudicating appeals or grievances related to the covered plan's prescription drug benefits;
recordkeeping related to the covered plan's prescription drug benefits; and
performing regulatory compliance with respect to the covered plan's prescription drug benefits under the contract or arrangement.
As discussed above, pharmacy benefit management encompasses a number of services related to developing drug formularies, negotiating with drug manufacturers for rebates and other discounts, negotiating with pharmacies, and processing claims and other functions for covered plans. The examples provided in the definition are intended to describe the services expansively to ensure comprehensive disclosures are made. Consequently, the definition specifies that whether the person providing the services identifies itself as a PBM is not dispositive of the requirement to disclose. Additionally, a person will be a covered service provider by virtue of performing any of the services identified in the definition; covered service provider status does not depend on comprehensively providing all the services set forth in the definition.
The definition in the final rule was revised from the proposal based on comments stating that certain examples included in the proposed definition were too broad. Commenters identified the following examples as ones that in isolation may identify service providers that should not be considered to provide pharmacy benefit management services: “processing and payment of claims for prescription drugs;” “adjudicating appeals or grievances related to the covered plan's prescription drug benefits;” “recordkeeping related to the covered plan's prescription drug benefits;” and “regulatory compliance with respect to the covered plan's prescription drug benefits under the contract or arrangement.” One commenter, for example, said that health reimbursement account (HRA) service providers may process and pay claims for prescription drugs as part of their account administration, but the commenter did not believe the Department should cover HRA service providers as providers of pharmacy benefit management services.
The Department is persuaded by the examples provided by these commenters that the examples may be too broad in isolation, and has accordingly revised the definition of pharmacy benefit management services. Under the revised definition, certain services described in the examples will, standing alone, be considered pharmacy benefit management services. Those services are: acting as a negotiator or aggregator of rebates, fees, discounts, and other price concessions for prescription drugs; establishing or maintaining prescription drug formularies; establishing or maintaining pharmacy networks, through contract or otherwise, including a mail order pharmacy, a specialty pharmacy, a retail pharmacy, a nursing home pharmacy, a long-term care pharmacy, and an infusion or other outpatient pharmacy, to provide prescription drugs; and performing utilization review and management, including the instituting or processing of prior authorization requests for drugs, step therapy protocols, patient compliance analyses, conducting therapeutic intervention, and administering generic and biosimilar substitution programs. These services can be considered core pharmacy benefit management services.
The Department revised the example regarding utilization review and management based on comments suggesting that the example should be expanded to be comprehensive. In the final rule, the words “instituting or” were added before “processing of prior authorization requests for drugs,” so that the example extends to “
instituting or
processing of prior authorization requests for drugs” and the word “biosimilar” was added to the phrase regarding administering generic substitution programs, so that the example reads “administering generic
and biosimilar
substitution programs.”
Other examples in the definition will be considered pharmacy benefit management services only if they are performed “in conjunction with” the core services. Those services are: processing and payment of claims for prescription drugs; adjudicating appeals or grievances related to the covered plan's prescription drug benefits; recordkeeping related to the covered plan's prescription drug benefits; and performing regulatory compliance with respect to the covered plan's prescription drug benefits under the contract or arrangement. Under this approach, entities who provide these services along with the core pharmacy benefit management services would consider the compensation from these services when determining if the $1,000 threshold is met for status as a covered service provider. Compensation received in connection with these services would be disclosed under the various disclosure provisions in the final rule.
Some commenters focused on the example regarding “performing regulatory compliance” and asked whether, under that example, providers of legal services would be considered covered service providers. The revised definition should make clear that attorneys and other providers of legal services would generally not be considered providers of pharmacy benefit management services under the final rule. The definition is intended to encompass entities that perform any of the core services described above and also provide regulatory compliance—for example, ensuring compliance with the rebate pass through requirements of ERISA section 408(b)(2)(C) when that section takes effect. Under the definition of pharmacy benefit management services in the final rule, it is not necessary for an entity to provide all the services described in the examples. One commenter said the word “and” connecting the examples might suggest that all such examples must be satisfied for the definition to apply. The Department has replaced “and” with “or” and, under the language of the definition as revised, the Department does not believe there is potential for confusion.
Commenters suggested that the Department make other changes to this definition in the final rule. One commenter said that the example “acting as a negotiator or aggregator of rebates, fees, discounts and other price
(
printed page 69113)
concessions for prescription drugs” is unnecessarily broad and could encompass negotiators of price concessions whose services are separate from the procurement and management of prescription drug coverage traditionally associated with pharmacy benefit management services. The commenter also said any definition should be clear that pharmacies themselves are not pharmacy benefit management service providers. In the Department's view, acting as a negotiator or aggregator of rebates, fees, discounts and other price concessions for prescription drugs is a core component of pharmacy benefit management services so it has retained that aspect of the definition as proposed. The Department understands that pharmacies do not perform the core services as described above and therefore agrees that they would not be considered providers of pharmacy benefit management services under the final rule.
Several commenters asked for specific items to be added to the definition. Suggestions included adding a reference to administration of a pharmacy benefit, in whole or in part, to the definition; adding a reference to establishing or maintaining prescription drug formularies that require beneficiaries to apply to manufacturer patient assistance-related programs and adding a reference to activity of a provider of pharmacy benefit management services or an affiliate that manages, co-manages, or private-labels pharmaceutical products. The Department has not adopted these changes because it believes the existing language in the definition is adequate to cover the activities suggested by commenters. For example, administration of a pharmacy benefit is specifically referenced in the general language in paragraph (d)(1), which states “the term `pharmacy benefit management services' means services necessary for the management or administration of a covered plan's prescription drug benefits (including the covered plan's provision of prescription drugs through the plan's medical benefit) . . .” Paragraph (d)(2)(ii) provides that pharmacy benefit management services include “[e]stablishing or maintaining prescription drug formularies” which the Department believes is broad enough to cover establishing or maintaining prescription drug formularies that require beneficiaries to apply to manufacturer patient assistance-related programs as well as selecting PBM-affiliated pharmaceutical products for the formulary.
One commenter suggested the definition of pharmacy benefit management services should include a rebuttable presumption under which a health plan service provider providing what generally may be considered pharmacy benefit management services as illustrated by the examples would be presumed to be a covered service provider unless reasonably determined not to be by the applicable group health plan fiduciaries. Another commenter suggested a special rule under which pharmacy benefit management services would not include activities performed by “an integrated health care delivery system that includes a nonprofit health insurance issuer in which enrollees primarily use pharmacies that are entirely owned and operated by the nonprofit health insurance issuer.” The Department has not adopted the rebuttable presumption because it does not believe a responsible plan fiduciary should be in a position to excuse a particular entity from being considered a covered service provider. The Department also has not adopted the special rule for the nonprofit health insurance issuer described by the commenter because it was not persuaded that covered plans entering into that arrangement would not benefit from the disclosures under the final rule.
There were additional comments on how the definition of pharmacy benefit management services should be phrased. One commenter suggested that the definition should reference subsidiaries, parents, and affiliates of the entity providing pharmacy benefit management services. The Department does not believe that is necessary because the final rule has a definition of “affiliate” that includes these entities.
One commenter believed that the final rule should clarify that the definition of pharmacy benefit management services relates to prescription drugs reimbursed under the medical benefit, and specifically that the following compensation streams are covered: compensation received by PBMs, TPAs, carriers, specialty pharmacies, and affiliated entities in connection with medical-benefit drugs; rebates, administrative fees, and other payments tied to physician-administered or specialty drugs; provider-side revenue, including markups, reimbursement differentials, and site-of care-related compensation; and any other direct or indirect remuneration arising from the management, distribution, or reimbursement of such drugs.
The Department believes the definition in the final rule adequately includes that reference in the language. In paragraph (d)(1) of the final rule, the definition states: “the term `pharmacy benefit management services' means services necessary for the management or administration of a covered plan's prescription drug benefits (
including the covered plan's provision of prescription drugs through the plan's medical benefit
) . . . .” (Emphasis added).
1.4.2. Affiliates, Agents and Subcontractors—Paragraph (m)
The final rule's defined terms “affiliate,” “agent,” and “subcontractor” identify parties other than the covered service provider that may perform pharmacy benefit management services and may receive compensation in connection with the contract or arrangement that the covered service provider has with a covered plan for pharmacy benefit management services. The services and compensation of these entities are required to be disclosed under the final rule. As noted above, the final rule places the obligation on the covered service provider to make the disclosures, including to seek any required information from these parties as needed for the disclosure. Paragraph (c)(2) clarifies that affiliates, agents, and subcontractors of covered service providers do not, themselves, become covered service providers as a result of providing services pursuant to the contract or arrangement.
[
141

Under paragraph (m)(1) of the final rule, an affiliate is an entity that “directly or indirectly (through one or more intermediaries) controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with such person or entity; or is an officer, director, or employee of, or partner in, such person or entity.” The definition states that unless otherwise specified, an “affiliate” in the regulation refers to an affiliate of the covered service provider. In other contexts, the Department has said “control” refers to the power to exercise a controlling influence over the management or policies of a person other than an individual.
[
142
]
Paragraph (m)(5) defines a subcontractor as a “person or entity (or an affiliate of such person or entity) that is not an affiliate of the covered service provider and that, pursuant to a contract or arrangement with the covered service provider or an affiliate, reasonably expects to receive $1,000 or more in compensation for performing one or more services described pursuant to paragraph (d) of this section provided
(

for by the contract or arrangement” with the covered plan. Accordingly, under the definition, an affiliate of a subcontractor would also be considered a subcontractor for purposes of the regulation, including the disclosure requirements. This means that compensation to a subcontractor's affiliate must be disclosed if received in connection with the pharmacy benefit management services provided to the covered plan.

29 CFR 2550.408b-2(c)
).
[

Although parties performing services provided for under the contract or arrangement on behalf of the covered service provider should generally fall within the broad term “subcontractor,” the additional defined term “agent” is included based on the concern that, in the context of pharmacy benefit management services, entities that receive undisclosed compensation in connection with a covered service provider's contract or arrangement with a covered plan for pharmacy benefit management services may not technically fall within the definition of an “affiliate” or a “subcontractor,” or may take the position that they do not. i.e.

Many commenters supported an approach in the regulation that would result in comprehensive disclosure of compensation associated with pharmacy benefit management services. Some commenters specifically referenced challenges to transparency associated with vertically integrated providers of pharmacy benefit management services.
Regarding the goal of comprehensive disclosures, some commenters said the phrasing of the definitions of “affiliate,” “subcontractor,” and “agent” might have loopholes, particularly with respect to rebate aggregators, GPOs, and similar entities. For example, some commenters said the definition of “affiliate” referenced common control but might not cover entities that have contractual relationships with a provider of pharmacy benefit management services. Some commenters suggested that the Department should specifically identify rebate aggregators, GPOs, and similar entities as entities for which compensation must be reported, regardless of their relationship with the covered service provider. One commenter said that if the Department did not narrow the definitions of these entities, it should provide a safe harbor for affiliates and subcontractors that receive compensation solely in the form of arm's length, market-rate fees for discrete services performed under separate commercial contracts, without discretion to influence formulary placement, plan design, or compensation structures applicable to the covered plan.
After considering comments on these definitions, the Department decided to retain the definitions as proposed, based on the view that they will ensure comprehensive disclosure of compensation received in connection with a covered service provider's contract or arrangement with a covered plan for pharmacy benefit management services, consistent with the goals of this rulemaking and the language of section 408(b)(2)(B), as amended. The Department did not eliminate the definitions of affiliates and subcontractors, or switch to the defined term “applicable entity,” because ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) specifies that affiliates' and subcontractors' services and compensation must be disclosed. The Department additionally agrees with commenters who believed that the term “agent” is needed in the context of a rule requiring disclosure of compensation in connection with a covered service provider's contract or arrangement with a covered plan for pharmacy benefit management services. The term “agent” is needed to ensure that compensation received by rebate aggregators, GPOs, and similar entities would be disclosed, even if such parties may take the position that they are not “affiliates” or “subcontractors.” As one commenter described, these entities act on behalf of providers of pharmacy benefit management services in negotiating, aggregating, and receiving manufacturer remuneration.
With respect to commenters who believed that the final rule might require disclosure of compensation of affiliates who do not have any involvement in the pharmacy benefit management services, the Department points to the regulatory text that provides for disclosure of the various forms of compensation received by the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor “in connection with” the service contract or arrangement. As discussed in greater detail below, the Department intends that “in connection with” will be interpreted broadly to cover compensation that is received based in whole or in part on the service contract or arrangement. If the standard is not satisfied with respect to compensation received by an affiliate, then disclosure is not required.
Some commenters addressed proposed paragraph (c)(2) which stated that “no person or entity is a `covered
(
printed page 69115)
service provider' solely on the basis of providing services as an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor of the covered service provider.” Some commenters supported this provision as providing clarity regarding which party has the obligation to provide the required disclosures. Another commenter asked the Department to delete this provision to ensure that all such parties will provide the required disclosures, noting that it was not clear what recourse covered plans would have if such parties did not provide the required information and data. A few other commenters also expressed concern about whether covered service providers would be able to obtain information from other parties in the pharmaceutical supply chain to supply the required disclosures to the covered plan.
The Department has retained paragraph (c)(2) in the final rule, as proposed, as a matter of consistency with ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) which also places the responsibility for disclosure on the entity with the direct relationship with the covered plan. This structure does not, however, absolve affiliates, agents, and subcontractors from supplying the information required by ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) or this regulation. For the covered service provider to participate in and receive compensation in connection with these contracts and arrangements, these parties must all be prepared to make the required disclosures so that contracts and arrangements with covered plans do not result in prohibited transactions. Responsible plan fiduciaries of covered plans that do not receive required disclosures under the final rule may take advantage of the administrative exemption that involves notifying the Department about covered service providers' failures to meet their disclosure obligations.

145
