In response, the Department notes that ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) does not provide an exemption from the disclosure requirements for small service providers. Also, to the extent that these smaller covered service providers provide services to smaller employers or smaller self-insured group health plans, the Department believes these burdens are alleviated by the more limited scope of the final rule extending the regulatory disclosure requirements only to larger self-insured group health plans.
1.5. Affiliated Providers of Brokerage or Consulting Services—Paragraph (c)(1)(ii)
Paragraph (c)(1)(ii) of the final rule identifies as covered service providers parties described in paragraph (c)(1)(i) or their affiliates that enter a contract or arrangement with a covered plan to provide advice, recommendations, or referrals of pharmacy benefit management services. These covered service providers have the obligation under the final rule to disclose their services and compensation and to allow for an audit, as discussed below. This provision in the final rule is unchanged from the proposal.
The Department's stated purpose in the proposal for including these entities as covered service providers was to address concerns about brokers and consultants receiving payments from parties they are recommending, which may be undisclosed to their covered plan clients. The Department stated that these arrangements have high potential for conflicts of interest that warrant disclosure. The Department further stated that to the extent that PBMs as described in paragraph (c)(1)(i) of the proposal, or their affiliates, also provide “brokerage services” or “consulting” to self-insured group health plans regarding pharmacy benefit management services, the Department had determined that special provisions under the rule would be needed. The Department said that these entities should be included in the definition of covered service providers under the rule to ensure that conflicts associated with the affiliation are disclosed and, further, to allow affiliated brokers and consultants to determine the extent of their obligations under the statutory exemption in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B).
Commenters who addressed inclusion of brokers and consultants as covered service providers suggested that a meaningful approach to disclosures for these parties would involve disclosure of the total net cost of the entire benefit for the upcoming year. Commenters expressed that this would provide a simple data point that would allow responsible plan fiduciaries to easily compare competing service provider bids even across different business models that may, or may not, incorporate rebate guarantees. The Department considered these comments but determined not to add a total net cost type of disclosure to the final rule. These comments and the Department's responses are discussed in section E.3.11.1 of this preamble.
2. Overview of Covered Service Provider Obligations Under This Final Rule
2.1. General
Under this final rule, covered service providers will be required to provide specified disclosures to responsible plan fiduciaries of covered plans and also permit the responsible plan fiduciaries to conduct an audit for accuracy of the disclosures. The disclosures will generally focus on the services provided, the compensation received, and the arrangements with other parties in the pharmaceutical supply chain.
[
146
]
The disclosures will be provided on an initial basis prior to the covered plan entering into the service contract or arrangement, or an extension or renewal, and then on a semiannual basis thereafter (or quarterly, at the plan's request).
With respect to brokers and consultants that are affiliated with providers of pharmacy benefit management services and recommend those services (covered service providers under paragraph (c)(1)(ii)), the required disclosures under the final rule will ensure that the responsible plan fiduciaries that may hire these brokers or consultants for their advice, recommendations, and referrals, are aware of the other sources of compensation that the brokers and consultants may be receiving, also so as to evaluate the potential impact on their services to the plan and the reasonableness of their compensation.
2.2. Breadth of Disclosure Obligation
Throughout the final rule, the disclosure obligation is phrased in terms of compensation “in connection with” the service contract or arrangement. This language largely mirrors the corresponding provisions in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) which require disclosure of direct compensation and indirect compensation reasonably expected to be received “in connection with” the services provided.
[
147
]
The Department intends that the language “in connection with” will be construed broadly and consistently with how the Department construes the language in its service provider disclosure regulation for pension plans (
29 CFR 2550.408b-2(c)(1)
). The Department stated in the preamble to that rule that: “[t]o the extent a covered service provider reasonably expects that
(
printed page 69116)
compensation will be received, which is based in whole or in part on its service contract or arrangement with the covered plan, the compensation will be considered `in connection with' such contract or arrangement.”
[
148
]
Some commenters on the Department's proposal said that a broad and comprehensive disclosure obligation was critical and suggested additional language that they thought would be needed to ensure the intended breadth, such as using “as a result of” instead of “in connection with.” Some commenters suggested a string of words such as “in connection with, as a result of, or in any way connected with, services provided to the plan” to ensure broad disclosure.
The Department has considered these comments but has determined to retain the proposed language “in connection with” to describe the breadth of the disclosure obligation. The Department believes there is value to using language like that of ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) as well as the service provider disclosure regulation for pension plans (
29 CFR 2550.408b-2(c)(1)
). The Department believes the interpretive position stated above, under which compensation will be required to be disclosed if it is (or will be) received, based in whole or in part on its service contract or arrangement with the covered plan, is appropriate to ensure comprehensive disclosure. The Department does not think that “as a result of” or other suggested wording is clearly broader.
Relatedly, in the preamble to the proposal, the Department requested comment on payments from drug manufacturers that may be based on a structure of incentives not solely related to the contract or arrangement with the self-insured group health plan.
[
149
]
The Department sought comment on whether the final rule should specify that such disclosures would be made on a pro-rata basis.
Several commenters said that it is common for providers of pharmacy benefit management services to negotiate rebates and other manufacturer payments on the basis of participants across multiple plan sponsors, so these commenters supported a pro-rata approach as a way for responsible plan fiduciaries to assess the compensation the provider is receiving in connection with a particular covered plan. One commenter said the Department should specify that pro-rata allocation based on an objective and consistently applied metric—such as enrollment share, utilization share, or claims volume—constitutes a compliant disclosure methodology. A few other commenters thought that a pro-rata disclosure might not relate to the actual rebate structure with respect to a particular covered plan and therefore may have limited value as a disclosure to responsible plan fiduciaries. In response, the Department has added text to the final rule in paragraph (e)(3) and paragraph (g)(2) clarifying that indirect compensation includes “compensation based on a structure of incentives not solely related to the contract or arrangement with the covered plan[.]” Thus the Department confirms that such compensation must be disclosed, but has not further specified that it must be disclosed on a pro-rata basis versus another reasonable method.
2.3. Disclosure of Monetary Amounts
Paragraph (k) of the final rule
[
150
]
provides information about the manner of disclosure, including a requirement that disclosures must be “clear and concise, free of misrepresentation, and contain sufficient specificity to permit evaluation of the reasonableness of the service contract or arrangement.” For required descriptions of compensation amounts, paragraph (k) provides that these descriptions must be expressed as a monetary amount and may be estimated to the extent that the actual amount is not reasonably ascertainable but shall contain sufficient information and specificity to permit evaluation of the reasonableness of the compensation received by the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent or a subcontractor.
The Department intends that disclosures of a monetary amount (even if estimated) in this context, furnished with the specificity required under paragraph (k), will further the transparency goals of this rulemaking which are intended to facilitate a responsible plan fiduciary's assessment of reasonableness of compensation and potential for or existence of conflicts of interest in the provision of pharmacy benefit management services. This would also foster a fairer prescription drug market that lowers costs.
Several commenters strongly supported this aspect of the proposal with one commenter taking the position that the disclosure of a monetary amount is the most important provision in the rulemaking. Some commenters said that formulas and percentages can be used by providers of pharmacy benefit management services to obscure compensation received. One commenter said that the Department should specifically provide that compensation estimates should be “grounded in good faith assumptions based on contractually defined methodologies, historical utilization and rebate experience or other information reasonably available at the time of disclosure.” Other commenters supported flexibility to use alternative methodologies and said this is how compensation arrangements are structured. A commenter said there would be no greater need to finalize this more prescriptive standard for PBM disclosures than in other contexts.
The Department agrees with the commenters who said that disclosure of a monetary amount is preferable to a formula or other methodology and has finalized that provision in paragraph (k) as proposed. The Department believes that the responsible plan fiduciaries of the large self-insured group health plans that are covered plans under the final rule will have sufficient resources to analyze the more detailed disclosures of monetary amounts. The Department believes that the commenter's suggested language (that the estimates should be “grounded in good faith assumptions based on contractually defined methodologies, historical utilization and rebate experience or other information reasonably available at the time of disclosure”) provides helpful guidance to covered service providers and has added it to paragraph (k) in the final rule.
2.4. Structure of the Final Rule
The specific elements of the disclosure and audit provisions are discussed in greater detail below. Paragraph (e) of the final rule establishes initial disclosure requirements. Paragraph (f) is reserved for initial disclosure requirements for fully insured group health plans. Paragraph (g) establishes semiannual disclosure obligations. Paragraph (h) is reserved for semiannual disclosure obligations for fully insured group health plans. Paragraph (i) establishes a requirement for the covered service provider to provide certain information upon request of the responsible plan fiduciary of the covered plan. Paragraph (j) establishes the audit rights that must be provided to the covered plan under the service contract or arrangement. Paragraph (k) addresses the manner of disclosure and paragraph (l) addresses
(
printed page 69117)
disclosure errors. Paragraph (m) provides definitions for certain terms used in the regulation.
Overall, the disclosures are intended to provide responsible plan fiduciaries of covered plans with a fuller picture of the terms under which the services will be provided, so they can assess both the reasonableness of the compensation in light of the services being (or to be) provided and the potential for or existence of conflicts of interest that may impact the quality of services provided. The Department believes that these disclosures will provide necessary information to responsible plan fiduciaries of these larger self-insured group health plans who are required to determine that the services contract or arrangement meets the standards for an exemption under ERISA section 408(b)(2).
3. Initial Disclosure Requirements—Paragraph (e)
Paragraph (e) of the final rule
[
151
]
sets forth the initial disclosure requirements. Covered service providers of pharmacy benefit management services are required under the final rule to produce these disclosures to the responsible plan fiduciary, in writing, no later than the date that is reasonably in advance of the date on which the contract or arrangement is entered, extended, or renewed. For extensions and renewals, 90 calendar days is deemed “reasonably in advance,” absent an agreement between the covered service provider and the plan to a longer timeframe.
The final rule, in some instances, requires disclosure of amounts reasonably expected to be paid to the covered service provider or an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor. As noted above, paragraph (k) requires descriptions of compensation to be expressed as a monetary amount—for example, $1,000. The amounts can be provided as an estimate, to the extent that the actual amount is not reasonably ascertainable; but in any event, the disclosures must contain sufficient information and specificity to permit evaluation of the reasonableness of the compensation to be received by the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor. Estimates shall be grounded in good faith assumptions based on contractually defined methodologies, historical utilization and rebate experience, or other information reasonably available at the time of disclosure.
3.1. Time Period for Initial Disclosure, Extensions and Renewals
The Department proposed that a reasonable period of time for responsible plan fiduciaries to receive the initial disclosure in the context of extensions and renewals of the contract or arrangement would be 30 days. This timeframe was intended to align with to other disclosure requirements in the Title XXVII of the Public Health Service (PHS) Act, Chapter 100 of the Internal Revenue Code, and Part 7 of ERISA that require 30-day timelines for disclosures, including the summary of benefits and coverage (SBC) requirements under PHS Act section 2715, as added by the Affordable Care Act and incorporated into ERISA section 715 and Code section 9815, for renewals, reissuances and reenrollments.
[
152
]
Aligning the timing requirements with other disclosures that group health plans and issuers already provide was intended to minimize compliance burdens by streamlining the collection of similar data and disclosure for multiple purposes during the same cadence. The Department sought comment on the proposed timing requirements for the initial disclosure including whether additional specificity would be needed for the timing of the disclosure outside of the context of contract extensions and renewals.
While one commenter supported the proposed 30-day time frame, a few other commenters said that plan fiduciaries would need disclosure at an earlier date to inform initial contract negotiations. Commenters offered different suggested longer time frames, including 60 or 90 days in advance of the date of contract, extension or renewal; 60 days from request of the responsible plan fiduciary; or, for extensions and renewals, sufficiently in advance of the earliest contractual deadline by which the plan fiduciary must act to avoid automatic renewal. A few commenters suggested timeframes that would allow disclosures after execution of the contract, while others emphasized that the disclosures must be prospective to assist responsible plan fiduciaries in assessing the reasonableness of the contract or arrangement.
The final rule provides that 90 days in advance of the extension or renewal is reasonable, to ensure that plan fiduciaries have sufficient time to review the disclosures as part of the contracting process. The Department agrees with the commenters who said that initial disclosures should be provided in advance of the contract to be useful to responsible plan fiduciaries. The Department selected a specific number of days (
i.e.,
90 days) prior to the extension or renewal because it has an advantage of simplicity over some of the other commenters' suggestions and would allow time for plan fiduciaries to solicit competing bids and evaluate information in the disclosures to prudently select a service provider. Under the final rule, parties remain free to negotiate for a longer period.
The Department did not propose any specific time frame for what would be deemed reasonable in the context of new contracts or arrangements. Although some commenters suggested some specific time frames, as noted above, the Department does not believe it is necessary to establish a default timeframe as that timing can be more easily managed by the responsible plan fiduciary who is considering entering into a contract or arrangement with a new covered service provider.
3.2. Description of Services
Under paragraph (e)(1), the initial disclosure must include a description of each pharmacy benefit management service, or of the advice, recommendations, or referrals regarding the provision of pharmacy benefit management services to be provided to the covered plan pursuant to the contract or arrangement. This provision mirrors the provision in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B)(iii)(I).
[
153
]
Full disclosure of the services is essential so that the responsible plan fiduciary can satisfy its duties under ERISA at the outset of the contract or arrangement and its ongoing duty to monitor. Full disclosure helps ensure that both parties have a common understanding of the services to be performed as part of the contract or arrangement. Absent full disclosure of services, questions may arise as to whether a responsible plan fiduciary has effectively approved otherwise discretionary behavior by the covered service provider.
Full disclosures are also important for covered service providers. Depending on the pharmacy benefit services being provided, if they are not performed in accordance with parameters established under the contract or arrangement with the covered plan, the provider may have assumed discretionary authority or control over the administration of the
(
printed page 69118)
covered plan. Providers who exercise such discretionary authority or control fall within the definition of a fiduciary under ERISA section 3(21)(A) and are subject to ERISA's fiduciary duties in section 403 and 404, and the prohibited transaction provisions in ERISA section 406. Therefore, it is crucial that disclosures be complete and accurate and carefully written in a manner that conforms with the plain language requirements in paragraph (k) of the final rule. When disclosures meet these standards, both parties to the contract or arrangement are more likely to have a common understanding of their roles and limitations under the contract or arrangement and the law.
Relatively few commenters addressed the general requirement in the proposal to provide a description of services to be provided to the covered plan pursuant to the contract or arrangement. One commenter asked the Department to add specificity regarding the level of detail required, after further stakeholder input. Another commenter suggested that the description should have increased granularity to specify which entity (
i.e.,
the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor) will be providing the services and the compensation to be received by service. The Department believes that the requirement in the final rule is clear and straightforward, and it determined not to increase complexity by adding further requirements specifying the level of detail to be provided or requiring the disclosures to identify which entity will be providing the services. Therefore, the Department is finalizing the description of services disclosure as proposed.
Some commenters identified certain policies and practices that may be implemented and administered by providers of pharmacy benefit management services that the commenters believed should be disclosed under the final rule. Examples include utilization management; cost sharing policies; and use of copay accumulators, copay maximizers or alternative funding programs. The Department views these as examples of services that are offered by providers of pharmacy benefit managers and agrees that initial disclosure under the final rule of the services to be provided would include disclosure of these types of services that will be implemented and administered by covered service providers with respect to a covered plan.
3.3. Direct Compensation
Under paragraph (e)(2), the initial disclosure must include a description of direct compensation the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor reasonably expects to receive in connection with the pharmacy benefit management services under the contract or arrangement. Specifically, the final rule requires a description of the amount of all direct compensation, both in the aggregate and by service, that the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor reasonably expects to receive on a semiannual (or quarterly, upon the covered plan's request) basis in connection with pharmacy benefit management services under the contract or arrangement. An example is an administrative fee calculated on a per-participant, per-month basis. ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B)(iii)(III) likewise provides for a description of direct compensation reasonably expected to be received by the covered service provider, an affiliate, or a subcontractor.
[
154
]
For purposes of paragraph (e)(2) of the final rule, the term “direct compensation” means compensation received directly from the covered plan or from the plan sponsor on behalf of the covered plan regardless of whether such compensation is paid from plan assets. It is important to ensure that all direct compensation is disclosed, regardless of the source of the payment, to avoid frustrating the purposes of this final rule because service providers to covered plans sometimes are paid, in whole or in part, directly from the general assets of the employer sponsoring the covered plan as opposed to a plan asset trust. Consequently, responsible plan fiduciaries may find it challenging to assess the overall reasonableness of the covered service provider's compensation if this source of revenue is excluded from disclosure.
The Department revised paragraph (e)(2) of the final rule so that the reporting period is semiannual or, at the request of the covered plan, quarterly. This change was made in other paragraphs throughout the final rule to align with the reporting period in ERISA section 726.
3.3.1. Bundled Services Arrangements
In the proposal, the Department requested comments as to whether the requirements under the proposed rule for disclosure of direct compensation as defined in paragraph (e)(2) would ensure sufficient disclosure of information for bundled services, or whether the description of direct compensation under paragraph (e)(2) for a bundled services option should include additional information, such as the bundled discounted value along with a description of services provided in the bundle.
A number of commenters said the Department should require covered service providers to unbundle and disclose compensation attributable to each discrete service, rather than permitting a single aggregate figure. Some commenters provided examples of scenarios that they believed necessitated unbundling. For example, one commenter asserted that bundled service arrangements may be used to obscure the cost of the services and that unbundling is especially important to uncover potential preferential pricing to affiliates. Another commenter believed that it is important for plan fiduciaries to understand the portion of a bundled service fee attributable to administrative fees to ensure that the plan is not paying twice for the same administrative service.
Other commenters were less sure that unbundling would be helpful or appropriate. One commenter stated that pharmacy benefit services are commonly offered on a full-service basis and requiring unbundling would be hypothetical and could mislead plan fiduciaries. A different commenter supported permitting covered service providers to disclose an aggregate figure with respect to direct compensation on the basis that the commenter believed this is the approach permitted by ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B).
Upon consideration of these comments, the Department determined to add a provision in paragraph (e)(2) of the final rule stating that bundled services or aggregated compensation arrangements must include a reasonable and good faith allocation of the compensation associated with each service in the bundle. This is consistent with the overarching standard in paragraph (e)(2) which provides that the disclosure must include a description of the amount of all direct compensation “both in the aggregate and by service” that the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor reasonably expects to receive. This standard is more specific than the statutory provision in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) but in the Department's view it is appropriate for the large self-insured group health plans that are covered plans under the final rule to receive more detailed information. The
(
printed page 69119)
Department also believes it is appropriate for covered service providers to make a reasonable and good faith allocation of the compensation associated with each of the services, despite the fact that these services may commonly be offered on a full-service basis. The Department does not share the commenter's concern about the potential for misleading plan fiduciaries; rather, unbundling may benefit group health plans by giving them the opportunity to consider a competitive bidding approach for each service, allowing them to design a plan that meets their unique needs to deliver costs savings and efficiencies. Allowing bundled services or aggregated compensation arrangements without specificity about the compensation associated with each service in the bundle, on the other hand, risks creating an unwarranted loophole for certain arrangements.
3.4. Indirect Compensation
The final rule includes a new paragraph (e)(3) entitled “Indirect Compensation” under which there are four subparagraphs listing disclosure obligations as follows: (i) payments from drug manufacturers, (ii) spread compensation, (iii) pharmacy recoupment, and (iv) price protection agreements. Subparagraphs (i)-(iv) correspond to proposed paragraphs (e)(3)-(6). These subparagraphs are discussed in the next sections of the preamble. Disclosure of indirect compensation is required under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B)(iii)(IV), which provides that disclosures must include a description of indirect compensation reasonably expected to be received by the covered service provider, an affiliate, or a subcontractor in connection with the services disclosed under the statute, as well as a description of the arrangement pursuant to which the indirect compensation is paid, the services for which the indirect compensation will be received, and an identification of the payer of the indirect compensation.
[
155
]
The Department introduced the paragraph heading “Indirect Compensation” in the final rule for consistency with ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B)—which distinguishes direct versus indirect compensation—and also in response to comments that asked for clarification of the distinction between the two.
Paragraph (e)(2) of the final rule includes a definition of “direct compensation” which is compensation received directly from a covered plan or from the plan sponsor on behalf of the plan (regardless of whether such compensation is paid from plan assets). The disclosures identified in paragraph (e)(3) of the final rule would be considered indirect compensation. Paragraph (e)(3) also makes clear that indirect compensation includes amounts based on a structure of incentives not solely related to the contract or arrangement with the covered plan.
[
156
]
As discussed above, this language is intended to ensure disclosure of rebates and other payments that may be based on a number of participants across multiple plan sponsors.
3.5. Payments From Drug Manufacturers
Under subparagraph (e)(3)(i), the initial disclosure must include a description of the monetary amount of any rebate, fee, alternative discount or other remuneration reasonably expected to be received from any drug manufacturer, distributor, wholesaler, or rebate aggregator (or other purchasing entity designed to aggregate rebates) by the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor, in the aggregate and for each drug on the formulary, in connection with the contract or arrangement with the covered plan. The disclosure must cover each semiannual period (or quarter) under the contract or arrangement and must disclose both amounts reasonably expected for claims incurred during the period and amounts reasonably expected that are related to utilization of such drug spending. For example, this disclosure will include any amounts the covered service provider reasonably expects to receive based on achieving utilization thresholds like volume-based rebates. The disclosure must specify both the amount that is reasonably expected to be passed on to the covered plan and, if applicable, the plan sponsor, and the amount that will be retained by the covered service provider, affiliate(s), agent(s), or subcontractor(s).
Under subparagraph (e)(3)(iv), the initial disclosure also must also include a description of any inflation protection or price protection agreements that the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor has entered with any drug manufacturer, distributor, wholesaler, or rebate aggregator (or other purchasing entity designed to aggregate rebates), regarding prescription drugs dispensed under the service contract or arrangement with the covered plan. The disclosure must specify the amount reasonably expected to be retained by the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor in connection with each prescription drug product and under each such contract or arrangement and the price protection amount that will be passed on to the covered plan and, if applicable, plan sponsor, for each semiannual period (or quarter). The disclosure must cover amounts reasonably expected to be received for claims reasonably expected to be incurred during the period and amounts reasonably expected to be received related to utilization of such drug or spending on such drug. The Department separated the disclosure required under subparagraph (e)(3)(iv) from the disclosure required under subparagraph (e)(3)(i) because of the contingent nature of inflation and price protection.
The disclosure required by these provisions would be intended to cover any and all payments reasonably expected to be received from drug manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers, or rebate aggregators (or other purchasing entities designed to aggregate rebates), by the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor in connection with their services to the covered plan, regardless of how they are characterized. The term “agent” is intended to capture rebate aggregators and GPOs, to the extent they may take the position that they do not fall within the definition of affiliate or subcontractor, so that reasonably expected payments to those entities in connection with the services contract or
(
printed page 69120)
arrangement would be part of the initial disclosures.
In the proposal, the disclosure obligation was phrased in terms of “payments” from drug manufacturers and aggregators. The Department sought comments on whether the provisions in proposed paragraph (e)(3) and proposed paragraph (e)(6) adequately described the type of payments that may be received in this respect. The Department also sought comment on whether the broad term “payments” would be sufficient to define the disclosure obligation or whether more specificity would be needed to ensure full disclosure.
Many commenters responded to the proposed requirement for disclosure of payments from drug manufacturers and aggregators to a covered service provider. Commenters expressed both support and concern as to the forms of compensation to be disclosed as a manufacturer payment, the granularity of information reported, and the interaction of the disclosures with other requirements introduced by the CAA, 2026.
Several commenters said the Department should adopt the proposed disclosure of manufacturer payments in both the aggregate and for each drug on the formulary, with some commenters suggesting that additional granularity in disclosures would be necessary. These commenters generally encouraged the Department to broadly construe the types of compensation to be disclosed under this provision to ensure the disclosure would cover all manner of compensation paid by drug manufacturers. While many commenters supported use of broad and general language to describe the disclosure obligation, some also suggested either exemplary or enumerated breakouts delineating information into categories of compensation such as the common types of payments (
e.g.,
administrative fees, data fees, and access fees), discounts, and other compensation structures, to avoid the possibility that the disclosure requirements could be evaded through reclassification of manufacturer payments as various types of fees or alternative forms of compensation not explicitly in connection with the service contract or arrangement. A few commenters emphasized the need to ensure that disclosure obligation included amounts retained by GPOs, which the Department confirmed in an earlier preamble paragraph describing the disclosure obligation.
Several commenters suggested that additional disclosure elements be added. A few commenters suggested that disclosure include information about the manufacturer's net price, which would assist fiduciaries in evaluating the components of drug costs including remuneration to providers of pharmacy benefit management services. One commenter recommended that the final rule should require disclosure of information related to the specific manufacturer rebate contract the covered service provider would apply to claims for drugs submitted to a plan and the amount of rebates, on a per-National Drug Code basis, applicable to such rebate contract. Another commenter said that the final rule should require disclosure of manufacturer payments to break out the amounts retained and passed through at the level of each entity in the supply chain; require disclosure of the ownership, governance, and compensation structure of all entities involved in negotiations for manufacturer rebates or price concessions; and break out manufacturer payments made to the covered service provider and its affiliated entities separately.
The Department has finalized the provisions regarding disclosure of payments from drug manufacturers in subparagraphs (e)(3)(i) and (e)(3)(iv) with modifications. In the final rule, the requirement to disclose manufacturer payments in subparagraph (e)(3)(i) is phrased in terms of rebates, fees, alternative discounts or other remuneration. Further, both subparagraph (e)(3)(i) and (e)(3)(iv) refer to payments from drug manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers, or rebate aggregators (or other purchasing entities designed to aggregate rebates). These changes provide additional specificity as to the type of payments and the types of payors that would result in the required disclosures. This terminology also aligns with terminology in ERISA sections 408(b)(2)(C) and 726.
[
157
]
Additionally, the reporting period is a semiannual period or, at the request of the plan, a quarter, which aligns with the reporting period in ERISA section 726(b).
[
158
]
The Department did not identify any additional specific payment types in the regulatory text as requested by some commenters (
e.g.,
administrative fees, data fees, and access fees) based on the view that “other remuneration” is a broad term that would encompass all such payments and that it was desirable to use the same terms as ERISA sections 408(b)(2)(C) and 726. The Department also did not add a requirement to disclose the specific rebate contract associated with the payments as one commenter suggested. Such contracts would be available as part of an audit, which the Department believes strikes the correct balance in terms of the burden of the disclosure requirements.
[
159
]
Some commenters said that an initial disclosure of manufacturer payments reasonably expected on a per-drug basis, as had been proposed, would be speculative and thus of limited use to responsible plan fiduciaries assessing the reasonableness of compensation for a contract or arrangement under ERISA section 408(b)(2). The commenters also said this approach was burdensome and generally misaligned with the comparable provisions regarding payments from drug manufacturers introduced by the CAA, 2026, which were only on a retrospective basis, and risked exposing sensitive information to be used for anti-competitive purposes. Some commenters said the Department should permit the disclosure in the aggregate, or by therapeutic category or formulary tier, rather than at the per-drug level using the requirements set forth in that section. A few commenters said that the new subparagraph (C) of ERISA section 408(b)(2), as added by the CAA, 2026 amendments, will require full rebate pass-through to group health plans and thereby will address concerns about a potential misalignment of incentives between covered service providers and group health plans related to manufacturer payments. Commenters said this obviated the necessity for the granular disclosure of
(
printed page 69121)
such payments under the Department's rule.
The Department did not eliminate the initial disclosure of manufacturer payments altogether or revise the rule to permit an aggregate initial disclosure based on therapeutic category or formulary tier, as some commenters suggested. The fact that ERISA section 726 is limited to a retrospective disclosure does not indicate that the Department's final rule should have a similar scope. Rather, the Department believes that the prospective disclosures are consistent with ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) because they serve a distinct purpose in assisting responsible plan fiduciaries in assessing the reasonableness of the contract or arrangement and the compensation of the covered service provider and its affiliates, agents, and subcontractors at the time of contracting and in monitoring these contracts or arrangements thereafter. This disclosure of manufacturer payments for each drug on the formulary is important to assess the compensation to providers of pharmacy benefit management services and their affiliates, agents and subcontractors for each such drug.
[
160
]
An aggregate disclosure, on the other hand, might permit a covered service provider to obscure the covered service provider's financial incentives to select a particular prescription drug for the formulary.
It is important to note that in the final rule, these detailed disclosures are required only for covered plans, which are generally the larger self-insured group health plans (
i.e.,
the plans of specified large employers and the specified large plans) but also do not include group health plans established by a plan sponsor that is, or that is affiliated with, a drug manufacturer, distributor, wholesaler, rebate aggregator (or other purchasing entity designed to aggregate rebates). As discussed elsewhere, the Department has mirrored the approach Congress took in the CAA, 2026 amendments regarding which responsible plan fiduciaries should receive the detailed disclosures. The more limited scope of the final rule should mitigate some concerns regarding the administrative burden to covered service providers of providing information on manufacturer payments and to responsible plan fiduciaries of reviewing such information as well as concerns about anti-competitive behavior.
To assist covered service providers that will need to make the detailed initial disclosures under subparagraphs (e)(3)(i) and (iv), the Department also added a new sentence to paragraph (k)(2) providing guidance on the methodology of developing the estimate, as suggested by a commenter. That sentence provides that “estimates shall be grounded in good faith assumptions based on contractually defined methodologies, historical utilization and rebate experience, or other information reasonably available at the time of disclosure.” The final rule also includes confidentiality provisions that are designed to address concerns about redisclosure of rebate information and use of such information for purposes unrelated to the covered plan's contract or arrangement, as discussed in section E.8 and E.9 of this preamble.
A few commenters directly addressed disclosure of price-protection agreements, with one commenter in favor of the disclosure as a measure of informing fiduciaries about how these agreements may influence behavior of providers of pharmacy benefit management services regarding higher list prices even when net price is offset by rebates. A few other commenters said the CAA, 2026 amendments did not require disclosure of these agreements, indicating Congress' view that disclosure would not be necessary for responsible plan fiduciaries in their review and evaluation of pharmacy benefit manager services arrangements. The Department believes that disclosure of these agreements is likely to provide insight regarding drug pricing-related incentives to responsible plan fiduciaries of the larger self-insured group health plans and is necessary to assess the reasonableness of compensation under the contract or arrangement required under the statutory exemption contained in ERISA section 408(b)(2). Therefore, the Department has retained this requirement in the final rule. The Department is also of the view that the disclosure of these agreements will help responsible plan fiduciaries analyze the full impact on participant costs and promote the use of lower cost alternatives.
Finally, the Department acknowledges that when the rebate pass-through provision in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(C) becomes effective, there likely will be increased transparency into rebate arrangements and other payments from drug manufacturers, and possibly reduced reliance on them. The Department does not see that potential development as a reason to eliminate the disclosure altogether. The Department believes it is still important to require transparency regarding how the payments are being handled for responsible plan fiduciaries to satisfy their fiduciary duties and the reasonableness assessment required under the statutory exemption. In this regard, the Department notes that ERISA section 408(b)(2)(C) will require the rebates, fees, alternative discounts, and other remuneration not only to be passed through to the covered plans but also to be fully disclosed to such plans.
[
161
]
The Department anticipates that requiring those disclosures in this regulation will make the transition to that disclosure process smoother, once those provisions (under section 408(b)(2)(C)) become fully effective, and envisions that it will leverage such disclosures in any future rulemaking or guidance implementing section 408(b)(2)(C) to minimize duplicative regulatory requirements.
3.6. Spread Compensation
Subparagraph (e)(3)(ii) of the final rule includes several disclosure requirements related to spread compensation. Under this subparagraph, the initial disclosure must include a list of drugs on the formulary, and for each drug: the contracted compensation to be paid by the covered plan for the drug to the covered service provider or an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor; the contracted compensation to be paid to the pharmacy by the covered service provider, or an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor, on behalf of the group health plan; and the difference between the two. This difference is defined in the final rule as spread compensation. Subparagraph (e)(3)(ii) further requires a description of the amount of spread compensation reasonably expected to be received by the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent and a subcontractor in connection with the service contract or arrangement, for claims filed during each semiannual period (or quarter), both in the aggregate and for each drug on the formulary, and for each pharmacy channel (
i.e.,
retail pharmacy, mail order pharmacy, and specialty pharmacy) available under the contract or arrangement. The subparagraph additionally requires the disclosure to include a description of arrangements, incentives, contractual provisions, and policies that will be implemented under the service contract or arrangement that direct patients to pharmacies that are affiliates of the covered service provider.

The Department sought comments on the requirements under the proposed rule for disclosure of spread compensation, including whether the provision required disclosure of information sufficient to assess reasonableness and what challenges would arise from a covered service provider providing, or a responsible plan fiduciary reviewing, this level of disclosure. The Department also sought comments on whether arrangements with retail, mail order, and specialty pharmacies are sufficiently similar to one another so that dividing disclosures into these three channels is efficient, and whether greater transparency would incentivize the use of a pass-through pricing or a flat-fee compensation model.
Many commenters said the spread pricing disclosure provisions should be adopted in the final rule as a means of improving transparency into this historically opaque PBM revenue stream. Commenters expressed the view that the availability of such information would allow plan fiduciaries to better assess compensation arrangements consistent with their obligations under ERISA. A few commenters believed that transparency into spread compensation would incentivize the adoption of pass-through pricing and flat fee models with one commenter suggesting the Department should consider exempting or requiring reduced disclosure for providers using those models. One commenter observed that incorporating drug-level spread disclosure in the final rule could be consistent with and complementary to the requirement in ERISA section 726, enabling fiduciaries to perform both prospective review and retrospective verification of such amounts. Another commenter observed that spread compensation may not be addressed by the rebate-pass through provision in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(C), so disclosure will be important to understand this revenue stream that will continue to exist after the rebate-pass through provision takes effect.
Several commenters agreed with the Department's designation of three pharmacy channels—retail, mail order and specialty—in the proposal for spread pricing disclosure. However, some commenters believed it would also be important to break out PBM-affiliated versus non-affiliated pharmacies within these channels. Commenters said this would allow responsible plan fiduciaries to identify incentives in these arrangements and assess their impact on plan costs. Several commenters said the Department should require disclosure of arrangements, incentives, and contractual provisions that may direct patients to affiliated pharmacies or higher-spread channels. Another commenter said that the Department should also break out disclosure of spread by drug category (generic, brand, and specialty).
Other commenters said that the Department's proposal to require disclosure with respect to spread compensation reasonably expected for all formulary drugs across each pharmacy channel would impose extreme administrative burden upon covered service providers. Commenters said responsible plan fiduciaries would be overwhelmed with the expanse of data, could not meaningfully process such information to evaluate the overall reasonableness of the arrangement, and could face increased litigation risk based on having received such detailed information. Several commenters said they would support disclosure of aggregate amounts of spread compensation by pharmacy channel. Commenters also suggested that the Department permit disclosure of spread compensation as a percentage of drug spend rather than a dollar amount.
Commenters also made recommendations that they said would better align the final rule with the CAA, 2026 amendments. A few said the Department should not require any initial disclosure of spread pricing on the basis that initial disclosures are not part of the CAA, 2026 statutory framework. One commenter said if the Department proceeded with this element of the initial disclosure, it should clarify methodologies for initial estimations and provide specific guidance to clarify “reasonably expected.”
In the final rule, the Department has revised the disclosure of spread compensation to align with the structure and phrasing of the similar requirement in ERISA section 726(b)(2)(A)(i)(I)-(III).

Thus subparagraph (e)(3)(ii)(A) requires a list of drugs on the formulary; the contracted compensation to be paid by the covered plan to the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor for each drug (identified by National Drug Code); the contracted compensation to be paid to the pharmacy by the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor for each such drug (identified by National Drug Code); and the difference between the two. To align with ERISA section 726, the Department also revised the reporting period so that it is a semiannual period (or at the request of the plan, a quarter).
Although the final rule requires disclosure of spread by pharmacy channel (retail, mail order, and specialty), the Department did not differentiate PBM-affiliated pharmacies versus non-affiliated pharmacies for purposes of the spread compensation disclosure provisions in the final rule because the Department was not convinced that this additional disclosure regarding spread compensation would be the easiest way for responsible plan fiduciaries to evaluate the potential for steering or pricing variations involving affiliated pharmacies. Rather, the Department believes that a more direct, narrative disclosure as suggested by some commenters may assist responsible plan fiduciaries; so for that reason, subparagraph (e)(3)(ii)(C) was added to the final rule requiring disclosure of arrangements, incentives, contractual provisions and policies that will be implemented under the service contract or arrangement that direct patients to pharmacies that are affiliates of the covered service provider. Additionally, as discussed below in section E.3.9 of this preamble, compensation reasonably expected to be received by pharmacies that are affiliated with a covered service provider when a covered plan's participants fill prescriptions at that pharmacy would be disclosed to the covered plan's responsible plan fiduciary as part of the category of “other” compensation. The Department did not require the disclosure to be categorized by drug category (generic, brand, and specialty) because that did not appear to be necessary in light of the disclosure at the individual drug level.
To address anticipated burdens in preparing the disclosures, some commenters requested limiting the disclosure obligation in the final rule to aggregate amounts of spread compensation by pharmacy channel. Other commenters suggested allowing disclosure of spread compensation as a percentage of drug spend rather than a dollar amount. The Department did not make these revisions because the

Department believes that concerns about administrative burden and utility to responsible plan fiduciaries are alleviated by the more limited scope of the final rule to the larger self-insured group health plans.
The Department also did not eliminate the initial disclosure regarding spread pricing altogether. Even though ERISA section 726 does not include initial disclosures, the Department determined that an initial disclosure of this important compensation stream was consistent with ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) and needed for responsible plan fiduciaries of covered plans evaluating the services contract or arrangement at the time of contracting. The Department included guidance on methodology in paragraph (k)(2) of the final rule which provides that “estimates shall be grounded in good faith assumptions based on contractually defined methodologies, historical utilization and rebate experience or other information reasonably available at the time of disclosure.”
The Department did not expressly exempt covered service providers using pass-through pricing and flat fee models as suggested by one commenter, but notes that covered service providers who do not reasonably expect to receive spread compensation would have no disclosure under this subparagraph of the final rule. PBM compensation models can change over time and be referred to by different names. By not providing a categorical exemption for certain models, the Department ensures that covered service providers provide disclosure under paragraph (e)(3)(ii) if they reasonably expect to receive such compensation.
3.7. Pharmacy Recoupment
Under subparagraph (e)(3)(iii) of the final rule, the initial disclosure must include a description of amounts of copay claw-back compensation and other retroactive adjustment to pharmacy reimbursement reasonably expected to be recouped from a pharmacy by a covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor in connection with prescription drugs dispensed under the contract or arrangement, for each semiannual period (or quarter). The final rule defines a copay claw-back as the dollar amount of the difference between a copayment or coinsurance amount paid to the pharmacy by a plan participant or beneficiary and the reimbursement to the pharmacy. Under subparagraphs (e)(3)(iii) and (k)(2), the disclosure must be expressed as a monetary amount per semiannual period (or quarter) and must specify the anticipated total number of transactions.
Where a covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor claws back any portion of a payment to a pharmacy made at point-of-sale and does not pass along the full amount recouped to the covered plan, information as to the value of any such amount recouped may not be otherwise available to a responsible plan fiduciary assessing the reasonableness of compensation under the contract or arrangement. For example, where the pharmacy's reimbursement price for dispensing a drug is less than the copayment made to the dispensing pharmacy by a participant or beneficiary and the covered plan's cost share for the drug is zero dollars, the responsible plan fiduciary may be unaware of the difference between the cost of the drug and the copayment that results in compensation to the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor recouping such difference. The Department believes that additional disclosure of the total number of transactions reasonably expected to occur in the reporting period would provide the responsible plan fiduciary key information needed to assess the pervasiveness of this practice and whether adjustments to the plan's cost sharing structure may be appropriate.
The Department sought comments on this disclosure element in the proposed rule, including whether the proposed provision's scope of required disclosure of information for copay claw-back payments would be sufficient to assess reasonableness and whether other types of recouped payments should be included. If commenters believed the final rule should require disclosure of information for recouped payments other than copay claw-backs, the Department asked the commenters to describe the type(s) of recouped payments recommended to be included and how disclosure of this information is necessary to assess the reasonableness of the compensation under the contract or arrangement.
A number of commenters said the initial disclosure of copay claw-backs would be an important compensation element for responsible plan fiduciaries to be aware of in connection with their assessment of a contract or arrangement. Several commenters asked the Department to take additional steps in the final rule related to recoupment of compensation from pharmacies—either to require disclosure of all types of retroactive payments imposed by pharmacy benefit management service providers on pharmacies or to outright prohibit such retroactive payments under ERISA. Commenters also asked the Department to expand the disclosure to cover additional types of recoupment mechanisms that generate compensation. Several commenters mentioned effective rate reconciliation, which they described as a practice whereby PBMs periodically adjust pharmacy reimbursement to match an “aggregate effective rate,” clawing back amounts previously paid. Commenters asking the Department to prohibit these payments pointed to the negative impact on plan participants and pharmacies. One commenter said the disclosure of copay claw-backs should be broken out by affiliated and non-affiliated pharmacies.
Other commenters said the proposed disclosure of copay claw-backs should not be adopted in the final rule because this type of compensation was not included in the disclosures outlined by Congress in the CAA, 2026 amendments. One such commenter said this was not a common feature of group health plan contracts or arrangements, so the Department should allow covered service providers to provide a simple negative response to that required disclosure category.
The Department believes that compensation recouped from pharmacies should be disclosed to responsible plan fiduciaries of covered plans for purposes of assessing the reasonableness of a contract or arrangement to provide pharmacy benefit management services. The Department was persuaded by commenters that, to ensure comprehensive disclosure, the requirement should be expanded to include any other retroactive adjustment to pharmacy reimbursement reasonably expected to be recouped from a pharmacy in connection with prescription drugs dispensed under the service contract or arrangement. In response to the commenter who believed this to be uncommon, the Department confirms that a covered service provider who does not reasonably expect to receive this type of compensation would not make a disclosure under this subparagraph of the final rule.
The Department did not revise the requirement in the final rule to require a breakdown of pharmacy recoupments from affiliated versus nonaffiliated pharmacies. The Department has determined to address the issues associated with PBM-affiliated pharmacies in subparagraph (e)(3)(ii)(C) which requires a description of arrangements, incentives, contractual provisions and policies that will be
(
printed page 69124)
implemented under the service contract or arrangement that direct patients to pharmacies that are affiliates of the covered service provider.
The Department did not eliminate this disclosure element of the rule even though the CAA, 2026 amendments do not include specific disclosures regarding recoupment of compensation from pharmacies. The Department believes that such disclosures are appropriate under ERISA section 408(b)(2) because they will assist responsible plan fiduciaries in assessing the reasonableness of the contract or arrangement and the compensation of the covered service provider and its affiliates, agents, and subcontractors at the time of contracting and in monitoring these contracts or arrangements thereafter. Moreover, comprehensive disclosure is consistent with ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), which requires disclosure of “all direct compensation” and “all indirect compensation” reasonably expected to be received by covered service providers, affiliates, and subcontractors.
3.8. Compensation for Termination of Contract or Arrangement
Under paragraph (e)(4) of the final rule, the initial disclosure must include a description of any compensation that the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor reasonably expects to receive in connection with termination of the contract or arrangement, and how any prepaid amounts will be calculated and refunded upon such termination. The provision on termination of compensation mirrors ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B)(iii)(VI).
[
163
]
In the Department's view, a determination of reasonableness necessitates that a responsible plan fiduciary be aware upfront of any termination costs or potential costs to a covered plan. Without this information, a responsible plan fiduciary cannot sufficiently evaluate the economic consequences of such termination to the covered plan. Paragraph (e)(4) will, for example, enable the responsible plan fiduciary to understand and ensure proper treatment of any rebates owed at the time of the termination. While covered service providers may recoup reasonable amounts for actual losses upon early termination of the contract or arrangement, no contract or arrangement is reasonable if it does not permit termination by the covered plan without penalty on reasonably short notice under the circumstances to prevent the covered plan from becoming locked into a contract or arrangement that has become disadvantageous.

Commenters on the Department's proposal generally did not address termination fees in any detail but several expressed the view that the comprehensive approach to disclosure in the proposal—including the termination fees—would assist responsible plan fiduciaries in fulfilling their statutory obligations. One commenter said visibility into costs of termination are needed for fiduciaries to understand the financial implications of ending the arrangement. Another commenter asked the Department to expand the disclosure to specify certain elements would be covered such as different impacts for different types of terminations, whether the compensation is direct or indirect, and the details of what entity is paying the compensation, what entity is receiving it, and how the compensation relates to the covered plan's arrangement. A few commenters on the other hand said the Department should not include this disclosure in the final rule because it is not a compensation element specified for disclosure in ERISA section 726, with one commenter expressing concern that this provision would invite regulatory scrutiny of lawful contractual provisions negotiated at arm's-length.
The Department agrees with commenters who said that disclosure of compensation reasonably expected in connection with termination of the contract or arrangement is a necessary component of comprehensive disclosure for responsible plan fiduciaries of covered plans determining the reasonableness of the contract or arrangement. Further, this disclosure element is consistent with ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), so the Department believes that including it in the final rule will not materially increase the likelihood regulatory scrutiny of these contractual provisions. As stated elsewhere, the Department believes that ERISA section 408(b)(2) assists responsible plan fiduciaries in assessing the reasonableness of the contract or arrangement and the compensation of the covered service provider and its affiliates, agents, and subcontractors at the time of contracting and in monitoring these contracts or arrangements thereafter. On the other hand, the Department is not persuaded that there is value commensurate to the burden associated with adding additional specific elements to the disclosure of termination compensation, such as whether the compensation is direct or indirect, and the details of what entity is paying the compensation, what entity is receiving it, and how the compensation relates to the covered plan's arrangement, as suggested by one commenter. For these reasons, the Department has adopted this disclosure in the final rule as proposed.
3.9. Other Compensation
Paragraph (e)(5) provides a catch-all provision for any compensation not disclosed under paragraphs (e)(1)-(4). The disclosure must include a description of any such compensation that the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor reasonably expects to receive in connection with the contract or arrangement for the semiannual period (or quarter), regardless of whether such compensation is paid regularly or irregularly or from plan assets or is subject to any contingency or other condition. The disclosure must also include an identification of the payer of such compensation, an identification of the services for which such compensation will be received, and a description of the arrangement between the payer and the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor, as applicable, pursuant to which such compensation is paid.
Several commenters who supported comprehensive disclosure under the Department's rule expressed uncertainty that this aspect of the proposal would achieve the desired result. In particular, some thought the Department intended an aggregate disclosure that would not require specification of the particular amount of compensation and the source. A few other commenters did not think “other” was an appropriate category of compensation to be included in the final rule based on the fact that ERISA section 726 does not include that category of compensation, and the commenters were concerned that the category could be overbroad and interpreted to require disclosure of compensation from services other than pharmacy benefit management services.
In response to comments, the Department revised the wording of the “other compensation” category to make clear it is not an aggregate disclosure; the requirement is now to disclose “any” compensation not already disclosed under paragraphs (e)(1)-(4), along with the payer of the
(
printed page 69125)
compensation, the services for which it will be received, and a description of the arrangement pursuant to which it will be received. This specific disclosure is what the Department had intended. The Department also added the language “regardless of whether such compensation is paid regularly or irregularly or from plan assets or is subject to any contingency or other condition” to underscore the breadth of the disclosure obligation.
The Department did not eliminate the category of “other” compensation altogether in response to comments regarding alignment with the CAA, 2026 amendments. The Department believes that ERISA section 408(b)(2) serves a distinct purpose in assisting responsible plan fiduciaries in assessing the reasonableness of the contract or arrangement and the compensation of the covered service provider and its affiliates, agents, and subcontractors at the time of contracting and in monitoring these contracts or arrangements thereafter. Further, comprehensive disclosure is consistent with ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B), which requires disclosure of “all direct compensation” and “all indirect compensation” reasonably expected to be received by covered service providers, affiliates, and subcontractors. Under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) as amended by the CAA 2026, the Department has authority to address time, manner, and content of the disclosures.
In connection with this category of “other” compensation, the Department sought comments on whether it should specify any other type of compensation that may be received by covered service providers instead of having those items disclosed in the catch all “other” category. The Department specifically asked about disclosure requirements related to compensation received by entities providing pharmacy benefit management services in connection with copay maximizer, copay accumulator, or alternative funding programs. Many commenters said that the final rule should include a specific disclosure regarding these programs, as the commenters said copay maximizer, copay accumulator, and alternative funding programs generate an increasing amount of compensation to providers of pharmacy benefit management services, including in the form of per-claim or per-enrollee fees; administration or technology fees; spreads or retained margins; and gain-share or savings-based payments for the design, implementation, or administration of these programs. Commenters suggested that use of such programs should be disclosed to permit the responsible plan fiduciaries to make decisions regarding their use. A few other commenters suggested the programs should be prohibited.
Commenters also suggested that the final rule should identify other examples of compensation streams that should be disclosed, including compensation from float (
i.e.,
interest on funds held or transferred on behalf of the plan); compensation from PBM-affiliated pharmacies; compensation received from pharmacy benefit manager-affiliated prescription drugs that are dispensed to the covered plan under the service contract or arrangement; compensation from rebate claw-backs (for seeking a lower cost or clinically superior drug); compensation associated with prescription drugs covered by the plan but reimbursed under the medical benefit, such as rebates, administrative fees and other payments tied to physician-administered or specialty drugs; and others.
The Department carefully considered commenters' suggestions regarding additional disclosure categories but determined that a robust list of additional disclosure items would overly complicate the regulatory text. The Department determined that the broad category of “other” compensation would be preferable to avoid creating any definitional loopholes or other unforeseen consequences associated with adding additional disclosure categories. However, based on the list of additional compensation streams commenters identified, the Department is persuaded that the other compensation category is critical to ensuring full disclosure and therefore did not eliminate it as requested by some commenters.
3.10. Formulary Placement Incentives
Paragraph (e)(6) requires the initial disclosures to include specified information regarding formulary placement incentives. The purpose of paragraph (e)(6) is to assist responsible plan fiduciaries in evaluating the covered service provider's formulary selections and how the selections might be influenced by incentives, arrangements, and payments. While paragraph (e)(3)(i) requires covered service providers to provide a description of the
amounts of payments
reasonably expected to be paid by drug manufacturers or rebate aggregators in connection with the contract or arrangement, paragraph (e)(6) requires a
description of the arrangements
so that the responsible plan fiduciary can gain additional insight as to their impact. The disclosures are set forth in three subparagraphs, each of which address different aspects of formulary design and maintenance.
3.10.1. Subparagraph (e)(6)(i)
Under subparagraph (e)(6)(i), the initial disclosure must include a description of any formulary placement incentives and arrangements that the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor has entered with any drug manufacturer in connection with the contract or arrangement with the covered plan. The disclosure must also include an explanation of how the incentives and arrangements affect services to and are aligned with the interests of the covered plan and/or its participants and beneficiaries, such as by controlling prescription drug costs, providing clinically superior drugs, or both.
Formulary incentives or arrangements widely reported on in industry literature include concessions made by a drug manufacturer for including its drugs in a formulary, for tiering of drugs within a formulary, for excluding or tiering of other manufacturers' drugs within a formulary, and for treating a drug differently than therapeutically equivalent drugs (including biosimilar biological products) under a utilization management protocol. In addition, adding to a formulary a drug that is manufactured or co-manufactured by the PBM or an affiliate, in the view of the Department, would be a formulary placement incentive that triggers the disclosure required under subparagraph (e)(6)(i).
Under subparagraph (e)(6)(i), the covered service provider is required to provide an explanation of how the formulary placement incentives and arrangements affect services to and align with the interests of the covered plan and/or its participants and beneficiaries. The concept of alignment is inherently dependent on the specific facts and circumstances of the incentive or arrangement in question. However, examples of incentives or arrangements that are aligned with the interests of the covered plan and/or its participants and beneficiaries are those that aim to control prescription drug costs, provide clinically superior drugs, or both. In this regard, the Department notes that any given formulary placement incentive or arrangement can be aligned with the interests of the covered plan and/or its participants and beneficiaries based on a combination of the clinical value and cost-effectiveness of the associated drug, even though the drug is not necessarily clinically superior to all alternatives.
(

The Department anticipates that, in connection with developing these disclosures, covered service providers will carefully review the incentives and arrangements to determine how the incentives and arrangements would impact services to the covered plan. Likewise, covered service providers are required to determine that they could accurately disclose how the incentives and arrangements are aligned with the interests of the covered plan and/or its participants and beneficiaries, whether by contributing to controlling prescription drug costs, by providing clinically superior drugs, or both.
In the proposal, the Department requested comments on the proposed requirement to explain how formulary incentives and arrangements affect services to and are aligned with the interests of the covered plan and/or its participants and beneficiaries, and in particular whether commenters believed this requirement would contribute to the elimination of incentives and arrangements that are not aligned with the interests of the covered plan and/or its participants and beneficiaries. Further, to ensure that the final rule appropriately protects the interests of the participants in covered plans, the Department sought comment on whether any assertions of clinical superiority provided in the disclosure should be required to be accompanied by evidence. The Department also asked whether there are other examples of incentives or arrangements that align with the interests of the covered plan and/or its participants and beneficiaries (other than by controlling prescription drug costs, providing clinically superior drugs, or both) that should be specified in the regulatory text.
The Department received comments supporting the proposed requirement to disclose formulary incentives as a means of allowing responsible plan fiduciaries to understand incentives of pharmacy benefit management service providers associated with formulary decisions that may affect access to, and costs of, prescription drugs under the service contract or arrangement. Several commenters suggested that the final rule should specify that the required disclosure extends to how drug manufacturer payments impact tier placement, prior authorization, or step therapy, and may require drugs to be excluded from the formulary.
With respect to the proposed requirement to provide an explanation of how the incentives and arrangements affect services to and are aligned with the interests of the plan and/or its participants and beneficiaries, for example by controlling drug prices, providing clinically superior drugs, or both, some commenters agreed with the concept but believed that covered service providers may provide conclusory responses that might be of limited use. One commenter said that assertions of clinical superiority should be accompanied by peer-reviewed evidence or FDA recognized clinical data, and another commenter believed that evidence to support the assertion should be available upon request. However, several other commenters believed such claims could be supported by other methods such as a short evidentiary basis or a detailed analysis.
Other commenters expressed concerns about the burdens to the covered service provider and the potential market impact of the proposed disclosures. These commenters said that the disclosures may impact pharmacy benefit management service providers' ability to maintain competitive rebate leverage. Some commenters asked the Department to permit a narrative qualitative type of disclosure regarding formulary design principles rather than the disclosure of the incentive arrangements. Commenters also asked the Department to align with the approach taken by Congress in ERISA section 726, which focuses on a retrospective disclosure regarding the plan's highest spend drugs and involves standardized formulary placement rationales developed by the Secretary (along with the Secretary of Treasury and Health and Human Services).
