After considering these comments, the Department determined to finalize this paragraph as proposed, and has redesignated it as subparagraph (e)(6)(i) in the final rule. The Department believes there is value in covered service providers carefully reviewing the incentives and arrangements in light of the requirement to provide an explanation of how the incentives and arrangements affect services to and are aligned with the interests of the covered plan and/or its participants and beneficiaries. The Department did not require assertions of clinical superiority to be accompanied by any specific type of justification, to avoid additional costs and burden to covered service providers. The type of justification provided will be evaluated for persuasiveness by the responsible plan fiduciaries, who may seek additional information as they determine appropriate. The Department did not revise subparagraph (e)(6)(i) specifically to require the disclosure to address how incentives may address tier placement, prior authorization, and step therapy, and may result in drugs being excluded from the formulary and other related matters because the Department believes that the language of the required disclosures in subparagraph (e)(6)(i) and (ii) (discussed below) is broad enough to capture such information.
One commenter said that the final rule also should specify that formulary placement driven by lowest net cost to the plan and participant combined, after all compensation to the pharmacy benefit management service provider, would be most aligned with plan and participant interests. The Department did not add this additional language to the regulatory text because cost was already addressed in the language of subparagraph (e)(6)(i) regarding controlling prescription drug costs.
The Department decided to retain the disclosure of the incentive arrangement rather than a narrative qualitative type of disclosure regarding formulary design principles, as suggested by some commenters, because the Department was not convinced that a narrative would allow the responsible plan fiduciary to assess the incentives associated with formulary decisions that may affect access to, and costs of, prescription drugs under the service contract or arrangement.
The Department did not eliminate this disclosure altogether to align with ERISA section 726, as some commenters suggested. The Department believes this disclosure has value as a component of the initial disclosure so that plan fiduciaries will have the information at the time of contracting, which is key to making the reasonableness determination required under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B). The Department believes that the burden described by commenters will be alleviated by the more limited scope of the final rule to the larger self-insured group health plans and that concerns about potential market impact are addressed by the confidentiality provision in paragraph (k)(4).

3.10.2. Subparagraph (e)(6)(ii)
Under subparagraph (e)(6)(ii), the initial disclosure also must include an identification of reasonably available therapeutically equivalent alternatives (including biosimilar biological products) for any drug on the formulary with respect to which the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor reasonably expects to receive any payment by the manufacturer or rebate aggregator that is not passed through to the covered plan. This provision also requires the covered service provider to explain the reason for omitting such alternatives from the covered plan's formulary.
The purpose of this provision is to provide the responsible plan fiduciary with information on the constitution of the formulary and the extent to which its overall composition was influenced by lower cost and/or clinical efficacy, as discussed above, as opposed to financial incentives. For instance, when the formulary contains a drug for which the covered service provider will receive a payment from the drug manufacturer (and not pass the payment through to the covered plan), subparagraph (e)(6)(ii) requires the subject disclosure to identify reasonably available therapeutically equivalent alternatives or biosimilar biologic products that do not similarly compensate the covered service provider. This disclosure thus will enable responsible plan fiduciaries to evaluate the way the covered service provider has designed the formulary and the extent to which its composition might be overly influenced by conflicts of interests that impact the quality or performance of services and that require mitigation. The mere fact that alternatives without manufacturers' payments may exist in the marketplace is not dispositive of an unreasonable contract or arrangement; therefore, subparagraph (e)(6)(ii) requires the disclosure to explain the reason for their omission from the formulary, such as the alternatives having lower clinical efficacy, higher pricing, or inadequate supply.
In the final rule, the Department has required identification of reasonably available therapeutically equivalent alternatives modifying the proposal to include “
biosimilar biological products,”
based on several comments that said that as used by the Food and Drug Administration, the term “therapeutically equivalent alternatives” applies to small molecule drugs, and not biological products.
Subparagraph (e)(6)(ii) of the final rule does not define “identification” with respect to reasonably available alternatives. At a minimum, however, this identification must include enough information about the alternatives that the responsible plan fiduciary is able to consult a publicly available directory to complete a prudent analysis.
[
167

Typically, this will include the manufacturer's name, the generic or trade name of the drug, and dosage form. The disclosure is required to include only a reasonable number of alternatives, not every alternative on the market.
The Department requested comments on whether the final rule should contain an explicit standard with respect to the number of alternatives versus allowing the contracting parties the leeway to establish parameters on their own. One commenter said the rule should have a minimum standard such as requiring identification of at least three therapeutically equivalent alternatives with the lowest net cost available on the market, rather than leaving this to negotiation. Another commenter supported leaving this to the contracting parties but said the final rule should provide that defining therapeutic equivalents by reference to the Orange Book maintained by the Food and Drug Administration would be considered a reasonable approach. Based on limited commenter feedback, the Department determined that requiring a specific number of alternatives to be identified may prove too prescriptive, so it determined to allow the contracting parties to determine parameters. The Department agrees with the commenter who suggested that reference to the Orange Book maintained by the Food and Drug Administration would be considered a reasonable approach.
Other commenters on the proposal also said the Department should align its approach with that of ERISA section 726(b)(2)(A)(iii), which will require notification of changes in the formulary placement compared to the prior year, or should withdraw its proposed disclosure altogether in light of that statutory provision. The Department did not adopt a provision in which the disclosure focused on formulary placement compared to the prior plan year because a change in a formulary placement is not the focus of subparagraph (e)(6)(ii) and that type of disclosure would not yield any information in the case of a new contract or arrangement. The Department did not eliminate this disclosure altogether as a means of aligning with ERISA section 726 because the Department believes this disclosure has value as a component of the initial disclosure so that plan fiduciaries will have the information at the time of contracting in order to conduct a reasonableness assessment under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B).
3.10.3. Subparagraph (e)(6)(iii)
Under subparagraph (e)(6)(iii), if the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor retains authority to modify the formulary during the term of the contract or arrangement 4—such as by adding or removing drugs or changing their tiering—the initial disclosure must include an explanation of the reasons for retaining such authority and the expected frequency of such changes. Further, the disclosure must state that the responsible plan fiduciary will be notified reasonably in advance of any modifications that, individually or in the aggregate, are reasonably expected to have a material impact on the reasonableness of compensation under the contract or arrangement. The disclosure also must notify the responsible plan fiduciary of the covered plan's right to terminate the
(
printed page 69128)
contract or arrangement on reasonably short notice under the circumstances.
The purpose of the advance disclosure requirement is to notify the responsible plan fiduciary sufficiently in advance of the upcoming formulary modification so that the responsible plan fiduciary can either consent or raise an objection. Modifying the formulary is an act of plan administration, with important consequences to the covered plan and its participants. The responsible plan fiduciary could not properly carry out its responsibilities under ERISA without this advance notice, and likewise the covered service provider might be exercising discretionary authority or responsibility in the administration of the covered plan if it unilaterally effected the modifications without the responsible plan fiduciary's consent.
With respect to this advance notice requirement, the proposed regulation did not specify a number of days “in advance” for the notice to be provided. The Department stated that ideally, the notice would be given sufficiently in advance so that responsible plan fiduciary has a reasonable period to consider the modification and consent or raise an objection. The Department requested comments on whether the final rule should provide more specificity regarding the timing of this advance notice, and stated that it was considering whether to require the notice to be furnished at least 75 days in advance of the change, to allow the covered plan to provide notice to plan participants at least 60 days prior to the date the upcoming material modification becomes effective, if required.
[
168
]
While several commenters supported the 75-day advance notice timeframe as providing responsible plan fiduciaries with sufficient time to evaluate the change before it takes effect, another commenter opposed the advance notice requirement stating that it could delay patient access to newly approved drugs. The commenters opposed to 75-day advance notice timeframe did not propose alternative timeframes. The Department determined, in light of concerns about prompt patient access to newly approved drugs, that it would not specify a timeframe for the advance notice provision in the final rule. Instead, it would leave the decision up to the responsible plan fiduciary and the covered service provider.
The advance notice requirement is triggered only with respect to formulary modifications that, individually or in the aggregate, are reasonably expected to have a material impact on the reasonableness of compensation under the contract or arrangement. In this way, the trigger is carefully tied to matters of compensation—the chief topic of ERISA section 408(b)(2).
For this purpose, subparagraph (e)(6)(iii) provides that the term “material” means an amount that is 5 percent or more, or such lower percentage or dollar amount that may be agreed to by the responsible plan fiduciary and set forth in writing in the contract or arrangement, of the aggregate compensation (on a semiannual basis, or at the request of the covered plan, quarterly basis) disclosed pursuant to subparagraph (e)(3)(i) of the final rule, adjusted for any increases previously disclosed under paragraph (e)(6). Thus, the base amount on which the materiality of the modification is judged would initially be the amount disclosed pursuant to subparagraph (e)(3)(i), but it would increase by the amount of any modifications disclosed under subparagraph (e)(6)(iii).
The following example illustrates how the base amount subparagraph (e)(6)(iii) adjusts as material modifications are made to the formulary. Assume that in advance of entering a contract with a covered plan, a covered service provider discloses pursuant to subparagraph (e)(3)(i) reasonably expected payments on a semiannual basis of 100 dollars. After entering the contract, a contemplated modification in the first semiannual period would result in an increase in compensation above the initially-disclosed amount (100 dollars) by two percent. Advance disclosure of this modification would not be required by subparagraph (e)(6)(iii), unless the parties had agreed to a two percent threshold. A contemplated modification in the second semiannual period would result in an increase in compensation above the initially-disclosed amount (100 dollars) by four percent. Because the aggregate of the second semiannual period modification (four percent increase to initially-disclosed amount) and the first semiannual period modification (two percent increase to initially-disclosed amount) collectively are expected to exceed five percent, advance notice of the second semiannual modification would be required under subparagraph (e)(6)(iii). The disclosure would need to describe the aggregate (six percent) increase to the initially-disclosed amount. Going forward, the five percent threshold in subparagraph (e)(6)(iii) would apply to the initially disclosed amount (100 dollars) plus the amount disclosed under paragraph (e)(6) (six dollars, or six percent of 100 dollars).
The Department proposed a materiality standard as a trigger to balance the amount of disclosure provided to responsible plan fiduciaries of covered plans. Without a materiality standard, the Department was concerned that responsible plan fiduciaries might be inundated with advance notices of formulary modifications. This concern was based on the understanding that PBMs make frequent changes to formularies.
The materiality standard has two components: it includes a ceiling of a five percent impact over the base amount, and it also allows for the covered service provider and responsible plan fiduciary to negotiate a lower threshold (dollar or percentage).
[
169
]
The Department understands that in other contexts, materiality is determined based on the significance to the impacted parties.
[
170
]
However, the Department also believes that covered service providers and responsible plan fiduciaries may appreciate a bright line rule as an alternative.
In the proposal, the Department sought comments on the proposed definition of materiality and whether commenters believed the approach taken in the proposal is workable and identifies an appropriate test for materiality. The Department asked whether the test for materiality in the proposal, which was based on a 5 percent increase over the estimated amount of expected rebates from manufacturers or aggregators, should be broadened to include other compensation, such as spread. The Department also asked about alternative tests for materiality, including whether it would be better to trigger advance disclosure on “any non-trivial changes in the formulary that could affect the covered service provider's own compensation.”
Several commenters suggested changes to the proposed approach to the materiality standard. A few commenters said the provision should be broadened to apply to material increases in other compensation such as spread. Other commenters said that the provision should also apply to material increases
(
printed page 69129)
in plan costs, cost-sharing, or utilization management structure.
A few commenters said the Department should eliminate the general materiality standard (
i.e.,
“the responsible plan fiduciary must be notified in advance of any modifications that, individually and in the aggregate,
are reasonably expected to have a material impact on
the reasonableness of compensation under the service contract or arrangement”) and instead use only a percentage threshold.
After considering comments on this paragraph, the Department decided to finalize it as proposed with a focus on formulary changes that materially impact rebates, fees, alternative discounts and other remuneration from drug manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers, and rebate aggregators (or other purchasing entities designed to aggregate rebates) that will be received by the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor. The Department did not expand the provision to apply to material increases in other compensation such as spread because it was not convinced that spread compensation is necessarily a driver of formulary changes such that changes should be brought to the attention of the responsible plan fiduciary in advance; rather, it is appropriate for material increases in spread compensation to be subject to the overage explanation in paragraph (g)(4). The Department did not require a disclosure based on material increase in plan costs or other factors such as cost-sharing because it determined that changes that will increase compensation for covered service providers (and affiliates, agents, or subcontractors) should be the focus of this disclosure under ERISA section 408(b)(2). The Department also did not replace the general standard that “the responsible plan fiduciary must be notified in advance of any modifications that, individually and in the aggregate,
are reasonably expected to have a material impact on
the reasonableness of compensation under the service contract or arrangement” with a percentage threshold, because it preferred to leave responsible plan fiduciaries the opportunity to negotiate a lower materiality threshold.
A few commenters opposed the disclosure in subparagraph (e)(6)(iii) as they said it was inconsistent with the statutorily mandated framework in the CAA, 2026. The Department disagrees that this provision exceeds its authority. As set forth above, modifying the formulary is an act of plan administration. To rely on the exemption when contracting with a plan to provide pharmacy benefit management services, ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) as amended by the CAA, 2026 in fact requires that PBMs as covered service providers make disclosures sufficient to permit the responsible plan fiduciary to assess the reasonableness of the compensation that is to be received. Without notice to the responsible plan fiduciary so that the fiduciary can monitor the service contract or arrangement and the covered service provider can avoid exercising discretionary authority or responsibility in the administration of the covered plan, the exemption cannot function, and a fiduciary cannot meet its duties under ERISA section 404.
3.11. Drug Pricing Methodology
Under paragraph (e)(7), the initial disclosure must include a description of the net price per course of treatment or single fill, such as a 30-day or 90-day supply, to the covered plan of each drug on the formulary, as defined by National Drug Code, after rebates, fees, alternative discounts, or other remuneration received from applicable entities, for each pharmacy channel, expressed as a monetary amount. If a monetary amount is not ascertainable, the covered service provider must disclose the methodology used by the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor, under the contract or arrangement, to determine the net price the covered plan will pay for each drug on the formulary, for each pharmacy channel, along with an objective means to verify the accuracy.
The final rule therefore requires the covered service provider to disclose the net price to the covered plan of each drug on the formulary by pharmacy channel, including mail order pharmacy, retail pharmacy, and specialty pharmacy. The net price refers to the total cost to the covered plan after rebates, fees, alternative discounts, or other remuneration received by applicable entities would be applied to the price paid by the plan. The covered service provider would disclose to the responsible plan fiduciary the net price of each drug as a monetary amount when such figures can be ascertained by available information.
In instances where a monetary amount cannot be ascertained by the covered service provider, the paragraph (e)(7) disclosure requirement may be satisfied if the covered service provider instead discloses the methodology that will be used to determine the cost to the covered plan and an objective means to verify the accuracy of that methodology. An example of this methodology would be a price determined by reference to AWP, and a direction to the plan as to where the AWP that will be used may be located. Depending on the specific pricing methodology being used, other examples of information that may be provided by the covered service provider, enabling the responsible plan fiduciary to verify the accuracy of the disclosed drug pricing methodology, could include pricing indices, rate schedules, benchmark formulas, or similar objective data sources.
The Department has no single specific list or benchmark in mind to satisfy this verification requirement. The covered plan and covered service provider are best situated, on a case-by-case basis, to establish solutions that meet their individual needs. The intent of this provision is to address the reported opacity in the pharmaceutical supply chain and to remedy the imbalance in bargaining power between covered plans and large providers of pharmacy benefit management services.
The paragraph (e)(7) disclosure requirements serve to establish price transparency to ensure a responsible plan fiduciary can effectively evaluate whether the contract or arrangement with the covered service provider is reasonable. The responsible plan fiduciary gains clear and upfront awareness of drug costs and can assess the fairness and predictability of such prices, preventing arbitrarily inflated net costs and enabling the selection of pricing models most aligned with the interests of the covered plan. Additionally, the (e)(7) provision limits opportunities for covered service providers to use non-transparent discretionary pricing formulas that could obscure the true costs of drugs on the formulary.
Commenters who supported this provision in the proposal said it would assist fiduciaries in evaluating drug pricing arrangements and formulary policies, and it would also ensure that pharmacy benefit managers do not implement discretionary pricing methodologies. One commenter particularly supported the ability of fiduciaries to verify the pricing information.
The Department had proposed disclosure of “net cost” to the covered plan of each drug on the formulary, for each pharmacy channel. The Department revised the language in the final rule to use the phrasing “the net price per course of treatment or single fill, such as a 30-day or 90-day supply to the plan . . . after rebates, fees, alternative discounts, or other remuneration” received from drug manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers, or rebate aggregators (or
(
printed page 69130)
other purchasing entities designed to aggregate rebates). The Department believes this is clearer than the phrasing “net cost” and the terminology aligns with ERISA section 726(b)(2)(A)(i)(VII).
One commenter who supported the disclosures recommended aligning pricing disclosure requirements under the rule with pricing disclosures required under ERISA section 726 and requested the Department clarify that the net cost of each drug be disclosed as the “average net unit cost.” The commenter did not describe how the average net unit cost related to the net cost language in ERISA section 726, so the Department declined to adopt that additional language.
In the proposal, the Department requested comments on whether the language in the proposed price disclosure provision provided sufficient clarity to covered service providers regarding their disclosure obligations or whether adjustments should be made. The Department asked whether, for example, the provision should specify how the term “drug” will be defined, and if so, the Department asked commenters to please provide suggested language. Several commenters suggested that the term drug be identified by reference to the National Drug Code. Some commenters specified that it should be at the 11-digit level (as opposed to the 5-digit or 9-digit level), which a commenter said is the standard identifier throughout the pharmaceutical supply chain and is necessary to prevent PBMs from aggregating disclosures and obscuring individual drug pricing. The Department has added a reference to the National Drug Code to paragraph (e)(7) in the final rule. The Department expects the disclosure to include the 11-digit code, as the industry standard, but has not included that specification in the final rule to avoid the potential that such specification could become outdated. Additionally, ERISA section 726 includes National Drug Code reporting without specifying the 11-digit code.
Commenters suggested additional changes that the Department did not accept. Several commenters suggested aggregate reporting of drug pricing information, including specific information by therapeutic category or pharmacy channel; and one commenter supported it as an addition to individual drug pricing, while another commenter suggested it as an alternative. The commenter who suggested it as an alternative to individual drug pricing said aggregate price disclosure would have the benefit of advancing transparency in a more targeted way while avoiding transmittal of commercially sensitive individual drug pricing information. A few commenters also said that this rule should require disclosure of net cost to include breakouts identifying whether a prescription was filled at a pharmacy owned by or affiliated with the covered service provider. The Department believes the disclosure of pricing information at the individual drug level in the final rule is appropriate as an initial disclosure to responsible plan fiduciaries contracting for pharmacy benefit management services. Additional disclosures such as aggregate disclosure by therapeutic category, pharmacy channel, or pharmacy affiliation would increase the burden to covered service providers.
Some commenters said that drug level disclosure would not be necessary for effective fiduciary oversight; would possibly overwhelm responsible plan fiduciaries; and would exceed the framework established by Congress in ERISA section 726, which requires pricing disclosure only for drugs for which a claim was filed. As discussed above, the Department believes that the paragraph (e)(7) disclosure requirements will assist responsible plan fiduciaries in their assessments of contracts or arrangements with providers of pharmacy benefit management services, including by allowing them to select drug pricing models most aligned with the interests of the self-insured group health plan, and limiting opportunities for covered service providers to use non-transparent discretionary pricing formulas that could obscure the true costs of drugs on the formulary. The Department believes disclosures under ERISA section 408(b)(2) assist responsible plan fiduciaries in assessing the reasonableness of the contract or arrangement and the compensation of the covered service provider and its affiliates, agents, and subcontractors at the time of contracting and in monitoring these contracts or arrangements thereafter.
Finally, commenters expressed concern about confidentiality of disclosures related to drug prices and drug pricing methodologies. The Department has adopted paragraph (k)(4) in the final rule that permits covered service providers to require responsible plan fiduciaries to require third parties and their subcontractors to execute reasonable confidentiality provisions preventing redisclosure by such parties and limiting use of such information to purposes related to the covered plan's contract or arrangement.
3.11.1. Net Effective Cost Disclosure
Several commenters recommended that the Department add a new provision to the final rule requiring covered service providers defined in paragraph (c)(1)(ii) (
i.e.,
brokers and consultants) to disclose information using a net effective cost model for bids to provide pharmacy benefit management services furnished as part of a request for proposal. These commenters said that bids submitted as part of a request for proposal for pharmacy benefit management services which focus on the value of rebates or other price concessions from drug manufacturers can obscure the total net cost incurred by a plan for providing its pharmacy benefit, as bids structured on securing sizable rebates for high-list-price drugs may still result in a higher cost to the plan than an option structured on using lower-list-price drugs, generics, or biosimilars. These commenters also said that requiring disclosure of bids using a net effective cost model would align the incentives of all parties in the supply chain and present competing models in a simple and comparable manner while preserving the various mechanisms used by covered service providers for negotiating price concessions and other factors to reduce the ultimate cost to the plan for providing a pharmacy benefit. The commenters proposed a definition of “net effective cost” for use in the regulatory text.
The Department considered these comments and concluded that a disclosure that is simple and would allow responsible plan fiduciaries to compare competing bids could be a helpful tool for responsible plan fiduciaries. However, the suggestion centered around a detailed and technical definition of net effective cost, and the Department was reluctant to adopt this disclosure as a requirement in the final rule based on limited comments.
3.12. Statement of Fiduciary Status
Under paragraph (e)(8), the initial disclosure must include, if applicable, a statement that the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor will provide, or reasonably expects to provide, services pursuant to the contract or arrangement directly to the covered plan as an ERISA fiduciary.
As relevant to this final rule, ERISA provides that a person is generally a fiduciary with respect to a covered plan to the extent he exercises any discretionary authority or discretionary control respecting management of such
(
printed page 69131)
plan or exercises any authority or control respecting management or disposition of its assets, or do so, or has any discretionary authority or discretionary responsibility in the administration of such plan.
[
171
]
In complying with paragraph (e)(8), therefore, the covered service provider should carefully consider whether it, or an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor, will meet this definition in its services to the covered plan.
The Department has previously explained in this respect that a person who performs “purely ministerial functions . . . within a framework of policies, interpretations, rules, practices and procedures made by other persons” is not a fiduciary under this test.
[
172
]
To avoid fiduciary status, a covered service provider should ensure that its services to the covered plan, and the services of its affiliates, agents, and subcontractors, are not discretionary, but instead operate within policies and procedures disclosed to and approved by the responsible plan fiduciary.
[
173
]
Multiple commenters expressed support for the proposal's broad disclosure requirement, indicating that transparency regarding fiduciary roles is essential to helping plan sponsors and fiduciaries clearly understand whether covered service providers or their affiliates have legal obligations to act in the best interest of the plan as required under ERISA. In their view, without knowing when fiduciary duties apply, plan sponsors cannot properly evaluate whether covered service provider's decisions are loyal fiduciary judgments or if financial incentives are influencing decision-making that may not be in the best interest of the plan.
Multiple other commenters generally opposed the statement of fiduciary status required under the proposal. A commenter noted that a statement of fiduciary status is not required under the disclosure provisions of the CAA, 2026, and that the statement seems to exceed the statutory purpose of ERISA section 408(b)(2). According to the commenter, it is immaterial to the framework under section 408(b)(2) whether or not the covered service provider believes it is a fiduciary. Some commenters suggested that the fiduciary status disclosure may cause confusion about ERISA's definition of fiduciary, which is well-understood to be a functional test. The commenters noted that disclosing a statement as to fiduciary status does not, by itself, create such status if the person does not meet the functional test, and that meeting the function test confers fiduciary status even without a statement. According to commenters, the initial disclosure could therefore mislead a responsible plan fiduciary into believing that a covered service provider is a fiduciary even if the purported fiduciary does not actually meet the functional test described in ERISA section 3(21).
A commenter suggested that the fiduciary statement should instead focus on those duties that the plan and covered service provider have separately and expressly agreed are fiduciary in nature. The commenter explained that any arrangement under which a plan fiduciary intends to confer on another entity the role of fiduciary would be the subject of a separate, explicit, and specific written undertaking agreed to by all parties. Another commenter similarly suggested that the statement should identify whether the covered service provider will provide services to the plan in a fiduciary capacity, or has entered into any agreement that could be construed as conferring discretionary authority or control over plan management or plan assets, which result in fiduciary status under ERISA section 3(21)(A). Another commenter suggested that the proposal should be modified to additionally require a negative disclosure when a covered service provider does not believe it is a fiduciary.
Commenters also requested several other clarifications and changes to the proposed requirement. A commenter requested clarification that a plan fiduciary, other than the PBM, is not liable for any failure of the PBM to provide the statement required by the regulation. Another commenter requested confirmation that the functional fiduciary test under ERISA section 3(21)(A) would still generally apply to pharmacy benefit service arrangements. A commenter also requested confirmation that ERISA makes clear that when a fiduciary is acting in a non-fiduciary capacity, such as when a PBM sells services to a plan, such activities are not a conflict of interest so long as they do not relate to the party's fiduciary role.
A commenter suggested that a covered service provider should be required to update their statements whenever there is a material change to the provider's fiduciary status or conflicts of interest or compensation, with materiality defined explicitly in relation to the affected plan sponsor. The commenter also recommended the fiduciary status statement requirement be changed to require semiannual and material event restatements, explaining that annual or even semiannual updates would be insufficient given the dynamic nature of PBM operations, vertical integration, and the frequency with which formulary and network changes can alter fiduciary analysis. The commenter also recommended that the regulation should be revised to indicate that the failure to acknowledge that the PBM is acting as a fiduciary is, itself, a breach of its fiduciary duty.
After reviewing the public comments, the Department has decided to include the disclosure of fiduciary status in the final regulation, and to not limit it to instances where fiduciary status is expressly agreed upon contractually. The Department agrees with commenters that argued the importance of responsible plan fiduciaries knowing whether a party will be providing or reasonably expects to provide services to the plan as an ERISA fiduciary, given the provider's heightened level of responsibility under ERISA. In the Department's view, this importance does not change based on whether a person is a functional fiduciary or expressly agrees by contract to perform fiduciary functions. The Department is not persuaded that disclosure of fiduciary status is inconsistent with section 408(b)(2) of ERISA. As indicated in both the proposal and elsewhere in this final rule, the statutory basis for this regulation includes section 408(b)(2)(B) of ERISA, which also contains a requirement to disclose if a covered service provider will provide, or reasonably expects to provide, services as a fiduciary within the meaning of section 3(21) of ERISA.
The Department does not share the concern of some commenters that an initial disclosure may mislead responsible plan fiduciaries into believing a covered service provider is a fiduciary even if the service provider does not actually meet the functional test described in section 3(21). As some commenters noted, the functional test for fiduciary status under section 3(21) is well understood. The Department's guidance and numerous court decisions make clear that a person is a fiduciary only to the extent it meets the functional
(
printed page 69132)
definition in the statute.
[
174
]
The disclosure requirement in the final regulation does not change the functional test for identifying fiduciaries. We also note that if a covered service provider fails to provide the statement of fiduciary status, the exemption at paragraph (n) of the final regulation is available for the responsible plan fiduciary.
The Department agrees with the commenter who said the statement of fiduciary status should be updated and has added a requirement to update this statement in the semiannual disclosure, in paragraph (g)(5) of the final rule. With respect to other suggestions to require additional disclosure of information, and updates to the information disclosures, the Department did not receive sufficient information from commenters for consideration. The Department has not made any changes in response to these comments.
3.12.1. Examples
A number of commenters supporting the proposal's statement of fiduciary status also suggested that the final rule include examples illustrating fiduciary status that may be taken on by PBMs. According to some, the proposal effectively allows PBMs, rather than responsible plan fiduciaries, to determine when they are acting as fiduciaries for purposes of the disclosure requirement. They indicated that the fiduciary status of a PBM performing PBM services is not always clear-cut in practice, and, as a result, similarly situated PBMs and responsible plan fiduciaries may reasonably reach different conclusions about whether specific conduct gives rise to fiduciary status that must be disclosed. Commenters cautioned that PBMs may adopt unduly narrow interpretations of fiduciary status, allowing activities that involve discretion or meaningful influence over plan assets, plan administration, or plan management to be characterized as non-fiduciary by default. Some also opined that PBMs often have evaded ERISA fiduciary duties by asserting they perform only “ministerial” functions, with one commenter suggesting that the Department provide further guidance on “ministerial” functions.
Some commenters said that the regulation could be strengthened if it includes examples of how PBMs function as fiduciaries. In their view, this would promote consistent application of the disclosure requirement and help responsible plan fiduciaries identify PBM fiduciary functions that are inconsistent with PBM pricing arrangements and increase the cost of medicines. Some commenters identified as possible examples for the regulation activities related to designing utilization management plans, designing pharmacy benefit networks, and developing other formulary changes that they believe can cause PBMs to operate as fiduciaries under ERISA.
With respect to fiduciary status, the proposal explained that ERISA provides that a person is generally a fiduciary with respect to a self-insured group health plan to the extent he exercises any discretionary authority or discretionary control respecting management of such plan or exercises any authority or control respecting management or disposition of its assets, or has any discretionary authority or discretionary responsibility in the administration of such plan.
[
175
]
However, a person who performs “purely ministerial functions . . . within a framework of policies, interpretations, rules, practices and procedures made by other persons” is not a fiduciary under this test.
[
176
]
Whether a person is a fiduciary under the function test depends on the surrounding facts and circumstances. Because the test is based on function, a person may be a fiduciary with respect to some activities, but not others. For example, as noted in the proposal, a covered service provider that unilaterally modifies a self-insured group health plan's formulary may be exercising discretionary authority or responsibility in the administration of the plan.
[
177
]
The Department believes providing more comprehensive guidance on fiduciary status, as requested by commenters, is beyond the scope of this regulatory project.
3.12.2. Conflicts Disclosure
In the proposal, the statement of fiduciary status also included a conflict-of-interest disclosure. Specifically, the proposal included a requirement to “disclose any activity or policy that may create a conflict of interest, including, for example, if such entity will benefit financially from drug substitution, from incentivizing use of affiliated pharmacies when other network pharmacies offer lower costs, or from step therapy or `fail first' protocols that require participants and beneficiaries to use drugs that generate greater manufacturer rebates than other therapeutically equivalent drugs on the formulary.”
A commenter questioned the need for the separate conflicts disclosure and the proposal's examples of potential conflicts in light of the CAA, 2026. The commenter explained that while the proposal suggested that such a conflict could include the use of a step therapy protocol requiring beneficiaries to use specific drugs to “generate higher manufacturer rebates than other therapeutically equivalent drugs,” manufacturer rebates are a means to lower plan costs. The commenter asserted that it is difficult to see how that scenario could be a “conflict of interest” because under the CAA, 2026's 100% rebate pass-through requirements, manufacturer payments associated with the plan's drug utilization flow entirely to the plan. The commenter observed that if a step therapy protocol results in greater manufacturer rebates, the plan receives 100% of that value. The commenter requested that the Department clarify that the conflict-of-interest disclosures relate to those areas in which the covered service provider serves as a fiduciary. In the commenter's view, that clarification would help avoid potential confusion around the types of examples provided in the proposal. Another commenter suggested that the conflicts disclosure should apply only to activities ancillary to the covered service provider's role as an expressly agreed upon fiduciary. Another commenter suggested that the conflicts of interest disclosure should be strengthened to require a description of the processes to identify and mitigate conflicts of interest, such as objective third-party evaluation of identified conflicts and management of recusals.
The Department decided not to include the conflict disclosure in the final rule. The Department had intended that the conflict disclosure would be applicable to activities and policies related to the covered service provider's services as a fiduciary. However, after consideration of comments on the proposed statement of fiduciary status and the conflict disclosure, the Department concluded that the totality of the other disclosures in the final
(
printed page 69133)
rule—particularly disclosures regarding the indirect compensation to be received by the covered service provider and its affiliates, agents, and subcontractors—will provide responsible plan fiduciaries with meaningful information to assess the potential conflicts of interest. Additional conflict disclosure associated with the statement of fiduciary status could prove duplicative and may therefore be confusing to responsible plan fiduciaries.
3.13. Statement of Audit Right
Under paragraph (e)(9), the initial disclosure must provide a statement of the covered plan's right to the audit described in paragraph (j) of the final rule and the procedures for requesting such an audit. Among other things, paragraph (j) ensures that the contract or arrangement does not contain terms that would impede the covered plan's ability to conduct an audit. As discussed in preamble section E.8., the right to audit the completeness and accuracy of the required disclosures is an essential part of the final rule's framework for establishing transparency in the marketplace for pharmacy benefit management services. Paragraph (e)(9) ensures that the responsible plan fiduciary is aware of the audit rights that are preserved in the regulation.
Several commenters said the audit provision exceeded the Department's statutory authority, and they submitted related comments saying that the initial disclosure should not include this statement of audit right. The Department has discussed the comments on its statutory authority below and has determined to adopt the audit provision in the final rule with modifications clarifying the scope of limitations for confidentiality agreements related to such an audit and the timing requirements for a service provider to provide the information required for the audit. Accordingly, the final rule also includes the required statement of audit right in the initial disclosure.
4. Initial Disclosure Requirements for Fully Insured Group Health Plans Reserved—Paragraph (f)
As discussed above, the regulatory initial disclosure requirements for fully insured group health plans are reserved. ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) continues to obligate all covered service providers, including group health plan issuers and related vendors who meet that definition, to comply with the statutory disclosure requirements to rely on the exemption.
5. Semiannual Disclosure Requirements—Paragraph (g)
Paragraph (g) of the final rule
[
178
]
requires semiannual (or at the request of the covered plan, quarterly) disclosures of the actual compensation received or reasonably expected to be received for the semiannual (or quarterly) period by the covered service provider and its affiliates, agents, and subcontractors in connection with the services provided under the contract or arrangement with the covered plan. This disclosure will serve an important purpose for the responsible plan fiduciary's monitoring obligations with respect to the services contract or arrangement with the covered plan.
Under the final rule, the semiannual (or quarterly) disclosure must cover amounts actually received during the period plus any amounts that are reasonably expected to be received in connection with services during the period. Language was added in the final rule to ensure full disclosure of amounts earned during the disclosure period, even if payment has not yet been received. This approach has the advantage of providing fiduciaries with a fuller picture of the compensation arrangements as compared to an approach based strictly on when compensation is received, which may be impacted by lagging payments. This also aligns with the approach in ERISA section 726, which bases certain disclosures on claims filed during the reporting period and requires disclosure of amounts received or expected to be received.
[
179
]
While selection of these covered service providers will be made based on the initial disclosures, which require disclosure of compensation “reasonably expected” to be received, the responsible plan fiduciary's ability to evaluate compensation actually received (or earned during the period but not yet received) is intended to facilitate ongoing oversight of the service arrangement.
[
180
]
The semiannual (or quarterly) disclosures would be required to be provided no later than 30 calendar days after the end of each six-month period (or, quarter) beginning on the date the contract or arrangement is entered, with respect to the preceding reporting period.
The content of semiannual disclosures generally tracks the specific categories of compensation that were included in the initial disclosures. Thus, these disclosures would address direct compensation (paragraph (g)(1)) as well as indirect compensation (paragraph (g)(2)), including but not limited to manufacturer payments, spread compensation, copay claw-backs and other pharmacy recoupment, and price protection agreements. Like the initial disclosures, the semiannual disclosures also contain a catch-all category for any “other compensation” not covered by the specific compensation categories (paragraph (g)(3)). The disclosure also must include an updated statement of fiduciary status, if applicable, to the extent not previously disclosed as part of the initial disclosures (paragraph (g)(5)), and would include a disclosure of the audit rights under the final rule (paragraph (g)(6)).
Unlike the initial disclosures, the semiannual disclosures would contain amounts of compensation actually received plus any amounts reasonably expected to be received for the semiannual (or quarterly) period for each of these categories. Compensation amounts should not be re-disclosed for a later period in which it is actually received. This clarification is so that covered service providers are not double reporting compensation under this final rule.
Semiannual disclosures must include an overage explanation, if applicable. Consistent with the purpose of these disclosures to assist responsible plan fiduciaries in their ongoing monitoring of the contract or arrangement, paragraph (g)(4) requires a disclosure if any category of compensation to the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor described in paragraph (g), in the aggregate, materially exceeds the corresponding estimate described in paragraph (e). Thus, for example, if the actual amount of spread compensation disclosed in the semiannual disclosure materially exceeded the amount identified in the initial disclosure, this overage explanation requirement would be triggered.
The overage explanation provision requires an identification of the amount of the overage (in the aggregate) and the reason for the overage. For this purpose, the term “materially” means 5 percent
(
printed page 69134)
or more, or such lower percentage or dollar amount as may be agreed to by the responsible plan fiduciary and set forth in writing in the contract or arrangement. This definition of materiality generally parallels the approach taken in paragraph (e)(6)(iii) (relating to the advance notification requirement for modifications to a formulary).
The overage explanation will help responsible plan fiduciaries by emphasizing areas where categories of compensation materially exceeded the parties' expectations at the outset of the contract or arrangement. A responsible plan fiduciary will be able to take the explanation into account when deciding on the continuing reasonableness of the contract and whether to continue the service relationship with the covered service provider.
The Department notes that the semiannual disclosure obligation is not directly stated in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B); however, the statute does require disclosure of changes to the information provided in the initial disclosures,
[
181
]
and the Department has the authority to regulate the timing of these disclosures. With respect to the compensation disclosures, changes to this information must be disclosed as soon as practicable, but generally no later than 60 calendar days from the date on which the covered service provider is informed of such change.
[
182
]
The Department believes that in the pharmacy benefit management context, it is more efficient to have a semiannual (or quarterly) disclosure that would provide all the compensation received in the prior 6 month period (or quarter), rather than a requirement to disclose changes on an ongoing basis.
As indicated above, the primary purpose of paragraph (g) is to ensure that responsible plan fiduciaries have more than just the estimates provided in the initial disclosure (before the contract or arrangement was even entered) under paragraph (e) of the final rule when conducting their statutory duty to monitor the ongoing reasonableness of the covered plan's service relationship with the covered serve provider. In this way, the final rule responds to those instances of reported opacity in the pharmacy benefits management industry.
5.1. Timing of the Disclosures
In the proposal, the Department asked for comments on ways to simplify or streamline the semiannual disclosure without compromising its stated purpose. The Department said it had considered and rejected the idea of proposing annual disclosures of compensation actually received, rather than semiannual disclosures, based on the understanding that pharmacy benefits management service contracts often are only one year in duration. Consequently, in such cases, a disclosure of actual compensation received after the expiration of the contract would seem to be of significantly less value to the responsible plan fiduciary than if it had been received during the term of contract, while the fiduciary's duty to monitor the reasonableness of the relationship is ongoing and, if needed, changes still can be made in response to these disclosures during the contract period.
A number of commenters supported the Department's proposal on the basis that it would facilitate monitoring by responsible plan fiduciaries and accountability of covered service providers at an appropriate interval before the parties would begin renegotiating their contract or arrangement. One commenter said the semiannual period was appropriate given that many service arrangements operate on annual contract cycles, and the semiannual disclosure would provide responsible plan fiduciaries with information that would be timely and actionable, whereas annual disclosures would occur too late to allow meaningful corrective action. Some commenters specifically supported the semiannual time frame as being consistent with the ERISA section 726 reporting period.
A few other commenters suggested semiannual disclosures would be too frequent, with one commenter suggesting that there should be an initial disclosure and thereafter annual disclosures prior to exercising any renewal or extension option. One commenter said that the proposed requirement to provide the disclosure 30 days after the end of the semiannual period would not allow the covered service provider to account for all payments since manufacturer payments may lag due to quarterly billing practices. One commenter asked the Department to make clear that payments received in a subsequent reporting period should be reported in that period if not previously reported.
In the final rule, the Department has retained the semiannual reporting period but also provides for a quarterly reporting period upon the request of the covered plan, in alignment with the reporting periods in ERISA section 726. The Department did not receive a significant number of comments objecting to the 30-day time frame for the disclosure and believes that prompt disclosure following the end of the reporting period is important, so it did not extend the time period for the semiannual (or quarterly) disclosure to be made. The covered service provider can report any amounts in a future semiannual (or quarterly) disclosure from a prior reporting period that were not previously reported. The Department notes, however, that the requirements in paragraphs (g)(2)(i) and (iv) as well as (g)(3) are phrased in terms of compensation received or
reasonably expected to be received.
5.2. Changes From the Proposal
Regarding the substance of the semiannual (or quarterly) disclosures, several commenters said that the Department should make changes that correspond to changes suggested for the initial disclosures, particularly regarding alignment with ERISA section 726. The final rule does generally incorporate corresponding changes to the initial disclosures, including those designed to align with ERISA section 726, all of which were discussed previously in this preamble section E.3.
One commenter suggested that covered service providers should provide an updated statement of fiduciary status whenever there is a change to the fiduciary status or related conflicts of interest. The Department agrees that disclosure of fiduciary status should be updated, but decided to include a requirement to update them in the semiannual (or quarterly) disclosure, not whenever a change happens. This disclosure appears in a new paragraph (g)(5) and is based on the wording of paragraph (e)(8) which is the corresponding initial disclosure.
5.3. Overage Explanation
Some commenters on the Department's proposal said the proposed overage explanation was appropriate and would assist responsible plan fiduciaries in monitoring the reasonableness of the compensation and the contract or arrangement. A few supportive commenters said additional consequences and enforcement options,
(
printed page 69135)
such as civil penalties, would be needed to ensure the overage explanations would not be incomplete or delayed.
A few commenters addressed the proposed materiality threshold of 5 percent. Some said it was appropriate, but others opined that it was either too high or too low. The commenter who said the 5 percent threshold was too high said that with six categories of compensation specified in the rule, covered service provider compensation could increase by up to 30 percent across the board with no overage explanation. A commenter who thought the 5 percent threshold was too low said that variations between projected and actual compensation are the natural result of changes in utilization and other factors over the course of the plan year. The commenter believed that ERISA section 408(b)(2) requires the contract or arrangement to be reasonable at the time it is entered into and does not require the fiduciary to precisely track prospective estimates. The commenter said the threshold should be significantly increased to at least 20 percent and be triggered by aggregate compensation increases not variations in individual categories. Further the commenter said the overage explanation should not be applied to manufacturer payments that are subject to the rebate pass-through to the covered plan.
In the final rule, the Department revised the language in the overage explanation to make clear the focus is compensation to the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor. The Department agrees with the commenter that the overage explanation should not be applied to payments that are passed through to the covered plan. The Department further determined that the approach in the proposal in which the materiality threshold applied to each category of compensation and required the covered service provider to explain the reason for the overage was a straightforward way to assist the responsible plan fiduciary in its monitoring of the service contract or arrangement. Providing for a disclosure based on aggregate overage across categories may result in an explanation that involves multiple reasons and is less clear.
With respect to potential enforcement or civil penalties, section E.13 of this preamble discusses consequences of noncompliance.
6. Semiannual Disclosure Requirements for Fully Insured Group Health Plans Reserved—Paragraph (h)
As discussed above, the regulatory semiannual disclosure requirements for fully insured group health plans are reserved. ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) continues to obligate all covered service providers, including group health plan issuers and related vendors who meet that definition, to comply with the statutory disclosure requirements to rely on the exemption.
