8. Right to Audit—Paragraph (j)
Paragraph (j)
[
188
]
establishes a right for covered plans to audit their covered service providers at least once per year. The purpose of the audit provision in the final rule is to enable responsible plan fiduciaries to verify the accuracy of the disclosures made under the final rule. In describing the scope of the audit provision, paragraph (j)(1) narrowly reflects this purpose. The Department chose not to limit a covered plan's ability to audit their covered service providers only with respect to each plan year to avoid foreclosing a covered plan's ability to cross-reference actual service delivery against compensation disclosures regardless of plan year to identify issues or concerns related to the accuracy of the disclosure, such as hidden costs, billing inconsistencies, or complete disclosure failures.
The final rule provides that the parties would share the audit costs as follows. The covered plan will be responsible for compensating the auditor. The covered service provider will bear the costs of providing the auditor with the information, data, and other materials needed to perform the audit. The Department believes this shared cost approach is fair, balanced, adequately protective of covered plans, and not unduly financially burdensome to covered service providers.
Under the final rule, the covered plans have the sole authority to select the auditor, and the covered service providers are prohibited from imposing limitations on the selection process. Likewise, the final rule broadly prohibits covered service providers from imposing restrictive conditions on the auditor, such as the location of the audit or the number of records to be provided, including contracts with retail pharmacies and drug manufacturers. The final rule, however, provides that the scope of the audit is limited to the disclosures made under the final rule.
The Department considers the audit provision to be necessary to ensure a proper and meaningful audit so that the accuracy of the disclosures can be verified. A right to audit the veracity of any and all disclosures made by the covered service provider to a responsible plan fiduciary as required by this regulation, including the responsibility of the covered service provider to deliver all necessary information to conduct such an audit, is an essential part of the rule's framework for establishing transparency in the marketplace for pharmacy benefit management services. As a general matter, the Department believes that covered service providers will be mindful of the regulation's audit rights when developing their disclosures, and the audit rights therefore are deliberately intended to result in disclosures that are more carefully constructed, robust, and transparent. Further, to the extent that an audit reveals information that was not previously disclosed or flaws in the disclosure, the responsible plan fiduciary can evaluate the additional information in assessing the reasonableness of the compensation and determining whether additional payments should have been passed through to the covered plan or whether to exercise other rights.
In this regard, responsible plan fiduciaries must periodically monitor compliance by covered service providers with the terms of their agreements and the reasonableness of their compensation under the agreements to ensure continuation of the agreement meets the requirements of ERISA section 408(b)(2) as well as the general fiduciary obligations under ERISA section 404. In satisfying its monitoring obligations, however, the responsible plan fiduciary retains discretion as to when, if at all, to request an audit of disclosures issued by the covered service provider. The right to conduct an audit does not need to be exercised. A responsible plan fiduciary may reasonably determine that the expense incurred by the plan to audit the covered service provider under this section outweighs the likely benefit to the plan resulting from such audit where additional circumstances suggesting the covered service provider is noncompliant with the terms of the contract or arrangement or the requirements of the regulation are absent.
8.1. General Comments
After considering comments on the proposal, the Department determined to finalize the audit provision with minor changes, as discussed below. Several commenters said that audits are essential for plan fiduciaries to assess the accuracy of the required disclosures. Commenters said that audits are already often standard practice, and the final rule will set expectations and requirements for auditing across service providers and responsible plan fiduciaries. Commenters also identified issues that have arisen in the absence of a clear audit right: PBMs sometimes limit responsible plan fiduciaries' discretion in choosing auditors or do not provide material information necessary for a complete audit. The Department finds these comments persuasive because of the role audits play already, the value commenters saw in the audit rights, and the opportunity to create a baseline standard for audits to help ensure that the disclosures required by the rule are accurate.
In the proposal, the Department sought comments on the scope of the audit considering the purpose of the rulemaking. Some commenters suggested that the Department expand the audit requirement so that plan fiduciaries would be able to use an audit to assess the extent to which service providers complied with the terms of their contract rather than limiting the audit to the accuracy of their disclosures. Other commenters said maintaining the proposed scope of the audit provision would be preferable and expanding beyond verification of required disclosures would be inconsistent with the objectives of the rule. The Department is not persuaded that the audit rights should extend beyond requiring needed information to validate the disclosures required in the rule. Such a requirement would be beyond the scope of the rule, which is designed to ensure plan fiduciaries have the information they need to assess whether the contract or arrangement is reasonable.
Some commenters said the proposed audit provision exceeded the Department's regulatory authority and therefore should not be included in the final rule. They said the Department's regulatory authority under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) is limited to “time, manner, and content” of the disclosures. Further, the commenters said that new ERISA section 408(b)(2)(C) contains audit rights that are limited to the rebate-pass through provision, which they believed suggested that Congress did not intend broader audit rights.
The Department does not agree that the final rule's provision preserving covered plans' audit rights exceeds its regulatory authority. Congress specified the Department's authority in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) with respect to the time, manner, and content of disclosures. In the Department's view, shared by many commenters, the audit provisions are necessary for responsible
(
printed page 69137)
plan fiduciaries to verify accuracy of the disclosures and thus fulfill their ERISA section 404 duties. The audit provisions also make the reasonableness determination meaningful to fulfill the purpose of the statutory exemption. The Department believes that in the context of pharmacy benefit management services, where, historically, indirect compensation streams have not been transparent, ensuring that covered plans can audit the detailed disclosures in the final rule furthers the goal of this rulemaking. Further, the Department retains authority under ERISA section 505 to issue regulations necessary or appropriate to carry out the provisions of Title I of ERISA.
8.2. Auditor Selection and Audit Costs
Some commenters asked the Department to permit covered service providers to place reasonable limits on auditor selection, including limitations related to conflicts of interest or other anticompetitive behaviors. One commenter said auditors should be prohibited from receiving contingency fees, such as compensation based on a percentage of rebate payments not remitted to the group health plan. Other commenters stressed the need for the responsible plan fiduciary to retain the right to engage the auditor of its choosing and not be subject to limitations placed by the covered service provider.
The Department agrees with commenters who said the auditor selection should be the sole responsibility of the responsible plan fiduciary. Such responsible plan fiduciaries are required under ERISA to make a prudent and loyal selection of an auditor as a plan service provider. The Department is concerned that if the final rule permitted covered service providers to impose additional limitations, such limitations could potentially be used to limit auditor selection in ways that are inconsistent with the covered plans' interests.
Some commenters also addressed the cost sharing provision in the proposal, under which the covered plan would pay for the selection and retention of the auditor and the covered service provider would pay for providing the requested information. Some commenters opposed this provision based on their interpretation that it would establish a 50-50 cost splitting requirement which they believed could involve the plan subsidizing the covered service provider's costs. Some commenters also believed that the approach in the proposal was inconsistent with the approach in new ERISA section 408(b)(2)(C) which provides that payment for the auditor shall not be made by the provider of pharmacy benefit management services. One commenter said the covered plan should bear all the costs of the audit including the cost of providing the requested information.
The Department believes these comments were based on misinterpretation of the proposed cost sharing provision. The Department did not intend to establish a strict 50-50 cost splitting requirement; rather, as stated above, the proposal provided that the covered plan would pay for the selection and retention of the auditor and the covered service provider would pay for the costs of providing the required information. The Department does not believe this approach is inconsistent with ERISA section 408(b)(2)(C) which also provides that the payment from the auditor shall not be made by the provider of pharmacy benefit management services. Therefore, the Department decided to adopt the cost sharing provision as proposed. The Department did not adopt the commenter's suggestion for the covered plan to bear the entire cost of the audit because we are concerned that approach would create a barrier to covered plans exercising audit rights.
In the proposal, the Department asked for comments on whether there are any circumstances in which the covered service provider should bear the entire cost of the audit, such as if the audit reveals a certain level of inaccurate disclosures. If commenters agreed, the Department asked how the final rule should identify a level of disclosure inaccuracy that would trigger the obligation for the covered service provider to bear the entire audit cost.
A few commenters expressed agreement with this approach but did not suggest a materiality threshold. One commenter suggested a threshold of a 5-percent deviation between disclosed and actual compensation in any of the categories, as an incentive for accurate disclosure. In considering these comments, the Department will not adopt a materiality standard without an objective threshold, based on the view that the lack of an objective threshold would lead to disputes related to whether a covered service provider would have the obligation to bear all the audit costs in any particular case. Moreover, the Department was not persuaded that the 5 percent threshold as suggested by one commenter represented a significant enough disparity to be used in the final rule as a threshold for the covered service provider to bear all the audit costs. Although the Department has used a 5 percent threshold for materiality elsewhere in the final rule, in those cases, the 5 percent threshold triggered an additional disclosure requirement. In the Department's view, a requirement that the covered service provider bear all the audit costs should not be based on the same threshold as provided for additional disclosures. Lacking more specific suggestions and considering the burden this would create, the Department declined to adopt a provision under which covered service providers would bear all audit costs.
8.3. Provision of Data and Confidentiality
Some commenters argued that the audit right as proposed was problematic as it could require service providers to provide sensitive or proprietary information to auditors and responsible plan fiduciaries. Several commenters suggested that the final rule explicitly provide that covered services providers may limit use of data to the group health plan's purposes, noting that the new ERISA section 408(b)(2)(C) has similar language allowing reasonable restrictions (as determined by the Secretary) on confidentiality related to rebate contracts to prevent re-disclosure of such contracts
or use of such information in audits for purposes unrelated to the section
. The Department notes that the audit provision in the proposal addressed confidentiality concerns by allowing “reasonable confidentiality agreements to prevent redisclosure of such information.” However, the Department believes adding additional language may help alleviate these concerns, so it has revised the language in paragraph (j)(3) of the final rule to allow “reasonable confidentiality agreements to prevent redisclosure of such information and to limit use of such information for purposes related to the covered plan's contract or arrangement.”
[
189
]
Some commenters expressed concern about the volume of information that may be requested as part of the audit and asked the Department to confirm that statistically valid sampling methodologies would be permitted. Other commenters said that sampling could be used to obscure potentially improper transactions. For the reason cited by this commenter, the Department determined not to expressly permit sampling under the final rule;
(
printed page 69138)
but it notes that the audit provision is limited to “all records, claims and transaction-level data, and other information
reasonably necessary
to confirm the accuracy of any disclosure made to comply with this section . . . .” (Emphasis added).
Several commenters addressed access to claims and payment data. Some asked the Department to ensure that auditors would not be limited from accessing claims and payment data as needed for verifying the accuracy of the disclosures. Others suggested a more affirmative obligation to provide this information. As proposed, the audit provision required the covered service provider to make available to the auditor “all records, data, and other information reasonably necessary to confirm the accuracy of any disclosure made to comply with this section, including contracts with retail pharmacies and drug manufacturers . . . .” Although the Department believes that this language preserves access to data needed to confirm accuracy of disclosure, and that the rule is sufficiently tailored to require an audit of only that information used to produce the required disclosures, a reference to claims and transaction-level data was added to the final rule for avoidance of doubt. Paragraph (j)(3) of the final rule therefore provides that the covered service provider shall make available to the auditor “all records, claims and transaction-level data, and other information . . .” In sum, plan fiduciaries' auditors need access to material information to assess the quality and accuracy of the disclosures, as required in the rule, and the comments illustrate the need for an audit right. The Department believes that the audit provision in the rule is properly scoped to meet the needs of plan fiduciaries.
8.4. Timeframes
As in the proposed rule, the audit provision in the final rule preserves the right to an audit “[n]ot less than once per year.” This approach leaves it to the parties to define “year” for this purpose,
e.g.
, contract year, calendar year, or plan year. The Department invited comments on whether the final rule should be more prescriptive on this point. Some commenters said it would be helpful to specify whether the reference to year meant contract year, plan year, or calendar year to avoid unnecessary disputes. One commenter noted that the audit provision in new ERISA section 408(b)(2)(C) is based on a “plan year” and recommended that the Department align with that approach. Other commenters suggested that the parties should retain flexibility to define the relevant “year.” The Department determined after consideration of these comments to finalize the provision as proposed. The Department believes that allowing the parties flexibility to define the relevant year is preferable to specifying an approach that may not work for all covered plans.
Another commenter asked the Department to confirm that the language in proposed paragraph (j)(6), which provided that “the scope of the audit may be limited to the period covered by the disclosures under this section,” was intended to mean that the scope of the audit could be limited to the period after the effective date of the final rule as applied to the particular covered service provider arrangement. The Department agrees that is the intent of this language and has changed “may be” to “is” for additional certainty.
One commenter asked the Department to define the period within which audit materials must be produced. Under proposed paragraph (j)(5), covered service providers would be required to provide information reasonably necessary to confirm the accuracy of disclosures within a “commercially reasonable period.” The commenter said the phrase “commercially reasonable period” could lead to disputes about compliance. The commenter suggested that the final rule should specify that requested audit materials must be provided within a defined outside period, such as no more than 60 calendar days after receipt of the request, absent extraordinary circumstances. The Department agrees with this commenter that it is preferable to state a specific period for compliance, coupled with an exception for extraordinary circumstances, and therefore has adopted the suggested 60-day timeframe absent extraordinary circumstances beyond the covered service provider's control.
8.5. Compliance With the Audit Requirement
Several commenters raised issues related to compliance with the audit requirement. One commenter asked for confirmation that failure to provide information in compliance with the audit provision would result in a prohibited transaction. Another commenter asked the Department to include a safe harbor protecting covered service providers from liability when information held by affiliates, agents, or subcontractors is not produced due to circumstances outside the covered service provider's control, provided the covered service provider exercises reasonable diligence to obtain and provide such information. In response, the Department confirms that a covered service provider's failure to provide information in compliance with the audit provision would result in a prohibited transaction, absent availability of another prohibited transaction exemption. In that event, the administrative prohibited transaction exemption granted in paragraph (n) of the final rule would be available to the responsible plan fiduciary to avoid liability. The covered service provider could be subject to a civil penalty under ERISA section 502(i), which authorizes the Secretary to assess a civil penalty on a party in interest in the case of a transaction prohibited by ERISA section 406. The Department declines to offer a safe harbor for such covered service providers but notes that its authority under ERISA section 502(i) is discretionary.
9. Manner of Disclosure—Paragraph (k)
Paragraph (k)
[
190
]
includes four separate provisions regarding the manner of disclosures under the regulation. Each is discussed below.
9.1. Plain Language
Paragraph (k)(1) specifies that all disclosures must be clear and concise, free of misrepresentations, and contain sufficient specificity to permit evaluation of the reasonableness of the contract or arrangement. The paragraph further specifies that, for example, the Department will consider the use of generic industry terms, jargon, or legalese, without definition, to lack the sufficient specificity required under the preceding sentence unless the language in question specifically refers to objectively determinable definitions, standards, or other similar guidelines that are publicly available or will be provided by the covered service provider to the responsible plan fiduciary free of charge and within a reasonable period of time following the request.
Commenters said disclosures should be clear, concise, and presented in plain language so that plan fiduciaries could understand and use them. Another commenter recommended requiring PBMs and related entities to define proprietary, specialized, or industry-specific terminology in plain language or link such terms to objective definitions. The Department agrees and therefore finalized as proposed.
9.2. Description of Compensation
With respect to descriptions of compensation required under the final
(
printed page 69139)
rule, paragraph (k)(2) requires that they must be expressed as a monetary amount (for example, $1,000) and may be estimated to the extent that the actual amount is not reasonably ascertainable. However, the disclosure must contain sufficient information and specificity to permit evaluation of the reasonableness of the compensation received by the covered service provider, an affiliate, an agent, or a subcontractor. Several commenters supported the requirement that compensation be expressed as a monetary amount, describing it as the single most important provision of this rulemaking. These commenters argued that formulas, percentages, and benchmark-based descriptions could obscure actual dollar flows and hinder meaningful transparency. Some commenters noted that their individual company experience demonstrates that monetary transparency is both feasible and commercially viable.
A few commenters supported the Department's service provider disclosure regulation for pension plans (
29 CFR 2550.408b-2(c)(1)
) and the statutory provision at ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) framework in lieu of a monetary amount. However, many other commenters disagreed, stressing that formulas and percentages obscure actual dollars flowing to and from a covered plan. Several commenters suggested that, if the actual amount of compensation is not reasonably ascertainable, the estimated compensation should be grounded in a good faith assumption based on contractually defined methodologies, historical utilization, and rebate experience, or other reasonable information available at the time of disclosure. The Department agrees. Comments on the proposed paragraph (k)(2) and the Department's responses are discussed in section E.2.3 of this preamble.
9.3. Machine-Readability Format
Paragraph (k)(3) of the final rule provides that upon request of a responsible plan fiduciary, descriptions of compensation must be provided in a machine-readable file within a reasonable time after such request. The rule defines “machine-readable file” as a digital representation of data or information in a file that can be imported or read by a computer system for further processing without human intervention, while ensuring no semantic meaning is lost. This requirement is designed to ensure that a responsible plan fiduciary can obtain information in this format if the responsible plan fiduciary determines that this will aid in its evaluation of the reasonableness of the contract or arrangement. Therefore, the contract or arrangement may not foreclose responsible plan fiduciaries from selecting the machine-readable format.
The Department received comments supporting this provision in the proposal. One commenter said the “upon request” approach strikes the correct balance because not every responsible plan fiduciary will have the capacity to process machine-readable data so requiring that format for all disclosures would be too burdensome.
Several commenters supported the use of machine-readable files to help facilitate actuarial analysis, benchmarking, comparison, oversight, and access to claims detail. A few commenters, however, argued that machine-readable files impose significant technical infrastructure costs on covered service providers. Others supported alternative formats to machine-readable files such as PDF, excel (.xlsx) and .csv files. Commenters explained that plain language disclosures can improve usability and comprehension for plan fiduciaries. Some commenters suggested that covered service providers should be required to provide information in formats negotiated and agreed upon by the covered plan. Several commenters requested the Department to establish a uniform, machine-readable schema to improve comparability, reduce ambiguity, and enhance usability.
In addition, several commenters said the Department should provide technical specifications with respect to the machine-readable format, with one commenter asking the Department to clarify that the Department's Transparency in Covered (TiC) prescription drug machine-readable file requirements, once implemented, will be deemed sufficient. The Department agrees that machine-readable files can be useful to a responsible plan fiduciary but is finalizing the “upon request” structure to balance the need for transparency against the administrative burden of requiring machine-readable files as a default for every disclosure. For those responsible plan fiduciaries who request machine-readable files, the Department is considering future guidance to adopt a standardized disclosure framework under this rulemaking.
Some commenters requested that the Departments define what is a “reasonable time” under Paragraph (k)(3). Some suggested 30 days from the close of the most recent applicable semiannual period, or thirty days from the date of request, or whichever is sooner. The Department agrees that 30 days seems commercially reasonable but is declining to adopt a definition of “reasonable time” under this rulemaking given the limited number of comments it received.
9.4. Confidentiality Agreements
Paragraph (k)(4) addresses confidentiality agreements. The paragraph states that, except as provided in paragraph (j)(3), the covered service provider and its affiliates, agents, and subcontractors may not impose restrictions on the covered plan's use of disclosures required under this section, or the contract or arrangement described in paragraph (c)(1) of this section, with specific exceptions. Namely, the covered contract or arrangement may require the responsible plan fiduciary to require third parties with whom it shares the disclosures (and any subcontractors of the third parties) to execute reasonable confidentiality agreements that prevent redisclosure and also limit use of the disclosures to purposes related to the covered plan's contract or arrangement. Further, paragraph (k)(4)(ii) of the final rule adds language clarifying that neither paragraph (k)(4) nor paragraph (j)(3) would restrict a covered plan, auditor, or a third party hired by the plan, or their subcontractors, from sharing information with State or Federal Government regulators or with legal counsel, even if the activities of those entities are unrelated to the purpose of a covered plan's contract or arrangement.
The primary purpose of paragraph (k)(4) is to ensure that covered service providers are not able to undermine responsible plan fiduciaries' efforts to evaluate their compensation by limiting the covered plan's ability to meaningfully use information in the disclosures, for example, by restricting responsible plan fiduciaries from sharing the information with other plan service providers, such as third-party auditors, consultants, attorneys, or advisors, and such service providers' subcontractors, for quality control, evaluation, comparing, benchmarking, renegotiating, and other purposes. At the same time, paragraph (k)(4) would protect covered service providers by ensuring covered plans take steps to prevent redisclosure of the information by third parties with whom covered plans share the disclosures (and the third parties' subcontractors), and use of the disclosed information for purposes unrelated to the covered plan's contract or arrangement.
Comments on confidentiality agreements addressed both the use of the disclosures by responsible plan
(
printed page 69140)
fiduciaries and by third parties. Some commenters believed it was very important to ensure that covered service providers did not prevent responsible plan fiduciaries from using the disclosures to compare service provider offerings, for example, and from sharing the disclosures with third party service providers, such as consultants and legal counsel, or third-party subcontractors, such as data analytics service providers. Other commenters expressed concern about how third parties may use the information in the disclosures in other contexts and asked the Department to permit covered service providers to require reasonable confidentiality agreements governing the plan's use of the disclosed information, including limiting the use for fiduciary purposes only. Commenters also referenced confidentiality provisions in ERISA section 726 and suggested a similar approach in the final rule.
The Department believes that the approach taken in the proposal generally strikes the correct balance in ensuring that responsible plan fiduciaries may share information with third party service providers (and their subcontractors) but also preventing further redisclosure. In response to commenters' concerns about how the information might be used by third parties, the Department has added language to the final rule permitting confidentiality agreements to limit use of disclosure information “to purposes related to the covered plans contract or arrangement.” This is similar to language added in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(C) which permits, in the context of the audit provision, reasonable restrictions (as determined by the Secretary) on confidentiality to prevent redisclosure of disclosed rebate contracts or use of such information in audits “for purposes unrelated to this section.” Under this language, service providers would not be able to use the disclosures in contexts other than services to the covered plan (with the exception for State and Federal Government regulators). In combination with the confidentiality provisions in the final rule's audit provision (paragraph (j)(3)), the Department believes this should, in large part, address commenters' concerns about confidentiality. The Department is concerned that commenters' suggestions to limit covered plans' and responsible plan fiduciaries' use of disclosure information to fiduciary oversight purposes might allow covered service providers to unnecessarily intrude on responsible plan fiduciaries' contracting processes, or could have other unintended consequences, and therefore did not incorporate any such limits.

Under the final rule, no contract or arrangement will fail to be reasonable under the regulation solely because the covered service provider, acting in good faith and with reasonable diligence, makes an error or omission in disclosing the information required pursuant to paragraphs (e), (g), or (j), so long as the covered service provider discloses the correct information to the responsible plan fiduciary as soon as practicable, but not later than 30 calendar days from the date on which the covered service provider knows of such error or omission. Under ERISA section 726, Congress has set forth privacy protections when entities providing pharmacy benefit management services on behalf of group health plans are required to disclose information with respect to the compensation those entities receive for those services and for the costs of drugs they place on the group health plan's formulary. As discussed in section D. of this preamble, there are similarities between ERISA section 726 and this final rule in the information required to be disclosed and in the parties disclosing and receiving the information, and thus the same privacy concerns that arise under ERISA section 726 apply to the disclosures in this final rule under ERISA section 408(b)(2) as well. Therefore, the Department is of the view that the HIPAA privacy protections contained in ERISA section 726, including the limitation to summary health information, only applies to the disclosures under this final rule. 13. Consequences of Non-Compliance and Proposed Administrative Class Exemption for Responsible Plan Fiduciary—Paragraph (n)
13.1. Statutory Framework
As directed by President Trump's
Executive Order 14273
,
Lowering Drug Prices by Once Again Putting Americans First,
this final rule aims to promote transparent pricing and create a fairer and more competitive prescription drug market that lowers costs and ensures accountability across the healthcare system. Responsible plan fiduciaries of covered plans will be able to use the disclosures in their process of selecting a provider of pharmacy benefit management services, engaging an affiliated broker or consultant, monitoring these service providers' operations and compliance with contractual obligations, and in analyzing the drivers of prescription drug costs.
In this regard, responsible plan fiduciaries must determine that service provider relationships involving the covered plan meet certain conditions in an exemption to avoid constituting a prohibited transaction under ERISA. Specifically, unless an exemption applies, the furnishing of goods, services, or facilities between a self-insured group health plan and a party in interest to the plan is a prohibited transaction under ERISA section 406(a)(1)(C). A person providing services to the self-insured group health plan is defined by ERISA to be a “party in interest” to the self-insured group health plan.
ERISA section 408(b)(2) exempts certain arrangements between ERISA-covered plans (including larger self-insured group health plans) and service providers that otherwise would be prohibited transactions under ERISA section 406. Section 408(b)(2) provides relief from ERISA's prohibited transaction rules for service contracts or arrangements between a plan and a party in interest if the contract or arrangement is reasonable, the services are necessary for the establishment or operation of the plan, and no more than reasonable compensation is paid for the services.
If the terms of an exemption are not satisfied, responsible plan fiduciaries entering into service arrangements with parties in interest to self-insured group health plans, and the parties in interest themselves, may be subject to enforcement action by the Department and imposition of a civil penalty.
[
194
]
The Department's enforcement will be aided by the requirement in the administrative class exemption in paragraph (n) (discussed in the next section) that plan fiduciaries report to the Department a covered service provider's non-compliance with the disclosure or audit provisions.
A number of commenters on the Department's proposed rule raised concerns that the prohibited transaction framework under which the rule was proposed would result in insufficient incentives for compliance by providers of pharmacy benefit management services and, relatedly, that the final rule placed too much responsibility on responsible plan fiduciaries to identify noncompliance. Some commenters referenced the need for civil penalties. In the Department's view, the approach in the final rule will allow the Department to be alerted to instances of noncompliance, but that is not the only means by which noncompliance could be discovered; and, the Department retains its investigative authority under ERISA. In addition, as set forth above, the Department has authority under ERISA section 502(i) to assess a civil penalty against a party in interest in the event of a prohibited transaction.
13.2. Administrative Class Exemption
The Department recognizes that there may be circumstances when a responsible plan fiduciary enters into (or extends or renews) a contract or arrangement that appears to meet the requirements of this final rule under ERISA section 408(b)(2), but the covered service provider fails to comply with its obligations, including by not disclosing the required information or failing to comply with an audit request. Without

The Department proposed an administrative class exemption in paragraph (n) to provide relief for responsible plan fiduciaries in the event covered service providers fail to comply with the regulation, consistent with the approach in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B)(viii) and the Department's service provider regulation for pension plans (
29 CFR 2550.408b-2(c)(1)(ix)
), both of which provide exemptions for responsible plan fiduciaries who do not receive necessary disclosures from covered service providers to their ERISA-covered plans or are impeded in their right to access information related to the contract or arrangement as required under the regulation.
After consideration of comments, as discussed below, the Department has determined to adopt paragraph (n) in the final rule,

with minor modifications. The exemption provides responsible plan fiduciaries with relief from the restrictions of ERISA section 406(a)(1)(C) and (D) if, among other things, the responsible plan fiduciary did not know that the covered service provider failed to comply with the final rule and “reasonably believed” that the regulatory requirements were satisfied.

Upon discovery of a failure to comply, the responsible plan fiduciary must take certain specified steps within designated timeframes, as described in paragraphs (n)(1) and (2), including notifying the Department of any failures that are not corrected within the designated timeframes. In this way, the administrative class exemption will facilitate oversight by the Department of those covered service providers that fail to comply with the regulation. Paragraphs (n)(3) and (4) set forth the timing, content and other requirements applicable to the notice required to be filed with the Department by the responsible plan fiduciary. The Department notes that parties seeking to avail themselves of the relief provided by the exemption would need to be able to demonstrate compliance with the conditions of the exemption.
In the proposal, the Department requested comments on the administrative class exemption. The Department received several comments in support of the administrative class exemption and its protection for fiduciaries acting in good faith. While some commenters suggested that the full burden of a covered service provider's failure to provide complete and accurate disclosures should fall on the covered service provider, many appreciated the balance between ensuring transparency and avoiding unfair liability for circumstances outside of the responsible plan fiduciary's control.
Some commenters requested that the notifications received by the Department from responsible plan fiduciaries should be used to bring enforcement actions against providers of pharmacy benefit management services that engage in noncompliance, evasion, or unreasonable compensation practices. According to a commenter, this proactive approach is necessary to deter such providers from improper disclosure. While the Department is not making any changes to the text of paragraph (n) to address this comment, the Department reiterates its position from the proposal that “[t]he Department's enforcement will be aided by the requirement . . . that plan fiduciaries report to the Department a service provider's non-compliance with the disclosure or audit provisions.”

If the PBM does not comply with the requirements of the regulation, the responsible plan fiduciary would be required to name the TPA under the administrative exemption. The commenter expressed concern that this exposes the TPA to liability for failures outside their control and could chill TPA-PBM subcontracting arrangements. 13.3. Terminating the Contract
Paragraph (n)(5) of the administrative exemption addresses the potential that the responsible plan fiduciary would terminate the contract or arrangement in connection with the covered service provider's failure to comply with its obligations under the final rule. It provides that if the covered service provider fails to comply with the written request to correct the failure within 90 calendar days of such request, the responsible plan fiduciary shall determine whether to terminate or continue the contract or arrangement consistent with its duty of prudence under ERISA section 404 and shall document the basis for that determination.
This provision is based on a similar provision in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B)(viii)(IV), and the Department's service provider regulation for pension plans, but it does not include language from these sources that suggests that a responsible plan fiduciary must always terminate a contract or arrangement with a noncompliant covered service provider if the failure to disclose relates to future services. Although the provisions in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B)(viii)(IV) and the Department's service provider regulation for pension plans provide that the contract or arrangement must be terminated as “expeditiously as possible, consistent with the duty of prudence,” the Department is wary of imposing an absolute requirement to terminate a contract as a condition of obtaining the prohibited transaction relief under paragraph (n) because it could cause concerns about the
(
printed page 69144)
responsible plan fiduciary's ability to prudently provide for plan benefits. Such a requirement to terminate could be read as precluding a responsible plan fiduciary from continuing a contract or arrangement for some period even if, taking into account surrounding facts and circumstances, it reasonably determines that it would be prudent and in the best interest of participants and beneficiaries to do so.
The Department solicited comments on this approach in the proposal and received several comments supporting the proposed administrative exemption's flexible approach. Commenters emphasized that requiring termination of a service provider contract could harm plan participants, including by denying their continuity in access to benefits and health care services. One commenter requested the Department add a condition that, absent extraordinary circumstances, a contract or arrangement with a noncompliant service provider should not extend beyond the end of the current plan year without corrective action. Another commenter suggested that the provisions in paragraph (n)(5) describing the termination of a services contract or arrangement should apply only when the fiduciary believes the noncompliance is material and requested that the Department confirm that a plan fiduciary is not required to terminate a service arrangement based solely on a material disclosure deficiency. The Department does not agree that there should be a specific “extraordinary circumstances” or “materiality” requirement governing whether the contract or arrangement should continue beyond the plan year, but instead thinks it is appropriate to retain the overarching requirement that a fiduciary would make this determination consistent with its duties of prudence and loyalty.
Some commenters supported the Department's flexible approach, but suggested that, in order to ensure such flexibility is not abused, the Department should add a requirement that the responsible plan fiduciary document its analysis of whether it is prudent to continue a service or arrangement with a PBM that has failed to comply with the applicable conditions. Documentation would allow the Department to monitor whether responsible plan fiduciaries do terminate contracts and thus determine whether the flexibility is being abused by fiduciaries who fail to act on disclosed non-compliance.
The Department is revising paragraph (n) to add this documentation requirement. As granted, paragraph (n)(5) reads, “If the covered service provider fails to comply with the written request under paragraph (n)(1)(ii) of this section within 90 calendar days of such request, the responsible plan fiduciary shall determine whether to terminate or continue the service contract or arrangement consistent with its duty of prudence under section 404 of the Act, and shall document the basis for that determination.” This documentation should not be a mere check the box exercise, but reflect the responsible plan fiduciary's considerations, alternatives, and how the responsible plan fiduciary will ensure no further compliance failures. Responsible plan fiduciaries should also retain the documentation in case a need arises to demonstrate to the Department compliance with the administrative class exemption.
Some commenters expressed concern about the timing requirements in the proposed administrative exemption, particularly that responsible plan fiduciaries notify the Secretary within 90 calendar days of a covered service provider's failure to comply. One commenter asked about interim protections for plans and beneficiaries during the 90-day period. Another commenter said that 90 days is an insufficient remediation period because a responsible plan fiduciary may not be able to find a replacement service provider within 90 days and would risk losing exemption protection.
The Department notes that nothing in the exemption requires plan fiduciaries to terminate or even decide whether to terminate a services contract or arrangement within 90 days. Responsible plan fiduciaries are required to request in writing that the covered service provider correct the failure “upon discovering that the covered service provider failed to meet any requirement.” If the covered service provider fails to comply with that requirement within 90 calendar days of the request, then the responsible plan fiduciary must notify the Secretary of the failure and determine whether to terminate the contract. At all times, the responsible plan fiduciary must continue to act in the interests of the plan, its participants and beneficiaries.
13.4. Findings
The Department is granting the administrative class exemption in paragraph (n) pursuant to its authority under ERISA section 408(a) and in accordance with the procedures set forth in
29 CFR part 2570, subpart B
(
89 FR 4662
(Jan. 24, 2024)). The attention of interested persons is directed to the following: (1) the fact that a transaction is the subject of an exemption under ERISA section 408(a) does not relieve a fiduciary, or other party in interest with respect to a self-insured group health plan, from certain other provisions of ERISA, including any prohibited transaction provisions to which the exemption does not apply and the general fiduciary responsibility provisions of ERISA section 404 which require, among other things, that a fiduciary act prudently and discharge his or her duties respecting the plan solely in the interests of the participants and beneficiaries of the plan; (2) the Department finds that the administrative class exemption is administratively feasible, in the interests of self-insured group health plans and their participants and beneficiaries and protective of the rights of participants and beneficiaries of the self-insured group health plans; (3) the administrative class exemption is applicable only to transactions that satisfy the conditions specified in the exemption; and (4) the administrative class exemption is supplemental to, and not in derogation of, any other provisions of ERISA, including statutory or administrative exemptions and transitional rules. Furthermore, the fact that a transaction is subject to an administrative or statutory exemption is not dispositive of whether the transaction is in fact a prohibited transaction.
14. Statutory Authority for and Placement of the Final Rule
14.1. Statutory Authority
Section 408(b)(2)(A) of ERISA exempts from the prohibitions of ERISA section 406(a) “reasonable” contracts or arrangements with a party in interest, including a fiduciary, for office space, or legal, accounting, or other services necessary for the establishment or operation of the plan, if no more than reasonable compensation is paid. Section 408(b)(2)(B) of ERISA clarifies that, in the case of a covered service provider who provides services to group health plans no such contract or arrangement is “reasonable” unless the disclosure requirements in subparagraph (iii) of section 408(b)(2)(B) of ERISA are satisfied.
As originally enacted, ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) described two categories of covered service providers to group health plans, namely providers of “brokerage services” and “consulting services” with respect to certain sub-services, although these terms were undefined. CAA, 2026 amended ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) and broadened its scope to make clear that it encapsulated
(
printed page 69145)
a much wider array of covered service providers who provide services to group health plans, including providers of pharmacy benefit management services.
[
200
]
It also provided specific regulatory authority to the Secretary of Labor to address time, manner, and content of disclosures under that subsection.
[
201
]
Therefore, the Department is relying on its authority to regulate entities providing pharmacy benefit management services and entities providing advice, recommendations, or referrals regarding the provision of pharmacy benefit management services, and who are affiliated with providers of pharmacy benefit management services, pursuant to sections 505 and 408(b)(2)(B) of ERISA.
Several commenters argue the Department exceeded the statutory authority granted to it in ERISA section 408(b)(2) by extending beyond direct compensation paid by the plan for services. The Department disagrees.
As discussed in section C of this preamble, section 408(b)(2) provides relief from ERISA's prohibited transaction rules for service contracts or arrangements between a plan and a party in interest if the contract or arrangement is reasonable, the services are necessary for the establishment or operation of the plan, and no more than reasonable compensation is paid for the services. Section 408(b)(2)(B)(iii) closely tracks the Department's regulation for pension plan services arrangements. It requires covered service providers to group health plans to disclose the following to take advantage of the exemption: the services to be provided; the status of the covered service provider, an affiliate, or subcontractor as a fiduciary, if applicable; the direct and indirect compensation reasonably expected to be received by the covered service provider, their affiliates and their subcontractors; as well as allocations of compensation reasonably expected to be made among the covered service providers and its affiliates and subcontractors.
Several commenters noted that Congress acted in the CAA, 2026 amendments specifically to clarify the meaning and scope of “services” under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B). According to a comment submitted by the U.S. House Committee on Education and the Workforce in response to this rulemaking, Congress replaced the narrow “brokerage” and “consulting” terminology with a detailed and expansive list of services to confirm that ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) reaches the full range of services that affect plan participants' access to and cost of health benefits. To put it another way, Congress made these changes to section 408(b)(2)(B) so that covered service providers performing
any
of the services enumerated in the statute must disclose both direct and indirect compensation to a group health plan.
[
202
]
The Department is of the view that the CAA, 2026 did not alter these substantive disclosure obligations. Furthermore, in specifying that the disclosure obligation under the exemption extends to “indirect compensation,” Congress clearly intended that payments from third parties and the related arrangements under which such payments are made are appropriate and necessary subjects of disclosure. The Department is well within its authority to require disclosure of payments from, and arrangements with, drug manufacturers, third party administrators, and others. For these reasons, the Department disagrees that it exceeded the statutory authority granted to it in ERISA section 408(b)(2) by extending beyond direct compensation paid by the plan for services.
Several commenters also argue that ERISA section 726, as enacted by the CAA, 2026, preempts or limits the Department's ability to engage in this rulemaking. The Department disagrees.
As discussed in section D of this preamble, Congress added ERISA section 726, as part of the CAA, 2026. ERISA section 726 establishes new disclosure and reporting obligations for entities that provide pharmacy benefit management services to group health plans and health insurance issuers in Part VII of ERISA, outside of the prohibited transaction framework in Part IV of ERISA.
As one stakeholder commented, section 726 of the CAA, 2026 contains no preemptive language; it does not prohibit the Department from rulemaking under ERISA section 408(b)(2), nor does it state that its provisions are exclusive or that other disclosure regimes are barred. Congress was aware of the
E.O. 14273
(Apr. 2025) directing the Department to improve employer health plan fiduciary transparency through rulemaking. Prior to enacting the CAA, 2026, Congress could have prohibited the Department from rulemaking under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B) or it could have included preemptive language—it intentionally did not. Instead, Congress
doubled down
and strengthened the Secretary's authority to issue regulations governing the time, manner, and content of the required disclosures by covered services providers to group health plans required under ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B)(iii).
Even so, in addition to its authority under ERISA section 408(b)(2), the Department has the express authority under ERISA section 505 to “prescribe such regulation as [it] finds necessary and appropriate” and to “define accounting, technical and trade terms.” This authority is undisturbed by the new provisions of the CAA, 2026.
For these reasons, the Department disagrees that Congress preempted this rule or limited the Department's rulemaking authority by passing ERISA section 726, as enacted by the CAA, 2026.
A few commenters argued that the Department failed to provide adequate notice of its legal theory after the passage of the CAA, 2026. The Department disagrees. Contrary to commenters' assertions, the proposed rule clearly identified ERISA section 408(b)(2) and section 505 as the source of the Department's authority to prescribe these regulations.
A few commenters also asserted that the Department somehow changed its legal theory when it extended the comment period for this rule by 15 days, following the enactment of the CAA, 2026. This mischaracterizes the Department's actions. After Congress enacted the CAA, 2026, the Department extended the comment period for 15 days for the express purpose of allowing stakeholders to evaluate and comment on whether the rule should be adjusted due to the new statutory provisions. The Department chose to draw the public's attention to the CAA, 2026 and specifically seek comments on the interaction with the proposal to ensure robust public input on that matter. Commenters had notice and a full opportunity to submit comments on the interaction with the CAA, 2026, including the statutory authority, as evidenced by the substantial volume of
(
