AGENCY:
U.S. International Trade Commission.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
Notice is hereby given that the U.S. International Trade Commission (“Commission”) has determined to review-in-part a final initial determination (“FID”) of the presiding administrative law judge (“ALJ”). The Commission requests briefing from the parties on certain issues under review, as set forth in this notice. The Commission also requests written submissions from the parties, interested government agencies, and other interested persons on the issues of remedy, the public interest, and bonding, under the schedule set forth below. The Commission has also determined to extend the target date for completion of the investigation to January 14, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jonathan D. Link, Esq., Office of the General Counsel, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436, telephone (202) 205-3103. Copies of non-confidential documents filed in connection with this investigation may be viewed on the Commission's electronic docket (EDIS) at
https://edis.usitc.gov
.
For help accessing EDIS, please email
EDIS3Help@usitc.gov
.
General information concerning the Commission may also be obtained by accessing its internet server at
https://www.usitc.gov
.
Hearing-impaired persons are advised that information on this matter can be obtained by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal on (202) 205-1810.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Commission instituted this investigation on June 23, 2025, based on a complaint filed on behalf of Estelgia, LLC (“Estelgia”) of Dover, Delaware.
90 FR 26608-09
(June 23, 2025). The complaint, as supplemented, alleges violations of section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended,
19 U.S.C. 1337
(“section 337”), in the importation into the United States, the sale for importation, and the sale within the United States after importation of certain Wi-Fi routers, Wi-Fi devices, mesh Wi-Fi network devices and components thereof by reason of the infringement of certain claims of U.S. Patent Nos. 7,936,714 (“the '714 patent”); 11,246,016 (“the '016 patent”); 10,735,973 (“the '973 patent”); 10,531,518 (“the '518 patent”); 9,775,164 (“the '164 patent”); and 9,277,591 (“the '591 patent”). The complaint, as supplemented, further alleges that an industry in the United States exists as required by the applicable Federal Statute. The Commission's notice of investigation names seven (7) respondents: Linksys Holdings, Inc. and Linksys USA, Inc. (collectively, “Linksys Respondents”) of Irvine, CA; ASUStek Computer Inc. of Taipei City, Taiwan and ASUS Computer International of Fremont, CA (collectively “ASUS”); D-Link Corporation of Taipei, Taiwan and D-Link Systems, Inc. of Irvine, CA (collectively, “D-Link Respondents”); and Plume Design Inc. (“Plume”) of Palo Alto, CA.
Id.
at 26609. The Office of Unfair Import Investigations (“OUII”) is also named as a party in this investigation.
On December 19, 2025, the Commission terminated the Linksys Respondents from the investigation based on a settlement agreement.
See
Order No. 12 (Nov. 25, 2025),
unreviewed by
Comm'n Notice (Dec. 19, 2025).
On January 29, 2026, the Commission terminated claim 14 of the '714 patent; claims 1-5, 7-17, and 20 the '016 patent; claims 2, 3, 5-7, 10, and 13 of the '973 patent; claims 12 and 13 of the '518 patent; claims 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13-15, 17-21, 23, 25, 27, 28, and 30-33 of the '164 patent; and claims 1, 2, 5, 9, 10, 12, and 14-20 of the '591 patent from the investigation based on the withdrawal of allegations by Estelgia.
See
Order No. 17 (Jan. 6, 2026),
unreviewed by
Comm'n Notice (Jan. 29, 2026).
On March 17, 2026, the Commission terminated the '016, the '518, the '164, and the '591 patents from the investigation based on the withdrawal of allegations by Estelgia.
See
Order No. 20 (Feb. 19, 2026),
unreviewed by
Comm'n Notice (Mar. 17, 2026).
On April 27, 2026, the Commission terminated the D-Link Respondents from the investigation based on a consent order.
See
Order No. 30 (Mar. 26, 2026),
unreviewed by
Comm'n Notice (Apr. 27, 2026).
On August 6, 2026, the ALJ issued the FID finding a violation of section 337 by respondents ASUS and Plume (collectively “Respondents”). On August 18, 2026, Respondents and OUII each filed a petition for review of the FID, while Estelgia filed a contingent petition for review. On August 26, 2026, Estelgia and Respondents each filed responses. On September 2, 2026, OUII filed its response.
Having reviewed the record of the investigation, including the FID and the parties' submissions to the ALJ and to the Commission, the Commission has determined to review-in-part the FID. Specifically, the Commission has determined to review the FID's findings on (1) the construction of the preamble of claim 13 of the '714 patent and related subsidiary findings, including infringement by ASUS and Plume and the technical prong of the domestic industry requirement; (2) indirect infringement by ASUS of claim 13 of the '714 patent; (3) infringement by ASUS and Plume and the technical prong of the domestic industry requirement for the claim elements “prioritizing the one or more channels . . . based on the measured channel condition” and “assigning . . . at least one channel having a lower priority to a second UE having a lower priority for communication” in the asserted claim of the '973 patent; (4) written description and obviousness of the '973 patent; and (5) the economic prong of the domestic industry requirement.
The Commission has determined not to review, and thus adopts, the FID's findings regarding invalidity for the '714 patent. With respect to the FID's finding that Sorrells-836 in view of Sorrells-296 does not render claim 13 of the '714 patent obvious, the Commission has further determined that Respondents did not present in their post-hearing briefs the additional arguments in Respondents' petition for review regarding a motivation to use MMDS and IEEE 802.11, and therefore Respondents have waived these arguments. The Commission has determined not to review the remainder of the FID's findings.
The Commission has also determined to extend the target date for completion of the investigation to January 14, 2027.
Finally, the Commission requests a response to the following questions. The parties are requested to brief their positions with reference to the applicable law and the existing evidentiary record.
(1) For the '973 patent, whether the “based on” language in claim elements 1[d] and 8[f] has a different meaning than the “based, at least in part, on”
(
printed page 68979)
language in claim elements 1[b], 1[e], 1[f], 8[d], 8[g], and 8[h].
(2) For the '973 patent, explain whether the FID's finding regarding written description that “both parties' experts acknowledge that `when you're prioritizing a band, and you're selecting a band, you're selecting a channel in a band. You don't transmit or communicate on a band. You communicate on channels in bands' ” (FID at 137) can be reconciled with its obviousness finding that “Novak's network may comprise `multiple bands,' including `the interleaved communication channels of the TV bands'—but it does not disclose prioritization of the channels, as opposed to the bands” (FID at 167)
(3) Explain whether Estelgia submitted into evidence any foreign plant and equipment and/or labor or capital investments, including contract manufacturing, relating to manufacturing of the DI products and whether Estelgia provided any DI economic prong analysis that considers such foreign investments.
(4) Please discuss the following statutory terms and the evidence of record pertaining to these terms:
a. whether the statutory language of section 337(a)(3)(A) “plant and equipment,” in view of the legislative history and judicial precedents, defines the physical “plant and equipment” to be limited to land, buildings, machinery, apparatus, and fixtures employed in the physical production or industrial activity in the United States concerning articles protected by the asserted patents;
b. whether the statutory language of section 337(a)(3)(B) “employment of labor,” in view of the legislative history and judicial precedents is confined to the employment of a subset of workers who are wage earners engaged in physical production or industrial activity in the United States with respect to articles protected by the asserted patents;
c. whether the statutory language of section 337(a)(3)(B) “employment of . . . capital,” in view of the legislative history and judicial precedents, is confined to the employment of capital goods and capital expenditures not otherwise accounted for by categories of capital assets and expenditures other than those recited in subsections 337(a)(3)(A) or (C); and
d. whether the evidence of investments and employment in the categories so defined indicates that they are “significant” as required in subsections 337(a)(3)(A) and (B).
The parties are invited to brief only the discrete issues requested above. The parties are not to brief other issues on review, which are adequately presented in the parties' existing filings.
In connection with the final disposition of this investigation, the statute authorizes issuance of,
inter alia,
(1) an exclusion order that could result in the exclusion of the subject articles from entry into the United States; and/or (2) cease and desist orders that could result in the respondents being required to cease and desist from engaging in unfair acts in the importation and sale of such articles. Accordingly, the Commission is interested in receiving written submissions that address the form of remedy, if any, that should be ordered. If a party seeks exclusion of an article from entry into the United States for purposes other than entry for consumption, the party should so indicate and provide information establishing that activities involving other types of entry either are adversely affecting it or likely to do so. For background, see
Certain Devices for Connecting Computers via Telephone Lines,
Inv. No. 337-TA-360, USITC Pub. No. 2843, Comm'n Op. at 7-10 (Dec. 1994).
The statute requires the Commission to consider the effects of that remedy upon the public interest. The public interest factors the Commission will consider include the effect that an exclusion order and a cease and desist order would have on: (1) the public health and welfare, (2) competitive conditions in the U.S. economy, (3) U.S. production of articles that are like or directly competitive with those that are subject to investigation, and (4) U.S. consumers. The Commission is therefore interested in receiving written submissions that address the aforementioned public interest factors in the context of this investigation.
If the Commission orders some form of remedy, the U.S. Trade Representative, as delegated by the President, has 60 days to approve, disapprove, or take no action on the Commission's determination.
See
Presidential Memorandum of July 21, 2005,
70 FR 43251
(July 26, 2005). During this period, the subject articles would be entitled to enter the United States under bond, in an amount determined by the Commission and prescribed by the Secretary of the Treasury. The Commission is therefore interested in receiving submissions concerning the amount of the bond that should be imposed if a remedy is ordered.
Written Submissions:
The parties to the investigation are requested to file written submissions on the questions identified in this notice. Parties to the investigation, interested government agencies, and any other interested parties are encouraged to file written submissions on the issues of remedy, the public interest, and bonding. Such submissions should address the recommended determination by the ALJ on remedy and bonding.
In its initial submission, Complainant is also requested to identify the remedy sought and Complainant is requested to submit proposed remedial orders for the Commission's consideration. Complainant is further requested to provide the HTSUS subheadings under which the accused products are imported, and to supply the identification information for all known importers of the products at issue in this investigation. All initial written submissions, from the parties and/or third parties/interested government agencies, and proposed remedial orders from the parties must be filed no later than close of business on November 12, 2026. All reply submissions must be filed no later than the close of business on November 19, 2026. Opening submissions from the parties are limited to 30 pages. Reply submissions from the parties are limited to 15 pages. All submissions from third parties and/or interested government agencies are limited to 10 pages. No further submissions on any of these issues will be permitted unless otherwise ordered by the Commission.
Persons filing written submissions must file the original document electronically on or before the deadlines stated above pursuant to
19 CFR 210.4(f)
. Submissions should refer to the investigation number (Inv. No. 337-TA-1454) in a prominent place on the cover page and/or the first page. (
See
Handbook for Electronic Filing Procedures,
https://www.usitc.gov/​documents/​handbook_​on_​filing_​procedures.pdf
). Persons with questions regarding filing should contact the Secretary, (202) 205-2000.
Any person desiring to submit a document to the Commission in confidence must request confidential treatment by marking each document with a header indicating that the document contains confidential information. This marking will be deemed to satisfy the request procedure set forth in Rules 201.6(b) and 210.5(e)(2) (
19 CFR 201.6(b)
& 210.5(e)(2)). Documents for which confidential treatment by the Commission is properly sought will be treated accordingly. Any non-party wishing to submit comments containing confidential information must serve those comments on the parties to the investigation pursuant to the applicable
(
printed page 68980)
Administrative Protective Order. A redacted non-confidential version of the document must also be filed with the Commission and served on any parties to the investigation within two business days of any confidential filing. All information, including confidential business information and documents for which confidential treatment is properly sought, submitted to the Commission for purposes of this investigation may be disclosed to and used: (i) by the Commission, its employees and Offices, and contract personnel (a) for developing or maintaining the records of this or a related proceeding, or (b) in internal investigations, audits, reviews, and evaluations relating to the programs, personnel, and operations of the Commission including under 5 U.S.C. Appendix 3; or (ii) by U.S. government employees and contract personnel, solely for cybersecurity purposes. All contract personnel will sign appropriate nondisclosure agreements. All nonconfidential written submissions will be available for public inspection on EDIS.
The Commission vote for this determination took place on October 28, 2026.
The authority for the Commission's determination is contained in section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (
19 U.S.C. 1337
), and in Part 210 of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure (
19 CFR part 210
).
By order of the Commission.
Issued: October 28, 2026.
Lisa Barton,
Secretary to the Commission.

AGENCY:
Office of Child Care, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
ACTION:
Request for public comments.
SUMMARY:
The Administration for Children and Families (ACF) is requesting a 3-year reinstatement with changes to information collection: Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) Quality Progress Report (QPR)—(Office of Management and Budget #0970-0517, expiration December 31, 2024).
DATES:
Comments due January 4, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
In compliance with the requirements of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, ACF is soliciting public comment on the specific aspects of the information collection described above. You can obtain copies of the proposed collection of information and submit comments by emailing
infocollection@acf.hhs.gov
.
Identify all requests by the title of the information collection.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Description:
The CCDF QPR annually collects information from states and territories to describe investments to improve the quality of care available for children from birth to age 13. This report is one of the primary oversight mechanisms for an estimated $4.2 billion in CCDF funding invested in overall quality improvement activities and $605 million in CCDF funding in fiscal year 2023 dedicated to improving the supply and quality of care for infants and toddlers. The report meets the requirements in the Child Care and Development Block Grant (CCDBG) Act of 2014 for Lead Agencies to submit an annual report that describes how quality funds were expended, including the activities carried out and the measures used to evaluate progress in improving the quality of child care programs and services.
Outcomes from the information collected will primarily be used to support program administration and oversight and inform technical assistance and support for states and territories.
The new form reduces duplication and the overall volume of information requested from states compared to prior years, and asks clearer, more specific questions with examples to better capture quantitative outcomes, while continuing to collect information that is required by law.

Unified Carrier Registration Plan
TIME AND DATE:
November 5, 2026, 10:30 a.m.-2:30 p.m., Eastern time.
PLACE:
This meeting will be held at the Graduate by Hilton Providence, 11 Dorrance Street, Providence, RI 02903.
STATUS:
This meeting will be open to the public.
MATTERS TO BE CONSIDERED:
The Unified Carrier Registration Plan Governance Task Force (the “Task Force”) will conduct a meeting to continue its work in developing and implementing the Unified Carrier Registration Plan and Agreement. The subject matter of this meeting will include:
PROPOSED AGENDA
I. Call to Order—UCR Plan Governance Task Force Chair
The UCR Governance Task Force Chair will welcome attendees, call the meeting to order, call roll for the task force, confirm whether a quorum is present, and facilitate self-introductions.
II. Verification of Publication of Meeting Notice—UCR Executive Director
The UCR Executive Director will verify the publication of the meeting notice on the UCR website and distribution to the UCR contact list via email followed by the subsequent publication of the notice in the
Federal Register
.
III. Review and Approval of Task Force Agenda and Setting of Ground Rules—UCR Plan Governance Task Force Chair
For Discussion and Possible Task Force Action
The Governance Task Force Agenda will be reviewed, and the Task Force will consider adoption.

I. Executive Summary
A. Purpose and Coverage of the Proposed Rule
Under Operation Stork Speed, FDA is taking steps to enhance its efforts to ensure the ongoing quality, safety, nutritional adequacy, and resilience of the domestic infant formula supply (
https://www.fda.gov/​food/​infant-formula-homepage/​operation-stork-speed
). As part of this effort, FDA conducted a scientific review of a subset of nutrient requirements for infant formula to ensure that infant formula provides adequate nutrition to support the growth and development of infants from birth through 12 months of age while avoiding excessive intakes that could pose health risks. This is the first comprehensive update and review of infant formula nutrients by the FDA since 1998 and part of FDA's strategic, phased approach to evaluating available scientific evidence for a comprehensive review of infant formula nutrients, as announced as part of Operation Stork Speed. This proposed rule assesses 8 of the 30 required nutrients in infant formula. The proposed rule, if finalized, would amend the minimum and/or maximum levels of four required nutrients—iodine, vitamin A, vitamin D, and manganese—and establish a maximum level for manganese. Additionally, the proposed rule, if finalized, would change the unit of measure for vitamin A and vitamin D, change the permitted source to meet the vitamin A requirement, and amend the content of the required labeling. This action also includes a comprehensive assessment of four additional nutrients—chloride, selenium, potassium, and sodium—for which we conclude that the current required levels remain appropriate. FDA intends to address the remaining infant formula nutrient specifications through subsequent proposed rules followed by one final rule covering all infant formula nutrient requirement changes. Lastly, the proposed rule, if finalized, would amend infant formula labeling requirements to change the unit of measure for vitamin A from International Units (IU) to microgram Retinol Activity Equivalents (μg RAE), and change the unit of measure for vitamin D from IU to micrograms (μg). The rule would also provide that vitamin A and vitamin D content may be voluntarily declared in IU in parentheses immediately following the declarations in μg RAE and μg, respectively.
Additionally, in accordance with the OMB “Final Information Quality Bulletin for Peer Review” (
https://www.federalregister.gov/​documents/​2005/​01/​14/​05-769/​final-information-quality-bulletin-for-peer-review
), FDA intends to conduct an external peer review on all influential scientific information used to inform development of any final rule.
B. Summary of the Major Provisions of the Proposed Rule
The proposed rule, if finalized, would:
Increase the required minimum level of iodine in infant formula from 5 µg/100 kilocalories (kcal) to 15 µg/100 kcal and decrease the required maximum level of iodine from 75 µg/100 kcal to 50 µg/100 kcal;
Change the unit of measure for vitamin A in infant formula from IU to μg RAE (1 IU retinol = 0.3 μg RAE);
Decrease the required minimum level of vitamin A in infant formula from 250 IU/100 kcal (75 μg RAE/100 kcal) to 70 μg RAE/100 kcal (233 IU/100 kcal) and decrease the required maximum level from 750 IU/100 kcal (225 μg RAE/100 kcal) to 120 μg RAE/100 kcal (400 IU/100 kcal);
Limit permitted forms of vitamin A that contribute to minimum and maximum vitamin A content from both preformed vitamin A and
beta
-carotene to preformed vitamin A only;
Change the unit of measure for vitamin D in infant formula from IU to μg (1 IU = 0.025 μg);
Increase the required minimum level of vitamin D in infant formula from 40 IU/100 kcal (1 μg/100 kcal) to 2 μg/100 kcal (80 IU/100 kcal) and increase the required maximum level from 100 IU/100 kcal (2.5 μg/100 kcal) to 3 μg/100 kcal (120 IU/100 kcal);
Decrease the required minimum level for manganese in infant formula from 5 μg/100 kcal to 1 μg/100 kcal and establish a maximum level for manganese in infant formula of 50 μg/100 kcal.
C. Legal Authority
We are issuing this proposed rule consistent with our authority in sections 201(z), 403(j), 412(i), and 701(e) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) (
21 U.S.C. 321(z)
,
343(j)
,
350a(i)
, and
371(e)
).
D. Costs and Benefits
This proposed rule, if finalized, would update the nutrient specifications for infant formula to reflect the best available scientific evidence on infant nutritional requirements and safe intake levels. Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin essential for calcium absorption, skeletal mineralization, and the prevention of rickets. Clinical symptoms of vitamin D deficiency include hypocalcemia (
i.e.,
low blood calcium levels), hypophosphatemia (
i.e.,
low blood phosphorus levels), tetany, and rickets. We quantify benefits to formula-fed infants from avoided healthcare costs associated with vitamin D deficiency-induced late-onset hypocalcemia. This approach captures the most severe and acute clinical manifestation of vitamin D deficiency and therefore represents a lower bound on the rule's total societal benefits. Additional benefits include reduced risk of inadequate iodine intake, excessive vitamin A exposure, and excessive manganese exposure in formula-fed infants; these benefits are described qualitatively. We quantify costs to infant formula manufacturers from relabeling, reformulation, and administrative costs associated with Before First Processing notification submissions. Additional costs would include FDA review costs associated with those submissions. We estimate that the annualized benefits over 10 years would range from $18.8 million to $171.7 million, with a primary estimate of $80.9 million, at a 7 percent discount rate and from $20.9 million to $191.0 million, with a primary estimate of $90.0 million, at a 3 percent discount rate. The annualized costs would range from $8.4 million to $31.7 million, with a primary estimate of $17.6 million, at a 7 percent discount rate and from $8.3 million to $31.6 million, with a primary estimate of $17.6 million, at a 3 percent discount rate.

III. Background
The Infant Formula Act of 1980 added section 412 of the FD&C Act, establishing requirements for infant formulas, including nutrient content requirements, and authorizing the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) to revise these requirements. In the
Federal Register
of October 30, 1985 (
50 FR 45106
), FDA issued a final rule revising the infant formula nutrient requirements of the Infant Formula Act of 1980 (Pub. L. 96-359, 94 Stat. 1190), which was codified at § 107.100 (
21 CFR 107.100
). In 1995, FDA's Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition (CFSAN), now known as the Human Foods Program (HFP), contracted the Life Sciences Research Office (LSRO) of the American Society for Nutritional Sciences to provide evidence-based recommendations on compositional requirements for infant formula, with Health Canada serving as a cosponsor. The assessment was conducted in consultation with expert scientists and professional organizations. The 1998 LSRO Panel report represents our last comprehensive review of the required infant formula nutrients although comprehensive updates to the nutrient requirements were not proposed after the report (Ref. 1). In 2015, we updated the table in § 107.100 to add the mineral selenium to the list of required nutrients and to establish minimum and maximum levels of selenium in infant formula (
80 FR 35834
, June 23, 2015). The table in § 107.100 specifies that infant formulas must contain 30 nutrients; the table specifies minimum levels for each nutrient and maximum levels for 10 of the 30 nutrients.
On March 18, 2025, HHS and FDA announced “Operation Stork Speed,” a set of actions and initiatives to expand options for safe, reliable, and nutritious infant formula for American families, including a comprehensive infant formula nutrient review (
https://www.fda.gov/​food/​infant-formula-homepage/​operation-stork-speed
).
On May 14, 2025, FDA issued a Request for Information (RFI) as a first step in the comprehensive nutrient review process (
90 FR 20475
, May 14, 2025). Specifically, the RFI sought information that would help us determine whether there is a need to revise the existing nutrient requirements in § 107.100, taking into consideration any new scientific data or information related to infant formula nutrients, including international infant formula standards. The comment period closed on September 11, 2025.
IV. Legal Authority
Section 412(i) of the FD&C Act establishes requirements for the nutrient content of infant formula. Section 412(i) of the FD&C Act contains a table listing the required infant formula nutrients with respective minimum and, as applicable, maximum required levels. Section 412(i)(2) of the FD&C Act authorizes the Secretary, and by delegation the Commissioner of Food and Drugs (Commissioner), to revise the list of required nutrients and to revise the level of any required nutrient. In addition, section 412(i)(1) of the FD&C Act, as amended by the Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act of 2022 (commonly referred to as FDORA (
Pub. L. 117-328
)), requires the Secretary, and by delegation the Commissioner, to review the table of required nutrients “every 4 years as appropriate,” taking into consideration “any new scientific data or information related to infant formula nutrients, including international infant formula standards.” The table of required nutrients is codified at § 107.100.
The nutrition information labeling requirements for infant formula are codified at § 107.10 (
21 CFR 107.10
). If finalized, the proposed rule would amend the label required in § 107.10(a)(2) to change the unit of measure for vitamin A in infant formula from IU to μg RAE and to change the unit of measure for vitamin D in infant formula from IU to μg. The rule would also amend § 107.10(b)(1) to provide that vitamin A and vitamin D content may be voluntarily declared in IU in parentheses immediately following the declarations in μg RAE and μg, respectively. “Infant formula” is defined as a food for “special dietary use” under section 201(z) of the FD&C Act. Under sections 403(j) and 701(e) of the FD&C Act for foods for special dietary uses, the Secretary, and by delegation the Commissioner, may prescribe regulations requiring information concerning the vitamin and mineral content of the food to be provided on the label to fully inform purchasers as to the value of the food for such uses. Thus, FDA has the authority to revise the statement of the content of nutrients required for infant formula labeling in § 107.10 under sections 201(z), 403(j), 412(i), and 701(e) of the FD&C Act. If the proposed revisions to § 107.10 are finalized, FDA will provide an opportunity for filing objections and requests for a formal evidentiary public hearing under
21 CFR part 12
.
V. Description of the Proposed Rule
A. Scope
The proposed rule, if finalized, would apply to products that meet the statutory definition of “infant formula” in section 201(z) of the FD&C Act. Section 201(z) of the FD&C Act defines infant formula as “a food which purports to be or is represented for special dietary use solely as a food for infants by reason of its simulation of human milk or its suitability as a complete or partial substitute for human milk.” FDA regulations define an “infant” as a person not more than 12 months of age (
21 CFR 105.3(e)
and
106.3
).
B. Approach and Assumptions Used in Scientific Assessments
The proposed rule evaluates eight of the 30 required nutrients in infant formula. For each nutrient, FDA reviewed the physiological role and health consequences of deficiency or excess, relevant nutrient reference values from major expert bodies, human milk composition data, international regulatory standards, and recent scientific evidence. This nutrient-by-nutrient approach culminates in an evidence evaluation and rationale section that explains FDA's basis for either proposing changes to current minimum and/or maximum specifications or concluding that existing levels remain appropriate.
In sections V.C through V.J of this document, we present FDA's nutrient-specific evaluations, including the scientific basis for proposed changes to minimum and maximum specifications and the rationale for maintaining current specifications where appropriate. These nutrient-specific
(
printed page 69044)
evaluations are based on comprehensive nutrient-specific assessments, which we reference herein and have included in the docket. As required by section 412(i)(1) of the FD&C Act, FDA considered scientific information and data since the last comprehensive review of infant formula in 1998 as well as infant formula nutrient requirements in international standards. FDA also reviewed and considered comments submitted in response to the RFI.
FDA conducted a comprehensive evidence scan of peer-reviewed literature using the PubMed database to identify English-language publications regarding chloride, iodine, manganese, potassium, selenium, sodium, vitamin A, and vitamin D. Searches were individually constructed to account for the distinct characteristics of each nutrient. The queries utilized specific Medical Subject Headings (commonly referred to as MeSH) and keywords focused on general pharmacokinetics, nutritional requirements, deficiency, and toxicity for human infants 0 to 12 months of age. To capture updated evidence, search parameters targeted literature published from the end of the previous 1998 LSRO report review periods through May 2026. This corresponded to search start dates of 1989 for manganese; 1992 for vitamin D; 1995 for chloride, potassium, sodium, vitamin A, and iodine; and 2015 for selenium, which corresponds to FDA”s final rule, “The Addition of Minimum and Maximum Levels of Selenium to Infant Formula and Related Labeling Requirements” (
80 FR 35834
, June 23, 2015). FDA considered study design among other factors when prioritizing the literature reviewed, which included meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials, clinical trials, and observational studies. While, for example, traditional literature reviews and case reports were generally excluded from the primary evidence scan used to evaluate nutrient specifications, FDA notes that such literature was incorporated where necessary to provide clinical, historical, or toxicological context. The population of interest focused on healthy, full-term infants. This target population included infants with low birth weight or who were small for gestational age but excluded preterm infants and those with conditions requiring specialized formulas. Finally, the selected outcomes prioritized evidence regarding minimum dietary requirements, maximum safe levels, clinical signs of deficiency or toxicity, and adverse nutrient interactions.
To evaluate nutrient reference values, FDA considered recommendations from several expert bodies, including the National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM), the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), the Australian National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC)/New Zealand Ministry of Health (MoH), and the German, Austrian, and Swiss nutrition societies (D-A-CH). These organizations, utilizing expert committees, develop nutrient reference values, including Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs), which are science-based benchmarks used to assess and plan diets for healthy populations. Grounded in rigorous expert review across multiple countries and methodologies, these values serve as appropriate inputs for evaluating both the adequacy and safety of nutrient intakes in infant populations.
Nutrient reference values developed by these expert committees include several types of recommendations: Estimated Average Requirement (EAR), Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA), Adequate Intake (AI), and Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL). The EAR represents the average daily intake estimated to meet the needs of half of healthy individuals in each life stage. EFSA uses an equivalent term, Average Requirement (AR). The RDA is derived mathematically from the EAR (EAR plus two standard deviations) and is set to meet the needs of nearly all (97-98 percent) healthy individuals (Ref. 2); the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations/World Health Organization (WHO) and EFSA use equivalent terms: the Recommended Nutrient Intake (RNI) and Population Reference Intake (PRI), respectively (Refs. 3, 4). When insufficient scientific evidence exists to establish an EAR—and thus an RDA—an AI is established instead, based on experimentally derived intake levels or observed mean nutrient intakes in healthy populations (Ref. 2). The UL represents the highest average daily intake level likely to pose no risk of adverse health effects (Ref. 2). These reference values provide science-based benchmarks for assessing both the adequacy and safety of nutrient intakes in infant populations and are incorporated into each nutrient section if available.
FDA considered human milk composition data, where appropriate, as a primary source of evidence, recognizing that human milk serves as the gold standard for infant nutrition during, at minimum, the first 6 months of life, and that most nutrient AIs for infants are based on observed nutrient concentrations in human milk.

Mature human milk is the stage of lactation established approximately 2 weeks postpartum, following colostrum and transitional milk, and is characterized by a relatively stable nutrient composition compared with earlier phases (Ref. 5). For the purposes of FDA's review, human milk collected 21 days or more postpartum was considered mature. In addition, for the purposes of this review, FDA converted nutrient concentrations in human milk from per liter (L) to per 100 kcal using an assumed energy density of approximately 650 kcal/L for mature human milk. This value represents a well-supported midpoint estimate that is consistent with the range of values reported across multiple independent data sources and accounts for the natural variability in human milk energy content across lactation stages and populations (Refs. 6, 7, 8, 9, 10). FDA acknowledges that this value represents a midpoint within a range of plausible estimates and commits to updating this reference value as new, nationally representative data from North American populations become available. Therefore, FDA requests comment on the use of approximately 650 kcal/L in mature milk for calculations performed in this proposed rule including the references that were used to derive this value.
Two recent publications provide updated human milk nutrient composition data that were considered in this review, along with other relevant studies as discussed in the sections
(
printed page 69045)
below. The Mothers, Infants and Lactation Quality (MILQ) study was designed to establish reference values for nutrient concentrations in human milk from well-nourished women with minimal nutrient supplementation and dietary fortification across geographically diverse populations. The study collected human milk samples from 1,242 women in Bangladesh, Brazil, Denmark, and The Gambia at multiple time points throughout the first 8.5 months of lactation (Ref. 11). Concentrations of macronutrients, water-soluble vitamins, fat-soluble vitamins, and minerals were quantified using validated analytical methods. Milk volume was measured simultaneously, enabling calculation of total nutrient transfer to the infant (Ref. 11). The other study developed interim human milk nutrient profile data (iHMNutD) for use in North American food composition databases through a literature synthesis of eligible North American data from three previously published systematic reviews covering the period 1980-2022 and one large Canadian biomonitoring study (Ref. 8). Data were restricted to mature milk from term-born infants collected within the first 6 months of lactation using nutrient-specific collection and analytical methods. Values were reviewed by subject matter experts and accompanied by data flags to communicate uncertainty where data were limited (Ref. 8).
FDA reviewed international infant formula standards and recommendations from Codex Alimentarius, the European Union (EU), Australia, New Zealand, Canada, and China, among others, to inform its assessment of appropriate nutrient specifications while also considering differences in methodology and regulatory philosophy. Codex Alimentarius and some non-U.S. countries use the term “infant formula” to refer to formula intended for infants 0-6 months of age and the term “follow-on formula” to refer to formula intended for infants 6-12 months of age. In the United States, there is not a regulatory distinction between formula intended for infants 0-6 months of age and formula intended for infants 6-12 months of age; both are considered “infant formula,” as defined in
21 CFR 106.3
and section 201(z) of the FD&C Act. We considered data on nutrient function and interactions, clinical outcomes associated with deficiency or excess intake, U.S. dietary intake data, and other evidence relevant to evaluating minimum and maximum nutrient levels in infant formula. Where relevant, FDA notes distinctions between maximums and guidance upper levels (GULs) established in some international standards. Unlike maximums, GULs apply to nutrients for which sufficient information for a science-based risk assessment is not available; rather, they are derived based on meeting nutritional requirements of infants and an established history of apparent safe use. In general, from a nutrition perspective, it is best that nutrient contents in infant formulas do not exceed GULs unless higher levels cannot be avoided (Ref. 12).
To estimate infant exposure to nutrients from infant formula, FDA assumed typical infant formula intakes of 0.78 L/day for infants 0-6 months of age and 0.6 L/day for infants 7-12 months of age, accounting for the introduction of complementary foods in the second half of infancy. These intake volumes are based on observed consumption patterns in breastfed infants and are consistent with the assumptions used by NASEM (Ref. 2) and similar to assumptions used by other expert bodies in establishing nutrient reference values. Assuming a standard infant formula energy density of 20 kcal/oz (676 kcal/L), these volumes correspond to approximately 527 kcal/day for infants 0-6 months of age and approximately 406 kcal/day for infants 7-12 months of age. FDA requests comment on all aspects of its assumptions to calculate the kcal consumed per day for infants 0-6 months of age and infants 7-12 months of age, including the assumption of the energy density of infant formula.
For certain nutrients, FDA also considered a high consumer scenario based on data from three cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), using the 90th percentile of energy intake from infant formula among non-breastfed infants to evaluate potential nutrient exposures at the upper end of the consumption distribution (Refs. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18). Evaluation of typical consumption scenarios (
i.e.,
mean, representing the average diet) informed the assessment of minimum specifications to ensure adequate nutrient intakes, while both typical and high-consumer scenarios informed the assessment of maximum specifications to ensure appropriate safety margins.
C. Chloride
The current requirements for chloride in infant formula are a minimum level of 55 milligrams (mg)/100 kcal and a maximum level of 150 mg/100 kcal (§ 107.100). Based on our analysis of scientific information and data since the 1998 comprehensive study of infant formula nutrients (LSRO Panel report), including infant formula chloride requirements in international standards, we conclude that the required chloride levels in § 107.100 remain appropriate.
1. Background
Chloride is an essential mineral that serves critical physiological functions in infants, including maintenance of acid-base balance, regulation of fluid and electrolyte homeostasis, and production of hydrochloric acid for digestion (Refs. 19, 20). Chloride works closely with sodium, potassium, and bicarbonate as electrically charged particles in body fluids to help regulate membrane electrical charge, facilitate nutrient absorption, and generate signals in muscles and nerves (Ref. 20). Chloride also helps keep mucus moist and fluid in the lungs and other organs through a process controlled by the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator channel; when this channel malfunctions, it causes cystic fibrosis (Ref. 20). Most dietary chloride intake comes from sodium chloride (
i.e.,
table salt) added to food during processing or at the table (Refs. 19, 20).
a. Health Consequences of Chloride Deficiency
A deficiency in chloride can result in metabolic alkalosis (
i.e.,
a condition in which blood becomes excessively alkaline) (Ref. 21). The most well-documented cases of chloride deficiency in the United States occurred during 1978-1979, when approximately 150 infants in the United States developed hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis after consuming improperly formulated soy protein-based infant formulas (Ref. 22). These formulas contained chloride levels as low as 1-2 milliequivalents (mEq)/L (approximately 5-11 mg/100 kcal) (Refs. 22, 23, 24), and symptoms were observed in some infants consuming formula with 5.1 mEq/L (approximately 27 mg/100 kcal) (Ref. 1). Infants with acute chloride deficiency exhibited a failure to thrive, lethargy, loss of appetite, and weakness. Other laboratory abnormalities included low blood and urine chloride levels with metabolic alkalosis, low blood potassium levels, and red blood cells in the urine (Refs. 24, 25). This public health incident helped lead to the enactment of the Infant Formula Act of 1980 (Pub. L. 96-359).
Long-term followup studies of the infants in the United States affected by the chloride deficiency crisis identified subtle neurodevelopmental effects in children who experienced severe
(
printed page 69046)
chloride deficiency during infancy, particularly affecting language skills (Refs. 22, 26).
b. Health Consequences of Excess Chloride Intake
Hyperchloremia is a condition in which blood chloride levels exceed the normal range. Hyperchloremia typically results from medical disorders or clinical treatments rather than dietary chloride intake, and excessive chloride consumption through infant formula or other food is unlikely to be a cause of hyperchloremia (Ref. 20).
In its 2005 assessment, NASEM found no research examining the consequences of chronic overconsumption of chloride in infants (Ref. 19). Available evidence regarding harmful effects of excess chloride consumption in infants remains sparse. FDA's review identified no significant new scientific evidence concerning adverse outcomes from excessive dietary chloride consumption during infancy since NASEM's 2005 report (Ref. 27).
2. Nutrient Reference Values
a. NASEM (United States)
NASEM established AIs for chloride for infants in 2005 as part of its comprehensive report,
Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride, and Sulfate
(Ref. 19). NASEM established an AI of 180 mg/day for infants 0-6 months of age and an AI of 570 mg/day for infants 7-12 months of age. NASEM established these AIs based on the sodium content of human milk, assuming chloride adequacy in equimolar amounts to sodium, because most dietary chloride is consumed as sodium chloride. The calculation for infants 7-12 months of age accounted for the introduction of complementary foods at this age.
b. European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)
The EFSA Panel on Nutrition, Novel Foods and Food Allergens (NDA) published a comprehensive Scientific Opinion on dietary reference values for chloride in 2019 (Ref. 20), in which it established an AI of 300 mg/day for infants 7-11 months of age. EFSA did not establish an AI for chloride in infants 0-6 months of age, but, through a comprehensive review of human milk studies from others of term infants in Western populations, the EFSA Panel determined an approximate midpoint of chloride concentration in mature human milk to be 400 mg (11.3 millimole (mmol))/L and estimated infant intake of 320 mg/day from exclusive breastfeeding.
The EFSA Panel also reviewed a study that calculated physiological requirements of chloride in infants and that recommended an intake of 120 mg/day throughout the first year of life. EFSA noted that the amount of chloride provided by human milk during the first 6 months of life (approximately 320 mg/day) is substantially higher than this calculated physiological requirement, suggesting either that the approach underestimates actual needs or that human milk provides chloride beyond minimal physiological requirements (Ref. 20).
c. D-A-CH (Germany, Austria, Switzerland)
In 2017, D-A-CH established an AI for chloride of 300 mg/day for infants 0-4 months of age, and 450 mg/day for infants 4-12 months of age (Ref. 28). Because intake data from complementary foods were unavailable, the 4-12 months value was extrapolated from the 0-4-month group's values, adjusting for differences in average body weight.
d. UL
Establishing a UL requires evidence from studies that test multiple levels of intake and identify the point at which adverse effects begin to occur; however, available data were insufficient to support such a determination for chloride in infants (Ref. 19). Consequently, neither NASEM (Ref. 19) nor EFSA (Ref. 20) established a UL for chloride in infants. In its 2005 assessment, EFSA observed that chloride consumption levels in European populations surpassed the amounts needed for normal physiological function (Ref. 29). EFSA also recognized that higher consumption of chloride in the form of sodium chloride correlated with increased risk of high blood pressure (Refs. 20, 29). Nevertheless, EFSA determined that the available scientific evidence was inadequate to establish a specific numerical value for an upper limit (Ref. 20). Similarly, NASEM noted that “as with other nutrients, an intake of sodium or chloride markedly above the AI is not warranted” (Ref. 19).

The considerable variation in chloride recommendations across international expert bodies reflects fundamental differences in methodology and data sources (Ref. 27). Despite these methodological differences, all expert bodies used human milk composition as the primary basis for chloride AIs and assessed that there is insufficient evidence to establish a UL.
3. Human Milk Composition
Maternal diet and nutritional status do not affect how much chloride is present in human milk (Refs. 20, 30). Multiple studies have characterized chloride concentrations in mature human milk from mothers with term pregnancies. The direct measurements of chloride concentrations in mature human milk resulted in values ranging from 339 to 547 mg/L across individual study timepoints (Refs. 31, 32, 33, 34, 35) and a pooled weighted mean of 416 mg/L (n=5 studies and 139 participants) (Ref. 8) and reflect the natural variability observed in human milk.
The MILQ study (Ref. 36) provides comprehensive recent data on human milk mineral composition, from 1,242 women in Bangladesh, Brazil, Denmark, and The Gambia. The MILQ study
(
printed page 69047)
reported sodium concentrations, not chloride. In converting sodium to chloride on an equimolar basis, substantially lower values are obtained than with direct measurements of chloride in milk (Ref. 27).
The discrepancy suggests either that chloride and sodium may not be present in exactly equimolar amounts in human milk or that different analytical methods, study populations, or periods yield systematically different results. NASEM's approach of establishing chloride AIs based on equimolar conversion from sodium may underestimate actual chloride concentrations when based on sodium measurements alone (Ref. 27).
4. International Regulatory Standards for Infant Formula
Chloride specifications for infant formula vary among international regulatory bodies and expert organizations, though most align closely with Codex Alimentarius standards. The Codex Alimentarius Commission, a program that establishes internationally recognized standards, specifies a minimum of 50 mg/100 kcal and a maximum of 160 mg/100 kcal. These specifications apply to both infant formula (for 0-6 months of age) (Ref. 12) and follow-on formula (for 6-12 months of age) (Ref. 37). The EU, based on recommendations from EFSA (Ref. 7), specifies a minimum of 60 mg/100 kcal and a maximum of 160 mg/100 kcal (Ref. 38). The EU minimum assumes that infants 0-6 months of age consume 500 kcal/day and require 300 mg/day of chloride. Other countries have adopted or proposed to adopt specifications aligned with Codex Alimentarius, including Food Standards Australia New Zealand (Ref. 39), Health Canada (Ref. 40), and China (Ref. 41); however, China has different standards for follow-on formulas for infants 6-12 months of age (approximately 220 mg/100 kcal maximum for 6-12 months) (Ref. 42).
In its 1998 comprehensive review of infant formula nutrients, LSRO recommended a minimum of 50 mg/100 kcal and a maximum of 160 mg/100 kcal. The LSRO Panel based the minimum recommendation on the mean minus one standard deviation value for the chloride concentration of human milk, which was approximately 320 mg/L (48 mg/100 kcal) (Ref. 30), rounded up to 50 mg/100 kcal for the minimum specification. The LSRO Panel found no evidence to suggest that chloride is absorbed differently from infant formula compared to human milk, supporting the use of human milk composition data as the basis for the specification. For the maximum chloride content of 160 mg/100 kcal, the LSRO Panel based this on the 90th percentile of FDA analyses of infant formulas available at that time, rather than on safety concerns, as no evidence supported that excessive chloride intake caused adverse effects in children.

5. Recent Scientific Evidence on Chloride Intake
A 2006 analysis of electrolyte intake in infants from the 2002 Feeding Infants and Toddlers Study (FITS) reported mean chloride intakes of 290 mg/day for infants 4-5 months of age and 761 mg/day for infants 6-11 months of age based on equimolar conversion of sodium to chloride (Ref. 43). Mean intakes exceeded NASEM's AI for both age groups. For infants 6-11 months of age, chloride intakes ranged from approximately 50 percent of the AI at the 10th percentile (276 mg/day) to approximately 260 percent at the 90th percentile (1,493 mg/day). Although there are several limitations of the FITS study (Ref. 27), the FITS data nonetheless provide useful information demonstrating that most infants—whether breastfed or consuming infant formulas meeting current specifications—along with age-appropriate complementary foods, achieve chloride intakes that meet or exceed established AIs.
6. Evidence Evaluation and Rationale
Based on the review of available literature, NRVs, and international standards, we conclude that the current minimum level of 55 mg/100 kcal and maximum level of 150 mg/100 kcal for chloride in § 107.100 remain appropriate.
a. Maintaining the Minimum Specification of 55 mg/100 kcal
The current minimum required level of 55 mg/100 kcal of chloride provides a 2- to 11-fold margin above the deficiency-causing levels of 5-27 mg/100 kcal associated with the 1978-1979 chloride-deficiency crisis. Given the severity of the consequences of the chloride-deficiency crisis in 1978-1979 and the lack of functional biomarkers for chloride status (
i.e.,
early indicators of chloride inadequacy), we determine that the substantial margin is appropriate.
Although methodological variability exists in measuring chloride levels in human milk, human milk composition data support the current required minimum. The current minimum of 55 mg/100 kcal falls between and aligns well with direct chloride measurements in human milk (approximately 52 to 84 mg/100 kcal, with a pooled weighted mean of 64 mg/100 kcal) (Refs. 1, 8, 20, 28, 31 through 35). When chloride measurements are derived from converting sodium concentrations to chloride, the chloride measurements are far lower than direct chloride measurements, suggesting that chloride and sodium are not present in exactly equimolar amounts in human milk (Refs. 8, 27, 36). Given the uncertainty associated with chloride measurements
(
printed page 69048)
derived from converting sodium concentrations to chloride, the current minimum appropriately reflects direct chloride measurement data while providing a conservative safety margin.
The current minimum ensures that infant formula provides chloride intakes that pose low risk of deficiency relative to established AIs (Ref. 27). Our current specification of 55 mg/100 kcal falls within the international consensus range, and no compelling evidence from other jurisdictions suggests that lowering the minimum would provide any benefit. Doing so would reduce the safety margin above the established deficiency threshold without corresponding nutritional justification (Ref. 27).
b. Maintaining the Maximum Specification of 150 mg/100 kcal
The current maximum of 150 mg/100 kcal substantially exceeds the median human milk chloride content while maintaining a prudent upper limit for sole-source infant nutrition. No compelling evidence supports either raising or lowering this specification (Ref. 27).
Although expert bodies have not established a UL for chloride in infants due to limited data (Refs. 19, 20, 29), the absence of an established UL reflects insufficient dose-response data regarding adverse effects rather than confirmation that all intake levels are safe (Ref. 27).
The current maximum provides a substantial margin above the chloride content of human milk (Ref. 27). FDA's current maximum of 150 mg/100 kcal provides an additional conservative margin below both LSRO's recommendation and the international standard of approximately 160 mg/100 kcal.
History of use and available intake data support safety at the current maximum. The current maximum would provide 791 mg/day for a 0-6-month-old infant and 609 mg/day for a 6-12-month-old infant consuming typical daily infant formula intakes. These chloride amounts have not been associated with adverse effects in clinical use since the chloride requirements were established in the Infant Formula Act of 1980. An analysis of 2002 FITS data (Ref. 43) reported mean sodium intakes corresponding to estimated chloride intakes of 290 mg/day (4-5 months of age) and 761 mg/day (6-11 months of age), although these estimates included intake from all dietary sources, not solely infant formula.
We have considered whether raising the maximum to align with the international consensus of approximately 160 mg/100 kcal would be warranted and conclude that it is not necessary to ensure adequate infant nutrition. While such harmonization could provide modest additional manufacturing flexibility and align U.S. standards with international regulatory agencies, the difference between the current U.S. maximum and the international standard is relatively small (6.7% or 10 mg/100 kcal). No evidence suggests that the current maximum is inadequate, constrains appropriate formulation, or that chloride intakes between 150 and 160 mg/100 kcal provide nutritional advantages to infants beyond those achieved at the present maximum of 150 mg/100 kcal. Manufacturers have successfully met the current specification since the 1980s without reported difficulties. Therefore, we conclude that the slightly lower maximum provides an additional conservative margin without imposing undue manufacturing constraints (Ref. 27).
c. Consideration of the Evidence Base
We acknowledge several uncertainties in the evidence base that support maintaining the current specifications. There is wide variability in reported human milk chloride concentrations across studies (171-547 mg/L or approximately 26-84 mg/100 kcal for mature milk) primarily from discrepancies between direct chloride measurements and sodium-based estimates, lack of functional biomarkers for chloride status, and individual variability in infant requirements. Given these uncertainties, the serious consequences of dietary chloride deficiency, and the lack of evidence of adverse effects from current specifications, we believe a conservative approach is warranted and that the current required minimum level of 55 mg/100 kcal and maximum level of 150 mg/100 kcal should be retained (Ref. 27).
D. Selenium
At the time FDA initially established nutrient specifications for infant formula, selenium was not recognized as an essential nutrient and was not one of the nutrients required by statute in infant formula. However, in 1989, an RDA for selenium for infants 0-6 months of age was established (Ref. 44), and in 2000, AI levels and ULs were established for infants 0-6 and 7-12 months of age (Ref. 45). In 2015, FDA added selenium as a required nutrient in infant formula with a minimum of 2 µg/100 kcal and a maximum of 7 µg/100 kcal (see
80 FR 35834
, June 23, 2015). Based on our analysis of the scientific information and data since the addition of minimum and maximum levels of selenium to the infant formula requirements in 2015, including infant formula selenium requirements in international standards, we conclude that the required selenium levels in § 107.100 remain appropriate.
1. Background
Selenium is an essential trace element for humans that functions largely through its incorporation into proteins known as selenoproteins. The known biological functions of selenium include defense against oxidative stress, regulation of thyroid hormone action, and regulation of the oxidation/reduction status of vitamin C and other molecules (Ref. 46). Selenium also provides protective effects against toxicity of certain elements—including arsenic, lead, cadmium, and mercury—by facilitating urinary excretion, reducing oxidative damage, and forming biologically inactive complexes with these elements (Refs. 45, 47, 48). Infant selenium status is influenced by geographic variation in the selenium content of soil and water, which shapes maternal selenium intake and, in turn, the selenium content of human milk. As a result, the selenium intake of breastfed infants varies by geographic location (Ref. 46).
a. Health Consequences of Selenium Deficiency
Keshan disease, a cardiomyopathy that occurs almost exclusively in children, has been associated with selenium deficiency. Keshan disease has been reported in areas of China where the population has severe selenium deficiency (Refs. 46, 49;
78 FR 22442
at 22443, April 16, 2013). Selenium deficiency has also been identified throughout the lifespan in those who receive long-term parenteral nutrition (
i.e.,
intravenous nutrition) not adequately supplemented with selenium. Deficiency signs and symptoms include macrocytosis, loss of skin and hair pigmentation, and, in severe cases, cardiomyopathy (Ref. 46).
b. Health Consequences of Excess Selenium Intake
Chronic selenium toxicity (selenosis) is rare but has been observed in adults consuming diets containing excess levels of selenium due to selenium supplementation (Ref. 46). Reported characteristics include hair and nail brittleness and loss, gastrointestinal upsets, skin rash, garlic breath odor, fatigue, irritability, and nervous system abnormalities. Acute selenium toxicity
(
printed page 69049)
is rare, and the few reports in the literature of acute fatal or near fatal selenium poisoning in adults occurred secondary to accidental ingestion of selenium (Ref. 45).
2. Dietary Reference Intakes
a. NASEM
In 2000, NASEM established AI and UL values for selenium for infants as part of its comprehensive report,
Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin C, Vitamin E, Selenium, and Carotenoids
(Ref. 45). NASEM did not find sufficient evidence to calculate an EAR for selenium for infants during the first year of life and, therefore, did not have a basis to set an RDA for selenium for infants. This contrasts with the 1989 Food and Nutrition board recommendation, which had established an RDA for infants extrapolated from adult values (Ref. 44). NASEM's 2000 report instead determined that, due to the lack of functional criteria of selenium status in infants to accurately reflect dietary intake, recommended intakes should be based on an AI reflecting observed mean intakes of infants fed principally with human milk.
NASEM established an AI of 15 µg/day for infants 0-6 months of age and an AI of 20 µg/day for infants 7-12 months of age. NASEM's basis for deriving an AI for the first 6 months of life was the average intake by full-term infants born to healthy, well-nourished mothers and exclusively fed human milk (Ref. 45). The AI for infants 7-12 months of age was derived from using the data of infants 0-6 months of age, extrapolated upward to account for increased body size and the introduction of complementary foods.
NASEM established a UL of 45 µg/day for selenium for infants 0-6 months of age by relying on the concentration of selenium in human milk, which is not associated with known adverse effects. The UL of 60 µg/day for infants 7-12 months of age was extrapolated to account for increased body size (Ref. 45).
b. EFSA
EFSA published dietary reference values for selenium in 2014 (AI) and 2023 (UL) (Refs. 50, 51). EFSA did not establish an AI for selenium in infants 0-6 months of age. For infants 7-11 months of age, EFSA established an AI of 15 µg/day (Ref. 49).
EFSA established ULs of 45 µg/day for infants 4-6 months of age and 55 µg/day for infants 7-11 months of age. EFSA acknowledged that there are no direct data to support derivation of a UL for infants; however, given that there is no evidence that infants are more susceptible to selenium toxicity than adults, the EFSA Panel considered it appropriate to extrapolate ULs from adults to infants (Ref. 51). The EFSA Panel noted that these ULs are consistent with human milk concentrations.
c. FAO/WHO
The joint FAO/WHO Consultation established RNI levels of 6 µg/day for infants 0-6 months of age and 10 µg/day for infants 7-12 months of age based on the selenium content of human milk from international surveys, which averaged 18.5 μg/L, combined with data on milk consumption by exclusively breastfed infants (Ref. 3).
d. D-A-CH (Germany, Austria, Switzerland)
In 2015, D-A-CH established an AI for selenium of 10 µg/day for infants 0-4 months of age, based on the selenium content of human milk. Values were adjusted for body weight to establish an AI of 15 µg/day for infants 4-12 months of age. No UL was determined (Ref. 52).
e. Australian NHMRC/New Zealand MoH
Australia and New Zealand established AIs and ULs in 2005 (Ref. 53). The AI of 12 µg/day for infants 0-6 months of age was calculated by multiplying the average intake of human milk (0.78 L/day) and the average selenium content in human milk of 15 µg/L based on several key studies (Refs. 54, 55, 56). The AI of 60 µg/day for infants 7-12 months of age was extrapolated from that of the younger infants on a metabolic weight basis, with considerations for the introduction of complementary foods.
The UL for young infants was based on the studies showing that a human milk concentration of 60 µg/L was not associated with adverse effects (Ref. 57). This gives a no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) of 47 µg/day (7 µg/kg body weight).

3. Human Milk Composition
a. Selenium Concentration in Human Milk
Maternal diet and nutritional status affect the amount of selenium present in human milk. The average selenium content of mature human milk sampled between 2- and 6-months lactation appears to be relatively constant within a population group. However, selenium content in human milk varies greatly based on maternal selenium intakes, including variability in selenium soil content (Ref. 45).
(
printed page 69050)
There is wide interindividual variation in the selenium content of human milk, and the selenium content of hind milk (
i.e.,
milk at the end of an infant feeding) is greater than that of the fore milk (
i.e.,
milk at the beginning of the feeding). Studies report average selenium concentrations of mature human milk of 10 to 23 µg/L (with a range of 6 to 39 µg/L) (Refs. 45, 49).
b. Recent Data
The MILQ study (Ref. 36) reported a pooled median selenium concentration of 9 µg/L in human milk collected from mothers of infants 1-6 months of age, representing only 50 percent of the NASEM reference concentration of 18 µg/L used to establish the current AI. The study suggested that the current NASEM AI may overestimate selenium concentrations in human milk from well-nourished populations and called for updated recommendations informed by these study data (Ref. 36). The iHMNutD study reported a pooled weighted mean selenium concentration which converted to approximately 20.4 µg/L (Ref. 8). A 2019 study (Ref. 58) measured milk selenium concentrations in lactating Chinese women across three regions with varying selenium status. Among mothers with optimal selenium intake, the Beijing milk concentration was 27.8 μg/L; combined with an average milk volume of 0.55 L/day, this yielded a calculated AI of 15.29 μg/day for Chinese infants 0-3 months of age, consistent with the current Chinese AI of 15 μg/day for infants 0-6 months of age.
4. International Regulatory Standards for Infant Formula
Selenium specifications for infant formula vary among international regulatory bodies and expert organizations (table 4). The Codex Alimentarius Commission specifies a minimum of 1 µg/100 kcal and a GUL of 9 µg/100 kcal for infant formula (0-6 months of age) (Ref. 12), and a minimum of 2 µg/100 kcal and GUL of 9 µg/100 kcal for follow-on formula (6-12 months of age) (Ref. 37). The EU specifies a minimum of 3 µg/100 kcal and a maximum of 8.6 µg/100 kcal (Ref. 38). Other countries have adopted or proposed to adopt specifications aligned with Codex Alimentarius, including Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ) (Ref. 39), Health Canada (Ref. 40), and China (Refs. 41, 42).
The 1998 LSRO Panel report recommended a minimum selenium requirement of 1.5 µg/100 kcal and a maximum of 5 µg/100 kcal. The minimum value approximated the estimated value for the mean minus one standard deviation for the selenium concentration in human milk in countries in which selenium deficiency has not been recognized in breastfed infants. This recommended minimum level would provide an estimated 7.5 µg/day of selenium for young infants exclusively fed infant formula, an amount below the 1989 RDA (10 µg/day). The LSRO Panel was aware that there were disparities between some of its recommendations for nutrient levels in infant formulas and the 1989 RDAs; however, the history of use for a large population in which selenium deficiency had not been reported was regarded as a reasonable basis for recommending a minimum value for selenium in infant formula (Ref. 1;
78 FR 22442
at 22443, April 16, 2013).
The 1998 LSRO Panel report recommended a maximum selenium level for infant formula of 5 µg/100 kcal (33.5 µg/L). This recommendation was based on the upper limit of the range of selenium in human milk, which was considered to represent a history of use for a large population in which selenium toxicity had not been reported. The LSRO Panel report also indicated that, on a body weight basis, this level is far below the intake associated with the development of selenosis in adults (Ref. 1;
78 FR 22442
at 22444-22445).
