5. Recent Scientific Evidence on Selenium Intake
A randomized dose-response trial of healthy term infants from birth to 16 weeks of age fed infant formula containing selenium at three different concentrations and a breastfed reference group found that infants fed the formula containing a selenium level of 1.9 µg/100 kcal received sufficient selenium to meet their nutritional needs and that much of the selenium above the level of 1.9 µg/100 kcal was eliminated from the body (Ref. 59). An analysis of a randomized controlled trial investigating maternal selenium status during pregnancy and lactation in relation to infant birth outcomes across
(
printed page 69051)
898 mother-infant dyads in Guatemala, India, and Pakistan concluded that maternal selenium supplementation did not impact serum selenium concentrations in populations at high risk for deficiency, suggesting that supplementation may not overcome the impact of low dietary intake and the high demands of pregnancy and early lactation (Ref. 60). However, the authors noted that larger studies in high-risk regions are needed to further clarify the relationship between maternal selenium deficiency and infant outcomes (Ref. 60).
6. Evidence Evaluation and Rationale
Based on our review of available scientific data, information, and international standards, we conclude that the current minimum of 2 µg/100 kcal and maximum level of 7 µg/100 kcal for selenium in § 107.100 remain appropriate.
a. Maintaining the Minimum Specification of 2 µg/100 kcal
The current minimum of 2 µg/100 kcal is based primarily on two sources of evidence. First, NASEM's AI of 15 µg/day for infants 0-6 months of age, converted to an energy basis assuming 100 kcal/kg body weight/day intake, yields approximately 2.1 µg/100 kcal. FDA rounded this to 2 µg/100 kcal for the minimum specification (Refs. 45, 49). The current minimum provides adequate selenium to meet established AIs. For a 0-6-month-old infant consuming a typical daily infant formula intake, infant formula at the minimum specification provides 10.5 µg/day, which represents 70 percent of the NASEM AI of 15 µg/day (Refs. 45, 49). While this percentage may appear modest, it is important to note that the AI is based on the mean intake from human milk and is intended to meet or exceed the needs of nearly all individuals in the population (Refs. 45, 49). Second, the randomized dose-response trial described in section V.D.5 of this document provides direct clinical evidence supporting this minimum level, demonstrating that 1.9 µg/100 kcal was sufficient to achieve selenium status indicators comparable to breastfed infants (Ref. 59). Additionally, the current minimum also aligns well with international standards (Ref. 49).
Moreover, recent evidence from the MILQ study suggests that the pooled median total selenium intake from human milk is 7.3 µg/day from 1 to 6 months postpartum, representing only 49 percent of the NASEM AI (Ref. 36). This finding raises questions about whether the NASEM AI may overestimate infant selenium requirements, as the MILQ study population of well-nourished mothers and healthy, normally developing infants showed no evidence of selenium deficiency despite intakes well below the established AI. However, the current minimum specification of 2 µg/100 kcal, providing 10.4 µg/day, exceeds the MILQ median intake by 42 percent, offering a conservative margin of safety.
The minimum specification also accounts for potential differences in bioavailability. The U.S. minimum was established as a level providing sufficient amounts to account for potential differences in bioavailability among various infant formula types, including a conservative estimate of 50 percent relative bioavailability of selenium from soy protein-based formulas compared to human milk (Ref. 1). This conservative approach ensures that all formula types, regardless of protein source, provide adequate selenium.
Human milk composition data support the current minimum. The current minimum of 2 µg/100 kcal exceeds the estimated median value of 1.3 µg/100 kcal from the MILQ study by approximately 54 percent, providing a safety margin to account for population variability and potential differences in bioavailability (Refs. 36, 49). The MILQ study authors noted that the substantially lower concentrations as compared with NASEM estimates suggested that the differences may be due to maternal dietary selenium intake, which varies with regional soil selenium content (Ref. 36). The lower MILQ study values as compared with other studies may reflect populations with lower selenium intake rather than indicating that lower concentrations are adequate (Refs. 8, 36, 49, 58). Data from other well-nourished populations (Refs. 8, 58) support selenium concentrations closer to the NASEM reference value. The wide geographic variability in human milk selenium concentrations underscores the importance of maintaining a minimum specification that ensures adequacy across diverse populations and accounts for the serious health consequences of selenium deficiency, including Keshan disease (Ref. 49).
b. Maintaining the Maximum Specification of 7 µg/100 kcal
The current maximum is based on safety considerations. NASEM established a UL of approximately 7 µg/kg/day for infants 0-6 months of age, which approximates 7 µg/100 kcal (Ref. 45). The UL is defined as “the highest daily intake level that is likely to pose no risk of adverse health effects in almost all individuals in a life stage group” (Ref. 45). NASEM established this UL by relying on data on the concentration of selenium in human milk, which is not associated with known adverse effects.
The current maximum substantially exceeds median human milk content while maintaining a prudent limit (Ref. 49). Although the current maximum is approximately 5.4 times the median human milk concentration from the MILQ study population, the studies conducted in mothers with optimal selenium intake (North American data) and from well-nourished populations (in China) reported reference values of approximately 3.1 µg/100 kcal and 4.2 µg/100 kcal, respectively (Refs. 8, 49, 58). Relative to these higher reference values from populations with optimal selenium intake, the current maximum of 7 µg/100 kcal represents approximately 2.3 times the North American median and 1.7 times the concentration in milk from optimally nourished Chinese mothers.
The current maximum is conservative compared to most international standards. The current maximum is lower than the Codex Alimentarius GUL, the FSANZ GUL, and the Health Canada, EU, and China maximums (Ref. 49). The LSRO recommendation of a maximum selenium level for infant formula of 5 µg/100 kcal was based on the upper limit of the range of selenium in human milk and represented a history of use for a large population in which selenium toxicity had not been reported. The current maximum is higher than the LSRO recommendation but aligns with the NASEM UL, reflecting a conservative approach based on safety considerations while providing additional manufacturing flexibility (Ref. 49).
History of use also supports safety at the current maximum. The current maximum has demonstrated safety in practice since the level went into effect in 2016. Manufacturers have successfully met the current specification since 2016 without reported difficulties, suggesting that the current maximum does not impose undue constraints.
c. Consideration of the Evidence Base
There is wide variability in reported human milk selenium concentrations across studies and geographic regions, reflecting differences in maternal selenium intake, which is highly dependent on regional soil selenium
(
printed page 69052)
content. There are limited recent data from U.S. populations specifically, methodological variability across studies, and uncertainty about bioavailability differences between infant formula types and human milk. Recent evidence suggests that populations at high risk of selenium deficiency may have higher needs during pregnancy and lactation that cannot be easily met through supplementation alone and that selenium status can decline substantially during lactation even with supplementation (Ref. 60). Given these uncertainties, the associated consequences of dietary selenium deficiency (
i.e.,
Keshan disease), the potential for selenium status to decline during lactation, and the lack of evidence of adverse effects from current specifications, we believe a conservative approach in maintaining the required minimum level of 2 µg/100 kcal and maximum level of 7 µg/100 kcal is warranted.
E. Iodine (Proposed § 107.100(a))
The current requirements for iodine in infant formula are a minimum level of 5 µg/100 kcal and a maximum level of 75 µg/100 kcal (§ 107.100). Based on our analysis of scientific information and data since the 1998 comprehensive study of infant formula nutrients (Ref. 1), including infant formula iodine requirements in international standards, we propose to amend § 107.100(a) to increase the required minimum to 15 µg/100 kcal and decrease the required maximum to 50 µg/100 kcal.
1. Background
Iodine is an essential micronutrient whose primary physiological role is as an essential component of the thyroid hormones that regulate protein synthesis, enzymatic activity, and metabolic processes critical to normal growth and development (Refs. 1, 61). In infants, thyroid hormones are particularly important for myelination of the central nervous system, which is most active in the perinatal period and during early postnatal development; iodine deficiency during this critical window can irreversibly impair neuromotor development (Ref. 62).
Iodine (I
2
) refers to the elemental form, while iodide (I−) is the reduced, ionic form that predominates in food, water, and the body. Most dietary iodine is rapidly converted to iodide in the gastrointestinal tract prior to absorption (Ref. 62). Infant formula and human milk contain iodine primarily in the iodide form. In regulatory and nutritional contexts, the term “iodine” is used conventionally to refer to total iodine intake regardless of chemical form, and this convention is followed throughout this document.
a. Health Consequences of Iodine Deficiency
Iodine deficiency disorders identified throughout the lifespan include intellectual disability, hypothyroidism, goiter, cretinism, and varying degrees of growth and developmental abnormalities resulting from inadequate thyroid hormone production (Ref. 62). Fetal iodine deficiency resulting in cretinism occurs in areas where endemic goiters exist, generally in association with iodine intakes less than 25 µg/day (Ref. 1). Infants are among the most vulnerable populations for iodine deficiency because their intrathyroidal iodine stores are small, daily thyroid hormone turnover rates per body weight are higher than at any other time of life, and they are entirely dependent on dietary iodine from human milk or infant formula (Refs. 61, 62). Deficiencies of vitamin A, selenium, or iron can exacerbate the effects of iodine deficiency (Refs. 61, 62).
b. Health Consequences of Excess Iodine Intake
High iodine intakes have been associated with thyroiditis, goiter, hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, and sensitivity reactions (Ref. 62). Excess iodine can be harmful to infants, particularly premature infants, because excretion mechanisms may be unable to accommodate high intake levels, potentially resulting in transient hypothyroidism (Refs. 1, 61).
2. Nutrient Reference Values
a. NASEM
NASEM established AI values for iodine for infants in 2001 based on the observed mean iodine intake of infants exclusively fed human milk (Ref. 62). NASEM established an AI of 110 µg/day for infants 0-6 months of age and an AI of 130 µg/day for infants 7-12 months of age. The AI for infants 7-12 months of age was extrapolated from the AI for younger infants using a metabolic weight ratio (Ref. 62). NASEM judged the UL to be not determinable for infants due to insufficient data on adverse effects and concern about the infant's ability to handle excess amounts (Ref. 62).
b. EFSA
EFSA published dietary reference values for iodine in 2014 (Ref. 63). EFSA did not establish an AI for iodine in infants 0-6 months of age, during which period exclusive breastfeeding is assumed to provide an adequate iodine supply. For infants 7-11 months of age, EFSA established an AI of 70 µg/day based on the urinary iodine concentration (UIC) threshold (100 µg/L) from school-age children, extrapolated to infants using age-adjusted urinary volumes and body weight. The EFSA Panel concluded that an iodine intake of 90 µg/day is adequate for the majority of infants, and, since there is no reason to assume that infants from birth to 6 months of age need more iodine than infants in the second half of the first year of life, an intake of 70 µg/day is adequate for the majority of infants from birth to 12 months of age (Ref. 63). EFSA did not establish a UL for iodine for infants.
c. WHO
WHO, together with the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) and the International Council for Control of Iodine Deficiency Disorders (ICCIDD), established an RNI of 90 µg/day for children under 5 years of age (0-59 months) based on physiological evidence that positive iodine balance requires iodine intake of at least 15 µg/kg/day, approximating 90 µg/day for a 6-month-old infant weighing 6 kg (Refs. 64, 65). The recommended value supports normal thyroid hormone production without stressing the iodide trapping mechanism. While a UL for infants was not established, daily intakes exceeding 180 µg/day were not expected to provide additional health benefit and may be associated with impaired thyroid function. However, the Consultation set upper limits of probable safe intake for infants at 150 µg/kg/day (0-6 months of age) and 140 µg/kg/day (7-12 months of age) (Ref. 64).
d. D-A-CH (Germany, Austria, Switzerland)
D-A-CH established a reference value for daily iodine intake for infants of 80 µg/day for infants 0-12 months of age in 2025 (Ref. 66). This value represents a doubling of the previous D-A-CH reference value of 40 µg/day. According to the D-A-CH reference values, the updated iodine recommendation for infants differs methodologically from the previous reference value and allows the revised reference value to be expressed as a recommended intake rather than an estimated value (Refs. 61, 66). No UL was determined.
e. Australian NHMRC/New Zealand MoH
Australia and New Zealand established AIs for iodine in 2006 (Ref. 53). The AI for infants 0-6 months of age was calculated by multiplying the
(
printed page 69053)
average intake of human milk (0.78 L/day) by the average concentration of iodine in human milk (115 µg/L), consistent with the 2001 recommendation (Ref. 64), in addition to other studies, yielding an AI of 90 µg/day. The AI for infants 7-12 months of age was extrapolated from that of younger infants using a metabolic weight ratio, yielding an AI of 110 µg/day. No UL was determined (Ref. 53).

The variation in iodine recommendations across international expert bodies reflects differences in methodology, data sources, and the timing of each review (Ref. 61). A key methodological difference across all bodies is the degree to which human milk iodine data are used as the primary reference. Unlike many other minerals, iodine in human milk is not homeostatically regulated (
i.e.,
automatically kept at a consistent level by the body) but directly reflects maternal iodine status and population-level iodine exposure. Consequently, human milk iodine concentrations vary substantially across populations and over time, and the choice of reference population for human milk data has a direct and substantial effect on the resulting AI (Refs. 36, 61, 67).
3. Human Milk Composition
There is wide variability in milk iodine concentrations across populations, driven by differences in national salt iodization policies, dietary patterns, geographic variability, and dietary supplement use (Ref. 61). Consequently, no single human milk iodine concentration can be considered universally representative. The large, multi-country MILQ study ultimately chose not to generate pooled iodine reference values or percentile curves because of this between-country variability, unlike its approach to other minerals (Ref. 36).
4. International Regulatory Standards for Infant Formula
Iodine specifications for infant formula vary considerably among international regulatory bodies and expert organizations (see table 6). The current U.S. specification of 5 µg/100 kcal (minimum) to 75 µg/100 kcal (maximum) is an outlier relative to international standards. Specifically, the U.S. minimum falls below the current minimum thresholds established by major international regulatory frameworks, while the U.S. maximum exceeds their corresponding upper levels.
Across the international regulatory frameworks assessed, minimum iodine specifications range from 10 to 15 µg/100 kcal, while maximum levels or GULs range from 29 to 60 µg/100 kcal. Codex Alimentarius, FSANZ, and Health Canada share identical specifications (10 µg/100 kcal minimum; 60 µg/100 kcal maximum or GUL) (Refs. 12, 37, 39, 40). China also has a maximum of 60 µg/100 kcal with a higher minimum of 15 µg/100 kcal (Refs. 41, 42). The EU specifies the narrowest range, with a minimum of 15 µg/100 kcal and a maximum of 29 µg/100 kcal (Ref. 38). The EU minimum was derived from EFSA's 2014 scientific opinion, which determined that a minimum iodine content of 14 µg/100 kcal (rounded up to 15 µg/100 kcal) is necessary for an infant consuming approximately 500 kcal/day to achieve an adequate intake of 70 µg/day (Ref. 7).
The 1998 LSRO Panel report recommended a minimum of 8 µg/100 kcal and a maximum of 35 µg/100 kcal (Ref. 1). The LSRO minimum was based on the then-current RDA for iodine of 40 µg/day for infants 0-6 months of age, which translates to 8 µg/100 kcal for a 5 kg infant consuming 100 kcal/kg/day (Ref. 44). Human milk was not used as the reference standard. Data obtained from iodine balance studies further support this level, estimating the dietary requirement at no more than 8.6 µg/kg/day (Ref. 1). The LSRO recommended maximum of 35 µg/100 kcal represented approximately the 75th percentile of FDA analyses of marketed formulas and was considered the lowest feasible value at the time (Ref. 1). The LSRO Panel considered the U.S. maximum of 75 µg/100 kcal to be too high.

5. Recent Scientific Evidence on Iodine Intake
The most direct evidence on iodine requirements in early infancy comes from a 2016 balance study in formula-fed infants 2-5 months of age (Ref. 68). The study found that zero iodine balance was achieved at approximately 70 μg/day and found iodine retention to be linear up to 300 μg/day with no evidence of down-regulation (Ref. 68). These findings led the authors to propose an EAR of 72 μg/day and an RDA of 80 μg/day, suggesting the current AI of 110 μg/day for infants 0-6 months of age may be set too high. The study also proposed a urinary iodine concentration threshold of approximately 125 μg/L as indicative of adequacy, slightly above the WHO cutoff of 100 μg/L (Ref. 68). An additional study to evaluate iodine status in settings with universal salt iodization supports these estimates (Refs. 61, 69).
Moreover, a 2022 secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial (Ref. 70) provided independent corroboration of the proposed EAR. Median UICs were greater than or equal to 100 μg/L at all ages from 1 to 12 months, and more than 98 percent of infants met the proposed EAR of 72 μg/day. These findings support the appropriateness of the lower estimated iodine requirement derived from the 2016 balance study (Refs. 61, 68, 70).
These newer estimates are broadly consistent with established reference values. WHO, together with UNICEF and ICCIDD, established an RNI of 90 µg/day for children under 5 years of age (0-59 months) and identified a UIC of greater than or equal to 100 μg/L as indicative of adequate iodine nutrition, while noting that daily intakes exceeding 180 μg/day are not expected to provide additional health benefit (Refs. 64, 65). A narrative review of the literature from 1960 to 2007 proposed an iodine requirement of greater than or equal to 15 μg/kg/day (≥90 μg/day) for full-term infants (Ref. 71). Further, the 2016 balance study suggests that the true AR may sit somewhat below the established RNI, though the difference between the proposed RDA (80 μg/day) and the established RNI (90 μg/day) is modest, and both fall below NASEM's current AIs of 110 and 130 μg/day.
Studies conducted in populations with high environmental iodine exposure have documented adverse thyroid outcomes in infants and young children at elevated iodine intakes. A cross-sectional study documented subclinical hypothyroidism in 7.4 percent and elevated thyroglobulin in 15.8 percent of participants 6-24 months of age in a population with high environmental iodine exposure (Ref. 72). An observational study found that high iodine intakes were associated with subclinical hypothyroidism in 9 percent of children and elevated thyroglobulin in 13 percent at 3-year followup (Ref. 73).
The excess iodine exposures represented in these studies arise primarily from environmental sources and supplementation rather than from infant formula, and, in some cases, involve intake levels far exceeding those achievable through formula feeding alone. The studies were also conducted in populations with iodine exposure profiles markedly different from typical U.S. infants, limiting direct generalizability. Nevertheless, the thyroid and growth outcomes observed across these populations provide useful context for understanding the biological consequences of sustained elevated iodine intake in early infancy, a period of particular vulnerability to disruption of thyroid function (Ref. 61).
6. Evidence Evaluation and Rationale
a. Rationale for Increasing the Minimum Specification to 15 μg/100 kcal
The current minimum specification of 5 µg/100 kcal has not been updated since 1985 (
50 FR 45106
, October 30, 1985) and is no longer supported by more recently available scientific evidence. At this level, an infant 0-6 months of age would receive only approximately 26 µg/day of iodine, representing 24 percent of the NASEM AI of 110 µg/day (Ref. 62) and 29 percent of the WHO RNI of 90 µg/day (Ref. 65) (see table 7). An infant 6-12 months of age would receive approximately 20 µg/day at the current minimum, representing 16 percent of the NASEM AI of 130 µg/day and 23 percent of the WHO RNI of 90 µg/day. Intakes at both age groups fall below even the experimentally derived EAR of 72 µg/day (Ref. 68), representing 37 percent and 28 percent of that threshold for infants 0-6 months and 6-12 months of age, respectively, the most conservative available estimate of average iodine requirement. The 1998 LSRO Panel also recommended a higher minimum of 8 µg/100 kcal based on the then-current RDA of 40 µg/day for infants 0-6 months of age (Ref. 1).

FDA acknowledges that, at typical intake volumes, the proposed minimum of 15 µg/100 kcal does not fully meet the NASEM AI or WHO RNI for either age group, reflecting a challenge of setting a minimum specification for a nutrient with varying nutrient reference values among expert bodies. The NASEM AIs are based on the mean intake from human milk and are intended to reflect observed intakes in healthy populations rather than a minimum requirement threshold. The proposed minimum is intended to ensure an adequate iodine provision consistent with the best available evidence on iodine requirements in infancy (Ref. 61).
The current U.S. minimum of 5 µg/100 kcal is the lowest of any major regulatory jurisdiction. All other major international regulatory frameworks have established minimums of 10 to 15 µg/100 kcal: Codex Alimentarius, FSANZ, and Health Canada specify a minimum of 10 µg/100 kcal, while the EU and China specify a minimum of 15 µg/100 kcal (table 6). The proposed minimum of 15 µg/100 kcal aligns with the standards from the EU and China and represents a scientifically supported improvement over the current U.S. minimum.
Since the 1998 LSRO Panel report (Ref. 1), the evidence base has expanded substantially (see Refs. 68, 69, 70, 74) and consistently supports a minimum above the current 5 µg/100 kcal (Ref. 61). Additionally, a few comments in response to FDA's 2025 RFI on nutrient requirements for infant formula express support for increasing the minimum iodine level (
90 FR 20475
, May 14, 2025).
b. Rationale for Decreasing the Maximum Specification to 50 µg/100 kcal
The current FDA maximum of 75 µg/100 kcal has not been revised since 1985 (
50 FR 45106
, October 30, 1985). At this level, an infant 0-6 months of age consuming a typical daily infant formula intake would receive approximately 396 µg/day of iodine, and an infant 6-12 months of age consuming a typical daily infant formula intake would receive approximately 305 µg/day. These levels substantially exceed upper levels of probable safe intake (Ref. 75), as well as estimated intakes associated with subclinical thyroid dysfunction in several applicable studies (Refs. 72, 73).
The limitations of the current maximum are further illustrated by NHANES-derived estimates of energy intake from infant formula among high consumers (Refs. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18). At the 90th percentile of energy intake from infant formula (836 kcal/day for infants 0-6 months of age and 794 kcal/day for infants 6-12 months of age), the current maximum of 75 µg/100 kcal would provide iodine intakes of approximately 627 µg/day and 596 µg/day, respectively.
These findings reinforce the need for a significant downward revision of the maximum specification, particularly given the absence of a formal UL for infants and the linear iodine retention observed across intake levels (Ref. 69). Because no UL has been established for infants by any major international expert body (Ref. 62), the safety margin between the current maximum and any established toxicity threshold cannot be precisely quantified, a significant limitation that further underscores the need for a decrease (Ref. 61).
As discussed in section V.E.5 of this document, other major international regulatory frameworks have established GULs or maximums substantially below the current U.S. maximum of 75 µg/100 kcal: Codex Alimentarius, FSANZ, Health Canada, and China specify a GUL or maximum of 60 µg/100 kcal, and the EU specifies a maximum of 29 µg/100 kcal (table 6). In 1998, the LSRO Panel report explicitly concluded that the current maximum of 75 µg/100 kcal was too high and recommended a maximum of 35 µg/100 kcal based on the 75th percentile of FDA analyses of marketed formulas at the time (Ref. 1). The proposed maximum of 50 µg/100 kcal represents a substantial reduction from the current maximum and falls within international consensus and available scientific evidence to reduce risk of excessive exposure while allowing manufacturing flexibility.
Since the 1998 LSRO Panel report, several lines of evidence have emerged that support reducing the maximum specification. A Technical Consultation document noted that daily intakes exceeding 180 µg/day are not expected to provide additional health benefit and may be associated with impaired thyroid function (Ref. 75). Consistent with this, studies conducted in populations with high environmental iodine exposure have documented adverse thyroid outcomes in infants and young children at elevated iodine intakes (Refs. 72, 73). A balance study (Ref. 68) further found that iodine retention was linear across all intake levels up to 300 µg/day, with no evidence of homeostatic down-regulation (
i.e.,
the body's ability to automatically reduce absorption or increase excretion to prevent excess buildup) at higher intakes, suggesting that infants do not have robust mechanisms to limit iodine retention at high intakes and that higher formula iodine concentrations may result in proportionally higher retention with uncertain long-term consequences. FDA considers that these findings, while derived from populations with environmental iodine excess rather than formula-fed infants, provide the best available evidence for understanding the biological consequences of sustained elevated iodine intake in early infancy and collectively support a significant downward revision of the maximum (Ref. 61).
At 50 µg/100 kcal, an infant 0-6 months of age consuming a typical daily infant formula intake would receive approximately 264 µg/day of iodine, and an infant 6-12 months of age consuming a typical daily infant formula intake would receive approximately 203 µg/day of iodine. Among higher consumers, NHANES-derived estimates of energy intake from infant formula indicate that, at the 90th percentile of energy intake from infant formula (836 kcal/day for infants 0-6 months of age and 794 kcal/day for infants 6-12 months of age), the proposed maximum of 50 µg/100 kcal would permit iodine intakes of approximately 418 µg/day and 397 µg/day, respectively (Refs. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 61).
FDA acknowledges that these intakes exceed 180 µg/day, the level above which additional health benefits are unlikely (Ref. 75); however, they are below the probable safe upper limits of 150 µg/kg/day for infants 0-6 months of age (reference weight: 6 kg) and 140 µg/kg/day for infants 7-12 months of age (reference weight: 8.9 kg). Using the reference weights identified in the report, these correspond to absolute upper limits of approximately 900 µg/day and 1,246 µg/day, respectively (Ref. 64). In populations with excess environmental exposure to iodine, reports of subclinical hypothyroidism in infants and young children have been documented (Refs. 72, 73). However, the evidence from these studies is derived from populations with environmental iodine excess rather than routine feeding of formula-fed infants, and the generalizability of these findings to U.S. formula-fed infants is uncertain. Because no UL has been established for infants, the percentage of UL at the proposed maximum cannot be calculated: a significant limitation that FDA acknowledges. The proposed maximum reflects a conservative approach based primarily on international regulatory alignment, rather than a formally derived safety margin (Ref. 61).

F. Potassium
The current requirements for potassium in infant formula are a minimum level of 80 mg/100 kcal and a maximum level of 200 mg/100 kcal (§ 107.100). Based on our analysis of scientific information and data since the 1998 LSRO Panel report (Ref. 1), including infant formula potassium requirements in international standards, we conclude that the required potassium levels in § 107.100 remain appropriate.
1. Background
Potassium is an essential nutrient that serves critical physiological functions in infants, including regulation of cell volume, membrane transport, cardiac conduction, nerve signaling, and muscle contraction (Ref. 76). Most of the potassium in the body is found inside cells; potassium and sodium are interrelated and function together across cell membranes to regulate cell volume and membrane transport. Potassium also plays a role in regulating water and acid-base balance in the blood and tissues (Ref. 76). Potassium metabolism is tightly controlled over a wide range of dietary intakes, primarily regulated via the kidneys. Assessing potassium status is difficult because most potassium in the body resides inside cells, and no sensitive biomarker exists that can characterize the distribution of potassium requirements in healthy populations (Refs. 76, 77).
a. Health Consequences of Potassium Deficiency
Hypokalemia (
i.e.,
low blood potassium; serum potassium ≤3.5 mmol/L) can result from inadequate intake, excessive losses, or transcellular shifts in potassium. Hypokalemia from dietary inadequacy alone is rare in healthy individuals because the kidney efficiently conserves potassium at low dietary intakes (Ref. 77). Potassium depletion studies conducted in adults over short periods have shown that very low intakes (0-390 mg/day) can lead to hypokalemia. Inadequate potassium intake may also contribute to impaired glycemic control (Ref. 78). However, in clinical settings, hypokalemia is more commonly caused by abnormal losses of potassium (renal or gastrointestinal) or medications promoting transcellular shifts (Ref. 76).
b. Health Consequences of Excess Potassium Intake
In healthy individuals with normal kidney function, excess potassium is efficiently excreted and toxicity from dietary sources is unlikely. Hyperkalemia (
i.e.,
high blood potassium) is of greater concern in individuals with chronic kidney disease, diabetes, heart failure, adrenal insufficiency, or those taking certain medications. In addition, there is no evidence that high intakes of potassium cause hyperkalemia or other adverse effects in adults with normal kidney function (Ref. 77).
2. Nutrient Reference Values
a. NASEM
NASEM published DRIs for water, potassium, sodium, chloride, and sulfate in 2005 and published an updated report specific to sodium and potassium in 2019 (Refs. 19, 76). Because no EAR could be established due to the absence of a sensitive biomarker of potassium status and limitations in available balance study data, the committee established AI values for potassium in infants based on estimated potassium intakes from human milk (Ref. 76). The AI for infants 0-6 months of age was set at 400 mg/day, derived by multiplying the average human milk intake (0.78 L/day) by the average human milk potassium concentration (515 mg/L) from a meta-analysis of 15 studies focusing on the first 6 months of lactation. The AI for infants 7-12 months of age was set at 860 mg/day, based on estimated intakes from human milk plus an estimated potassium intake from complementary foods of approximately 600 mg/day, derived from NHANES 2003-2010 and FITS 2016 data (Ref. 76). The AI for infants 0-6 months of age is unchanged from the 2005 DRI report, while the AI for infants 7-12 months of age was increased from 700 mg/day (2005) to 860 mg/day (2019), reflecting updated estimates of complementary food contributions (Refs. 19, 76).
No UL has been established for potassium in infants. The 2019 NASEM committee concluded that “there is insufficient evidence of potassium toxicity risk within the apparently healthy population to establish a potassium Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL)” (Ref. 76).
b. EFSA
The EFSA Panel established an AI of 750 mg/day for infants 7-11 months of age, extrapolated from the adult AI using isometric scaling and a growth factor (Ref. 79). No AI was established for infants 0-6 months of age. The EFSA NDA Panel estimated an approximate midpoint potassium concentration in mature human milk of 500 mg/L based on data from multiple studies of women from Western countries (Ref. 79).
c. D-A-CH
The D-A-CH reference values established estimated values of 400 mg/day for infants 0-4 months of age and 600 mg/day for infants 4-12 months of age. The authors based the 0-4-month estimate on an average human milk intake of 750 mL/day and a mean potassium content of 500 mg/L. They calculated the 4-12-month estimate by extrapolating from the younger group's value and adjusting for differences in reference body weight (Ref. 80).
d. Australian NHMRC/New Zealand MoH
NHMRC/MoH (2006) (Ref. 53) derived the AI for infants 0-6 months of age as 400 mg/day, calculated by multiplying the average human milk intake (0.78 L/day) by the average human milk potassium concentration (500 mg/L). NHMRC/MoH derived an AI of 700 mg/day for infants 7-12 months of age, calculated by assuming an average 0.6 L/day of human milk intake plus 440 mg/day from complementary foods.

There is consistency across international bodies in the AI established for young infants (0-6 months of age). Divergence in AIs for older infants (7-12 months of age) across international bodies is primarily attributable to methodological differences in estimating potassium intake from complementary foods. EFSA used a different approach entirely, extrapolating from the adult AI using isometric scaling rather than observed infant intake data.
3. Human Milk Composition
Maternal dietary intake does not strongly influence human milk potassium concentrations (Ref. 76). Human milk potassium concentrations decline over the course of lactation (Ref. 79). Four sources informed the analysis of potassium concentrations in human milk: the 2019 NASEM meta-analysis (Ref. 76), the 2016 EFSA NDA Panel review (Ref. 79), the iHMNutD study (Ref. 8), and the MILQ study (Ref. 36).
In 2019, NASEM conducted a meta-analysis of 15 longitudinal and cross-sectional studies (1980-2017) and estimated mean potassium concentrations of 515 mg/L (95 percent confidence interval (CI): 472.76-557.81 mg/L) for the 0-6-month interval and 437 mg/L (95 percent CI: 367.89-505.22 mg/L) for the 7-12-month interval (Ref. 76). The 2016 EFSA Panel reviewed data from eight studies (1982-2012) and derived an estimate of approximately 500 mg/L as the midpoint concentration (Ref. 79). The iHMNutD study identified 10 eligible North American studies (1980-2024; total n = 905) and estimated a weighted mean potassium concentration of 573 ± 75 mg/L (Ref. 8). Additionally, the MILQ study, the most comprehensive recent data, reported a pooled median of 542 mg/L (interquartile range (IQR): 485-609 mg/L) from 1 to 6 months of lactation (Ref. 36).
Across all four sources, central estimates of potassium concentration in mature human milk ranged from approximately 500 to 573 mg/L (Refs. 8, 36, 76, 79). The NASEM estimate for human milk potassium content for infants 7-12 months of age (437 mg/L) (Ref. 76) was notably lower than the estimate for younger infants, consistent with the expected decline in potassium concentration over the course of lactation. While estimates derived from NASEM, EFSA, and the iHMNutD study show a degree of consistency, this convergence should be interpreted with some caution, as the three analyses draw from an overlapping body of foundational literature, particularly studies conducted in North American populations during the 1980s and 1990s (Ref. 77). The MILQ study (Ref. 36) provides broader geographic evidence consistent with the range of concentrations observed in North American estimates.
4. International Regulatory Standards for Infant Formula
The current U.S. minimum requirement for potassium aligns with the EU and meets or exceeds the minimum levels set by most other international bodies. The U.S. maximum of 200 mg/100 kcal exceeds most international standards, with only China's standard for infants 6-12 months of age (225 mg/100 kcal) surpassing it (see table 9).
In its 1998 comprehensive review, the LSRO Panel recommended a potassium range of 60-160 mg/100 kcal for infants 0-12 months of age. The recommended minimum was derived from the mean minus one standard deviation of potassium concentrations in mature human milk, with no evidence identified to suggest differences in potassium bioavailability between human milk and infant formula. The recommended maximum of 160 mg/100 kcal was based on the 90th percentile of FDA analyses of commercially available infant formulas at the time (Ref. 1).

5. Recent Scientific Evidence on Potassium Intake
Several U.S.-based national dietary surveys have assessed potassium intake in U.S. infants and toddlers, consistently demonstrating that most infants meet or exceed established AIs for potassium. Data are available primarily from three iterations of FITS (FITS 2002, 2008, and 2016) (Refs. 43, 81, 82, 83) and from NHANES 2009-2012 (Ref. 84).
Mean potassium intakes for infants 0-6 months of age generally met or exceeded the AI of 400 mg/day. Mean intakes ranged from approximately 570 to 700 mg/day across datasets. At the 10th percentile, intakes ranged from
(
printed page 69058)
approximately 387 to 414 mg/day across FITS 2008 and FITS 2016, close to the AI, suggesting that most infants in this age group had potassium intakes at or above the recommended level.
Mean potassium intakes for infants 7-12 months of age consistently exceeded the current AI of 860 mg/day and ranged from approximately 1,085 to 1,225 mg/day across three FITS iterations and NHANES 2009-2012. The 10th percentile of usual potassium intake ranged from approximately 650 to 791 mg/day across available studies, falling below the current AI of 860 mg/day. While most infants had adequate intakes, a small proportion had intakes near or below the AI.
Several methodological limitations should be considered. Potassium intake estimates rely on proxy-reported 24-hour dietary recalls subject to recall bias. Human milk volumes were not directly measured but estimated using standardized assumptions, and some analyses excluded the youngest infants from intake modeling. The available data do not include information on health outcomes associated with potassium intake levels. As such, the extent to which current intakes translate to clinical outcomes cannot be determined from these data alone (Ref. 77).
6. Evidence Evaluation and Rationale
Based on the review of available scientific data, information, and international standards, we conclude that the current minimum level of 80 mg/100 kcal and maximum level of 200 mg/100 kcal for potassium in § 107.100 remain appropriate.
a. Maintaining the Minimum Specification of 80 mg/100 kcal
The current minimum of 80 mg/100 kcal is consistent with human milk potassium concentrations and provides potassium intakes that meet or exceed established AIs when applied to typical formula consumption patterns. The most current estimates of human milk potassium concentration range from approximately 77 to 88 mg/100 kcal (derived from 500 to 573 mg/L at a typical energy density of 650 kcal/L) (Refs. 8, 36, 76, 77, 79). The current minimum falls within this range.
Applied to typical formula consumption patterns, the current minimum provides potassium intakes that meet or exceed NASEM (2019) AIs for both infant age groups. For an infant 0-6 months of age consuming a typical daily infant formula intake, the minimum specification of 80 mg/100 kcal provides approximately 422 mg/day, which is 105 percent of the AI of 400 mg/day. For an infant 7-12 months of age consuming a typical daily infant formula intake, the minimum provides approximately 324 mg/day from formula alone. When combined with the estimated complementary food contribution of approximately 600 mg/day (Ref. 76), total intake would be approximately 920 mg/day, which is 107 percent of the AI of 860 mg/day. These calculations demonstrate that the current minimum supports adequate potassium intake across the first year of life (Ref. 77).
Population intake data provide contextual support for maintaining the current minimum. Across several large national surveys, mean potassium intakes for infants 0-6 months of age ranged from approximately 570 to 700 mg/day, and for infants 6-12 months of age ranged from approximately 1,085 to 1,225 mg/day, with all mean estimates exceeding the respective AIs (Refs. 43, 81, 82, 83, 84).
The current U.S. minimum is consistent with or above international regulatory standards. FDA considered whether the minimum should be lowered to 60 mg/100 kcal to align with Codex Alimentarius, FSANZ, Health Canada, and LSRO; however, lowering the minimum to 60 mg/100 kcal would reduce the daily potassium intake from formula for infants 0-6 months of age to approximately 78 percent of the AI, reducing the margin of adequacy for infants consuming formula as their sole source of nutrition. Maintaining the current minimum of 80 mg/100 kcal is supported by human milk composition data and U.S. population intake data and falls within the range of minimums set by international standards. FDA has not identified evidence that the current minimum is nutritionally insufficient or presents manufacturing challenges.
b. Maintaining the Maximum Specification of 200 mg/100 kcal
The current maximum of 200 mg/100 kcal was originally established based on the potassium content of cow milk, which was considered to represent a significant but tolerable burden on the kidneys for healthy infants with normal renal function (Ref. 85). After reviewing the available scientific evidence, FDA concludes that this maximum remains appropriate (Ref. 77).
No authoritative body has established a UL for potassium in infants (Refs. 1, 76, 77, 79). However, the current maximum of 200 mg/100 kcal has been in effect since the 1980 Infant Formula Act was enacted without documented adverse effects attributable to potassium intake from infant formula in healthy infants (Ref. 77).
The current maximum of 200 mg/100 kcal provides a substantial margin above the potassium content of human milk (approximately 77-88 mg/100 kcal), positioned at approximately 227-260 percent of the mean mature human milk potassium content on a per-calorie basis (Ref. 77). Applied to typical infant formula daily consumption, the current maximum would provide approximately 1,054 mg/day for an infant 0-6 months of age and approximately 812 mg/day from formula alone for an infant 7-12 months of age. These intakes substantially exceed the AIs but remain well below the levels associated with adverse effects in healthy infants with normal renal function (Refs. 1, 77).
Internationally, maximum specifications range from 160 to 180 mg/100 kcal for infants 0-6 months of age and up to 225 mg/100 kcal for infants 6-12 months of age, with the U.S. maximum of 200 mg/100 kcal falling within the upper portion of this range (see table 9). FDA considered whether the maximum should be lowered to align with the international consensus range and concludes that such a change is not warranted at this time. No UL has been established for potassium in infants, no documented adverse effects from dietary potassium intake at the current maximum have been identified, and lowering the maximum would reduce manufacturing flexibility without a demonstrated safety benefit. The LSRO Panel's recommended maximum of 160 mg/100 kcal was based on the 90th percentile of FDA analyses of infant formulas on the market at that time, rather than on safety concerns (Ref. 1). FDA also considered whether the maximum should be raised and concludes this is not warranted. No evidence was identified suggesting that higher potassium levels in infant formula would provide nutritional benefits (Ref. 77).
c. Consideration of the Evidence Base
FDA acknowledges several uncertainties in the evidence base. No sensitive biomarker of potassium status has been identified that can be used to assess adequacy at the population level (Refs. 76, 79). The AIs for infants are derived from observed intake data rather than experimental determination of requirements, and the AI for infants 7-12 months of age is sensitive to assumptions about complementary food contributions. Human milk potassium concentrations vary across studies, stages of lactation, and populations. Population intake data are based on proxy-reported dietary recalls not linked to health outcomes. Given these limitations, FDA considers that

maintaining the current specifications, which have a demonstrated history of safe use, is appropriate in the absence of compelling evidence for change (Ref. 77).
G. Vitamin A (Proposed §§ 107.10(a)(2), (b)(1), and 107.100(a) and (g))
The current requirements for vitamin A in infant formula are a minimum level of 250 IU/100 kcal (75 μg RAE/100 kcal) and a maximum level of 750 IU/100 kcal (225 μg RAE/100 kcal) (
21 CFR 107.100
). Based on our analysis of scientific information and data since the 1998 LSRO Panel report (Ref. 1), including infant formula vitamin A requirements in international standards, we propose to decrease the required minimum to 70 μg RAE/100 kcal (233 IU/100 kcal) and decrease the maximum specification to 120 μg RAE/100 kcal (400 IU/100 kcal) for vitamin A in infant formula in § 107.100(a). We also propose changes to the unit of measure from IU to μg RAE in § 107.10(a)(2), (b)(1), and § 107.100(a). Finally, we propose to change which forms of vitamin A may contribute to the minimum and maximum vitamin A content calculations from both preformed vitamin A and
beta
-carotene to preformed vitamin A only in newly established § 107.100(g).
1. Background
Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin and essential nutrient that supports vision, immune function, cell growth and differentiation, and embryonic development (Ref. 86). These functions are especially critical during infancy, a period of rapid growth and immune system development. The term “vitamin A” encompasses preformed vitamin A (
i.e.,
retinol and retinyl esters) and provitamin A carotenoids such as
beta
-carotene, which the body can convert to active vitamin A. Infants are born with limited hepatic vitamin A stores even when mothers are well-nourished during pregnancy, making adequate postnatal intake from human milk or infant formula essential (Refs. 62, 86, 87, 88).
a. Factors Affecting Absorption
Preformed vitamin A absorption efficiency is generally 70-90 percent (Refs. 62, 87). However, exclusively formula-fed infants may absorb vitamin A less efficiently than breastfed infants because bile-salt-stimulated lipase (BSSL), which is present in human milk but absent from infant formula, facilitates hydrolysis of retinyl esters. Formula-fed infants rely solely on endogenous digestive enzymes for this process (Ref. 1). Unlike preformed vitamin A, the absorption and conversion of provitamin A carotenoids such as
beta
-carotene are far more variable (5-65 percent), depending on factors such as the food source, genetics, vitamin A status, and health status. The extent to which infants can absorb and convert
beta
-carotene to active vitamin A remains poorly understood (Refs. 62, 87, 89).
b. Health Consequences of Vitamin A Deficiency
Vitamin A deficiency (VAD) is a major public health concern in low- and middle-income countries, affecting an estimated 190 million preschool-age children globally (Ref. 90). Xerophthalmia is a well-documented consequence of VAD, encompassing a spectrum of ocular manifestations from night blindness to corneal ulceration and blindness (Refs. 87, 88, 91). VAD is also associated with increased morbidity and mortality from infectious diseases and impaired iron mobilization contributing to anemia (Refs. 62, 87, 91). In the United States and other high-income countries, clinical VAD is uncommon in healthy term infants receiving adequate nutrition, though infants with fat malabsorption disorders (
e.g.,
cystic fibrosis, cholestatic liver disease) are at elevated risk (Ref. 91).
c. Health Consequences of Excess Vitamin A Intake
Vitamin A is fat soluble and is stored primarily in the liver (Refs. 62, 87). Excessive intake of preformed vitamin A can cause hypervitaminosis A, a toxic condition caused by having too much vitamin A in the body. Provitamin A carotenoids are not associated with toxicity, because their absorption and conversion are downregulated at high intakes (Ref. 89). Acute toxicity in infants may manifest as bulging fontanelle, vomiting, irritability, and headache (Ref. 86). Chronic toxicity symptoms may include fatigue, loss of appetite, hair loss, bone pain, skin changes, and, in serious cases, liver damage, decreased bone mineral density, and increased intracranial pressure. In young children, doses as low as 450 μg/kg/day have been reported to cause hypervitaminosis A (Refs. 62, 88, 92).
2. Nutrient Reference Values
a. NASEM
NASEM established AIs for vitamin A in infants in 2001 based on the mean vitamin A intake of infants fed human milk, as no functional criteria of vitamin A status reflecting dietary response in infants have been demonstrated. The AI for infants 0-6 months of age was set at 400 μg RAE/day, derived from an average milk intake of 0.78 L/day and average human milk vitamin A concentration of 485 μg/L during the first 6 months of lactation. The AI for infants 7-12 months of age was set at 500 μg RAE/day, based on extrapolation from the 0-6-month AI plus estimated contributions from human milk and complementary foods. NASEM did not consider contribution of carotenoids in human milk in meeting the vitamin A requirement of infants (Ref. 61). The UL was set at 600 μg RAE/day for infants 0-12 months of age, derived from case reports of hypervitaminosis A in infants, with a lowest observed adverse effect level (LOAEL) of 6,000 μg/day and an uncertainty factor of 10 to account for the extrapolation from a LOAEL to a NOAEL. NASEM acknowledged this UL was deliberately conservative (Ref. 62).
b. EFSA
The 2015 EFSA Panel derived dietary reference values for vitamin A using a factorial approach (
i.e.,
multiplying together a series of known biological parameters) with pediatric-specific adjustments for body weight, liver/body weight ratio, and growth, yielding a PRI of 250 μg retinol equivalents (RE)/day for infants 7-11 months of age (Ref. 87). In 2024, EFSA proposed a UL of 600 μg RE/day for all infants 4-11 months of age, derived by allometric scaling from the adult UL (Ref. 89). EFSA noted that a UL of 500 μg RE/day for infants 4-6 months of age would be overconservative given that human milk secretion of retinol is estimated at 424 μg RE/day (midpoint concentration: 530 μg/L × 0.8 L/day) during the first 6 months of lactation (Ref. 89).
c. Australian NHMRC/New Zealand MoH
NHMRC/MoH derived AIs for vitamin A in infants based on human milk composition from a single multinational study (Ref. 53). The AI for infants 0-6 months of age was set at 250 µg retinol/day (as retinyl esters), based on an average human milk intake of 0.78 L/day and a retinol concentration of 310 µg/L. The AI for infants 7-12 months of age was set at 430 µg RE/day, based on an average human milk intake of 0.6 L/day (approximately 186 µg RE/day), plus an estimated 244 µg RE/day from complementary foods (including vitamin A from retinol and carotenoids). The UL for infants 0-12 months of age was set at 600 µg RE/day, derived from case reports of hypervitaminosis A in infants (Ref. 53).

d. FAO/WHO
The joint FAO/WHO Consultation estimated vitamin A requirements for infants from observed retinol intakes of breastfed infants in communities with good nutrition and no signs of deficiency (Ref. 3). Notably, due to insufficient data to derive mean requirements for any age group, the Consultation provided “recommended safe intakes” rather than true RNIs. The recommended safe intake for infants 0-6 months of age was set at 375 µg RE/day, based on an average human milk retinol concentration of approximately 1.75 µmol/L (503 µg/L × 0.75 L/day). The recommended safe intake for infants 7-12 months of age was increased to 400 µg RE/day, accounting for a decline in average milk intake to 0.65 L/day and increased mortality risk in vitamin A-deficient populations from 6 months of age onward (Ref. 3).

Authoritative bodies differ fundamentally on whether infant vitamin A requirements should be derived from observed intakes from human milk or through a factorial approach. NASEM (Ref. 62), FAO/WHO (Ref. 3), and NHMRC/MoH (Ref. 53) all used human milk composition, but the wide variation in mean retinol concentrations across studies explains why these bodies arrived at different values despite using the same general approach. None of the bodies reviewed incorporated provitamin A carotenoid contributions from human milk into reference values for infants 0-6 months of age due to unknown bioconversion efficiency in this age group. With respect to ULs, NASEM, NHMRC/MoH, and EFSA converged on 600 µg RAE/day or 600 µg RE/day despite different derivation methods, strengthening confidence in this value for evaluating maximum levels (Ref. 86).
FDA believes the NASEM AIs are the most appropriate choice for assessing minimum vitamin A requirements in infant formula, as they represent the most conservative estimates and best ensure that infant nutritional needs are met (Ref. 86).
3. Human Milk Composition
Vitamin A in human milk is present almost exclusively as retinyl esters in the lipid fraction of the milk (Ref. 93). Retinol concentration is highly dependent on fat content, is substantially higher in colostrum than in mature milk, and reflects both maternal vitamin A status and recent dietary intake (Ref. 93).
Three primary data sources inform FDA's assessment of vitamin A concentrations in mature human milk. These sources were selected based on recent publication dates, robust study designs, validated analytical methods, and inclusion of healthy, full-term mother-infant dyads (Ref. 86). A 2022 meta-analysis pooled data from 76 studies that used high-performance liquid chromatography-based retinol measurements totaling 9,171 samples across 33 geographically diverse countries (Ref. 94). Studies involving vitamin A supplementation were excluded. Country was identified as a significant source of variance (Ref. 94). The authors proposed the mean early mature milk concentration of 402.4 μg/L as the reference concentration for DRI revision in infants up to 6 months of age (Ref. 94). The MILQ study (Ref. 95) provides the most comprehensive recent data on retinol concentrations in human milk using validated analytical methods from well-nourished, unsupplemented populations across four countries. Median milk retinol concentrations were highest in early lactation (886 µg/L) and stabilized from 3 months onward (450-460 µg/L) (Ref. 95). The iHMNutD study reported a pooled weighted mean of 36.09 µg/100 g (approximately 372 µg/L) (Ref. 8); however, this value was based on a limited number of studies and participants, introducing uncertainty (Ref. 8).
FDA acknowledges several limitations relevant to the estimates from human milk studies that introduce uncertainty in cross-study comparisons, including small sample sizes, geographic variability, inconsistent collection protocols, and the absence of milk fat adjustment for retinol concentrations (see Ref. 86). Notwithstanding this, FDA considers that these three sources support a plausible range of approximately 370-460 μg/L (approximately 57-71 μg RAE/100 kcal) as the best current estimate of vitamin A concentration in mature human milk, with higher concentrations observed in early mature milk. This range informs FDA's proposed minimum vitamin A specification in infant formula.
4. International Regulatory Standards for Infant Formula
Vitamin A specifications for infant formula vary among international regulatory bodies and expert organizations, though most have adopted or proposed to adopt specifications that generally align with Codex Alimentarius standards (see table 11). The Codex Alimentarius specifies a minimum of 60 μg RE/100 kcal and a maximum of 180 μg RE/100 kcal for infant formula (for infants 0-6 months of age) (Ref. 12). For follow-on formula (for infants 6-12 months of age), Codex Alimentarius specifies a higher minimum of 75 μg RE/100 kcal with the same maximum (Ref. 37).
FSANZ and Health Canada specify the same maximum as Codex

Alimentarius but do not specify a higher minimum for infants 6-12 months of age, maintaining 60 μg RE/100 kcal for infants 0-12 months of age (Refs. 39, 40). The EU and China have higher minimums and/or lower maximums than Codex Alimentarius. The EU, based on recommendations from EFSA (Ref. 7), specifies a minimum of 70 μg RE/100 kcal and a maximum of 114 μg RE/100 kcal, applicable to both infant formula and follow-on formula (Ref. 38). The EU minimum of 70 μg RE/100 kcal was set to ensure that infants consuming approximately 500 kcal/day receive at least 350 μg RE/day (Ref. 7). The EU reduced the maximum from 180 μg RE/100 kcal to 114 μg RE/100 kcal (Ref. 96), resulting in a daily vitamin A intake of approximately 570 μg RE/day (assuming 500 kcal/day), just under the UL of 600 μg RE/day. China also specifies a lower maximum of 150 μg RE/100 kcal for infant formula (Ref. 41), although the maximum for follow-on formula is consistent with Codex Alimentarius (Ref. 42).
The LSRO Panel report recommended a minimum preformed vitamin A content of infant formulas of 60 μg RE/100 kcal and a maximum of 150 μg RE/100 kcal (Ref. 1), noting that a minimum above the estimated vitamin A concentration in human milk (approximately 30 μg RE/100 kcal) was appropriate to account for lower absorption efficiency in formula-fed infants due to the absence of BSSL (Refs. 1, 86).
