5. Recent Scientific Evidence on Vitamin A Intake
Several U.S.-based national dietary surveys have assessed vitamin A intake in U.S. infants and toddlers, including the FITS (FITS 2008 and FITS 2016) and NHANES (NHANES 2009-2012 and NHANES 2015-2020) (Refs. 81, 82, 84, 86, 97). Mean intakes for infants 0-6 months of age ranged from approximately 582 to 637 μg RAE/day, and for infants 6-12 months of age from approximately 669 to 794 μg RAE/day. Preformed vitamin A constituted 88 percent of total vitamin A intake for infants 0-6 months of age and 74 percent for infants 6-12 months of age, with the remainder derived from provitamin A carotenoids (Ref. 97). The proportion of infants with vitamin A intakes exceeding the UL ranged from 21 to 39 percent depending on study and age group (Refs. 81, 82, 84).
Important methodological differences must be considered when interpreting these data. Treatment of human milk varies substantially across studies. NHANES-based analyses exclude or cannot quantify human milk contributions, while FITS-based analyses estimate them through imputation. Infant dietary supplement inclusion differs across studies, and supplement use was reported in 8.8-23 percent of infants (Refs. 81, 82). Finally, carotenoid-derived vitamin A is disaggregated from preformed vitamin A only in one available study (Ref. 97), limiting comparisons of retinol versus carotenoid contributions.
Overall, the available studies support the conclusion that current vitamin A intakes in U.S. infants are adequate and that a significant proportion have
(
printed page 69062)
intakes approaching or exceeding the UL. It should be noted, however, that the available dietary intake data do not include information on health outcomes associated with vitamin A intake levels (Ref. 86).
6. Evidence Evaluation and Rationale
Based on the review of available scientific data, information, and international standards, we propose to decrease the current minimum specification for vitamin A from 75 to 70 μg RAE/100 kcal and to decrease the current maximum specification for vitamin A from 225 to 120 μg RAE/100 kcal in § 107.100. We also propose a change to the unit of measure for vitamin A in §§ 107.10(a)(2) and (b)(1) and 107.100 from IU to μg RAE. Finally, we propose a change to the form of vitamin A that may be used to meet the minimum and maximum vitamin A specifications in § 107.100 from both preformed vitamin A and
beta
-carotene to preformed vitamin A only in § 107.100(g) (see table 11).
a. Rationale for Changing the Unit of Measure From IU to µg RAE
Expert scientific bodies recommend expressing vitamin A intake in µg RAE rather than IU, as these weight-based units more accurately reflect the differing bioavailability and bioconversion of preformed vitamin A and provitamin A carotenoids. This approach has been widely adopted in dietary reference values and infant formula vitamin A specifications (tables 10 and 11). In the United States, vitamin A was expressed in RE in the 1989 National Research Council Recommended Dietary Allowances (Ref. 44). An RE is a standardized unit that captures how much bioavailable vitamin A the body derives from dietary sources. The RAE unit was introduced by the U.S. DRI Committee on vitamin A (Ref. 62) to reflect updated evidence on the bioavailability of provitamin A carotenoids. Under the RE system, 6 μg of
beta
-carotene was considered equivalent to 1 μg of retinol; under the RAE system, 12 μg of
beta
-carotene is required to yield 1 μg of retinol, meaning that the vitamin A activity attributed to provitamin A carotenoids is half the amount obtained when expressed in μg RAE compared to μg RE. Because preformed retinol contributes equally under both systems (1 μg retinol = 1 μg RE = 1 μg RAE), the practical effect of this change is that total vitamin A intake estimates are lower when carotenoid contributions are calculated using μg RAE rather than μg RE. The IOM recommended expressing vitamin A requirements in μg RAE rather than μg RE or IU to more accurately reflect the bioavailability of vitamin A from mixed diets and, accordingly, established the AIs for infants in μg RAE (Ref. 86).
In the United States, when included voluntarily on food (other than infant formula) and dietary supplement labels, vitamin A is declared in µg RAE following the recommendation from the NASEM Labeling Committee that the units of measure be consistent with the DRI (
81 FR 33742
at 33912, May 27, 2016);
21 CFR 101.9(c)(8)(iv)
) (Ref. 98). We are therefore proposing to change the units of measure for vitamin A in infant formula from IU to µg RAE, for consistency with both the DRI and U.S. nutrition labeling regulations for other foods. We believe this proposed change will benefit consumers, as it aligns the unit of measure for vitamin A in infant formula with that already used for general food and dietary supplement labeling in the United States, as well as infant formula labeling outside the United States. The IU may be voluntarily declared in parentheses immediately following the declaration in µg RAE, providing infant formula manufacturers with flexibility and supporting continuity for consumers accustomed to IU-based labeling. This change would also be more aligned with international regulatory standards. If only preformed vitamin A is permitted to meet the vitamin A requirement in infant formula, the adoption of µg RAE would not create a discrepancy with international organizations that use µg RE, since 1 µg RAE = 1 µg RE = 1 µg all-
trans
-retinol. The three units are numerically equivalent when applied solely to preformed retinol. FDA has developed a guidance document that provides detailed instructions to assist manufacturers in converting from IU to µg RAE (Ref. 99).
b. Rationale for Allowing Only Preformed Vitamin A To Meet Vitamin A Specifications
Current U.S. regulation allows
beta
-carotene to be used in infant formula as a source of vitamin A (§ 184.1245 (
21 CFR 184.1245
)). Other international expert bodies, aside from FSANZ, allow only preformed vitamin A as a source of vitamin A in infant formula (table 11). In its 1998 assessment, the LSRO recommended using only preformed vitamin A to meet the minimum requirements in infant formula (Ref. 1). NASEM did not include
beta
-carotene contributions when establishing the AI for vitamin A for infants because the bioconversion of carotenoids in milk and in infants is not known (Ref. 62). Because the efficiency with which infants convert
beta
-carotene to active vitamin A is unknown, relying on
beta
-carotene as a source of vitamin A in infant formula may put infants at risk of vitamin A deficiency if the assumed conversion does not occur as expected. Additionally, only preformed retinols are considered when establishing the UL for vitamin A, as provitamin A carotenoids are not known to cause vitamin A toxicity (Ref. 62). Thus, excluding
beta
-carotene from the calculated vitamin A content of infant formula would not increase the risk of vitamin A toxicity (Ref. 1, 62, 86). Therefore, FDA is proposing to amend § 107.100 to specify that vitamin A minimum and maximum levels must be met through preformed vitamin A only.
Beta
-carotene, if used in infant formula, shall not be considered to contribute to the required minimum and maximum levels of vitamin A in infant formula (proposed § 107.100(g)).
The use of
beta
-carotene in infant formula is addressed in § 184.1245(c)(2). FDA proposes to amend § 184.1245(c)(2) to list infant formula among the foods in which
beta
-carotene may be used at levels not to exceed current good manufacturing practice.
c. Decreasing the Minimum Specification From 75 µg RAE/100 kcal to 70 µg RAE/100 kcal
The proposed minimum specification of 70 µg RAE/100 kcal is supported by DRIs, human milk composition data, bioavailability considerations, manufacturing feasibility, and international standards, and provides an appropriate margin of nutritional adequacy for formula-fed infants. FDA relies on NASEM AIs as the most appropriate and conservative reference values for vitamin A requirements in infant formula. Notably, the AI is not equivalent to a minimum requirement, but rather it represents an intake assumed to be adequate based on observed intakes in healthy, breastfed infants (Ref. 62). At the proposed minimum, an infant 0-6 months of age consuming a typical daily infant formula intake would receive 369 μg RAE/day (92 percent of the NASEM AI of 400 μg RAE/day). For infants 6-12 months of age consuming a typical daily infant formula intake, the proposed minimum would provide 284 μg RAE/day from formula. NASEM estimated that complementary foods provide approximately 244 μg/day, yielding a combined intake of approximately 528 μg/day (106 percent of the NASEM AI of 500 μg RAE/day). FDA considers this level of intake adequate to meet the vitamin A needs of formula-fed infants 0-12 months of age, with a low risk of deficiency (Ref. 86).
(
printed page 69063)
Human milk composition data from multiple studies (Refs. 8, 94, 95) support a plausible range of approximately 370 to 460 μg retinol/L in mature human milk, corresponding to approximately 57 to 71 μg RAE/100 kcal. The proposed minimum of 70 μg RAE/100 kcal falls at the upper end of this range, indicating that formula-fed infants consuming formula at the proposed minimum would receive vitamin A at concentrations consistent with mature human milk from well-nourished populations. The proposed minimum also exceeds the LSRO recommendation of 60 μg RE/100 kcal and provides a buffer to account for potentially lower vitamin A absorption from formula due to the absence of BSSL (Ref. 86).
Lowering the minimum from 75 to 70 μg RAE/100 kcal also responds to manufacturing feasibility considerations. Manufacturers must account for nutrient degradation over shelf life, lot-to-lot variability in raw material potency, and inherent variation in blending and manufacturing processes when formulating infant formulas. In conjunction with the proposed maximum of 120 μg RAE/100 kcal, a minimum of 75 μg RAE/100 kcal would create an allowable manufacturing range of only 45 μg RAE/100 kcal. Reducing the minimum to 70 μg RAE/100 kcal widens this range to 50 μg RAE/100 kcal without compromising nutritional adequacy, reducing the risk of unintentional noncompliance during manufacturing (Ref. 86).
The proposed minimum of 70 µg RAE/100 kcal aligns with the EU minimum of 70 µg RE/100 kcal (Ref. 38); exceeds the Codex Alimentarius minimum for infant formula, the FSANZ minimum, the Health Canada proposed minimum, and the LSRO recommendation (all 60 µg RE/100 kcal) (Refs. 1, 12, 39, 40); and falls modestly below the Codex Alimentarius minimum for follow-on formula (75 µg RE/100 kcal) (Ref. 37). FDA's use of the NASEM AI as the primary reference value for assessing minimum requirements is consistent with the higher U.S. minimum relative to some international standards (Ref. 86).
FDA assesses that 70 µg RAE/100 kcal is consistent with available data on nutritional adequacy and appropriate as a minimum specification. At this level, estimated intakes for infants 0-6 months of age represent approximately 92 percent of the NASEM AI, within the 15 percent margin below the AI that has been used by other regulatory bodies to indicate low risk of nutritional inadequacy (Ref. 100).
d. Decreasing the Maximum Specification From 225 to 120 µg RAE/100 kcal
FDA's evaluation of the maximum is guided by the NASEM UL of 600 μg RAE/day for infants 0-12 months of age (Ref. 62), which is also supported by EFSA (Ref. 89) and NHMRC/MoH (Ref. 53). The NASEM UL was derived by applying an uncertainty factor of 10 to a LOAEL of 6,000 µg/day, identified from case reports of hypervitaminosis A in infants receiving supplemental preformed vitamin A.
At the current maximum of 225 μg RAE/100 kcal, estimated vitamin A intakes from infant formula substantially exceed the UL across all intake scenarios evaluated. U.S. dietary intake data from multiple national surveys consistently show that mean vitamin A intakes approach or exceed the UL and that 21-39 percent of infants have intakes above the UL (Refs. 81, 82, 84, 97). The current maximum also exceeds that of all other international regulatory standards, none of which permit a maximum above 180 μg RE/100 kcal.
FDA initially considered a maximum of 180 μg RAE/100 kcal, consistent with the Codex standard. However, at typical intake volumes, a maximum of 180 μg RAE/100 kcal would still result in estimated intakes from infant formula alone reaching 158 percent and 122 percent of the UL for infants 0-6 and 7-12 months of age, respectively, and as high as 251 percent and 238 percent of the UL among high consumers (90th percentile of energy intake from infant formula) (Refs. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18). EFSA found that regular consumption of infant formula at the previously permitted maximum of 180 μg RE/100 kcal would result in intakes exceeding the UL (Ref. 7). In the interest of maintaining an adequate safety margin, particularly for high consumers of infant formula, FDA proposes a lower maximum of 120 μg RAE/100 kcal.
At the proposed maximum of 120 μg RAE/100 kcal, estimated vitamin A intakes from infant formula at typical volumes represent 106 percent and 81 percent of the UL for infants 0-6 and 7-12 months of age, respectively. Among high consumers (90th percentile of energy intake) (Refs. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18), estimated intakes from infant formula alone reach 167 percent and 159 percent of the UL for the 0-6-month and 7-12-month age groups, respectively. While intakes exceed the UL under higher intake scenarios, the safety margin relative to the LOAEL improves substantially from approximately 2.9- to 3.2-fold at the current maximum to approximately 4.9- to 9.5-fold at the proposed maximum.
FDA acknowledges that no available data suggest that routine intake of infant formula at current vitamin A levels is associated with adverse events, and that U.S. dietary intake studies did not assess health outcomes associated with vitamin A intake levels (Refs. 81, 82, 84, 86, 97). Nevertheless, FDA considers it appropriate to limit unnecessary exposure to preformed vitamin A above the UL, particularly among high consumers.
The proposed maximum of 120 µg RAE/100 kcal falls within the range of international maximum specifications, which extend from 114 µg RE/100 kcal (EU) to 180 µg RE/100 kcal (Codex Alimentarius, Health Canada, and FSANZ) (Refs. 12, 37, 39, 40) and is below the LSRO recommendation of 150 µg RE/100 kcal (Ref. 1). The proposed maximum of 120 µg RAE/100 kcal is higher than the corresponding EU specification of 114 µg RE/100 kcal. This range is intended to provide manufacturers with sufficient operational flexibility to account for manufacturing overages, nutrient losses during processing, and shelf-life variability while ensuring appropriate vitamin A intakes across the U.S. infant population. FDA acknowledges that, despite a reduction of more than 46 percent from the current maximum, estimated vitamin A intakes among high consumers of infant formula may continue to exceed the UL at the proposed maximum. The safety margin relative to the LOAEL ranges from approximately 4.9- to 9.5-fold across intake scenarios evaluated (Ref. 86).
FDA acknowledges several important uncertainties in the evidence base underlying the proposed specifications for vitamin A in infant formula. The NASEM AI and UL were each derived from a limited number of studies with few participants, and the UL was deliberately set conservatively using a LOAEL rather than a NOAEL (Ref. 62). Human milk retinol concentrations vary substantially across studies, reflecting the influence of lactation stage, milk fat content, maternal vitamin A status, and geographic differences in diet and supplementation practices. The efficiency of vitamin A absorption from infant formula relative to human milk has not been precisely quantified, and the bioconversion efficiency of
beta
-carotene in infants remains unknown (Refs. 62, 95). Finally, none of the available U.S. dietary intake studies assessed health outcomes associated with vitamin A intake levels, limiting the ability to assess health outcomes at current intake levels. Given these
(
printed page 69064)
uncertainties, FDA has taken a conservative approach by only slightly decreasing the current minimum to preserve the margin of nutritional adequacy and implementing a large reduction in the maximum that is supported by the available safety evidence and falls within the range of current international maximum specifications (Ref. 86).
H. Sodium
The current requirements for sodium in infant formula are a minimum level of 20 mg/100 kcal and a maximum level of 60 mg/100 kcal (§ 107.100). Based on our analysis of scientific information and data since the 1998 comprehensive study of infant formula nutrients, including infant formula sodium requirements in international standards, we conclude that the required sodium levels in § 107.100 remain appropriate.
1. Background
Sodium is an essential nutrient. It plays a critical role in regulating extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure homeostasis, and it is important for the absorption of amino acids, small peptides, and monosaccharides (Refs. 76, 101, 102). Together with chloride and potassium, sodium maintains osmotic and acid-base balance between intracellular and extracellular compartments and is necessary for transporting solutes across membranes and generating electrical signals in the musculoskeletal and nervous systems (Refs. 101, 102, 103). Sodium also interacts with calcium, as increasing sodium intake has been shown to increase urinary calcium excretion, which may negatively affect bone health (Refs. 76, 101, 102). Approximately 95 percent of total body sodium is extracellular, and the body absorbs approximately 98 percent of dietary sodium consumed across a wide range of intakes (Refs. 76, 101, 102). There is no sensitive or specific biomarker for sodium status, as blood sodium concentrations are tightly controlled by homeostatic mechanisms (Refs. 76, 101, 102).
a. Health Consequences of Sodium Deficiency
Hyponatremia, defined as a sodium concentration in the blood less than or equal to 135 mmol/L, is rarely due to dietary sodium intake; rather, it is typically due to disturbances in free water balance and the hormonal regulation of that balance (Refs. 76, 101, 102). Low dietary sodium intakes are rare in healthy populations because sodium chloride and other sodium salts are ubiquitous in the food supply. Sodium intakes of infants who participated in the 2002 FITS exceeded the AIs (Ref. 43). There are also adaptive physiological mechanisms that reduce sodium losses in urine, feces, and sweat at low intakes, and the term-newborn kidney has sufficient renal absorption and excretion capabilities to minimize obligatory sodium losses (Refs. 1, 76, 101, 102).
b. Health Consequences of Excess Sodium Intake
Hypernatremia, defined as a blood sodium concentration greater than 145 mmol/L, is typically a consequence of dehydration rather than excessive sodium intake (Ref. 76). In adults, excessive sodium intake has been linked to elevated blood pressure and increased risk of cardiovascular disease (Refs. 76, 101, 102). It has been suggested that sodium intake during infancy may influence future blood pressure and taste preferences for sodium; however, the current evidence is insufficient to establish an upper limit of intake for this age group, and more research is needed (Refs. 76, 101, 102).
2. Nutrient Reference Values
a. NASEM
NASEM updated AIs for sodium in infants in its 2019 report,
Dietary Reference Intakes for Sodium and Potassium
(Ref. 76). The AI for infants 0-6 months of age was set at 110 mg/day, based on an estimated mean human milk sodium concentration of 140 mg/L and an assumed average consumption of 0.78 L/day. The AI for infants 7-12 months of age was set at 370 mg/day, based on approximately 70 mg/day from human milk (at 110 mg/L and 0.6 L/day) plus an estimated 300 mg/day from complementary foods. No UL was established for sodium in infants. In 2019, NASEM expanded its DRI model toward establishing DRIs based on chronic disease risk reduction intakes (CDRRs); however, NASEM was unable to establish a CDRR for infants. The absence of a sodium UL reflects an evolution in the DRI model's approach to characterizing risk rather than a change in the evidence regarding risks associated with excessive sodium intake (Refs. 76, 102).
b. EFSA
EFSA published a comprehensive scientific opinion on dietary reference values for sodium in 2019 (Ref. 101). Because insufficient data existed from which an AR could be derived, EFSA established an AI of 200 mg/day for infants 7-11 months of age based on upward extrapolation of the estimated sodium intake of exclusively breastfed infants during the first 6 months of life (midpoint sodium concentration of 150 mg/L and assumed milk transfer of 0.8 L/day = 120 mg/day), adjusted using the ratio of average energy requirements for infants 3 and 9 months of age. EFSA did not establish an AI for infants 0-6 months of age due to insufficient data. No UL was established for sodium in infants (Ref. 101).
c. D-A-CH
In 2017, D-A-CH established estimated values for sodium intake of 130 mg/day for infants 0 to under 4 months of age based on a mean mature human milk sodium concentration of 170 mg/L and an assumed average daily intake of 750 mL of human milk. For infants 4 months to under 12 months of age, the estimated value of 200 mg/day was derived from the 0-4-month value adjusted for differences in average body weight, as complementary food intake data from Germany were unavailable. No UL was established for sodium in infants (Ref. 28).

All three expert bodies used human milk composition as the primary basis for infant sodium reference values, and none established a UL for sodium in infants (see table 12). The substantially higher NASEM AI for infants 7-12 months (370 mg/day) compared to EFSA (200 mg/day) and D-A-CH (200 mg/day) reflects a key methodological difference: NASEM incorporated estimates of sodium intake from complementary foods, while EFSA and D-A-CH applied body weight scaling or lacked complementary food intake data. All expert bodies acknowledged wide variability in reported human milk sodium concentrations across studies and populations, which complicates the derivation of precise reference values and underscores shared uncertainty in this area (Ref. 102).
3. Human Milk Composition
a. Sodium Concentration in Mature Human Milk
There is no clear correlation between maternal dietary sodium intake and human milk sodium concentrations (Ref. 104). Direct measurements of sodium concentrations in mature human milk across individual study timepoints ranged from approximately 82 to 297 mg/L, reflecting natural variability in human milk (Ref. 102).
b. Recent Data
The iHMNutD study, based on literature synthesis covering mature milk from 21 to 180 days postpartum, included 12 studies with 924 participants with applicable sodium data (Ref. 8). The pooled weighted mean sodium concentration was 14.73 ± 6.99 mg/100 g, which converts to approximately 152 ± 72 mg/L. Eleven of the 12 studies overlap with sources reviewed by EFSA (Ref. 101) and NASEM (Ref. 76) and are drawn from U.S. data sources. All studies with sodium data except the Maternal-Infant Research on Environmental Chemicals (MIREC) study were conducted before 2000, which was identified as a data limitation (Ref. 8).
The MIREC Study (Ref. 105) provides additional recent data from a large Canadian cohort. Samples were collected from 2007 through 2011, from 3.5 to 10 weeks postpartum. The geometric mean sodium concentration for the full sample set (n = 770) was 151 ± 70 mg/L, and for the DRI variable subset (n = 660) was 153 ± 71 mg/L. This study was included among the 12 studies evaluated in the iHMNutD study (Refs. 8, 105).
The MILQ study (Ref. 36) provides the most comprehensive recent data on human milk mineral composition. Median sodium concentrations were 140 mg/L at 1-2 months of age, 111 mg/L at 3-4 months of age, and 97 mg/L at 5-6 months of age, with a pooled 1-6-month median of 111 mg/L (IQR: 87-156 mg/L). Total daily median sodium intake from 1 to 6 months of age was 96.5 mg/day based on measured milk volumes (Ref. 36).
The pooled weighted mean of 152 mg/L reported by the iHMNutD study (Ref. 8) is broadly consistent with values from the MIREC study (151-153 mg/L) (Ref. 105) and converts to approximately 23 mg/100 kcal. The MILQ study pooled median of 111 mg/L corresponds to approximately 17 mg/100 kcal. Together, these values suggest a central reference range of roughly 17-23 mg/100 kcal as reflective of typical mature human milk composition (Ref. 102).
4. International Regulatory Standards for Infant Formula
Sodium specifications for infant formula are generally aligned among international regulatory bodies and expert organizations, and most are closely aligned with Codex Alimentarius standards. The Codex Alimentarius Commission specifies a minimum of 20 mg/100 kcal and a maximum of 60 mg/100 kcal for both infant formula (0-6 months of age) (Ref. 12) and follow-on formula (6-12 months of age) (Ref. 37). The EU, based on recommendations from EFSA (Ref. 7), specifies a minimum of 25 mg/100 kcal and a maximum of 60 mg/100 kcal (Ref. 38). Other countries that have adopted or proposed specifications aligned with Codex Alimentarius include FSANZ (20-59 mg/100 kcal) (Ref. 39) and Health Canada (20-60 mg/100 kcal) (Ref. 40). China specifies 30-59 mg/100 kcal for infants 0-6 months of age (Ref. 41) but has different standards for follow-on formula (6-12 months of age; see table 13) (Ref. 42).
In its 1998 comprehensive review, the LSRO Panel recommended a minimum of 25 mg/100 kcal and a maximum of 50 mg/100 kcal (Ref. 1). The LSRO Panel based the minimum on the 1989 RDA of 120 mg/day for infants less than 6 months of age, which for a 5-kg infant consuming 100 kcal/kg/day equates to 24 mg/100 kcal (rounded to 25 mg/100 kcal). The LSRO Panel was reluctant to use the mean minus one standard deviation approach typically applied to other nutrients due to high coefficients of variation in reported human milk sodium values. The recommended maximum of 50 mg/100 kcal was based on the 90th percentile of FDA analyses of infant formulas available at that time (Ref. 1).

5. Recent Scientific Evidence on Sodium Intake
Reported sodium intakes in U.S. infants 0-12 months of age consistently met or exceeded the NASEM AIs across datasets reviewed, including two iterations of FITS (FITS 2008 and FITS 2016) and one cycle of NHANES (NHANES 2009-2012) (Refs. 81, 82, 84). For infants 0-5.9 months of age, FITS 2016 reported a mean usual sodium intake of 214 mg/day (10th-90th percentile: 107-347 mg/day), and FITS 2008 reported a mean of 175 mg/day for 0-5 months of age (10th-90th percentile: 138-240 mg/day), both exceeding the NASEM AI of 110 mg/day. For infants 6-11.9 months of age, mean usual sodium intakes were higher across all three surveys: FITS 2016 reported a mean of 400 mg/day (10th-90th percentile: 207-634 mg/day), FITS 2008 reported 528 mg/day (10th-90th percentile: 165-1,104 mg/day), and NHANES 2009-2012 reported 497 mg/day (10th-90th percentile: 163-946 mg/day), all exceeding the NASEM AI of 370 mg/day. In FITS 2016, approximately 49 percent of older infants exceeded the AI, and the wide 10th-to-90th percentile ranges observed across all surveys, particularly for the 6-11-month age group, indicate substantial variability in sodium exposure across the infant population.
Several methodological considerations must be factored in when interpreting these data. Human milk sodium content is relatively low and fixed by imputed volume rather than directly measured, so there may be limited precision when estimating sodium intakes in breastfed infants. All three studies rely on proxy-reported 24-hour dietary recalls, subject to recall bias. The statistical methods used to estimate usual intake distributions differ slightly across studies, though the approaches are designed to remove within-person variation and are broadly comparable. Additionally, the AI for sodium in infants is derived from estimated mean intakes from human milk in healthy, exclusively breastfed infants rather than from experimental dose-response data; consequently, exceeding the AI does not necessarily indicate risk of adverse health effects. Taken together, the data indicate that mean sodium intakes in U.S. infants meet or exceed the NASEM AIs across both age subgroups.
6. Evidence Evaluation and Rationale
Based on our review of available scientific data, information, and international standards, we conclude that the current minimum level of 20 mg/100 kcal and maximum level of 60 mg/100 kcal for sodium in § 107.100 remain appropriate.
a. Maintaining the Minimum Specification of 20 mg/100 kcal
The current minimum specification of 20 mg/100 kcal is supported by human milk composition data, intake-based reference value approaches, and international regulatory standards. Recent North American data from the MIREC study (Ref. 105) and the iHMNutD study (Ref. 8) converge on a central estimate of approximately 23 mg/100 kcal, while the multinational MILQ study (Ref. 36) suggests a somewhat lower value of approximately 17 mg/100 kcal, together defining a central reference range of approximately 17-23 mg/100 kcal for mature human milk sodium content. The reaffirmed minimum of 20 mg/100 kcal falls within this range. Applying the current NASEM AI of 110 mg/day using the same intake-based approach used by the LSRO yields an estimate of 22 mg/100 kcal, consistent with the North American central estimate and further supporting the current minimum (Refs. 1, 76, 102).
The current minimum requirement ensures that infant formula provides sodium intakes that pose a low risk of inadequacy relative to established AIs. For an infant 0-6 months of age consuming a typical daily infant formula intake, formula at the minimum specification provides 105 mg/day of sodium, which is 96 percent of the NASEM AI of 110 mg/day for infants 0-6 months of age. For an infant 0-4 months of age, this consumption level provides 81 percent of the D-A-CH AI of 130 mg/day for that age subset. For a 6-12-month-old infant consuming a typical daily intake of infant formula, the minimum specification provides 81 mg/day from formula, which is 22 percent of the NASEM AI of 370 mg/day, 40 percent of the EFSA AI of 200 mg/day for 7-11-month-old infants, and 40 percent of the D-A-CH AI of 200 mg/day for 4-12-month-old infants. However, for infants 7-12 months of age, estimated sodium intake from complementary foods of approximately 300 mg/day (Ref. 76) would contribute substantially to total sodium intake, bringing the total daily intake to approximately 381 mg/day, which is 103 percent of the NASEM AI (Ref. 102).
The current minimum aligns with international standards. The U.S. minimum of 20 mg/100 kcal is the same as Codex Alimentarius, FSANZ, and Health Canada but lower than the EU minimum of 25 mg/100 kcal as well as China's minimum of 30 mg/100 kcal. The current U.S. specification of 20 mg/100 kcal falls within this international consensus range, and no compelling evidence from other jurisdictions suggests that changing the minimum would provide any benefit (Ref. 102).
b. Maintaining the Maximum Specification of 60 mg/100 kcal
The current maximum provides a substantial margin above the central estimates of sodium content of mature human milk (approximately 17-23 mg/100 kcal) (Refs. 8, 36, 105). The LSRO Panel's 1998 recommendation of 50 mg/100 kcal as a maximum, although lower than the current specification, was based on the 90th percentile of sodium content in infant formulas available at that time, rather than on safety concerns, as the LSRO Panel found no evidence that excessive sodium intake caused adverse effects at these levels (Ref. 1). Finally, it is unclear if the difference between 50 and 60 mg/100 kcal reflects any functional significance, and the current maximum is aligned with international standards (Ref. 102).
History of use and available intake data also support safety at the current maximum. At typical daily infant formula intake volumes, the current maximum would provide approximately 316 mg/day for an infant 0-6-months of
(
printed page 69067)
age and 244 mg/day for an infant 6-12 months of age. Findings from the 2016 FITS reported mean sodium intakes of 214 mg/day (0-6 months of age) and 400 mg/day (6-11 months of age) (Ref. 82), although these estimates included intake from all dietary sources, including infant formula and complementary foods (Ref. 102).
Further, no upper limit or CDRR has been established for infants, and the current specification has not been associated with documented adverse effects in contemporary populations since 1980 when the Infant Formula Act was enacted. The evidence base for characterizing sodium intake-response relationships in infants remains limited, and findings derived from adult populations were extrapolated to children but not to infants (Ref. 76). This indicates that the current maximum level is sufficient to ensure nutritional adequacy in U.S. infants without adverse effects. The specifications are well-positioned within international regulatory consensus, and we find no compelling new evidence demonstrating functional benefits of modification or documented adverse effects at current levels (Ref. 102).
c. Consideration of the Evidence Base
We acknowledge several uncertainties in the evidence base that supports maintaining the current specifications. There is variability in reported mature human milk concentrations for sodium across studies (82 to 297 mg/L), lack of a sensitive or specific biomarker of sodium status and intake, and individual variability in infant requirements (Ref. 102). Nevertheless, FDA concludes that the totality of available evidence, including contemporary human milk composition data, alignment with international standards, and the longstanding history of use without documented safety concerns, supports maintaining the current minimum and maximum sodium specifications.
I. Vitamin D (Proposed §§ 107.10(a)(2), (b)(1), and 107.100(a))
The current requirements for vitamin D in infant formula are a minimum level of 40 IU/100 kcal (1 µg/100 kcal) and a maximum level of 100 IU/100 kcal (2.5 µg/100 kcal) (§ 107.100). Based on our analysis of scientific information and data since the LSRO Panel's 1998 comprehensive study of infant formula nutrients (Ref. 1), including infant formula vitamin D requirements in international standards, we propose to increase the required minimum to 2 µg/100 kcal (80 IU/100 kcal) and to increase the required maximum to 3 µg/100 kcal (120 IU/100 kcal) in § 107.100. We also propose to change the primary unit of measure from IU to µg in §§ 107.10(a)(2) and (b)(1) and 107.100.
1. Background
Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin and essential nutrient important for calcium absorption, skeletal mineralization, and the prevention of rickets. The two major forms are vitamin D
2
(ergocalciferol), derived from plants and fungi, and vitamin D
3
(cholecalciferol), found in select animal-derived foods and synthesized in the skin with sunlight exposure. Both forms are also found in dietary supplements and fortified foods (Refs. 91, 106, 107). Vitamin D is generally present at low levels in human milk (Refs. 95, 106, 107, 108).
Vitamin D is recognized as a prohormone, as it undergoes two reactions before becoming biologically active. The first, occurring in the liver, produces 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D; calcidiol), the major circulating form of vitamin D. The second, occurring in the kidney, converts 25(OH)D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25(OH)
2
D; calcitriol), the metabolically active form (Refs. 91, 106). The main function of calcitriol is to increase plasma calcium and phosphate, which are required for the mineralization of bone and the development and maintenance of skeletal health (Ref. 106). Calcitriol also regulates gene expression in a wide range of tissues throughout the body through binding to the vitamin D receptor (Ref. 106).
Serum 25(OH)D concentration is an indicator of total vitamin D exposure, which includes vitamin D intake from food and supplements, as well as synthesis from sun exposure (Ref. 106). The 2011 DRI report for calcium and vitamin D notes that while serum 25(OH)D cannot be considered a validated health outcome surrogate, it allows comparison of intake or exposure with health outcomes (Ref. 106). The DRI committee's review of data suggested that relative to bone health, individuals are at risk of deficiency at serum 25(OH)D concentrations below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL); some, but not all, individuals are potentially at risk for inadequacy at serum 25(OH)D concentrations between 30 and 50 nmol/L (12 and 20 ng/mL); practically all individuals are sufficient at serum 25(OH)D concentrations of at least 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL); and there may be reason for concern with serum 25(OH)D concentrations above 125 nmol/L (50 ng/mL) (Ref. 106). Consistent with NASEM's framework, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the Pediatric Endocrine Society endorse a target serum 25(OH)D of greater than or equal to 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) for vitamin D adequacy (Ref. 91). Deficiency is generally defined as a concentration below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) and insufficiency as 30-49 nmol/L (13-19 ng/mL) (Refs. 91, 106).
a. Health Consequences of Vitamin D Deficiency
Vitamin D deficiency results in inadequate skeletal mineralization. Clinical manifestations include hypocalcemia (
i.e.
, low blood calcium), hypophosphatemia (
i.e.
, low blood phosphorus), tetany (
i.e.
, involuntary spasms, muscle cramps, and twitching), rickets (a metabolic bone disease characterized by widening at the ends of long bones), rachitic rosary (a clinical and x-ray finding of bead-like swellings at the joints where the ribs meet the costal cartilage), skeletal deformities, lower limb deformities, and muscle weakness and pain (Refs. 91, 106). Because the periods of infancy and childhood represent critical windows of skeletal development, ensuring adequate vitamin D intake during these stages is essential to prevent these clinical outcomes, underscoring the importance of appropriate vitamin D in infant formula and early childhood nutrition. Serum 25(OH)D concentrations below 27-30 nmol/L are associated with increased risk of rickets when calcium intakes are limited (Refs. 106, 109, 110). No reports of clinical deficiency have been documented in infants receiving 400 IU/day of vitamin D, and this intake level generally maintains serum 25(OH)D above 50 nmol/L (Refs. 106, 108). Vitamin D deficiency may also manifest as hypocalcemic seizures. Although most commonly reported in breastfed infants, case reports have documented this outcome in formula-fed infants when compounding risk factors are present, including limited sun exposure, poor maternal vitamin D status during pregnancy, and low formula intake volumes (Refs. 108, 111, 112).
Populations at heightened risk for vitamin D deficiency include exclusively breastfed infants, infants with dark skin pigmentation, preterm infants, and infants with dietary fat malabsorption (Refs. 91, 106). Additional risk factors include reduced sunlight exposure, maternal vitamin D deficiency, sex, and having a mother who has given birth more than two times (Refs. 113, 114). A co-occurrence of multiple risk factors may substantially amplify risk (Ref. 113).
(
printed page 69068)
b. Health Consequences of Excess Vitamin D Intake
Excess vitamin D dietary intake can lead to hypervitaminosis D (
i.e.,
a toxic condition resulting from excessive vitamin D). In contrast, toxic levels of vitamin D do not occur from prolonged sun exposure, as thermal activation of previtamin D3 in the skin gives rise to multiple non-vitamin D forms that limit the formation of vitamin D (Ref. 106). Hypervitaminosis D leads to hypercalcemia (
i.e.,
high blood calcium) and hypercalciuria (
i.e.,
high urine calcium) and can eventually cause soft tissue calcification and renal and cardiovascular damage (Refs. 91, 106, 107). Symptoms of hypervitaminosis D in children are similar to those of hypercalcemia, including feeding difficulties, excessive or abnormal thirst and urine production, diarrhea, irritability, poor weight gain, and increased deep tendon reflexes (Ref. 1). In infants, excess intake for greater than 6 months may adversely affect linear growth (Refs. 106, 108).
c. Vitamin D
2
and Vitamin D
3
: Bioavailability Considerations
Both vitamin D
2
and D
3
are permitted for use in infant formula. The structural difference between the two forms does not affect intestinal absorption or the reaction required for activation to calcitriol, the biologically active form of vitamin D (Ref. 106). The available scientific literature on the relative bioavailability and potency of vitamin D
2
compared with vitamin D
3
in humans presents mixed findings. The 2011 NASEM DRI report concluded that “firm conclusions about different effects of the two forms of vitamin D cannot be drawn,” while observing that “it would appear that at low doses, D
2
and D
3
are equivalent, but at high doses, D
2
is less effective than D
3,
” in terms of raising the serum 25(OH)D concentration (Ref. 106). Data comparing the effects of vitamin D
2
and vitamin D
3
specifically in infants are limited. The EFSA NDA Panel, in its 2018 scientific opinion on the UL for vitamin D in infants, reviewed the available infant-specific evidence and concluded that “the limited data available on infants . . . do not allow a conclusion to be drawn on whether there is a difference between vitamin D
2
and D
3
as regards their impact on serum 25(OH)D concentrations in infants” (Ref. 115).
2. Nutrient Reference Values
a. NASEM
The 2011 NASEM DRI report established an AI for vitamin D of 400 IU (10 µg)/day for both infants 0-6 months of age and infants 6-12 months of age, as available data were insufficient to support derivation of an EAR for infants under 12 months of age (Ref. 106). This AI assumes minimal sun exposure contributing to vitamin D synthesis as well as adequate calcium intakes. Calcium and vitamin D are physiologically interdependent with respect to bone health outcomes, and an inadequacy in one may alter the body's handling of or response to the other (Ref. 106). Clinical studies have demonstrated that an intake of 400 IU (10 µg)/day is generally consistent with maintaining serum 25(OH)D concentrations above 50 nmol/L in infants, and no cases of clinical vitamin D deficiency have been reported at this level (Ref. 106).
The vitamin D AI for infants could not be derived from the nutrient content of human milk, as human milk does not provide a meaningful amount of vitamin D. Instead, the AI was based on evidence indicating that serum 25(OH)D “above 30 nmol/L, and more likely closer to 50 nmol/L, appears to cover adequately the needs of the majority of the infants and support normal bone accretion” (Ref. 106).
NASEM established separate ULs of 1,000 IU (25 µg)/day for infants 0-6 months of age and 1,500 IU (38 µg)/day for infants 6-12 months of age. The indicator selected for establishing these ULs was decreased linear growth. These ULs were derived from an NOAEL of approximately 1,800 IU (45 µg)/day established from mean intakes in a 1966 study, with an uncertainty factor of approximately 0.5 applied for infants 0-6 months of age to account for smaller body weight, and a 500 IU (12.5 µg)/day upward adjustment for infants 6-12 months of age to reflect their greater body mass and organ maturation (Ref. 116). NASEM acknowledged that decreased linear growth is a relatively insensitive endpoint and that dose-response relationships for adverse outcomes in infants are not well characterized (Ref. 106).
b. EFSA
In 2016, the EFSA NDA Panel established an AI for vitamin D of 10 µg/day for infants 7-11 months of age based on several trials conducted in mostly breastfed infants (Ref. 107). Two studies showed that supplementation with 10 µg/day of vitamin D
3
for at least 15 weeks led to achieved mean or median serum 25(OH)D concentrations of at least 80 nmol/L. This finding was consistent with conclusions from NASEM (Ref. 106) and recent trials that demonstrated that 10 µg/day of vitamin D
3
in primarily breastfed infants was adequate to achieve plasma/serum 25(OH)D concentrations of at least 50 nmol/L (Refs. 106, 107).
In 2018, EFSA revised the ULs for vitamin D in infants, establishing 25 µg/day for infants up to 6 months of age and 35 µg/day for infants 6 to less than 12 months of age. The EFSA Panel's systematic literature review of studies on four adverse health outcomes, specifically hypercalciuria, hypercalcemia, nephrocalcinosis (
i.e.,
abnormal deposits of calcium in the kidney tissue), and abnormal growth patterns, concluded that the available evidence on these endpoints was insufficient to derive a UL. The EFSA Panel instead used serum 25(OH)(D) concentration as an endpoint and concluded that a serum 25(OH)(D) concentration of 200 nmol/L or below is unlikely to pose a risk of adverse health outcomes in healthy infants. This value was not regarded as a toxicity threshold but rather as a conservative reference point from which the UL could be derived. The EFSA Panel estimated the proportion of infants expected to exceed this threshold at various intakes. The updated ULs apply to both vitamin D
2
and D
3
, though the dose-response analysis was based predominantly on vitamin D
3
supplementation data (Ref. 115).
c. Australian NHMRC/New Zealand MoH
NHMRC/MoH established an AI for vitamin D of 5 µg/day for infants 0-12 months of age. This recommendation assumes little to no sunlight exposure. The AI is based on the lowest dietary intake of vitamin D that is associated with a mean serum 25(OH)D concentration above 27.5 nmol/L. While a minimal intake of 2.5 µg/day may be sufficient to prevent rickets in infants 0-6 months of age, the AI was set at 5 µg/day to provide an additional margin of adequacy, as many infants at the lower intake level may still present with 25(OH)D concentrations within the range associated with rickets when sunlight exposure is absent. NHMRC/MoH noted that several studies have demonstrated that 5 µg/day is adequate for older infants and for formula-fed infants (Ref. 53).
The UL for vitamin D for infants 0-12 months of age was set at 25 µg/day, based on a NOAEL of 45 µg/day with an uncertainty factor of 1.8. The uncertainty factor reflects the small sample sizes and the relative insensitivity of the endpoint used (linear growth) in the studies informing the NOAEL (Ref. 53).

The joint FAO/WHO Consultation established a RNI of 5 µg/day for vitamin D for infants 0-6 months and 7-12 months of age (Ref. 3). This value was derived using plasma 25(OH)D as the primary indicator of vitamin D status, with the goal of maintaining concentrations above 27 nmol/L, the threshold associated with normal bone health. 3. Human Milk Composition
It is well established that human milk is generally not a meaningful source of vitamin D for infants. The MILQ study reported a pooled median antirachitic activity (
i.e.,
vitamin D activity to prevent or cure rickets) of 30.6 IU/L (approximately 0.765 µg/L; excluding Bangladesh, n = 1,461) in mature milk, representing only 61-77 percent of NASEM's estimated human milk vitamin D concentration of 40-50 IU/L (Ref. 95). The corresponding pooled median total infant intake from 1 to 6 months of age was 24.4 IU/day (0.61 µg/d), approximately 6 percent of the NASEM AI of 400 IU/day (Ref. 95). No eligible North American studies for total vitamin D in mature human milk were identified by the iHMNutD study. Only a single eligible North American study for 25(OH)D was identified (n = 21; mean: 0.13 µg/100 g; approximately 1.3 µg/L using the specific gravity of human milk of 1.031 g/mL). The authors cautioned that this 25(OH)D value is based solely on data from one study (Ref. 8). Globally, a 2026 systematic review similarly identified vitamin D as “the nutrient most vulnerable to inadequacy among exclusively breastfed infants” (Refs. 108, 117).
4. International Regulatory Standards for Infant Formula
International standards for vitamin D in infant formula are generally aligned with a minimum of 1 µg/100 kcal, with the exceptions of the EU and China (Refs. 38, 41, 42), which set higher minimums of 2 µg/100 kcal. Maximum specifications show somewhat greater variation, with the United States, Codex Alimentarius, the EU, and Canada sharing a common maximum of 2.5 µg/100 kcal for infants 0-6 months of age, while Codex Alimentarius, the EU, Australia, and Canada permit a higher maximum of 3 µg/100 kcal for older infants 6-12 months of age (Refs. 12, 37, 38, 39, 40, 118). China specifies a notably higher maximum of 5 µg/100 kcal for infants 0-12 months of age. Where rationale is provided, the allowance of a higher maximum for older infants reflects their greater tolerability for vitamin D, as evidenced by higher ULs established by NASEM for this age group, as well as their higher calcium requirements relative to younger infants (Refs. 40, 108).
In 1998, the LSRO Panel recommended a minimum of 40 IU (1 µg)/100 kcal and a maximum of 100 IU (2.5 µg)/100 kcal, based on long-standing use of the minimum in industrialized countries, elimination of nutritional rickets in formula-fed infants, and the 90th percentile of vitamin D content in commercially available formulas at the time (Ref. 1). In 2018, EFSA evaluated the safety of infant formula containing a maximum vitamin D content of 3 µg/100 kcal, the value established under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/127 (Ref. 38). EFSA found that some high-consuming infants under 4 months of age could receive intakes approaching or exceeding the UL of 25 µg/day from infant formula alone. Following the assessment, the European Commission lowered the maximum vitamin D level for infant formula for infants 0-6 months of age from 3 µg/100 kcal back to 2.5 µg/100 kcal (Refs. 115, 118).

5. Recent Scientific Evidence on Vitamin D Intake
A 2020 systematic review evaluating the effect of vitamin D supplementation in healthy, breastfed infants found evidence from six studies (n=334) indicating that supplementation at 400 IU/day was associated with a mean increase in serum 25(OH)D of 22.63 nmol/L (95 percent CI: 17.05 to 28.21) and a statistically significant reduction in the incidence of vitamin D insufficiency (serum 25(OH)D <50 nmol/L) (Risk ratio 0.57; 95 percent CI: 0.41 to 0.80) compared to placebo or no treatment (Ref. 119). The certainty of the evidence was rated as low to very low. This systematic review concluded that the evidence was insufficient to determine whether supplementation at this dose reduces deficiency (25(OH)D <30 nmol/L), improves bone mineral content, reduces the incidence of nutritional rickets, or affects growth (Refs. 108, 119).
A 2024 systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis (120 studies; 5,412 participants), sought to identify a minimum serum 25(OH)D threshold associated with reduced risk of nutritional rickets in children under 4 years of age (Ref. 110). A key contribution of this analysis was its ability to account for the confounding effect of dietary calcium intake on the risk of rickets. When analyses were restricted to children with adequate calcium intake, the serum 25(OH)D threshold at which sensitivity and specificity for rickets were simultaneously maximized was approximately 28 nmol/L. When the full dataset was considered, this threshold increased to 40 nmol/L, reflecting the elevated vitamin D requirement in the presence of inadequate dietary calcium. The authors concluded that a minimum serum 25(OH)D concentration of approximately 28 nmol/L represents a low risk of nutritional rickets for most children with adequate calcium intake, a finding consistent with the positions of NASEM (Ref. 106) and other agencies in the development of vitamin D dietary reference values (Refs. 108, 110).
A 2024 meta-regression analysis examined the relationship between total dietary vitamin D intake and serum 25(OH)D concentrations in children under 4 years of age (Ref. 120). The analysis used a multilevel, multivariable dose-response approach and included 31 randomized controlled trials enrolling healthy children who received vitamin D supplements or fortified foods. Studies were excluded if they enrolled premature/low birth weight infants or children with conditions such as rickets (Ref. 120). The trials covered a wide range of total vitamin D intakes (0.6 to 57 µg/day), with a median of 11 µg/day. To translate the dose-response model into population-level intake recommendations, the authors simulated 100,000 individual serum 25(OH)(D) responses at each vitamin D intake level. The modeling demonstrated that a total daily vitamin D intake of 10 µg/day (400 IU/day) would maintain serum 25(OH)D above 28 nmol/L in 97.3 percent of young children, and that an intake of 35 µg/day (1,400 IU/day) would result in fewer than 1.5 percent of individuals exceeding a serum 25(OH)D concentration of 200 nmol/L, a NOAEL with respect to hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria. The authors acknowledged that the overall certainty of evidence was rated as low (Ref. 120).
U.S. dietary intake data indicate that inadequate vitamin D intake is common among infants across feeding types. Analysis of NHANES data found that only approximately 27 percent of U.S. infants met AAP guidelines for vitamin D between 2009 and 2016 (Ref. 121). Data from the 2016 FITS indicate that vitamin D was one of only two nutrients for which mean total intakes (including supplements) did not exceed the AI. Mean intakes were approximately 260 IU/day (6.5 µg/day) for infants 0-5.9 months of age and 296 IU/day (7.4 µg/day) for infants 6-11.9 months of age, with only 17 percent and 24 percent of infants in these respective age groups meeting the AI (Ref. 82). A longitudinal study of infants enrolled in the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) found that despite the higher vitamin D intakes associated with formula feeding compared to breastfeeding, the proportion of formula-fed infants meeting the vitamin D AI ranged from only approximately 16-43 percent across time points (Ref. 122). Vitamin D supplementation was reported in only 4-5 percent of formula-fed infants.

6. Evidence Evaluation and Rationale
a. Rationale for Changing the Unit of Measure From IU to µg
Expert scientific bodies and international regulatory standards increasingly express vitamin D content in weight-based units (µg) rather than IU. Vitamin D specifications for infant formula currently must be expressed in IU (§ 107.10(a)(2)). In FDA's 2016 final rule revising the Nutrition and Supplement Facts labels, FDA replaced IUs with weight-based units for vitamin D on labels for conventional foods and dietary supplements, citing changes in understanding of vitamin activity and consistency with IOM DRI report units (
81 FR 33742
at 33912). FDA considers that the same scientific rationale supports expressing vitamin D specifications for infant formula in µg, consistent with current labeling regulations, NASEM DRI values, and international infant formula standards. The conversion factor of 40 IU = 1 µg is universally accepted. FDA proposes to amend § 107.10(a)(2) to require that vitamin D specifications be expressed in µg with voluntary declaration of IU equivalents provided parenthetically, supporting continuity for healthcare providers and caregivers accustomed to IU-based expressions (Ref. 108). FDA also proposes to amend the table at § 107.100(a) to reflect the unit of measurement for vitamin D as µg rather than IU.

Accordingly, FDA considers that expressing vitamin D content as total µg vitamin D is scientifically appropriate, as it represents the combined antirachitic activity provided to the infant. This approach is also consistent with international infant formula standards, which specify and declare vitamin D content in terms of total vitamin D rather than by individual form (table 15), and with current U.S. nutrition labeling regulations for conventional foods and dietary supplements, which similarly declare vitamin D on a total basis in µg. Therefore, FDA proposes to amend § 107.10(a)(2) to require that vitamin D be expressed in µg. FDA also proposes to amend § 107.10(b)(1) to permit voluntary declaration in IU in parentheses following the declaration in µg, and to remove the option of expressing vitamin D in µg cholecalciferol.
b. Rationale for Increasing the Minimum Specification to 2 µg (80 IU)/100 kcal
Multiple independent assessments support 10 µg (400 IU)/day as an appropriate vitamin D intake for infants. NASEM established an AI of 10 µg/day for infants 0-12 months of age, EFSA independently arrived at the same AI for infants, and dose-response modeling predicted that this intake level would maintain serum 25(OH)D above 28 nmol/L in 97.3 percent of young children (Ref. 120). These independent assessments using different methodological approaches all support 10 µg (400 IU)/day as the basis for the minimum vitamin D specification in infant formula (Ref. 108).
U.S. dietary intake data suggest risk for inadequate vitamin D intake among U.S. infants (Refs. 82, 108, 121, 122). Although dietary intake data carry inherent measurement limitations, findings across these studies, conducted in both WIC and non-WIC populations using different methodologies, are consistent in suggesting that a substantial proportion of U.S. infants, including those who are formula-fed, are at risk of vitamin D intakes below the AI (Ref. 108).
At the current minimum of 1 µg (40 IU)/100 kcal, an infant 0-6 months of age consuming a typical daily infant formula intake would receive approximately 5.3 µg (211 IU)/day from infant formula, representing 53 percent of the NASEM AI of 10 µg (400 IU/day). To achieve the full AI at the current minimum, an infant would need to consume approximately 1,000 kcal/day from formula, a volume substantially exceeding typical intake for this age group. For infants 6-12 months of age consuming typical daily infant formula intakes, vitamin D intake at the current minimum would be approximately 4.1 µg (163 IU)/day, representing only 41 percent of the AI. FDA considers these intakes insufficient to reliably meet vitamin D needs in either age group.
In contrast, at the proposed minimum of 2 µg (80 IU)/100 kcal, an infant 0-6 months of age consuming a typical daily intake of infant formula would receive 10.5 µg (422 IU)/day from infant formula, representing 105 percent of the NASEM AI. For infants 6-12 months of age consuming a typical daily intake of infant formula, vitamin D intake at the proposed minimum would be approximately 8.1 µg (324 IU)/day, representing approximately 81 percent of the AI from formula alone. FDA considers this level of intake from infant formula to be sufficient to support meeting the AI when accounting for the typical patterns of formula feeding as well as complementary food contributions in older infants.
The proposed minimum of 2 µg (80 IU)/100 kcal aligns with or exceeds international standards (table 15). Both the EU and China specify a minimum of 2 µg/100 kcal for infant formula. Codex Alimentarius, Australia, Canada, and the LSRO Panel specify a minimum of 1 µg/100 kcal. The LSRO Panel noted that the 1 µg (40 IU)/100 kcal minimum had eliminated nutritional rickets in formula-fed infants and, noting that the RDA for vitamin D was 300 IU/day at that time, found no scientific justification to recommend a change (Ref. 1). The NASEM AI and the available U.S. dietary intake data indicate that the current minimum does not reliably support attainment of the AI across the range of typical infant formula consumption volumes. FDA considers that the proposed minimum of 2 µg (80 IU)/100 kcal more appropriately supports infants in meeting current nutrient reference values.
c. Rationale for Increasing the Maximum Specification to 3 µg (120 IU)/100 kcal
FDA's evaluation of the maximum is guided by the NASEM ULs of 25 µg (1,000 IU)/day for infants 0-6 months of age and 38 µg (1,500 IU)/day for infants 6-12 months of age. As discussed in section V.I.2.a of this document, NASEM used an endpoint of decreased linear growth (Ref. 106). NASEM noted that this endpoint is relatively insensitive and that newer data have not emerged to better characterize dose-response relationships or hypercalcemia risk in infants, representing a source of ongoing uncertainty (Ref. 106). EFSA established concordant ULs of 25 µg/day
(
printed page 69072)
for infants under 6 months of age and 35 µg/day for infants 6 to less than 12 months of age (Ref. 115). The modeling study similarly found that a daily intake of 35 µg/day would result in fewer than 1.5 percent of young children (under 4 years of age) exceeding serum 25(OH)D of 200 nmol/L (Ref. 120). The authors rated the overall certainty of evidence as low (Ref. 120). The convergence of assessments around similar ULs, despite differing methodologies, provides a consistent framework for evaluating the safety of the proposed maximum specification (Ref. 108).
i. Estimated Vitamin D Intakes at the Current and Proposed Maximum
At the current maximum of 2.5 µg (100 IU)/100 kcal, estimated vitamin D intakes from typical infant formula volumes represent approximately 53 percent and 27 percent of the ULs for infants 0-6 months of age and 7-12 months of age, respectively. Under a high-consumption scenario (
i.e.,
90th percentile of energy intake from infant formula based on NHANES data from 2015-2023), these estimates increase to 84 percent and 52 percent of the ULs for the same age groups, respectively, from infant formula alone. At the proposed maximum of 3 µg (120 IU)/100 kcal, estimated vitamin D intakes at typical consumption volumes represent approximately 63 percent and 32 percent of the ULs for infants 0-6 months of age and 7-12 months of age, respectively (table 16). For high consumers, estimated intakes at the proposed maximum reach approximately 100 percent and 63 percent of the ULs for infants 0-6 months of age and 7-12 months of age, respectively. When complementary foods are also considered for infants 7-12 months of age, total estimated vitamin D intake reaches approximately 68 percent of the UL. Across all scenarios evaluated, estimated vitamin D intakes at the proposed maximum do not appreciably exceed the UL for either age group (Ref. 108).
