ii. Comparison With International Regulatory Standards
FDA's proposed maximum of 3 µg (120 IU)/100 kcal for vitamin D in infant formula is consistent with most international regulatory standards for follow-on formula for infants 6-12 months of age but exceeds most international standards for formula intended for infants 0-6 months of age. Codex Alimentarius, Australia, Canada, and the EU all permit a maximum of 3
(
printed page 69073)
µg/100 kcal for older infants (6-12 months of age), reflecting that age group's greater tolerability for vitamin D. The EU reduced its maximum for formula intended for infants 0-6 months of age from 3 µg/100 kcal to 2.5 µg/100 kcal following an EFSA safety assessment finding that some high-consuming infants in that age group may exceed the UL at the higher maximum. China specifies a notably higher maximum of 5 µg/100 kcal for all infants 0-12 months of age. The LSRO Panel's 1998 recommendation of 2.5 µg (100 IU)/100 kcal was based on the 90th percentile of vitamin D content in commercially available infant formulas at the time (Ref. 108).
Unlike most international frameworks, U.S. regulations do not distinguish between infant formula for infants 0-6 months of age and follow-on formula for infants 6-12 months of age. In the United States, all infant formulas must meet the nutrient specifications in § 107.100 and be suitable for infants from birth through 12 months of age. Accordingly, the proposed maximum of 3 µg/100 kcal would apply across the full infant age range, including younger infants 0-6 months of age who have a lower UL (25 µg/day) than older infants 7-12 months of age (38 µg/day) (Ref. 108).
iii. Safety Considerations for Younger Infants
EFSA's intake assessment for infants aged 0 to less than 4 months of age used high formula consumption values multiplied by median reference body weights, yielding estimated vitamin D intakes of approximately 19-25 µg/day at 1 month of age and 23-29 µg/day at 4 months of age. EFSA's approach, designed to characterize intake among high consumers in the context of European feeding practices, differs from FDA's exposure analysis, which is based on the 90th percentile of energy intake from infant formula among U.S. infants. EFSA's 2018 UL evaluation used a serum 25(OH)D concentration of 200 nmol/L as a conservative reference point rather than a toxicity threshold, predicting that 0-4 percent of infants under 6 months of age would exceed this level at intakes of 20-25 µg/day. FDA estimates that vitamin D intake among high-consuming U.S. infants 0-6 months of age at the proposed maximum is approximately 25.1 µg/day, which is at the NASEM UL. FDA considers this safety margin acceptable for younger infants, noting that the NASEM UL was derived from a relatively insensitive endpoint using a conservative uncertainty factor and that NASEM acknowledged limitations in the underlying evidence (Ref. 108). FDA is not aware of evidence of adverse effects at or near this level under current conditions of use. Nevertheless, FDA acknowledges residual uncertainty due to limited data on the dose-response relationship for adverse outcomes in infants 0-6 months of age and invites comment on whether a more conservative maximum should be considered for this age group.
iv. Manufacturing and Analytical Feasibility
The proposed maximum of 3 µg/100 kcal, paired with a proposed minimum of 2 µg/100 kcal, provides a manufacturing operating range of 1 µg (40 IU)/100 kcal. A 1 µg/100 kcal operating range between the minimum and maximum is intended to provide manufacturers sufficient flexibility to account for processing and shelf-life considerations while maintaining vitamin D intakes within a nutritionally appropriate and safe range across the U.S. infant population. Comments received in response to FDA's 2025 RFI on infant formula nutrient requirements support these manufacturing feasibility concerns (
90 FR 20475
). Multiple comments from industry stakeholders highlighted that vitamin D is a sensitive nutrient, since it degrades easily under certain conditions, with one reporting that it is less stable in the presence of protein hydrolysates or free amino acids, and that manufacturing variability and shelf-life losses necessitate formulating above the label claim, supporting the need for an adequate operating range between the minimum and maximum. Several of these comments recommended increasing the U.S. maximum to 3 µg (120 IU)/100 kcal, noting that the current U.S. maximum of 2.5 µg (100 IU)/100 kcal has proven insufficient to support manufacturing flexibility while reliably meeting the minimum label claim.
FDA's proposed range is also informed by considerations of analytical method performance and the ability to reliably verify regulatory compliance. A 2022 statistical assessment re-evaluated performance data from the multi-laboratory validation study of AOAC Method 2016.05/ISO 20636:2018, the current state-of-the-art analytical method for determining vitamin D content in infant formula. That study found that the narrower EU regulatory range of 2 to 2.5 µg/100 kcal presents significant compliance verification challenges: even when formula is accurately manufactured at the midpoint of that range (2.25 µg/100 kcal), approximately 18 percent of test results would be expected to indicate noncompliance due solely to analytical method variability (Ref. 123). In contrast, the Codex Alimentarius range of 1 to 2.5 µg/100 kcal was associated with a predicted noncompliance rate of less than 1 percent at the regulatory midpoint (Ref. 123). These findings indicate that maintaining the current maximum of 2.5 µg/100 kcal while raising the minimum to 2 µg/100 kcal is not analytically feasible using current validated methods (Ref. 123).
Applying the statistical methodology of the 2022 assessment previously discussed to the proposed 2 to 3 µg/100 kcal range, FDA estimates a predicted noncompliance rate of approximately 1.6 percent at the regulatory midpoint of 2.5 µg/100 kcal, assuming an average method reproducibility of 8.2 percent reproducibility relative standard deviation (Refs. 108, 123). FDA considers this to support the analytical feasibility of the proposed range and invites comment and data on analytical performance within the proposed range.
These manufacturing constraints also have direct nutritional implications. The AAP noted that, given manufacturing variability, shelf-life losses, and label claim requirements, it has proven difficult for infants to meet the full AI of 10 µg (400 IU)/day through typical infant formula intakes under the current allowable range, which the AAP characterized as too narrow. With label declarations commonly set at approximately 1.5 µg (60 IU) or 1.75 µg (75 IU)/100 kcal, manufacturers have difficulty ensuring that the label claim is maintained through end of shelf life without approaching or exceeding the current maximum of 2.5 µg (100 IU)/100 kcal, leaving only 25 to 40 IU/100 kcal of headroom for manufacturing overages (Ref. 91).
FDA acknowledges that the proposed range of 2 to 3 µg/100 kcal spans the same absolute width of 1 µg (40 IU)/100 kcal as the range the AAP described as insufficient. However, FDA considers that the proposed range addresses this concern not by widening the range, but by raising the minimum to 2 µg/100 kcal, which shifts the entire operating band upward, better positioning manufacturers to achieve label claims consistent with meeting the AI at typical consumption volumes. FDA invites comment on whether the proposed minimum-to-maximum range of 2 to 3 µg (80-120 IU)/100 kcal is sufficient to ensure that infants consuming typical volumes of infant formula can reliably meet the AI of 10 µg (400 IU)/day while addressing manufacturing variability and shelf-life losses. Specifically, FDA requests data and information on: (1)
(
printed page 69074)
whether the proposed 1 µg (40 IU)/100 kcal operating range is adequate to accommodate typical manufacturing overages and nutrient degradation over shelf life; (2) whether an alternative minimum or maximum should be considered, and if so, what scientific, technical, or operational data support such an alternative; and (3) whether the proposed maximum of 3 µg (120 IU)/100 kcal poses a risk of excessive vitamin D intake for infants 0-6 months of age (Ref. 108).
d. Consideration of the Evidence Base
FDA acknowledges significant uncertainties in the evidence base underlying its proposed vitamin D specifications for infant formula. The NASEM ULs were derived from a limited number of older studies using decreased linear growth, which it acknowledged as a relatively insensitive endpoint, and the dose-response relationship between vitamin D intake and adverse outcomes in infants is not well characterized (Refs. 106, 108). Additionally, differing consumption assumptions between FDA and EFSA led EFSA, but not FDA, to find that high-consuming infants under 4 months of age may exceed the UL at the proposed maximum of 3 µg/100 kcal. Exposure estimates do not account for vitamin D from sunlight. This is a conservative assumption with respect to the minimum specification, as any cutaneous vitamin D synthesis would supplement formula intake and reduce the risk of inadequacy. However, it is not conservative with respect to the maximum, as appreciable UV-B exposure would contribute to serum 25(OH)D concentrations beyond those estimated from formula intake alone.
Additionally, the estimates do not account for concurrent vitamin D supplementation. Currently, the AAP recommends that infants consuming less than 1,000 mL/day of infant formula receive routine vitamin D supplementation (Ref. 91). Thus, infants receiving both formula at or near the proposed maximum plus a vitamin D supplement could have total intakes that approach or exceed the UL, particularly among younger infants (Ref. 108). As an example, an infant 0-6 months of age consuming infant formula at the proposed maximum of 3 µg/100 kcal at approximately 780 mL/day would receive an estimated 15.8 µg/day from formula alone, and when combined with a standard 10 µg supplement, total intake would reach approximately 25.8 µg/day, marginally exceeding the UL of 25 µg/day (Ref. 108). FDA acknowledges this co-exposure scenario as a source of residual uncertainty and invites comment and associated data on the prevalence of concurrent formula feeding and vitamin D supplementation at volumes below the AAP threshold, and on whether additional labeling or guidance measures should be considered to address this scenario.
J. Manganese (Proposed § 107.100(a))
The current requirement for manganese in infant formula is a minimum level of 5 µg/100 kcal (
21 CFR 107.100
). There is no maximum level established. Based on our analysis of scientific information and data since the 1998 comprehensive study of infant formula nutrients (Ref. 1), including infant formula manganese requirements in international standards, we propose to decrease the required minimum level for manganese to 1 µg/100 kcal and establish a maximum level for manganese in infant formula of 50 µg/100 kcal in § 107.100.
1. Background
Manganese is an essential trace mineral found in all tissues and is required for normal amino acid, lipid, protein, and carbohydrate metabolism. Manganese functions as a cofactor for key metalloenzymes, including arginase, glutamine synthetase, pyruvate carboxylase, and manganese superoxide dismutase, supporting antioxidant defense, energy production, immune function, and neurological activity (Refs. 124, 125, 126). Manganese is integral to the synthesis of neurotransmitters, including dopamine, glutamate, and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), that are essential for neural signaling and survival (Refs. 126, 127). During fetal and infant development, manganese is also essential for skeletal and connective tissue formation, as well as for carbohydrate, protein, and lipid metabolism during periods of rapid growth (Refs. 126, 127, 128).
Manganese concentrations and bioavailability differ substantially across infant feeding sources. Human milk contains relatively low manganese levels (approximately 3-10 µg/L), cow milk-based formulas contain intermediate concentrations (approximately 30-50 µg/L), and soy protein-based formulas contain the highest levels (approximately 200-300 µg/L)—up to 100 times that of human milk (Refs. 125, 126, 127). In infant formulas, manganese is present in the divalent form (
i.e.,
an oxidation state that allows for chemically bonding with two other atoms or groups), in contrast to human milk, in which it is predominantly in trivalent form, (
i.e.,
an oxidation state which can chemically bond with three other atoms or groups), resulting in less controlled absorption from infant formula (Refs. 126, 127). Iron status modulates manganese uptake, as both minerals share common transporters. Iron deficiency, the most clinically significant driver of manganese excess in infants, increases the amount of these shared intestinal transporters produced in cells and increases manganese absorption, while adequate iron stores reduce manganese uptake (Refs. 124, 126, 128, 129, 130, 131). Route of exposure also significantly influences manganese absorption, distribution, and tissue retention (Refs. 126, 132). The scientific literature lacks consensus on optimal biomarker selection for assessing manganese status (Refs. 126, 133).
a. Health Consequences of Manganese Deficiency
Acquired manganese deficiency in human infants is considered extremely rare given the manganese concentrations present in human milk, infant formula (Refs. 126, 127), and food, with no reported cases in the scientific literature to date (Refs. 125, 126). Animal models on manganese deficiency have documented impaired growth, skeletal abnormalities, neonatal ataxia (
i.e.,
an irreversible congenital defect characterized by a lack of normal coordination of movements and loss of equilibrium), impaired glucose tolerance, altered lipid and carbohydrate metabolism, and compromised immunity, as well as low red blood cell count, hemoglobin, and hematocrit (
i.e.,
the percentage of total blood volume made up of red blood cells) (Refs. 62, 126, 134, 135, 136, 137).
b. Health Consequences of Excess Manganese Intake
Although manganese deficiency data in humans are largely derived from animal studies, the primary concern for infants and children centers on the well-documented toxic effects of manganese excess (Refs. 126, 138). The developing brain is especially vulnerable to manganese imbalances, as manganese preferentially accumulates in the basal ganglia, and disruptions during critical neurodevelopmental windows can produce lasting alterations in dopamine and GABA metabolism (Refs. 126, 127). This vulnerability is compounded in neonates (
i.e.,
early infancy) by immature biliary excretion, the primary route of manganese elimination, limiting the infant's capacity to clear excess manganese. Potential adverse effects of excess manganese exposure
(
printed page 69075)
are discussed further, below, in section J.5 of this document.
2. Nutrient Reference Values
a. NASEM
NASEM established AI values for manganese for infants in 2001 (Ref. 62). For infants 0-6 months of age, NASEM established an AI of 3 µg/day based on the manganese content of human milk from well-nourished mothers (3.5 µg/L) and typical milk consumption patterns (0.78 L/day) and rounding, reflecting that no cases of manganese deficiency have been observed in full-term infants exclusively breastfed in the United States or Canada. The higher AI of 600 μg/day for infants 7-12 months of age accounts for complementary foods containing higher manganese concentrations than human milk (Refs. 62, 126).
b. EFSA
Due to insufficient evidence to establish an AR and, by extension, a PRI, the EFSA NDA Panel proposed an AI. For infants 7-11 months of age, the EFSA Panel determined an AI range of 0.02-0.5 mg/day (20-500 µg/day) (Ref. 139). This range accounts for the broad spectrum of manganese intake levels that appear to support adequate nutrition and is informed by several sources: upward extrapolation from manganese intakes in exclusively breastfed infants, observed manganese consumption in infants at 6 and 12 months of age, and values derived from extrapolating the adult AI through isometric scaling (Ref. 139). EFSA did not establish an AI for younger infants (Ref. 139).
c. Australian NHMRC/New Zealand MoH
NHMRC/MoH established an AI of 3 µg/day for infants 0-6 months of age, calculated by multiplying the average human milk intake (0.78 L/day) by the average manganese concentration in human milk (3.5 µg/L) and rounding. For infants 7-12 months of age, NHMRC/MoH established an AI of 0.6 mg/day (600 µg/day), which was derived using two methods. The first method used consumption estimates for infants at 6 and 12 months of age (0.071 and 0.08 mg/kg, respectively) (Ref. 140), which, applied to reference weights of 7 and 9 kg, yielded total manganese intakes of 0.5 and 0.72 mg/day (from human milk and complementary food). The second method used body weight adjustment to extrapolate from adult data, producing an estimate of 0.567 mg/day. As noted above, the AI for the 7-12-month age group is significantly higher than that for the 0-6-month group because human milk contains lower concentrations of manganese than the complementary foods introduced into older infants' diets (Refs. 53, 126).
d. UL
NASEM was unable to determine ULs in infants because of the lack of data on adverse effects in infancy and concern about infants' ability to handle excess amounts (Ref. 62). Similarly, NHMRC/MoH did not set ULs, noting that the gap between the oral exposure levels known to cause effects in humans and animals and the estimated intake from food is narrow (Ref. 53).
In 2023, the EFSA NDA Panel conducted an updated scientific opinion on the UL for manganese and concluded that a UL for manganese could not be established (Ref. 141). In the absence of adequate data to establish a UL, EFSA derived safe levels of intake based on observed dietary intakes among high consumers (95th percentile) as an indication of the highest level of intake at which there is reasonable confidence in the absence of adverse effects. For infants, EFSA adopted a conservative approach because of insufficient data to determine when manganese homeostatic processes become fully mature, calculating the average of all available 95th percentile estimates across countries for infants 4 months to less than 12 months of age. This yielded a “safe level of intake” of 2 mg/day (2,000 µg/day) for manganese intake from all dietary sources, including fortified foods and food supplements, for this age group. EFSA noted that this safe level of intake is more limited in application than a UL because the intake level at which the risk of adverse effects begins to increase is not defined (Ref. 141).

3. Human Milk Composition
Multiple studies have characterized manganese concentrations in mature human milk from mothers with term pregnancies. Across most study populations largely conducted outside of North America, reported manganese concentrations generally ranged from approximately 2 to 16 µg/L (Refs. 126, 142). One data source reported substantially higher manganese concentrations: a 1991 Philippines subcohort study reported approximately
(
printed page 69076)
39.55 µg/L (Ref. 143), which may have reflected either a positive bias in reported manganese concentrations or environmental contamination. FDA does not consider this dataset to be representative of the physiological range of manganese in human milk from the broader population (Ref. 126).
More recently, the 2024 MIREC study reported manganese concentrations in mature human milk from a Canadian pregnancy cohort, which is the largest published study of human milk mineral composition from a high-income country using methods meeting eligibility criteria for reference value development (Ref. 105). The average (±standard deviation) manganese concentration in human milk was approximately 1.99 ± 2.93 µg/L in the full dataset and 1.96 ± 1.74 µg/L in the subset of participants who met the DRI applicability criteria. These values were calculated as geometric means and converted to a volume-based measure using the density of human milk (1.032 g/mL). FDA considers these data to be a substantially stronger evidentiary basis for characterizing the physiological range of manganese in human milk from a North American population, as compared to the broader data set described above, based on sample size and population/location. Accordingly, FDA intends to rely primarily on these data to inform the minimum and maximum specifications for manganese in infant formula (Ref. 126).
4. International Regulatory Standards for Infant Formula
International regulatory bodies are largely aligned on manganese specifications for infant formula (table 18). Codex Alimentarius specifies a minimum of 1 µg/100 kcal and a GUL of 100 µg/100 kcal, applicable to both infant formula (0-6 months of age) and follow-on formula (6-12 months of age) (Refs. 12, 37). The EU specifies a minimum of 1 µg/100 kcal and a maximum of 100 µg/100 kcal (Ref. 38). Australia, Canada, and China have adopted or proposed specifications aligned with Codex, with the exception that China specifies a higher minimum of 3 µg/100 kcal for infant formula for infants 0-6 months of age (Refs. 39, 40, 41, 42). In 2005, the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN) International Expert Group recommended a minimum of 1 µg/100 kcal and a lower maximum of 50 µg/100 kcal, citing infants' underdeveloped excretory capacity and the risk of bioaccumulation (Ref. 144). In 1998, the LSRO Panel recommended a minimum of 1 µg/100 kcal and a maximum of 100 µg/100 kcal.

5. Recent Scientific Evidence on Manganese Intake
a. Evidence of Toxicity (Neurotoxicity)
There are two distinct exposure frameworks that often occur simultaneously or over extended periods: (1) aggregate exposure, which involves a single chemical received through multiple routes or pathways simultaneously; and (2) cumulative exposure, which involves multiple chemicals acting on the same target system (Ref. 145). In the case of infant manganese exposure, both frameworks are relevant. Exposure routes include infant formula, drinking water, prenatal transfer, and airborne sources (Ref. 126). Neurodevelopmental effects are modified by co-exposures to other metals and nutrients such as selenium, lead, arsenic, and iron (Refs. 130, 146, 147, 148, 149).
Manganese becomes neurotoxic at elevated levels, and infants represent a uniquely vulnerable population due to their immature biliary excretion, higher intestinal absorption rates, and developing blood-brain barrier (Refs. 124, 127, 147, 150). Evidence from multiple prospective cohort studies, reviews (Refs. 133, 146, 147, 148, 151, 152, 153, 154, 155), and risk assessments (Refs. 156, 157) consistently demonstrate that excess prenatal and postnatal manganese exposure is associated with deficits in cognitive, motor, language, and social-emotional development in children (Ref. 158). Both manganese deficiency and manganese excess impair neurodevelopment, making it challenging to define a single, universal toxicity threshold (Ref. 126). The threshold at which manganese transitions from beneficial to harmful varies across studies but has been identified at approximately 24-28 µg/L in maternal blood at delivery for psychomotor outcomes (Ref. 152) and at cord serum manganese concentrations greater than 9.1 µg/L for neonatal neurobehavioral deficits (Ref. 148).
Regulatory and health-based thresholds for manganese exposure in infants have been established or proposed across studies and vary widely (Ref. 126). All current thresholds carry significant uncertainty, as they are largely extrapolated from animal studies or adult dietary data, and no threshold has been specifically validated for human infants across the full range of exposure routes and co-exposure conditions encountered in real-world settings.
Available evidence indicates that full neurological recovery from excess manganese exposure is unlikely when exposure is prolonged or occurs during critical periods of brain development (Refs. 126, 127, 133, 147, 159).
In addition to the limitations noted above regarding information about manganese toxicity, additional
(
printed page 69077)
limitations exist, such as study designs that preclude causal inference, the lack of a single validated biomarker, the potential for residual confounding by co-exposures, and inconsistent findings across studies and populations (Ref. 126).
b. Manganese Intakes From Water
Manganese occurs naturally in rocks, soil, groundwater, and surface water, with certain geographical regions in the United States exhibiting higher levels of manganese in the water (Ref. 160). Water manganese content is a significant consideration for formula-fed infants because water is used to reconstitute powdered and concentrated liquid infant formulas, and the total manganese intake reflects the contribution from water sources and infant formula. Powdered infant formulas, which represent most formula consumed by infants, require more water per unit volume than concentrated liquids, resulting in proportionally greater water-derived manganese intake. In a 2019 study, investigators analyzed data from 43,334 wells in the United States and estimated that 12.9 percent of groundwater samples exceeded the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Health Reference Level of 300 µg/L for manganese (Ref. 160). These findings were corroborated in a 2021 study at the state level, assessing water concentrations in Minnesota community public water systems, noting that 13 percent of U.S. groundwater samples exceeded this same threshold (Ref. 157). In the same 2021 paper, two additional international benchmarks applicable to the manganese content of water were highlighted: Canada's drinking water standard of 120 µg/L (Ref. 161) and a proposed WHO health-based guideline value of 80 µg/L (Ref. 162).
c. Manganese Intakes From Infant Formula
In 2019, a group of investigators measured manganese concentrations in infant formulas marketed in the United States and found ranges of 230-430 µg/L (36-65 µg/100 kcal) in cow milk-based formulas and 420-790 µg/L (64-120 µg/100 kcal) in soy protein-based formulas (Ref. 163). Researchers analyzing public drinking water in Minnesota and powdered infant formula samples also reported manganese concentrations of 69.8-291 µg/L and 306-531 µg/L for cow milk-based and soy protein-based infant formulas, respectively. Notably, the single amino acid-based formula included in the analysis contained the highest concentration at approximately 110 µg/100 kcal (Ref. 157). Based on these analyses, certain soy and amino acid-based formulas already exceeded the maximum specification of 100 µg/100 kcal set by other expert bodies (Ref. 126).
An important consideration is the combined exposure to manganese from both infant formula and drinking water used for reconstitution. When soy protein or amino acid-based formulas were reconstituted with water at the 95th percentile of Minnesota community water concentrations (562 µg/L), central tendency manganese intake estimates reached 156 percent and 213 percent, respectively, of the Minnesota Department of Health neonatal-based Reference Dose (RfD) (83 µg/kg/day) (Ref. 157). Upper-end estimates for all formula types, including cow milk-based formula, exceeded the RfD when reconstituted with water at the 95th percentile concentration (Ref. 157).
d. Manganese Intake
To characterize routine dietary manganese intakes among U.S. infants, FDA used food consumption data from the What We Eat in America/NHANES study covering 2017 to March 2020 (n = 332 infants 0-12 months of age) in conjunction with manganese concentration data from FDA's Total Diet Study (TDS) for fiscal years (FY) 2018-2020 (Refs. 164, 165, 166). Among infants 0-6 months of age (n = 169), the mean estimated daily manganese intake using mean TDS concentrations was 234 µg/day (10th percentile: 73 µg/day; 90th percentile: 601 µg/day). Among infants 7-12 months of age (n = 163), the mean estimated intake was 1,123 µg/day (10th percentile: 251 µg/day; 90th percentile: 1,991 µg/day) (Ref. 126).
6. Evidence Evaluation and Rationale
Based on the review of available scientific data, information, and international standards, we propose to decrease the current minimum specification for manganese in infant formula to 1 µg/100 kcal and to establish a maximum specification of 50 µg/100 kcal in § 107.100.
a. Rationale for Decreasing the Minimum Specification to 1 µg/100 kcal
At the current minimum manganese level, 5 µg/100 kcal, typical infant formula intakes provide approximately 26 µg/day and 20 µg/day for infants 0-6 months of age and 7-12 months of age, respectively. This represents 867 percent of the NASEM AI for infants 0-6 months of age (3 µg/day) and 3.3 percent of the AI for infants 7-12 months of age (600 µg/day). At the proposed minimum of 1 µg/100 kcal, the typical intake from infant formula is estimated to be 5.3 µg/day and 4.1 µg/day for infants 0-6 months of age and 7-12 months of age, respectively. These intakes exceed the AI for infants 0-6 months (176 percent AI) and would remain well below the AI for infants 7-12 months (0.7 percent AI). The notable discrepancy in AIs across the two age groups reflects variations in dietary exposure patterns (
i.e.,
older infants consuming complementary foods, which have higher concentrations of manganese) rather than a markedly distinct physiological requirement. Thus, FDA considers that manganese intakes at the proposed minimum of 1 µg/100 kcal are unlikely to present a risk of inadequacy for formula-fed infants in the 7-12-month age group (Ref. 126).
Manganese deficiency is rare in infants and has not been documented in healthy infants under normal dietary conditions. Cases of manganese deficiency are largely drawn from animal studies and rare genetic disorders affecting manganese transport. FDA considers that this limited evidence of deficiency under current intake conditions further supports the proposed reduction in the minimum specification (Ref. 126).
Central estimates of mature human milk manganese concentrations range from approximately 1.4 to 16 µg/L with recent North American data reflecting a mean concentration of 1.96 ± 1.74 µg/L (Ref. 105). Assuming an energy density of human milk of 650 kcal/L, the manganese content of human milk is approximately 0.3 µg/100 kcal based on the MIREC study (Ref. 105) mean, with the broader range of concentrations reported across studies corresponding to approximately 0.2 to 2.5 µg/100 kcal. The proposed minimum of 1 µg/100 kcal exceeds the mean manganese concentration of human milk on a per-kcal basis and remains within the range of concentrations reported across studies, providing a conservative margin above mean human milk concentrations (Ref. 126).
The current minimum of 5 µg/100 kcal exceeds all international standards assessed. The proposed minimum would align the U.S. minimum with international infant formula standards as well as recommendations from the LSRO Panel and ESPGHAN International Expert Group (table 18). Furthermore, the proposed decrease is supported by several comments recommending reducing or eliminating the minimum manganese requirement in response to FDA's 2025 RFI on nutrient requirements for infant formula (
90 FR 20475
, May 14, 2025).
(
printed page 69078)
b. Rationale for Establishing a Maximum Specification of 50 µg/100 kcal
Expert bodies, including NASEM and EFSA, have not established ULs for manganese in infants, citing insufficient dose-response data in human infant populations (Refs. 62, 141). Nevertheless, a substantial and growing body of evidence indicates that excess manganese exposure during infancy poses risks to neurodevelopment, and FDA considers that the weight of this evidence, along with the unique physiological vulnerabilities of infants and the aggregate nature of manganese exposure, supports establishing a maximum specification for manganese in infant formula (Ref. 126).
Manganese becomes neurotoxic at elevated levels, and infants represent a uniquely vulnerable population due to their immature biliary excretion, higher intestinal absorption rates, and developing blood-brain barrier (Refs. 125, 127). Evidence from multiple prospective cohort studies and reviews consistently demonstrates that excess prenatal and postnatal manganese exposure is associated with deficits in cognitive, motor, language, and social-emotional development in children (Refs. 133, 146, 147, 148, 151, 152, 153, 154, 155). FDA acknowledges that the dose-response relationship is complex and non-linear, that current health-based reference doses are largely extrapolated from neonatal animal studies rather than direct human infant data, and that causal inference from epidemiological literature remains limited by methodological constraints (Refs. 133, 156, 157). Nevertheless, FDA assesses that the consistency of associations across several independent cohorts, the biological plausibility based on manganese's known neurotoxic mechanisms, and the limited potential for full recovery from manganese-induced neurodevelopmental effects support a conservative approach to limiting manganese intake in infants.
Formula-fed infants may be exposed to manganese through several concurrent pathways, including infant formula, drinking water used to reconstitute powdered or concentrated liquid formulas, prenatal transfer, and inhalation (Refs. 147, 167). FDA considers that evaluating manganese intake from infant formula in isolation underestimates the total manganese burden experienced by formula-fed infants. As discussed in section V.J.5.b of this document, manganese occurs naturally in U.S. groundwater at variable concentrations (Ref. 160). Additionally, smaller community water systems, which comprise 97 percent of U.S. systems, have been shown to have significantly higher manganese concentrations than larger systems (Ref. 157). When infant formula is reconstituted with manganese-containing water, various combined contributions can result in total manganese intakes exceeding health-based reference doses (Refs. 126, 142, 155, 160).
At the proposed maximum of 50 µg/100 kcal, estimated manganese intakes from typical intake volumes of infant formula alone are approximately 264 µg/day and 203 µg/day for infants 0-6 months of age and 7-12 months of age, respectively, prior to any contribution from water or other sources (see table 19). Under a high-consumption scenario, defined here as the 90th percentile of energy intake from infant formula based on data from three NHANES cycles (Refs. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18), these estimates increase to approximately 418 µg/day and 397 µg/day for the same age groups, respectively, representing approximately 139-fold and 66 percent of the respective AI values (see table 19). The proposed maximum continues to provide manganese well above adequacy thresholds while substantially reducing the formula-derived contribution to aggregate exposure.

NHANES exposure estimates are based on the 90th percentile of energy intake from infant formula among non-breastfed infants 0-6 months (n = 235) and 7-12 months (n = 205) of age, using NHANES data (Refs. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18). Also, data from NHANES (2017-March 2020) and the TDS (2018-2020) suggest that infants may be routinely exposed to manganese at levels that substantially exceed the respective AIs for both age groups. This exposure accounts for all food sources, including complementary foods, infant formula, and human milk. FDA acknowledges that these estimates are subject to methodological limitations (Ref. 166) yet considers these intake data as contextual evidence in support of the proposed maximum.
Most major international regulatory bodies, including Codex Alimentarius, the EU, Australia, Canada, and China, have established a maximum or GUL of 100 µg/100 kcal (table 18). The LSRO Panel similarly recommended 100 µg/100 kcal (Ref. 1). FDA acknowledges this international consensus. However, FDA is concerned that this level may not fully account for aggregate infant exposure, particularly from drinking water used to reconstitute formula, or for the potentially higher absorption and retention of manganese in infants compared to the adults on whom adverse effect levels were based. FDA notes that the ESPGHAN International Expert Group reached a similar conclusion, recommending a maximum of 50 µg/100 kcal on the grounds that higher concentrations should be avoided given infants' immature
(
printed page 69079)
excretion mechanisms and the associated risk of bioaccumulation (Ref. 144).
Establishing a maximum specification for manganese in infant formula introduces manufacturing considerations that differ by protein source. Soy (
e.g.,
soy protein isolate) naturally contains high amounts of manganese, resulting in consistently higher manganese concentrations in soy protein-based formulas relative to cow milk-based formulas (Ref. 163). FDA acknowledges that the proposed maximum of 50 µg/100 kcal may represent the lowest technologically achievable level for soy protein-based formulas while maintaining adequate protein content. For cow milk-based formulas, which contain lower inherent manganese and for which manganese is typically added as a discrete ingredient (
e.g.,
manganese sulfate), greater formulation flexibility exists, and FDA does not expect that cow milk-based formulas would require formulation at or near the proposed maximum to meet nutritional requirements. It is also common for amino acid-based formulas to add manganese as a discrete ingredient, and FDA does not anticipate technological barriers to reformulation. FDA seeks comment on this proposed maximum, including data or information bearing on the feasibility of achieving lower manganese levels in soy protein-based infant formulas, which may include access to alternate sources of soy protein with lower manganese content.
c. Consideration of the Evidence Base
FDA acknowledges several important uncertainties in the evidence base supporting the proposed maximum. These include the absence of a validated UL for manganese in infants, the reliance on health-based reference doses extrapolated from neonatal animal studies, the lack of a single validated biomarker that captures total manganese body burden, the methodological limitations that preclude definitive causal inference regarding neurodevelopmental outcomes, variability in reported human milk manganese concentrations across studies, and the complexity of the dose-response relationship (Ref. 126). Despite these uncertainties, FDA is proposing to establish a lower maximum specification of 50 µg/100 kcal for manganese in infant formula (compared to 100 µg/100 kcal). FDA's recommendation is based on the weight of the available scientific evidence, including the consistency of associations between excess manganese exposure and adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes across independent cohorts, the unique physiological vulnerabilities of infants, and the aggregate nature of manganese exposure from multiple concurrent pathways, which together support a conservative approach to limiting manganese intake in this population.
VI. Proposed Effective/Compliance Dates
We intend that any final rule resulting from this rulemaking become effective 60 days after the date of the final rule's publication in the
Federal Register
. We propose a compliance date of 3 years after the effective date of the final rule completing our phased, comprehensive infant formula nutrient review to provide industry time to reformulate and relabel infant formula while recognizing the importance of updating the infant formula nutrient specifications. We invite comment on the proposed compliance date.

Executive Order 12866
.
Executive Order 14192
requires that any new incremental costs associated with certain significant regulatory actions “shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.” This proposed rule, if finalized as proposed, is expected to be an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action.
The Regulatory Flexibility Act requires us to analyze regulatory options that would minimize any significant impact of a rule on small entities. Because we cannot determine with certainty the magnitude of reformulation costs that small infant formula manufacturers would incur under this proposed rule, we find that the proposed rule may have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (Section 202(a)) requires us to prepare a written statement, which includes estimates of anticipated impacts, before proposing “any rule that includes any Federal mandate that may result in the expenditure by State, local, and tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100,000,000 or more (adjusted annually for inflation) in any 1 year.” The current threshold after adjustment for inflation is $193 million, using the most current (2025) Implicit Price Deflator for the Gross Domestic Product. This proposed rule would not result in an expenditure in any year that meets or exceeds this amount.
B. Overview of Benefits, Costs, and Transfers
This proposed rule, if finalized, would update the nutrient specifications for infant formula to reflect the best available scientific evidence on certain infant nutritional requirements and safe intake levels. If finalized, the proposed changes to the nutrient specifications would generate benefits primarily through (1) reducing the risk of vitamin D deficiency in formula-fed infants and (2) reducing the risk of inadequate iodine intake, excessive vitamin A exposure, and excessive manganese exposure across the formula-fed infant population. The primary quantified benefit is avoided healthcare costs from vitamin D deficiency-induced late-onset hypocalcemia, with a primary annualized estimate of $80.93 million at a 7 percent discount rate and $90.04 million at a 3 percent discount rate. If finalized as proposed, benefits of this rule would begin accruing in 2031, following the proposed 3-year compliance period. Additional benefits from iodine, vitamin A, and manganese specification changes are described qualitatively. The primary present value of quantified benefits is $568.43 million at a 7 percent discount rate and $768.08 million at a 3 percent discount rate.
Costs are one-time and borne by domestic and foreign infant formula manufacturers in the compliance year. The primary annualized cost estimate is $17.64 million at a 7 percent discount rate and $17.57 million at a 3 percent
(
printed page 69080)
discount rate. The primary present value of costs is $123.86 million at a 7 percent discount rate and $149.86 million at a 3 percent discount rate.

Title:
Infant Formula Nutrient Requirements.
Description:
Finalization of this rule to amend regulations in
21 CFR part 107
for nutrient products would revise OMB control number 0910-0256 with regard to the scope of activity applicable to labeling of these products. At the same time, consistent with
5 CFR 1320.3(b)(1)(v)
, we estimate a de minimis one-time burden for
[a]djusting the existing ways to comply with any previously applicable instructions and requirements.
Specifically, the proposed rule includes a mandatory unit change for vitamin A (from IU to µg RAE) and vitamin D (from IU to µg) that applies to all infant formula products regardless of whether nutrient levels change, such that all 326 UPCs would be subject to relabeling. We detail our estimates for this one-time reformulating cost here and in the PRIA. We note that we do not expect this to cause an ongoing increase in PRA burden above the current labeling requirements, but we seek comment on this assumption.
Relabeling costs were estimated using FDA's Labeling Cost Model (Ref. 169), updated to 2025 dollars. The model estimates per-UPC costs across labor, materials, inventory, and recordkeeping activities associated with a label change. All proposed label changes in this analysis are classified as minor changes, that is, changes confined to the Nutrition Facts panel that do not require multi-color redesign or modification of the principal display panel. The proposed changes, including updating declared values for vitamin D, vitamin A, iodine, and manganese and converting vitamin A and vitamin D declarations from IU-based to weight-based units, satisfy this definition.
The model distinguishes between coordinated and uncoordinated label changes. A coordinated change occurs when a manufacturer aligns a required regulatory label change with a planned voluntary relabeling cycle, avoiding prepress, design, and plate costs that would have been incurred regardless. An uncoordinated change occurs when a manufacturer must make a required label change outside of its normal voluntary cycle, incurring the full cost independently. Consistent with the model's empirical data showing that most products are voluntarily relabeled on a two-to-five-year cycle, we assume all label changes in this analysis are coordinated. Even under a coordinated change, manufacturers still incur administrative and recordkeeping costs associated with understanding the regulation, determining their response, and tracking the required change throughout the labeling process.
The estimated cost of a label change is $836 per UPC, with a 90 percent confidence interval between $226 and $1,942. We assume domestic and foreign entities incur the same per-UPC cost. Table 22 shows total estimated labeling costs by domestic and foreign origin.

XII. Request for Comments
We invite all interested persons to submit comments on any aspect of the proposed rule. In particular, we invite comment on the proposed changes to the minimum and/or maximum levels for iodine, vitamin A, vitamin D, and manganese; the proposal to establish a maximum level for manganese; the proposed changes to the unit of measure for vitamin A and vitamin D; the proposed change to the permitted source to meet the vitamin A requirement; and the proposed changes to the content of the required labeling. FDA also requests comment on maintaining the current required minimum and maximum levels in infant
(
printed page 69082)
formula for chloride, selenium, potassium, and sodium. Additionally, we invite comment on the following to further inform our phased, comprehensive infant formula nutrient review:
1. FDA is considering whether to require the inclusion of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and arachidonic acid (ARA) in infant formula. We invite comments supporting or opposing formal requirements for DHA and ARA, recommended minimum levels, ratios (
e.g.,
DHA:ARA ratio, amounts per 100 kcal), and any age- or formula type-specific considerations, along with scientific evidence supporting those recommendations.
2. FDA is considering whether alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) should be added as a required nutrient in infant formula given its role as an essential omega-3 fatty acid and precursor to longer-chain fatty acids such as DHA and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA). If ALA were required, its ratio to linoleic acid (LA) would also need to be considered, as the two fatty acids compete for the same metabolic enzymes. We invite comments on the scientific evidence supporting or opposing a formal requirement for ALA and its ratio to LA, including any relevant clinical, epidemiological, or alternative data.
3. FDA is considering the minimum and/or maximum iron levels currently required in infant formula and will review emerging evidence regarding iron's role in neurodevelopment, gut microbiome development, and potential risks at higher intake levels. We invite comments on whether current levels should be maintained, increased, or reduced and on the scientific literature or international standards supporting those positions.
4. FDA is considering whether iron requirements in formula should differ for specific populations of infants (
e.g.,
infants 0-6 vs. 7-12 months of age, infants with socioeconomic and nutritional risk factors). We invite comments on evidence supporting differentiated iron requirements for these groups and how FDA should approach establishing population-specific standards.
5. FDA is considering whether L-carnitine should be required in infant formula given its role in fatty acid oxidation and energy metabolism. We invite comments on the current state of the science regarding L-carnitine's essentiality in infant nutrition and what evidence would support or oppose establishing a formal requirement.
6. FDA is considering whether the proposed minimum and/or maximum nutrient specifications for infant formula present any manufacturing, reformulation, or analytical feasibility challenges for manufacturers, and invites submission of any supporting data or information relevant to this determination.
7. FDA invites data and information on the variability of nutrient levels in tap water and bottled water in the U.S. and how such variability should be considered in establishing minimum and maximum standards for nutrients in infant formula, such as chloride.
8. FDA invites comment on our proposal to change the unit of measure from IU to µg RAE for vitamin A and from IU to µg for vitamin D, and on the potential impact of these changes on consumers' understanding of infant formula labeling.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106759; File No. S7-2026-38]
October 28, 2026.
On October 26, 2026, Mizuho Capital Markets LLC (“MCM”) requested that the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) increase the maximum fixed-dollar amount of an security-based swap dealer's (“SBSD”) aggregate gross notional outstanding security-based swap (“SBS”) positions to qualify for Rule 18a-10's
[
1
]
alternative compliance mechanism (“ACM”) from $50 billion to $100 billion.
[
2
]
After considering the levels of SBS activity of SBSDs operating under Rule 18a-10, the Commission determines that it may be appropriate to change the maximum fixed-dollar amount for any SBSD eligible for Rule 18a-10 to $100 billion. Pursuant to Rule 18a-10(f)(2), the Commission is publishing this notice of the potential change to provide interested persons with an opportunity to comment.
I. Background
In 2019, the Commission adopted Rule 18a-1 and Rules 18a-3 through 18a-9 establishing capital, margin, segregation, recordkeeping, reporting, notification, and security count requirements applicable to SBSDs that are not banks and are not registered as broker-dealers (“stand-alone SBSDs”).
[
3
]
(
printed page 69027)
The Commission also adopted Rule 18a-10, which establishes an ACM pursuant to which a stand-alone SBSD that is registered as a swap dealer and predominantly engages in a swaps business may elect to comply with the capital, margin, segregation, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements of the Commodity Exchange Act (“CEA”) and the CFTC's rules in lieu of complying with Rules 18a-1 and Rules 18a-3 through 18a-9.
[
4
]
The Capital, Margin, and Segregation Release explains the rationale for the ACM as follows: “In light of the differences between the rules of the Commission and the CFTC, the Commission believes it is appropriate to permit such firms to comply with the capital, margin, and segregation requirements of the CEA and the CFTC's rules, provided the firm's [SBS] business is not a significant part of the [SBS] market and predominantly involves dealing in swaps as compared to [SBS]. In this circumstance, the CFTC's regulatory interest in the firm will greatly exceed the Commission's regulatory interest given the relative size of its swaps business as compared to its [SBS] business.”
[
5
]
To qualify to operate pursuant to Rule 18a-10, the stand-alone SBSD must: (1) be registered as an SBSD pursuant to section 15F(b) of the Exchange Act and the rules thereunder, (2) be registered as a swap dealer pursuant to section 4s of the CEA and the rules thereunder, (3) not be registered as a broker or dealer pursuant to section 15 of the Exchange Act and the rules thereunder, and (4) meet the conditions to be exempt from paragraph (f) of Exchange Act rule 18a-4.
[
6
]
In addition to these other conditions, the aggregate gross notional amount of the firm's outstanding SBS positions must not exceed the lesser of a maximum fixed-dollar amount or 10% of the combined aggregate gross notional amount of the firm's SBS and swap positions.
[
7
]
The maximum fixed-dollar amount was set at a transitional level of $250 billion for the first 3 years after the compliance date of the rule and then dropped to $50 billion thereafter unless the Commission issues an order: (1) maintaining the $250 billion maximum fixed-dollar amount for an additional period of time or indefinitely; or (2) lowering the maximum fixed-dollar amount to an amount between $250 billion and $50 billion.
[
8
]
In explaining the $50 billion fixed-dollar amount, the Commission stated its belief that “a stand-alone SBSD with a gross notional amount of outstanding [SBS] of no more than $50 billion will not be a significant participant in the [SBS] market.”
[
9
]
In contrast, the transitional $250 billion fixed dollar-amount was adopted to provide stand-alone SBSDs predominantly engaged in a swaps business “with a substantial amount of leeway to develop their [SBS] business without managing the level of that business to the lower $50 billion threshold,” as well as “additional time to transition from the $250 billion threshold to the $50 billion threshold or another threshold.”
[
10
]
Since more than 3 years have passed since the compliance date for Rule 18a-10, the current maximum fixed-dollar amount is $50 billion. For context, the gross notional amount of SBS outstanding on December 26, 2025 was approximately $7,265.144 billion.
[
11
]
The Capital, Margin, and Segregation Release stated that “[t]he Commission intends to analyze how significant . . . [SBSDs] are to the [SBS] market and broader securities markets based on their levels of their [SBS] activity. The analysis will consider the firm's individual and collective impact on the [SBS] market.”
[
12
]
The Commission is considering increasing the maximum fixed-dollar amount in paragraph (f)(1) of Rule 18a-10 from $50 billion to $100 billion. Rule 18a-10(f)(2) provides that if, after considering the levels of SBS activity of the SBSDs operating under the ACM, the Commission determines that it may be appropriate to change the maximum fixed-dollar amount, the Commission will publish a notice of the potential change.
[
13
]
II. Summary of the Request
In the Request, MCM asks the Commission to increase the maximum fixed-dollar amount of the aggregate gross notional outstanding SBS positions for any SBSD eligible for Rule 18a-10 from $50 billion to $100 billion.
[
14
]
In support of its Request, MCM states that it is one of two stand-alone SBSDs operating pursuant to the ACM in Rule 18a-10. MCM represents that its SBS activity represents only a small fraction of its overall derivatives business. From 2022 to 2024, its SBS activity represented less than 0.25% of the firm's total gross notional across SBS and swaps, and only 1.47% of the total active trade count. MCM states that the substantial majority of MCM's derivatives activity is conducted through its swap dealing business, which deals principally in interest rate and foreign exchange derivatives. MCM conducts a significant amount of business with commercial end users not required to post margin to MCM. Only roughly $0.4 billion of MCM's total $2.0 billion tier 1 capital is currently allocated to support SBS activity.
[
15
]
MCM provides the following reasons for increasing the maximum fixed-dollar amount in Rule 18a-10 to $100 billion:
[
16
]
Consistent with the Design of Rule 18a-10 and the Commission's Reserved Discretion:
The Commission expressly built flexibility into Rule 18a-10 to adjust the maximum fixed-dollar amount between $50 billion and $250 billion after reviewing the levels of SBS activity of firms operating under the ACM. Granting MCM's request would be a straightforward exercise of that authority.
Minimal Impact on the Broader SBS Market:
Because only a small number of firms operate under the ACM, and because MCM's SBS activity is a small fraction of its overall derivatives business, increasing the fixed-dollar amount would not distort the broader SBS market. The relief would also reflect the premise underlying the ACM—that, for a firm predominantly engaged in a swaps business, the CFTC's regulatory interest greatly exceeds the Commission's.
[
17
]
While granting relief
(
printed page 69028)
will likely have a small impact on the market, choosing not to grant relief is likely to subject MCM to substantial costs that could further incentivize migration of SBS activities into an already smaller cluster of the market, leading to decreased choice for counterparties. Additionally, since much of MCM's SBS activity is related to hedging and internal risk management, it is likely that counterparties and MCM and its affiliates as a whole will face substantial costs and difficulties when mitigating counterparty and hedging risks.
Promotes Regulatory Comparability:
Permitting MCM to continue to comply through the CEA and the CFTC's rules advances the Dodd-Frank Act's goal, of establishing and maintaining comparable minimum capital requirements across the Commission, the CFTC, and the prudential regulators to the maximum extent practicable.
[
18
]
Rule 18a-10 provides a unique ability to ease a regulatory burden while fostering harmonization across the securities industry. Relief in this instance furthers regulatory consistency by expanding existing coverage for similar derivatives products in a manner that is inherently coherent.
[
19
]
Preserves Safety, Soundness, and Liquidity While Reducing Duplicative Costs:
MCM would remain subject to the CFTC's comprehensive capital, margin, segregation, and risk management requirements, including its liquidity risk management requirements, so the relief would not compromise MCM's financial soundness. At the same time, the relief would spare MCM the cost and inefficiency of maintaining duplicative capital, margin, and segregation calculations under two regulatory regimes, reducing burdens on both MCM and the Commission's limited resources.
[
20
]
III. Solicitation of Comments
The Commission requests and encourages any interested person to submit comments regarding the potential change, including whether the Commission should increase the maximum fixed-dollar amount of the aggregate gross notional outstanding SBS positions for any SBSD eligible for Rule 18a-10 from $50 billion to $100 billion. In particular, the Commission solicits comment on the following questions:
1. Do commenters agree with MCM's reasons described in the Request for increasing Rule 18a-10's maximum fixed-dollar amount to $100 billion? Please explain why or why not.
2. Would increasing Rule 18a-10's maximum fixed-dollar amount to $100 billion be consistent with paragraph (f)(2) of Rule 18a-10, which requires the Commission to consider the levels of SBS activity of SBSDs operating under the rule? Please explain why or why not.
3. If Rule 18a-10's maximum fixed-dollar amount was increased to $100 billion, how significant could SBSDs relying on the ACM be to the SBS market and broader securities markets based on their SBS activity levels? What would be the individual and collective impact of these firms on the SBS market? Please explain.
4. Is there a maximum fixed-dollar amount that is lower or higher than the amount in the Request that the Commission should adopt, that accounts for the factors the Commission should consider in changing the maximum fixed-dollar amount? If so, please identify the amount and explain why it is appropriate.
Comments should be received on or before December 2, 2026. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​comments/​s7-2026-38/​notice-potential-change-increase-maximum-fixed-dollar-amount-alternative-compliance-mechanism
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include File Number S7-2026-38 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to File Number S7-2026-38. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method of submission. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules-regulations/​public-comments/​s7-2026-38

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Western Water Cooperative Committee, a Federal Advisory Committee, provides a forum for discussions between the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (“Corps”) and Western States regarding the operation of Corps projects and water rights and water laws of Western States. The Western Water Cooperative Committee will host an in-person meeting November 17 and 18, 2026, for the Committee to finalize the by-laws and discuss identified opportunities and proposed recommendations to avoid or minimize conflicts between Corps projects and state water rights and water laws. This meeting is open to the public.
DATES:
The Western Water Cooperative Committee will host an in-person meeting from 8:30 a.m. MST to 5:00 p.m. MST on Tuesday, November 17, and Wednesday, November 18, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
The Western Water Cooperative Committee will conduct an in-person meeting at the Homewood Suites Denver Downtown-Convention Center at 550 15th Street, Denver, Colorado. Comments or requests to speak at the meetings should be submitted in writing to the Designated Federal Officer (DFO) for the committee: Mr. Sean L. Smith, ATTN: CEEC, 441 G St. NW, Washington, DC 20314-1000; or by email at
WWCC@usace.army.mil
.
Alternatively, contact the Alternate Designated Federal Officer (ADFO): Ms. Virginia K. Rynk, ATTN: CEEC, 441 G St. NW, Washington, DC 20314-1000; or by email at
WWCC@usace.army.mil
.
Electronic mail is the preferred mode of submission.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
The DFO for the committee: Mr. Sean L. Smith, by telephone at 202-761-0301; and by email at
WWCC@usace.army.mil
;
or the ADFO, Ms. Virginia K. Rynk by telephone at 202-761-4741; and by email at
WWCC@usace.army.mil
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Committee meeting is being held under the provisions of the Federal Advisory Committee Act of 1972 (5 U.S.C., Chapter 10, as amended), the Government in the Sunshine Act of 1976 (
5 U.S.C. 552b
, as amended), and
41 CFR 102-3.150
.
Purpose of the Meeting:
The Committee is chartered pursuant to Section 8158 of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act (
33 U.S.C. 701b-17
) to ensure that the Corps flood control projects in Western States, as described in section 8158(b), are operated consistent with congressional directives by identifying opportunities to avoid or minimize conflicts between the operation of the Corps projects and water rights and water laws in such States.
Agenda:
At this meeting, the agenda will include the discussion and codification of the proposed by-laws, administrative topics, and discussion of identified opportunities and proposed recommendations to avoid or minimize conflicts between Corps project and state water rights and water laws.
Availability of Materials for the Meeting:
A copy of the agenda will be available on the website:
https://www.usace.army.mil/​Missions/​Civil-Works/​Project-Planning/​Legislative-Links/​WRDA-2022/​Western-Water-Cooperative-Committee/​
.
All meeting materials will be posted to the website after the meeting.
Public Accessibility to the Meeting:
Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 552b
, as amended, and
41 CFR 102-3.140
through
102-3.165
, this meeting is open to the public. Any interested person may participate in the meeting, file written comments or statements with the Committee, or make verbal comments during the public meeting, at the times, and in the manner permitted by the Committee, as set forth below.
Special Accommodations:
Individuals requiring any special accommodations related to the public meeting or seeking additional information about the procedures, should contact Mr. Smith, the Committee DFO, or Ms. Rynk, the ADFO, at the email addresses or telephone numbers listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section, at least five (5) business days prior to the meeting so that appropriate arrangements can be made.
Written Comments or Statements:
Pursuant to
41 CFR 102-3.105(j)
and 102-3.140 and section 10(a)(3) of the Federal Advisory Committee Act, the public or interested organizations may submit written comments or statements to the Committee about its mission and/or topics to be addressed in this public meeting. Written comments or statements should be submitted to Mr. Smith, the Committee DFO, or Ms. Rynk, the Committee ADFO, via electronic mail, the preferred mode of submission, at the addresses listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section in the following formats: Adobe Acrobat or Microsoft Word. The comment or statement must include the author's name, title, affiliation, address, daytime phone number, and reference to which meeting date the comment or statement is directed. Written comments or statements being submitted in response to the agenda set forth in this notice must be received by the Committee DFO or ADFO at least five (5) business days prior to the meeting so
(
printed page 68952)
that they may be made available to the Committee for its consideration prior to the meeting. Written comments or statements received after this date may not be provided to the Committee until its next meeting. Please note that because the committee operates under the provisions of the Federal Advisory Committee Act, as amended, all written comments will be treated as public documents and will be made available for public inspection.
Verbal Comments:
Members of the public will be permitted to make verbal comments during the in-person public meeting only at the time and in the manner allowed herein. If a member of the public is interested in making a verbal comment at the in-person meeting, that individual must submit a request, with a brief statement of the subject matter to be addressed by the comment, at least five business (5) days in advance to the Committee DFO or ADFO, via electronic mail, the preferred mode of submission, at the addresses listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section. The Committee DFO and ADFO will log each request to make a comment, in the order received, and determine whether the subject matter of each comment is relevant to the Committee's mission and/or the topics to be addressed in this public meeting. A 30-minute period near the end of the meeting will be available for verbal public comments. Members of the public who have requested to make a verbal comment and whose comments have been deemed relevant under the process described above, will be allotted no more than three (3) minutes during this period, and will be invited to speak in the order in which their requests were received by the DFO and ADFO.
