Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106761; File No. SR-NASDAQ-2026-089]
October 28, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 15, 2026, The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC (“Nasdaq” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III, below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
(
printed page 68993)
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend IM-8310-3 to provide for the public release of disciplinary complaints and disciplinary decisions (as defined in the proposed rule) on its website
Nasdaq.com
. The proposed rule change also would eliminate the $10,000 monetary threshold below which the Exchange currently does not release information or publish the disciplinary decision. Additionally, the proposed rule change would provide for the public release of eligibility decisions (as specified in the proposed rule) involving members or associated persons previously subject to statutory disqualification.
While these amendments are effective upon filing, the Exchange has designated the proposed amendments to be operative on November 14, 2026.
The text of the proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/​rulebook/​nasdaq/​rulefilings
,
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
Nasdaq IM-8310-3 (Release of Disciplinary Complaints, Decisions and Other Information) governs the release of disciplinary complaints, decisions, and other information by Nasdaq. In general, this proposed rule change seeks to promote broader accessibility of Nasdaq disciplinary complaints and disciplinary decisions (as defined in the rule). In particular, the proposed rule would provide for the public release of Nasdaq disciplinary complaints and temporary cease and desist notices. In addition, the proposed rule would conform IM-8310-3 to Nasdaq's existing practice of releasing specified categories of disciplinary decisions on its website. The proposed rule also would expand the release of disciplinary decisions by publishing temporary cease and desist decisions and orders and by eliminating the $10,000 threshold below which the Exchange currently does not release information or publish the disciplinary decision.
Under this proposed rule change, Nasdaq would publish copies of disciplinary complaints and disciplinary decisions instead of summaries of (
i.e.,
“information about”) such documents. By publishing copies of disciplinary complaints and disciplinary decisions on Nasdaq's website, the proposed rule would make it unnecessary to publish summaries of such documents instead of, or in addition to, such documents. In addition, the proposed rule change would conform IM-8310-3 to Nasdaq's existing practice of releasing eligible disciplinary decisions on its website.
The proposed rule also would define the terms “disciplinary complaint” and “disciplinary decision,” which current IM-8310-3 does not define. The Exchange believes that defining these terms would provide current and prospective members and associated persons with more clarity about the items that Nasdaq would publish under IM-8310-3.
The Exchange also proposes to provide for the public release of eligibility decisions (as specified in the proposed rule) involving members or associated persons previously subject to statutory disqualification. The Exchange believes that the public release of eligibility decisions involving members or associated persons previously subject to statutory disqualification will promote transparency by providing current and prospective members and associated persons with greater insight into the Exchange's decision-making process in resolving admissions applications by members and persons previously subject to statutory disqualification.
The proposed rule change is modeled after, and substantially similar to, the rules of several other Self-Regulatory Organizations (“SROs”), including Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (“FINRA”) Rule 8313 and New York Stock Exchange LLC (“NYSE”) Rule 8313. In particular, the rules of FINRA and NYSE provide for the public release of disciplinary complaints and disciplinary decisions, including disciplinary decisions that impose a monetary fine less than $10,000. Making disciplinary complaints and disciplinary decisions available to the public also would follow the practice of the Commission.
Background on Current IM-8310-3
If a party requests a copy of an identified disciplinary complaint or disciplinary decision issued by Nasdaq or any committee thereof, current IM-8310-3(a) requires Nasdaq to provide the requesting party with a copy of the requested document. Current IM-8310-3(a) does not provide for the release by Nasdaq of a copy of a disciplinary complaint issued by FINRA's Department of Enforcement on behalf of Nasdaq.
Current IM-8310-3(a)(1)-(4) detail the statement that accompanies the release of a disciplinary complaint, disciplinary decision, or information with respect to such a document. The accompanying statement varies depending, for example, on the type of document to be released or described (
i.e.,
disciplinary complaint vs. disciplinary decision), the finality of a disciplinary decision, and whether the Commission has stayed the effectiveness of sanctions imposed by Nasdaq.
Current IM-8310-3(b) and (c) provide that Nasdaq shall release “information” with respect to certain disciplinary complaints initiated by FINRA's Department of Enforcement on behalf of Nasdaq and with respect to certain disciplinary decisions of Nasdaq. Specifically, current IM-8310-3(b) provides that Nasdaq Regulation shall release to the public information with respect to any disciplinary complaint initiated by the FINRA Department of Enforcement acting on behalf of Nasdaq pursuant to the Nasdaq-FINRA Regulatory Services Agreement (“RSA”) that contains an allegation of a violation of a designated rule.
[
3
]
Nasdaq Regulation Department also may release information about any disciplinary complaint, or group of disciplinary complaints, that involve a significant policy or enforcement determination where Nasdaq's Chief Regulatory Officer deems the release of information to be in the public interest.
Current IM-8310-3(c)(1) provides that Nasdaq Regulation shall release to the public information regarding any disciplinary decision that: imposes a suspension, cancellation, or expulsion of a member; imposes a suspension or revocation of the registration of a person associated with a member; imposes a suspension or bar of a member or person associated with a member from
(
printed page 68994)
association with all members; imposes monetary sanctions of $10,000 or more upon a member or a person associated with a member; or contains an allegation of a violation of a designated rule as defined in current IM-8310-3(b). Current IM-8310-3(c)(1) also provides that Nasdaq Regulation shall release to the public information with respect to any temporary cease and desist order issued pursuant to the Rule 9800 Series. Nasdaq currently releases copies of the aforementioned categories of disciplinary decisions (principally, Letters of Acceptance, Waiver, and Consent) on its website
Nasdaq.com
.
[
4
]
In addition, current IM-8310-3(c)(1) provides that Nasdaq Regulation may release to the public information with respect to: any disciplinary decision (or group of decisions) that involve a significant policy or enforcement determination where Nasdaq's Chief Regulatory Officer deems the release to be in the public interest; any decision issued pursuant to the Rule 9550 Series imposing a suspension or cancellation of the member or a suspension or bar of the association of a person with a member, unless Nasdaq Regulation determines otherwise; and any disciplinary or other decision issued pursuant to the Rule 9000 Series (not specifically enumerated in current IM-8310-3(c)(1)) regardless of the sanction imposed, so long as the names of the parties and other identifying information is redacted.
Current IM-8310-3(c)(1)(A) and (B) establish the standards for public release of information in an appeal or review of a disciplinary decision where the underlying decision qualified for release but the appellate decision does not, or where the sanction imposed on some but not all of the respondents in a multi-respondent disciplinary matter qualifies for release. If the information about an underlying decision was released in unredacted form because the underlying decision met current IM-8310-3(c)(1)'s release criteria, current IM-8310-3(c)(1)(A) also requires the release in unredacted form of information about the appellate decision. In an appeal or review of a multi-respondent matter where information about the underlying disciplinary decision against a particular respondent qualified for release and was released in unredacted form, current IM-8310-3(c)(1)(B) requires the release of information in unredacted form with respect to that particular respondent's appeal or review. Nasdaq may release information to the public in redacted form about a respondent who does not meet the release criteria in current IM-8310-3(c)(1).
If a member or associated person appeals to the Commission from a Nasdaq decision imposing an expulsion, revocation, suspension, bar on associating with all members, or a monetary sanction of $10,000 or more, current IM-8310-3(g) provides that Nasdaq shall notify the membership and press as soon as possible after receiving the appeal. The notice must state whether the effectiveness of the Nasdaq Board's decision has been stayed pending the outcome of Commission proceedings. In the event of an appeal to the courts from a Commission decision that resolves a Nasdaq decision imposing an expulsion, revocation, suspension, bar on associating with all members, or a monetary sanction of $10,000 or more, current IM-8310-3(h) provides that Nasdaq shall notify the membership as soon as possible after receiving a formal notice of appeal. The notice must state whether the order of the Commission was stayed.
Proposed Rule Change
i. Definitions
Modeled after FINRA and NYSE Rules 8313, proposed IM-8310-3(a)(1) and (2) respectively define the terms “disciplinary complaint” and “disciplinary decision,” which current IM-8310-3 does not define. Under proposed IM-8310-3(a)(1), a “disciplinary complaint” means any complaint issued pursuant to the Rule 9200 Series or any notice issued pursuant to Rules 9400 or 9810.
[
5
]
The proposed inclusion of notice issued pursuant to Rule 9400 would result in the publication of notices seeking expedited suspension proceedings against a member alleged to have violated Nasdaq General 9, Section 53 (Disruptive Quoting and Trading Activity Prohibited). The proposed inclusion of notice issued pursuant to Rule 9810 would result in the publication of temporary cease and desist notices issued by Nasdaq Regulation or FINRA's Department of Enforcement. Current IM-8310-3 does not expressly provide for the publication of, or provision of information about, notice issued pursuant to Rules 9400 or 9810.
[
6
]
Proposed IM-8310-3(a)(2) defines “disciplinary decision” to mean:
any decision issued pursuant to the Rule 9000 Series, including decisions issued by a Hearing Officer, Hearing Panel, Extended Hearing Panel, Nasdaq Review Council, the Nasdaq Board, or any committee or subcommittee thereof; orders accepting offers of settlement; Letters of Acceptance, Waiver and Consent; suspension orders pursuant to Rule 9400; and temporary cease and desist decisions and orders pursuant to the Rule 9800 Series; provided, however, such term does not include decisions issued pursuant to the Rule 9550 Series, or decisions, notifications, or notices issued pursuant to the Rule 9520 Series, which are addressed by paragraphs (b)(2) and (b)(3) of this Rule. Minor rule violation plan letters issued pursuant to Rule 9216 are not subject to this Rule.
The proposed definition of “disciplinary decision” specifies which items would be subject to publication as “disciplinary decisions” pursuant to proposed IM-8310-3(b). The proposed definition excludes decisions issued pursuant to the Rule 9550 Series and decisions, notifications, or notices issued pursuant to the Rule 9520 Series, which items are addressed by proposed paragraphs IM-8310-3(b)(2) and (b)(3) (discussed below). The proposed definition also excludes minor rule violation plan (“MRVP”) letters from IM-8310-3, maintaining Nasdaq's current practice of not publishing, or releasing information about, such letters.
[
7
]
The proposed definition of “disciplinary decision” also does not cover exemptive-relief decisions issued under the Rule 9600 Series because Rule 9620 already governs the release of exemptive-relief decisions.
Proposed IM-8310-3(a)(3) would specify the terms that carry the same meanings as defined in existing Rule 9120, such as “Department of Enforcement,” “Hearing Panel,” “Nasdaq Regulation Department,” and “Nasdaq Review Council.”
ii. General Standards
Proposed IM-8310-3(b)(1)(i) provides that Nasdaq Regulation would release to
(
printed page 68995)
the public a copy of any disciplinary complaint issued by Nasdaq Regulation or FINRA's Department of Enforcement acting on behalf of Nasdaq.
[
8
]
The proposed release of disciplinary complaints would follow the practices of FINRA and NYSE, which release disciplinary complaints to the public under their respective Rules 8313(a). As noted above, Nasdaq proposes to release to the public a copy of the disciplinary complaint itself, mooting the need to release a summary of (that is, “information about”) such document.
While current Nasdaq IM-8310-3(a) requires releasing a copy of an identified disciplinary complaint issued by “Nasdaq or any committee thereof,” the proposed IM-8310-3(b)(1)(i) would reflect that FINRA's Department of Enforcement also may issue a disciplinary complaint on Nasdaq's behalf. The proposed rule also would specify the department within Nasdaq (namely, Nasdaq Regulation Department) that issues Nasdaq's disciplinary complaints. In addition to posting eligible disciplinary complaints and disciplinary decisions on Nasdaq's website (as specified in proposed IM-8310-3(c)(4), discussed in greater detail below), Nasdaq would continue to provide a requesting party with a copy of an identified disciplinary complaint or disciplinary decision of the Exchange, as provided in current IM-8310-3(a).
[
9
]
Under proposed IM-8310-3(b)(1)(ii), Nasdaq Regulation also would release to the public a copy of any disciplinary decision of the Exchange. Under proposed IM-8310-3(a)(2), disciplinary decisions of the Exchange would include those issued under the Rule 9000 Series by adjudicators within FINRA's Office of Hearing Officers acting pursuant to a Nasdaq-FINRA RSA. Expanding the availability of Nasdaq disciplinary decisions, this proposal would provide for the release to the public of all disciplinary decisions imposing a monetary penalty (eliminating the current $10,000 threshold below which the Exchange does not currently release or provide information about such decisions) as well as the release of temporary cease and desist decisions and orders.
[
10
]
As noted above, Nasdaq Regulation's public release of disciplinary decisions would moot the need to release a summary of (
i.e.,
“information about”) disciplinary decisions instead of, or in addition to, releasing such documents.
Proposed IM-8310-3(b)(2) provides that Nasdaq shall release to the public a copy of any statutory disqualification decision, notification, or notice issued by the Exchange or FINRA's Department of Member Regulation pursuant to the Rule 9520 Series that will be filed with the Commission. Current IM-8310-3 does not expressly provide for the publication of, or release of information about, decisions, notifications, or notices issued pursuant to the Rule 9520 Series. As noted above, Nasdaq Regulation's public release of a statutory disqualification decision, notification, or notice that will be filed with the Commission would moot the need to also release a summary of (
i.e.,
“information about”) such document.
[
11
]
Proposed IM-8310-3(b)(3) provides that Nasdaq shall release to the public information with respect to any suspension, cancellation, expulsion, limitation, prohibition, or bar imposed pursuant to the Rule 9550 Series that constitutes final Exchange action. This proposed provision replaces the discretionary release of information (“may release” under current IM-8310-3(c)(1)) with mandatory publication (“shall release” under proposed IM-8310-3(b)(3)), subject to Nasdaq Regulation's discretion not to publish such information in appropriate limited circumstances (detailed in Section 3(a)(iv) of this proposal). Proposed IM-8310-3(b)(3) also newly provides for the publication of information about a “limitation” or “prohibition” on a member's or associated person's access to services pursuant to the Rule 9550 Series or about the summary suspension or expulsion of a member organization or the summary revocation of the registration of a covered person for a failure to pay fines, other monetary sanctions, or costs pursuant to Rule 8320. By publishing information about a “limitation” or “prohibition” imposed under the Rule 9550 Series that constitutes final Exchange action, proposed IM-8310-3(b)(3) would govern comprehensively the publication of information about any sanction or preventative measure that may be imposed under the Rule 9550 Series.
[
12
]
Finally, proposed IM-8310-3(b)(4) newly provides that Nasdaq may release to the public a copy of any other disciplinary decision not governed by subsection IM-8310-3(b)(1) or (2) that is appealable to the Commission under Section 19(d). Proposed IM-8310-3(b)(4) aligns with NYSE Rule 8313(a)(4), except that proposed IM-8310-3(b)(4) does not mention exemptive-relief decisions because existing Nasdaq Rule 9620 already governs the release of exemptive-relief decisions, as noted above.
[
13
]
In addition, proposed IM-8310-3(b)(4) does not provide for publication of information about a disciplinary decision published under proposed IM-8310-3(b)(4) because Nasdaq believes that publishing the disciplinary decision itself moots the need to also release a summary of the disciplinary decision.
Given that proposed IM-8310-3(b)(1)(i) and (ii) broadly provide for the public release of the Exchange's disciplinary complaints and disciplinary decisions (as discussed in greater detail above), proposed IM-8310-3 omits current IM-8310-3(b)(1)'s and (c)(1)'s respective provisions permitting the release of information about a disciplinary complaint or disciplinary decision where Nasdaq's Chief Regulatory Officer deems the information release to be in the public interest and where the disciplinary complaint or disciplinary decision involves a significant policy or enforcement determination. As
(
printed page 68996)
discussed throughout this proposal, Nasdaq believes that releasing a copy of a disciplinary complaint or disciplinary decision makes it unnecessary to also release a summary of such document. In providing generally for the publication of the Exchange's disciplinary complaints and disciplinary decisions (as discussed in greater detail above) and omitting a provision that permits informational releases if the Exchange's Chief Regulatory Officer deems the informational release to be in the public interest, proposed IM-8310-3 aligns with NYSE Rule 8313 (which similarly does not provide for an informational release where a NYSE officer deems such a release to be in the public interest).
[
14
]
iii. Release Specifications
Proposed IM-8310-3(c)(1) and (2) are substantially similar to current IM-8310-3(a)(1)-(3), which they replace and supersede. Proposed IM-8310-3(c)(1) provides that copies of any disciplinary complaint released to the public pursuant to proposed IM-8310-3(b) shall indicate that a disciplinary complaint represents the initiation of a formal proceeding by the Exchange in which findings as to the allegations in the complaint have not been made and does not represent a decision as to any of the allegations contained in the complaint.
[
15 16
]
Proposed IM-8310-3(c)(2) provides that copies of, and information with respect to, any disciplinary decision or other decision, order, notification, or notice released to the public pursuant to proposed IM-8310-3(b) prior to the expiration of the time period provided for an appeal or call for review as permitted under Exchange rules or the Exchange Act, or while such an appeal or call for review is pending, shall indicate as appropriate that the findings and sanctions imposed therein are subject to review and modification by the Exchange or the Commission.
Proposed IM-8310-3(c)(3) is substantially similar to current IM-8310-3(k), which it replaces and supersedes. As a result of proposed IM-8310-3(c)(3), releases of information would identify the Nasdaq or Commission rule violated and the conduct constituting the violation. Under the proposed subparagraph (c)(3), the requirement that a “release” describe the rule violated and the conduct constituting the violation would apply only to “releases of information.” Nasdaq disciplinary complaints and disciplinary decisions necessarily identify the rules violated and the conduct constituting the violation, making it unnecessary for IM-8310-3(c)(3) to also cover Nasdaq disciplinary complaints and disciplinary decisions. For example, under Rule 9212, a disciplinary complaint must “specify in reasonable detail the conduct alleged to constitute the violative activity and the rule, regulation, or statutory provision the Respondent is alleged to be violating or to have violated.” Under Rule 9216, which governs letters of Acceptance, Waiver, and Consent (“AWCs”), an AWC must describe the “act or practice engaged in or omitted, the rule, regulation, or statutory provision violated, and the sanction or sanctions to be imposed.”
Proposed IM-8310-3(c)(4) specifies that Nasdaq would release disciplinary complaints, disciplinary decisions, information, notices, or any other items required to be released to the public pursuant to the Rule by posting such items on the Exchange's website. By posting such items to the Exchange's publicly accessible website, Nasdaq Regulation would satisfy the requirement to release to the public the documents and information specified in proposed IM-8310-3.
iv. Discretion To Redact Certain Information or Waive Publication
Proposed IM-8310-3(d)(1) provides that, notwithstanding proposed IM-8310-3(b) and (c)(4), the Exchange may, in its discretion and on a case-by-case basis, redact information that contains confidential customer information, including customer identities, or information that raises significant identity theft, personal safety, privacy, or other concerns that are not outweighed by investor protection concerns. While the Exchange anticipates that most redactions would protect the privacy of third parties, the more general term “other concerns” is intended to preserve the Exchange's flexibility to redact information outside the specified privacy- and safety-related categories but that the Exchange nevertheless determines warrants redaction after weighing investor protection concerns.
[
17
]
Current IM-8310-3 does not specifically provide for the redaction of information raising significant identity theft, personal safety, privacy, or other concerns after weighing such concerns against investor protection concerns.
Proposed IM-8310-3(d)(2) provides that, notwithstanding proposed IM-8310-3(b) and (c)(4), the Exchange may determine, in its discretion, to waive the requirement to release a copy of, or information with respect to, any disciplinary complaint, disciplinary decision or other decision, order, notification, or notice under those extraordinary circumstances where the release of such information would violate fundamental notions of fairness or work an injustice. This proposed subparagraph, which replaces and supersedes current IM-8310-3(c)(1), does not change the standard for waiving the public-release requirement,
i.e.,
it employs the same standard of “fundamental notions of fairness or work an injustice” as current IM-8310-3(c)(1). Given that proposed IM-8310-3(b) would provide newly for the release of disciplinary complaints, proposed IM-8310-3(d)(2)'s “fundamental notions of fairness or work an injustice” standard would apply newly to disciplinary complaints (not just disciplinary decisions, as does current IM-8310-3(c)(1)).
v. Other Items
Proposed IM-8310-3(e), titled “Notice of Appeals to the Commission of Exchange Decisions,” would replace and supersede current IM-8310-3(g). This proposed subparagraph provides that the Exchange shall provide notice to the public when a disciplinary decision of the Exchange is appealed to the Commission, and the notice shall state whether the effectiveness of the decision has been stayed pending the outcome of proceedings before the Commission. Proposed IM-8310-3(e) would expand the categories of appeals for which the Exchange would provide public notice of the appeal to include the appeal of all disciplinary decisions (as defined in proposed IM-8310-
(
printed page 68997)
3(a)(2), discussed above). In contrast, current IM-8310-3(g) more narrowly requires Nasdaq to notify its membership and the press of appeals to the Commission from Nasdaq disciplinary decisions only if the sanction is at least $10,000 or involves an expulsion, revocation, or suspension of a member or a bar on an associated person's associating with all members. While current IM-8310-3(g) requires Nasdaq to provide notice to the “membership and to the press,” proposed IM-8310-3(e) would require Nasdaq to provide notice to the public more broadly. As discussed above, Nasdaq would provide notice under proposed IM-8310-3(c)(4) by posting such notices on the Exchange's publicly accessible website.
Proposed IM-8310-3(f), titled “Notice of Appeal to the Courts of Commission Decisions,” would replace and supersede current IM-8310-3(h). This proposed subparagraph provides that the Exchange shall provide notice to the public if a decision by the Commission in a case previously appealed to it from a disciplinary decision of the Exchange is appealed to the courts, and the notice shall state whether the order of the Commission has been stayed. Proposed IM-8310-3(f) also would expand the categories of appeals for which the Exchange would provide notice of the appeal. While current IM-8310-3(h) requires providing notice of an appeal to the courts from a Commission decision involving Nasdaq's imposition of monetary sanctions of at least $10,000 or an expulsion, revocation, suspension, or bar of a member or associated person, proposed IM-8310-3(f) provides that Nasdaq would provide notice of appeal to the courts from any disciplinary decision of the Exchange (as defined in proposed IM-8310-3(a)(2)), even if the monetary sanction is less than $10,000. While current IM-8310-3(h) requires providing notice to the “membership,” proposed IM-8310-3(f) would require Nasdaq to provide notice to the public more broadly. As discussed above, Nasdaq would provide notice under proposed IM-8310-3(c)(4) by posting such notices on the Exchange's publicly accessible website.
Current IM-8310-3(e) would be renumbered to proposed IM-8310-3(h). Additionally, the proposed subparagraph (h) would reflect that FINRA's Office of Disciplinary Affairs may accept an AWC under Rule 9216 or an offer of settlement under Rule 9270 that imposes an expulsion or bar and that, consistent with proposed subparagraph IM-8310-3(b)(1), Nasdaq Regulation would release the disciplinary decision imposing the expulsion or bar. Nasdaq Regulation's authority to release the disciplinary decision imposing an expulsion or bar immediately upon approval would remain unchanged.
Current IM-8310-3(i), which would be renumbered to proposed IM-8310-3(j), would clarify that Nasdaq will provide public notice of specified Commission orders only in cases previously appealed to the Commission from a decision of Nasdaq. Consistent with the elimination of the $10,000 threshold for publishing disciplinary decisions, Nasdaq also would notify the public as soon as possible after receiving a Commission order imposing any monetary sanction in a case that originates from a Nasdaq disciplinary decision. As discussed above, Nasdaq would provide notice under proposed IM-8310-3(c)(4) by posting such notices on the Exchange's publicly accessible website.
The text of current IM-8310-3(d), (f), and (j) would remain unchanged but would be renumbered as follows: current subsection IM-8310-3(d) would become subsection IM-8310-3(g); current subsection IM-8310-3(f) would become subsection IM-8310-3(i); and current subsection IM-8310-3(j) would become subsection IM-8310-3(k).
The text and numbering of current IM-8310-3(l) would remain unchanged.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
18
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
19
]
in particular, in that it is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general to protect investors and the public interest. By providing for the publication of Nasdaq disciplinary complaints and expanding the category of disciplinary decisions published on Nasdaq's website, the proposed rule makes disciplinary complaints and disciplinary decisions more readily accessible to member firms, associated persons, the securities industry, and the public at large. In doing so, Nasdaq's proposed rule promotes just and equitable principles of trade and protects investors and the public interest.
Specifically, the Exchange believes that greater access to Nasdaq disciplinary decisions will provide valuable guidance and information to member organizations, associated persons, investors, and the securities industry generally. The publication of disciplinary decisions can deter and prevent misconduct by firms and improve overall business standards in the securities industry, as well as allowing prospective firm customers to consider firms' and representatives' disciplinary histories when deciding whether to conduct business with them. In addition, the publication of disciplinary decisions allows member organizations to use that information in educating their compliance staffs and informing their compliance procedures that involve similar business lines, products, or industry practices. Eliminating the $10,000 monetary threshold below which the Exchange does not currently release disciplinary decisions also would align the Exchange's publication rule with those of FINRA and NYSE.
The Exchange believes that the public release of Nasdaq disciplinary complaints (including temporary cease and desist notices) on Nasdaq's website will allow member firms to more quickly identify conduct that Nasdaq Regulation views as violating applicable Nasdaq or Commission rules and, if necessary, to curtail sooner similar conduct in which the member firms may be engaged. The Exchange also believes that prospective customers of a member firm would benefit from the opportunity to review a disciplinary complaint, accompanied by an appropriate statement noting that the complaint's factual allegations remain unadjudicated, as the prospective customers consider whether to conduct business with the member firm. Publishing the disciplinary complaint or the disciplinary decision itself often will provide member firms and the public with more detail about the violative conduct (or allegedly violative conduct in the case of a disciplinary complaint) than would a summary of the document.
In addition, the Exchange believes that defining the terms “disciplinary complaint” and “disciplinary decision” will provide member firms and associated persons with greater clarity about which discipline-related items the Exchange would publish, thereby removing impediments to and perfecting the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system and, in general, protecting investors and the public interest. Similarly, the Exchange believes that the incorporation in proposed IM-8310-3(a)(3) of specified definitions from Rule 9120 would promote consistency and clarity by making clear that Rule 9120's
(
printed page 68998)
definitions apply to such defined terms when used in proposed IM-8310-3.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change involves the administration of the Exchange's disciplinary procedures and raises no competitive concerns. Rather than addressing competitive issues, the proposed rule change would make Nasdaq disciplinary complaints and disciplinary decisions more readily available to member firms, associated persons, investors, and the public at large.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were either solicited or received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
20
]
and subparagraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 thereunder.
[
21
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-NASDAQ-2026-089 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NASDAQ-2026-089. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-NASDAQ-2026-089 and should be submitted on or before November 23, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
22
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

3
]
notice is hereby given that, on October 20, 2026, NYSE American LLC (“NYSE American” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have
(
printed page 69029)
been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend the NYSE American Options Fee Schedule (“Fee Schedule”) to waive the maximum combined Floor Broker credits paid for QCC trades and rebates paid through the Manual Billable Rebate Program for the month of October 2026. The proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
www.nyse.com
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of those statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The purpose of this filing is to amend the Fee Schedule to waive the maximum combined Floor Broker credits paid for QCC trades and rebates paid through the Manual Billable Rebate Program for the month of October 2026.
The Exchange imposes a limit on the maximum combined Floor Broker credits paid for QCC trades and rebates paid through the Manual Billable Rebate Program per month per Floor Broker firm (the “Cap”).
[
4
]
In 2025, the combined limit was $3,000,000. However, based on continuing open outcry volumes on the Exchange throughout 2025, the Exchange increased the combined limit to $4,000,000.
[
5
]
Shortly thereafter, and for the same reason (
i.e.,
elevated open outcry volume), the Exchange waived the Cap for the months of January and February 2026.
[
6
]
Shortly thereafter, and again to address continued elevated open outcry volumes, the Exchange further increased the Cap to $5,500,000 in March 2026.
[
7
]
Because open outcry volumes on the Exchange are again significantly elevated, the Exchange proposes to waive the Cap for the month of October 2026 and to use the period during which the Cap is waived to evaluate further adjustments to the amount of the Cap.
[
8
]
As with previous waivers, the proposed waiver is being adopted in anticipation of Floor Broker firms reaching the Cap before month's end and potentially redirecting their order flow away from the Exchange. In the absence of the proposed waiver, Floor Broker firms may choose to re-direct such order flow to a competing market. Accordingly, the purpose of the proposal is to encourage Floor Broker firms to continue to direct open outcry transactions to the Exchange, despite increasing industry volumes making it less difficult to reach the Cap (even at the most recently increased amount).
Although the Exchange cannot predict with certainty how many Floor Broker firms would be impacted by this change, the Exchange believes that the proposed changes would incent Floor Brokers to continue to direct their order flow to the Exchange, thus increasing liquidity to the benefit of all market participants.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
9
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and (5) of the Act,
[
10
]
in particular, because it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its members, issuers and other persons using its facilities and does not unfairly discriminate between customers, issuers, brokers or dealers.
As a threshold matter, the Exchange is subject to significant competitive forces in the market for options securities transaction services that constrain its pricing determinations in that market. The Commission has repeatedly expressed its preference for competition over regulatory intervention in determining prices, products, and services in the securities markets. In Regulation NMS, the Commission highlighted the importance of market forces in determining prices and SRO revenues and, also, recognized that current regulation of the market system “has been remarkably successful in promoting market competition in its broader forms that are most important to investors and listed companies.”
[
11
]
There are currently 20 registered options exchanges competing for order flow. Based on publicly available information and, excluding index-based options, no single exchange has more than 16% of the market share of executed volume of multiply-listed equity and ETF options trades.
[
12
]
Therefore, currently no exchange possesses significant pricing power in the execution of multiply-listed equity and ETF options order flow. More specifically, in September 2026, the Exchange had 12.39% market share of executed volume of multiply-listed equity and ETF options order flow. In such a low concentrated and highly competitive market, no single options exchange possesses significant pricing power in the execution of option order flow.
The proposed waiver of the Cap is reasonable because it is designed to encourage the role performed by Floor Brokers in facilitating the execution of orders via open outcry, a function that the Exchange wishes to support for the benefit of all market participants, and would allow the Exchange time to evaluate further changes to the amount of the Cap. Absent the proposed waiver, the Exchange believes that as soon as
(
printed page 69030)
Floor Brokers reach the Cap, they are likely to re-direct order flow away from the Exchange, which may adversely impact other market participants trading on the Exchange. To the extent that the proposed waiver encourages Floor Brokers to facilitate transactions on the Exchange instead of on a competing market, all market participants participating on the Exchange would benefit from the increased liquidity. The Exchange believes the proposed waiver should continue to incent Floor Brokers to encourage market participants to aggregate their executions at the Exchange as a primary execution venue. To the extent that the proposed change achieves its purpose in attracting more volume to the Exchange, this increased order flow would continue to make the Exchange a more competitive venue for order execution, thus improving market quality for all market participants.
The Exchange believes the proposed waiver of the Cap is an equitable allocation of its fees and credits and is not unfairly discriminatory because the proposal is based on the amount and type of business transacted on the Exchange. Floor Brokers are not obligated to execute manual transactions and QCCs to earn rebates and credits applied toward the Cap. However, the proposed waiver is designed to continue to encourage the role performed by Floor Brokers in facilitating the execution of orders via open outcry, a function that the Exchange wishes to support for the benefit of all market participants.
To the extent that the proposed waiver of the Cap continues to attract manual transactions and QCCs to the Exchange, this increased order flow would continue to make the Exchange a more competitive venue for order execution. Thus, the Exchange believes the proposed waiver would improve market quality for all market participants on the Exchange and attract more order flow to the Exchange, thereby improving market-wide quality and price discovery. The resulting increased volume and liquidity would provide more trading opportunities and tighter spreads to all market participants and thus would promote just and equitable principles of trade, remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system and, in general, protect investors and the public interest.
Finally, the Exchange believes that it is subject to significant competitive forces, as described below in the Exchange's statement regarding the burden on competition.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
In accordance with Section 6(b)(8) of the Act, the Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change would impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. Instead, as discussed above, the Exchange believes that the proposed changes would encourage the submission of additional liquidity to a public exchange, thereby promoting market depth, price discovery and transparency and enhancing order execution opportunities for all market participants. As a result, the Exchange believes that the proposed change furthers the Commission's goal in adopting Regulation NMS of fostering integrated competition among orders, which promotes “more efficient pricing of individual stocks for all types of orders, large and small.”
[
13
]
Intramarket Competition.
The proposed waiver of the Cap would apply equally to all similarly situated Floor Brokers. To the extent that there is an additional competitive burden on non-Floor Brokers, the Exchange believes that any such burden would be appropriate because Floor Brokers serve an important function in facilitating the execution of orders in open outcry and price discovery for all market participants.
Intermarket Competition.
The Exchange operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can readily favor one of the other 19 competing options exchanges if they deem the Exchange's fee levels to be excessive. In such an environment, the Exchange must continually adjust its fees to remain competitive with other exchanges and to attract order flow to the Exchange. Based on publicly available information, and excluding index-based options, no single exchange has more than 16% of the market share of executed volume of multiply-listed equity and ETF options trades.
[
14
]
Therefore, currently no exchange possesses significant pricing power in the execution of multiply-listed equity and ETF options order flow. More specifically, in September 2026, the Exchange had 12.39% market share of executed volume of multiply-listed equity and ETF options trades.
[
15
]
The Exchange believes that the proposed waiver of the Cap reflects this competitive environment because it is designed to continue to incent Floor Brokers to direct manual and QCC transactions to the Exchange, to provide liquidity and to attract order flow. To the extent that Floor Brokers are encouraged to utilize the Exchange as a primary trading venue for all transactions, all Exchange market participants stand to benefit from the improved market quality and increased opportunities for price improvement. The Exchange notes that it operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can readily favor competing venues. In such an environment, the Exchange must continually review, and consider adjusting, its fees and credits to remain competitive with other exchanges. For the reasons described above, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule change reflects this competitive environment
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were solicited or received with respect to the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change is effective upon filing pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)
[
16
]
of the Act and subparagraph (f)(2) of Rule 19b-4
[
17
]
thereunder, because it establishes a due, fee, or other charge imposed by the Exchange.
At any time within 60 days of the filing of such proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B)
[
18
]
of the Act to determine whether the proposed rule
(
printed page 69031)
change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-NYSEAMER-2026-95 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSEAMER-2026-95. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSEAMER-2026-95 and should be submitted on or before November 23, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
19
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106758; File No. SR-MX2-2026-09]
October 28, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that, on October 19, 2026, MX2 LLC (“MX2” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange is filing with the Commission a proposed rule change to amend Rule 11.23, (“Trading Halts Due to Extraordinary Market Volatility/Market-Wide Circuit Breakers”) concerning the resumption of trading following a Level 3 Market-Wide Circuit Breaker (“MWCB”) halt (“Level 3 Market Decline”) in connection with the industry's expansion of trading hours to 23 hours per day, 5 days per week (“23/5 Trading”). The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5 and is available on the Exchange's website at
https://info.memxtrading.com/​regulation/​rules-and-filings/​
.
(
printed page 69022)
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 11.23(b)(2) concerning the resumption of trading following a Level 3 Market Decline in connection with the industry's expansion of trading hours to 23/5 Trading. Some exchanges, including the Exchange's affiliate exchange, MEMX, LLC (“MEMX”), are planning to offer overnight trading,
[
3
]
and as a result, the uniform Level 3 Market Decline rules of each exchange are being modified, as explained further below.
Background
The MWCB mechanism under Rule 11.23 provides an important, automatic mechanism that is invoked to promote stability and investor confidence during a period of significant stress when U.S. securities markets experience extreme broad-based declines. All U.S. equity exchanges and FINRA (collectively, the self-regulatory organizations or “SROs”) adopted uniform rules relating to the MWCB mechanism in 2012, which are designed to slow the effects of extreme price movement through coordinated trading halts across U.S. securities markets when severe price declines reach levels that may exhaust market liquidity.
[
4
]
Such market-wide circuit breakers provide for trading halts in all U.S. cash equity and equities options markets during a severe market decline as measured by a single-day decline in the S&P 500 Index during regular trading hours.
Pursuant to Rule 11.23, a market-wide trading halt will be triggered if the S&P 500 Index declines in price by specified percentages from the prior day's closing price of that index. Currently, the triggers are set at three circuit breaker thresholds: 7% (Level 1), 13% (Level 2), and 20% (Level 3). A market decline that triggers a Level 1 or Level 2 halt after 9:30 a.m. ET and before 3:25 p.m. ET would halt market-wide trading for 15 minutes, while a similar market decline at or after 3:25 p.m. ET would not halt market-wide trading. If a Level 3 Market Decline occurs at any time during the trading day, trading in all stocks will halt on the Exchange for the remainder of the trading day, and will resume the following trading day at 7:00 a.m. ET.
Proposal
The Exchange now proposes to amend Rule 11.23 to reflect extended trading hours under 23/5 Trading. On December 6, 2026, several exchanges, including MEMX, intend to offer new overnight trading sessions that would be available from 9:00 p.m. ET to 4:00 a.m. ET, significantly increasing their hours of operation in response to customer demand.
As discussed, consistent with the uniform rules in place across all SROs, current Rule 11.23(b)(2) provides that if a Level 3 Market Decline occurs at any time during the trading day, the Exchange shall halt trading in all stocks on the Exchange for the remainder of the trading day. Currently, that means that the earliest that any exchange would re-open trading after a Level 3 Market Decline is 4:00 a.m. ET the following day, since no SROs are open for trading before 4:00 a.m. ET.
Unless amended, when 23/5 Trading is launched, the current rule's reference to halting “for the remainder of the trading day”
[
5
]
would require SROs participating in 23/5 Trading to re-open trading at an earlier time,
i.e.,
9:00 p.m. ET on the same calendar day, when those SROs' systems would generally become available for overnight trading. The Exchange does not believe that this is an expected or desired result and is therefore amending this rule in coordination with the other SROs such that trading on any SRO will not resume until 4:00 a.m. ET or later on the following trading day, consistent with current market practice. This proposed rule change is therefore not intended to make any substantive changes to the MWCB mechanism. Rather, the proposed rule change would preserve the current resumption time following a Level 3 Market Decline.
To effect this change, the Exchange proposes to delete the language in Rule 11.23(b)(2) that provides that trading in all stocks will halt on the Exchange “for the remainder of the trading day” if a Level 3 Market Decline occurs at any time during the trading day, and replace it with new language that explicitly provides that trading in all stocks would halt on the Exchange until 4:00 a.m. Eastern Time on the following trading day.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes the proposal is consistent with the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to the Exchange and, in particular, the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act.
[
6
]
Specifically, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
7
]
requirements that the rules of an exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
The MWCB mechanism described in Rule 11.23 is an important, automatic mechanism that is invoked to promote stability and investor confidence during periods of significant stress when U.S. securities markets experience extreme broad-based declines. The proposed rule change, when applied uniformly by all SROs, would ensure that the current 4:00 a.m. ET resumption time following a Level 3 halt continues to apply under 23/5 Trading, notwithstanding current rule text implying that the resumption time would coincide with the start of overnight trading on SROs operating an overnight session.
Rather than leave the rule in place as is, which would result in an earlier resumption time than originally contemplated when the rule was adopted, the Exchange, the other U.S. equity exchanges, and FINRA met alongside industry representatives to determine the appropriate resumption time. Following those discussions, the collective decision was made to retain the 4:00 a.m. ET resumption time,
(
printed page 69023)
notwithstanding the fact that an earlier resumption time would be possible with the introduction of 23/5 Trading. The proposed rule change codifies this decision into the Exchange's rules. The Exchange understands that the other SROs have filed similar proposed rule changes. As a result, the market as a whole, including on- and off-exchange, will continue to be subject to harmonized rules for the resumption of trading following a Level 3 Market Decline.
While the SROs had previously decided to tie the resumption time following a Level 3 halt to the earliest SRO opening time, the upcoming transition to 23/5 Trading raises various concerns that warrant a change from the current approach.
First, the Exchange notes that the MWCB mechanism was designed to provide a cooling-off period where market participants would be provided with additional time to evaluate the market events that led to the decline before determining how to position their trading activity for the next day. With the introduction of 23/5 Trading and the start of overnight trading on some SROs at 9:00 p.m. ET, however, this cooling-off period could be materially shortened, reducing one of the key benefits that the MWCB mechanism was designed to provide in the first place. Rather than shorten the cooling-off period and risk this benefit, the Exchange believes the market would be better served by a change to the length of the associated trading halt that mirrors current market practice. Under the proposed rule, as is the case today, after a Level 3 halt, all SROs would re-open trading at 4:00 a.m. ET or later, and no SRO would offer an overnight trading session starting on the day of a Level 3 halt.
Second, overnight trading may be subject to different liquidity and participation considerations than the current pre-market sessions that start at or after 4:00 a.m. ET. Notably, while retail investors have expressed interest in overnight trading, the Exchange expects that institutional investors will take more time to transition to a round-the-clock model. However, such institutional participation may be of heightened importance following a Level 3 halt, as these investors are likely to have views on the underlying market events that led to the Level 3 Market Decline in the first place. The Exchange is concerned that opening during hours that such participants do not normally trade may impact the quality of price discovery at a time of significant market volatility. Waiting until 4:00 a.m. ET to resume trading would facilitate broader participation and therefore price discovery.
Finally, the Exchange notes that the Commission recently approved an amendment to the Plan to Address Extraordinary Market Volatility (“LULD Plan”) that would establish new price protections from 9:00 p.m. ET to 4:00 a.m. ET.
[
8
]
While these price bands would help to assure a fair and orderly market during normal market conditions, it is possible that they would instead prevent normal price discovery following a Level 3 Market Decline. Rather than allowing trading to resume with such price bands in effect, which would represent a change from the current trading reopening following a Level 3 Market Decline, the Exchange believes that requiring SROs to wait until 4:00 a.m. ET to resume trading would ensure that price discovery can occur unimpeded during pre-market trading, as it does today, which may further inform prices going into the opening auction and regular market hours trading following a Level 3 halt.
Given the factors discussed above, the Exchange believes that trading in all securities on the Exchange should not resume before 4:00 a.m. ET on the trading day after a Level 3 halt. This decision, which the Exchange understands will also be reflected in the rules of the other SROs, would promote a fair and orderly market at a time of significant market volatility, and thereby protect investors and the public interest. In addition, while the actual Level 3 resumption time would not be changing in practice—as proposed, the current resumption time and future resumption time would both be 4:00 a.m. ET at the earliest—the Exchange believes that it is appropriate to amend its rules to ensure that its rules reflect the upcoming changes due to 23/5 Trading. Without this change, market participants may mistakenly believe that the Exchange intends for trading to re-open on overnight trading exchanges at 9:00 p.m. ET following a Level 3 halt. The proposed rule change would therefore facilitate operational transparency while providing for a fair and orderly market.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act because the proposal would ensure the continued, uninterrupted operation of a consistent mechanism to halt trading across U.S. securities markets. Further, the Exchange understands that the other SROs have filed proposed rule changes to ensure a consistent resumption time at 4:00 a.m. ET across markets. Thus, the proposed rule change will help to ensure consistency across market centers without implicating any competitive issues.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
9
]
and subparagraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 thereunder.
[
10
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
(
printed page 69024)
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-MX2-2026-09 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-MX2-2026-09. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-MX2-2026-09 and should be submitted on or before November 23, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
11
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106756; File No. SR-NYSENAT-2026-28]
October 28, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1)
[
1
]
of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)
[
2
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
3
]
notice is hereby given that on October 22, 2026, NYSE National, Inc. (“NYSE National” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend the bylaws of the Exchange to (a) remove the requirement that the fair representation director be an ETP Holder or Person Associated with an ETP Holder; (b) make a conforming change to the title; and (c) update a cross reference. The proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
www.nyse.com
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of those statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend the Eighth Amended and Restated By-laws of the Exchange (the “Bylaws”) to (a) remove the requirement that the fair representation director be an ETP Holder or Person Associated with an ETP Holder;
[
4
]
(b) make a conforming change to the title; and (c) update a cross reference.
Nominating Committee
The Exchange proposes to remove the requirement, in the first sentence of Article III, Section 3.4(b) (Nomination and Election), that the Nominating Committee
[
5
]
publish the names of ETP Holders or Persons Associated with an ETP Holder as its nominee for Non-Affiliated Director.
[
6
]
Rather, it would be able to name the individual of its choice as its nominee.
Currently, the Nominating Committee is limited to someone who is currently an ETP Holder or Person Associated with an ETP Holder. For example, the Nominating Committee cannot name someone who was until recently, but is not at present, a Person Associated with an ETP Holder. The proposed change would give the Nominating Committee more options: they still could name an ETP Holder or Person Associated with an ETP Holder Participant but could name another individual as well.
The Exchange proposes to amend the first sentence of Article III, Section
(
printed page 69002)
3.4(b) so that the Nominating Committee may name individuals of its choice as nominees. More specifically, the Exchange proposes to make the following change (proposed addition underlined, proposed deletion in brackets):
The Nominating Committee shall publish the name(s) of one or more [ETP Holders or Persons Associated with an ETP Holder (in any combination)]
individuals
as its nominee(s) for Non-Affiliated Directors of the Board of Directors of the Exchange.
The proposed change would be consistent with the New York Stock Exchange LLC and NYSE American LLC, affiliates of the Exchange, which have no equivalent requirement.
[
7
]
The Exchange notes that the proposed change also would be consistent with the governing documents of other self-regulatory organizations, such as the Nasdaq Stock Market LLC
[
8
]
and CBOE BYX Exchange, Inc.
[
9
]
Title
The Exchange proposes to make a non-substantive technical and conforming change to the title of the Bylaws, to replace “Eighth” with “Ninth.”
Cross Reference
The Exchange proposes to make a non-substantive corrective change to a cross-reference in Article V, Section 5.7, from a reference to Section 3.5 (Chairman) to a reference to Section 3.4. Section 3.5, which the section currently refers to, does not address the Nominating Committee “approving and submitting names of candidates for election to the position of Non-Affiliated Director” unlike Section 3.4, which does.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Exchange Act,
[
10
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(1)
[
11
]
in particular, in that it enables the Exchange to be so organized as to have the capacity to be able to carry out the purposes of the Exchange Act and to comply, and to enforce compliance by its exchange members and persons associated with its exchange members, with the provisions of the Exchange Act, the rules and regulations thereunder, and the rules of the Exchange. The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b)(3) of the Exchange Act,
[
12
]
in that it would ensure a fair representation of its members in the selection of its directors and administration of its affairs. The Exchange also believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b)(5) of the Exchange Act,
[
13
]
in that it is designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
The Exchange believes that the change would enable it to be so organized as to have the capacity to be able to carry out the purposes of the Exchange Act and would ensure a fair representation of its members in the selection of its directors and administration of its affairs because it would allow the Nominating Committee to name the individuals of its choice as its nominees, and not be limited to individuals that are currently ETP Holders or Persons Associated with an ETP Holder. The proposed changes would allow the Exchange to ensure that it remains in compliance with the Exchange Act.
[
14
]
The Exchange believes that for the same reason the rule change would remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system and, in general, protect investors and the public interest, as it would remove the limitation, and therefore give the Nominating Committee more options.
The proposed change to Section 3.4(b) would make the Bylaws consistent with the New York Stock Exchange LLC and NYSE American LLC, affiliates of the Exchange, which have no equivalent requirement.
[
15
]
The proposed change to the title and cross-reference in Section 5.7 (“Non-Substantive Changes”) are non-substantive changes that do not impact the governance or ownership of the Exchange. The Exchange believes that the proposed Non-Substantive Changes would enable the Exchange to continue to be so organized as to have the capacity to carry out the purposes of the Exchange Act and comply and enforce compliance with the provisions of the Exchange Act by its members and persons associated with its members, because making the Non-Substantive Changes would contribute to the orderly operation of the Exchange by adding clarity and transparency to the Bylaws, ensuring that market participants can more easily navigate, understand and comply with the governing documents of the Exchange. For the same reason, the Exchange believes that the proposed Non-Substantive Changes would remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system and, in general, protect investors and the public interest. The proposed rule changes would reduce potential investor or market participant confusion.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Exchange Act. The proposed rule change is not intended to address competitive issues but rather is concerned solely with ensuring that the Nominating Committee has more options in naming its nominees and making Non-Substantive changes to the Bylaws.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were solicited or received with respect to the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The Exchange has filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
16
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
[
17
]
Because the proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative prior to 30 days from the date on which
(
printed page 69003)
it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, if consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest, the proposed rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii) thereunder.
[
18
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of such proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B)
[
19
]
of the Act to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-NYSENAT-2026-28 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSENAT-2026-28. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSENAT-2026-28 and should be submitted on or before November 23, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
20
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.
